units.la: Ad Nobili prudentiâ amp!lissimum Virum Dominum BERNHARDVM à GEISMAR REIPUB. WARBURGENSIS Consulem dignissimum, Dominum ac amicum obseruandum OTHONIS CASMANNI PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, endowed with noble prudence, Lord BERNHARD VON GEISMAR, most worthy Consul of the Republic of Warburg, my lord and esteemed friend: the preface of Otto Casmann.

units.la: Rnamentum[?] ac decus insigne Warburgensium Reipub. Nobili prudentiâ amplissime Vir, Domine & Amice honorande, semper duxi & depradicavi GEISMARIORUM nobilem & de ipsa præclarè promeritam gentem. Quantâ, me Christe, autoritate, quæ Magistratus est apex, quantâ fide, quamq; felici dexteritate, longo eam tempore administrarit: Magnus ille omnibus bonis Bernhardus à Geismar avunculus tuus, cujus ut habes nomen, ita virtutum affectaris vestigia, unanimi agnoscunt consensu cives. Quanta etiam religione, prudentia, quamq; commodâ humanitate ad clavum ejusdem sessitarit [?] Optimus parens tuus P.M. Evergetes meus singularis, D. Conradus à Geismar, non ignorant, qui amabilem candidi pectoris integritatem cognorunt. Ne itaq;, ô Consul nunquam satis laudatis prognate parentibus, Domine & amice honorande, Ampl. tuam à me humilioris sortis homine, qui se suo Artaxerxi fatetur Sinetam, appellari mireris. Etenim quadruplicis continemur conjunctionis vinculo. Primum communis patria (cujus nomen suave, suavior fruitio) nos hanc lucem primùm videntes conjunxit. Natura me docet illud Poëta verum esse:
units.tr: Ornament and distinguished glory of the Republic of Warburg, most eminent man of noble prudence, honoured lord and friend, I have always thought of and proclaimed the noble family of the Geismars, which has deserved so well of its country. With what authority, by Christ, which is the summit of the magistracy, with what fidelity and what happy dexterity your uncle, that great man Bernhard von Geismar, whose name you bear and whose virtues you strive to follow, administered it for a long time, the citizens unanimously acknowledge. With what piety, prudence and agreeable courtesy he held the helm, your most excellent father, my own singular benefactor, Lord Conrad von Geismar, well knows, as do all who have known the lovable integrity of his candid heart. Therefore, O Consul, born of parents never praised enough, lord and honoured friend, do not wonder that your Honour is addressed by me, a man of humbler lot, who confesses himself Sineta to his Artaxerxes. For we are bound together by a fourfold tie. First, a common homeland (whose name is sweet, and whose enjoyment is sweeter) joined us, who first saw this light. Nature teaches me that the poet's words are true:

units.la: Nescio quâ natale solum dulcedine cunctosDucit, & immemores non sinit esse sui.
units.tr: I know not by what sweetness the native soil draws all men, and never lets them forget themselves.

units.la: Patriam diligo, at careo: interim si non corpore, mente saltem sæpius ad Saxa Ithacæ cum Ulysse propero, cum Agamemnone ad Mycenarum nobiles muros; Et ingemisco dicens: Bene age, Salve, Valeq.
units.tr: I love my homeland, but I am parted from it. Meanwhile, if not in body, at least in mind, I often hasten to the rocks of Ithaca with Ulysses, and with Agamemnon to the noble walls of Mycenae; and I sigh, saying: Fare well, be well, farewell.

units.la: Solatur me sæpius Seneca meus: Patriam, inquiens, meam transfire non possum: Omnium una est: Extra hanc nemo projici potest: In quamcunq; terram venio, in meam venio. Pueritia dein annos suaviter singularis con-strinxit amor, quem naturalis ita conciliavit propensio, ut Alexis ultro delegerit & dilexe-rit me Coridonem, ordinis dico plebei puerum.
units.tr: My Seneca often consoles me: "I cannot cross over from my homeland," he says. "There is one homeland for all; no one can be cast out of it. Wherever I come to, I come to my own." Then, in boyhood, a singular love bound me pleasantly through the years, which natural inclination so won over that Alexis of his own accord chose and loved me, Corydon, a boy of the common rank I mean.

units.la: Jam vero
units.tr: Now indeed

units.la: Difficile est primum subito deponere amorem.
units.tr: It is hard to lay aside a first love all at once.

units.la: Arctius postea adolescentiam nostram in Scholis studiorum uspiam communio & benevola animorum societas colligavit: Magna eius est vis in voluntatum conjunctione. Hisce ego studiis, propitia DEI providentia adhuc innutrior, immoror, & fortasse immoriar, quibus prodesse, quibus possum, nocere autem nemini, est animus; Te interim ad amplissi-mos Patriæ Reipub. honores evecto, quos ut tibi gratulor, ita tu fasces ejus Reipub. cum laude geris, ut onera leves ferasq. Denique ea me Tibi devinxit relationis mutuæ affectio, quæ est inter eum, qui beneficium confert, & eum, qui accipit. Et laudatissimus P. M. Parens tuus, & tu filius ejus multum mihi honorandus sæpiuscule Musis meis miserè afflictis succurre-re non estis dedignati. Eum vobis elegistis,
units.tr: Later, our youth was more closely bound together in the schools of whatever place of study, by common pursuits and a kindly fellowship of minds; great is its power in the union of wills. In these studies, still being nourished by the favourable providence of GOD, I linger, and perhaps shall die, devoted to whatever I can do for others and harm no one, which is my purpose. Meanwhile you have been raised to the most distinguished honours of your fatherland's Republic, and as I congratulate you on them, so you bear its fasces with credit, so that you lighten its burdens and bear them. Finally, that mutual feeling of obligation has bound me to you, which exists between the one who confers a benefit and the one who receives it. And your most praiseworthy father, and you his son, whom I must greatly honour, did not disdain to come often to the aid of my Muses, sorely afflicted. You have chosen that for yourselves,

units.la: gratus gratis qui beneficium accepit, reddere non potuit. In votis quidem esset, si in fatis & viribus.
units.tr: He who has received a kindness freely, though grateful, could not repay it gratis. It would indeed be my wish, if fate and my powers allowed.

units.la: En itaque, ô Consul, qua tua est humanitas Ampl. Tuam eum permittas jam, ea qua par observantia, compellare, quem Tibi natalis soli jus, quem primi amoris dulcis memoria, quem studiorum olim jucunda societas, quem deniq; animi grati ad remunerandum obligata propensio obstrinxit.
units.tr: Behold, then, O Consul, by the kindness that is yours, may your Honour now permit me to address you with the respect that is due, you whom the right of native soil, the sweet memory of early affection, the pleasant fellowship of former studies, and finally the inclination of a grateful mind bound to repay, have bound to me.

units.la: At vero quid feram ego Sineta Mnemoni? quid retribuā Evergeta olim meo? Manibus meis hauste aquam; In censu meo literario aliud donum offerendū cum jam non occurrat, en Munusculum literarium, fortè satis levidense, (quod quasi tamen Tibi ne sordeat) fero.
units.tr: But what shall I, Sineta, bring to Mnemon? What shall I return to my former benefactor, Evergetes? I poured water over his hands. Since no other gift from my literary store presents itself to offer, behold a little literary present, perhaps rather slight, which I bring, so that it may not seem contemptible to you.

units.la: At inquies: Reipub. ego deploratissimis hīs temporibus mihi commissā, inter tot difficultates, turbas & pericula, operam & curam impendo: mihi quid cum natura mysteriis? quid cum Physicorum Musis philosophicis? Curia mea alias curas, difficilia hæc tempora alia postulant studia.
units.tr: But you will say: I devote my labour and care to the Republic committed to me in these most desperate times, amid so many difficulties, disturbances and dangers. What have I to do with the mysteries of nature? What with the philosophical Muses of the natural philosophers? My office has other cares; these difficult times demand other studies.

units.la: Scio equidem, quo splendidior est & divinior Reipub. administratio, eo ipsam solere laboriosiorem & difficiliorem esse, quippe cui communis humani generis hostis diabolus cumpri-mis mis jolet esse infestus. Magnum & arduum opus, gubernare, & in primis hoc seculo. Ne igitur vires consternet & exhauriat omnes, in reme-dium cedat honesti oblectamenti solatium. Quod-nam vero honestius viro politico oblectamen-tum, quàm interdum è Curia, curarum splen-dido, & saepe misero Theatro, secedere in uni-versa Natura à Conditore DEO mirabiliter extructum Theatrum, ut admirandorum Dei operum contemplatione animum suum recreans ad ipsum assurgat Architectum Deum, eumque glorificet? Non quidem abs re dixit Plato no-ster; Magnis licet honoribus colatur Magistra-tus, ipsum tamen multis malis & incommodis agitari, gaudium furunculi instar habere, la-tente inflammatione micantem, nec liberum ac tranquillum spiritum ducere: His tamen malis nec penitus, nec semper prudens immo-ratur ac immoritur, sed molestiam aliquando cum jucunda quadam recreatione animi commutat, alteramque altera temperat. Nam
units.tr: I indeed know that the more splendid and divine the administration of a commonwealth, the more laborious and difficult it is wont to be, since the devil, the common enemy of mankind, is especially hostile to it. Governing is a great and arduous task, especially in this age. Lest it wear down and exhaust all one's strength, let the solace of an honourable delight serve as a remedy. What delight could be more honourable for a political man than sometimes to withdraw from the Curia, the splendid and often wretched theatre of cares, into that theatre of the whole of Nature which God the Creator has wonderfully built, so that, refreshing his mind by contemplating the admirable works of God, he may rise up to God the Architect and glorify him? Not without reason our Plato said: though the magistrate is honoured with great dignities, yet he is harassed by many evils and troubles, has joy like a little boil, glittering with a hidden inflammation, and does not draw a free and tranquil breath. Yet the wise man does not dwell on these evils wholly, nor always; he sometimes exchanges annoyance for a pleasant recreation of the mind, and tempers the one by the other. For

units.la: Quod caret alterna requie, durabile non est, Si nunquam cesses tendere, mollis eris.
units.tr: What lacks alternating rest is not durable: if you never cease to strain, you will become brittle.

units.la: Deliciis vero physicis ad refectionem quid aptius? His laxandi animi causa oblectare se li-cet etiam sarcinam ferenti consulare. Utinam vero Nucleus hic à me Enucleatus & tibi jam oblatus ejusmodi esset, ut non, dum pulverem Musarum Scholasticarum redolet, sua brevi-tate, quâ contractus, tædium ac nauseam ani-mo ad magna vadenti pareret.
units.tr: What is more suitable for refreshment than physical delights? For the sake of relaxing the mind one may amuse oneself with these, just as one may console the bearer of a burden. Would that this Nucleus, which I have shelled out and now offer to you, were of such a kind that it would not, while it smells of the dust of the scholastic Muses, by its very brevity, by which it is compressed, produce weariness and nausea in a mind that is bent on great matters.

units.la: Accipe tamen hunc, quem Nomini tuo, ô Consul Bernharde, consecratum mitto Naturæ nucleum philosophicum fronte serenâ. Ut enim mittam, beneficia tua animi mei inclinantem affectum urgent: Gratæ mentis vicem reponere qualemcunque satago: Tu verò ut benignè, quod mitto, accipias, inveteratus tuus in me amor suadet, humanitasque invi-tat. Proinde, te non aversa facie chartace-um hoc munus, sed animo & vultu veteris tui Casmanni studiosissimo accepturum spero. Vale & fave. Stadæ Kal. Januarii, Anno à partu Virginis 1 6 0 5 [?]. Cujus ineuntis jam anni initium felix faustumq;, medium felicius & faustius, extremum felicissimum & fau-stissimum tibi cum omnibus tuis largiatur præpotens DEUS, faxitq; ut Paternæ digni-tatis hæres, Reipub. Patriæ nostræ à Vari illius Romani castris appellatæ lumen ac columen sis diuq; maneas.
units.tr: Accept, however, this philosophical kernel of Nature, which I send, consecrated to your name, O Consul Bernhard, with a serene brow. For although I send it, your benefits press upon my inclined feeling: I strive to make some return, however small, for a grateful mind. That you should receive kindly what I send, your long-standing love for me urges and your humanity invites. Therefore I hope you will receive this paper gift not with averted face, but with the mind and countenance of your old and most devoted Casmann. Farewell and favour me. Stade, Kalends of January, in the year from the Virgin's childbirth 1605 [?]. May almighty GOD grant you and all yours a happy and auspicious beginning to the year now starting, a happier and more auspicious middle, and a most happy and most auspicious end; and may you, heir to your father's dignity, long remain the light and pillar of our Republic, named after that Roman camp of Varus.

units.la: ELENCHVS CAPITVM NATVRÆ MYSTERIORVM Nuclei.
units.tr: INDEX OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE NUCLEUS OF THE MYSTERIES OF NATURE

units.la: Disseritur Capite
units.tr: The chapter treats of

units.la: 1. De corpore Naturali, ubi de Natura & actione naturæ varia.
units.tr: 1. Of the natural body, where of nature and of the various actions of nature.

units.la: I. PARS PHYSICÆ, scilicet ACROAMATICA.
units.tr: I. PART OF PHYSICS, namely the ACROAMATIC part.

units.la: 2. De corporum naturalium Principiis externis & internis.
units.tr: 2. On the external and internal principles of natural bodies.

units.la: 3. De communibus affectionibus Corp. Nat. & quidem primo de Mutabilitate, Motu Physico vario & Quiete.
units.tr: 3. On the common affections of natural bodies, and first on mutability, varied physical motion and rest.

units.la: 4. Secundo de finitate, scilicet, Loco & Tempore physico.
units.tr: 4. Second, on finitude, namely physical place and time.

units.la: 5. De propriis affectionibus corporum Naturalium, nempe Qualitatibus manifestis & occultis.
units.tr: 5. On the proper affections of natural bodies, namely manifest and occult qualities.

units.la: 6. De qualitatibus actualibus Sensilibus, actualibus Tactilibus primis.
units.tr: 6. On the actual sensible qualities, the first actual tactile qualities.

units.la: 7. De Qualitatibus tactilibꝰ Secundis, Variis.
units.tr: 7. On the second and various tactile qualities.

units.la: 8. De Visibilibus qualitatibus, Luce & Coloribus.
units.tr: 8. On visible qualities, light and colours.

units.la: 9. De Qualitate audibili, scilicet Sono.
units.tr: 9. On the audible quality, namely sound.

units.la: 10. De Qualitate gustatili, scilicet Sapore.
units.tr: 10. On the gustatory quality, namely flavour.

units.la: 11. De Qualitate odorabili, scilicet Odore.
units.tr: 11. On the odorous quality, namely smell.

units.la: II. PARS PHTSICÆ, COSMOGRAPHIA Physica.
units.tr: II. PART OF PHYSICS: PHYSICAL COSMOGRAPHY.

units.la: Cap.i. agitur : De Mundo, & quidem Prima ac suprema ejus parte, Cœlo, cujus doctrina Ouranographia.
units.tr: Chapter 1 treats of the world, and first and highest of its parts, the heavens, whose doctrine is called Ouranography.

units.la: 2. De Stellis in cœlo, earumq; natura & proprietatibus : Quarum doctrina dicitur Astrologia.
units.tr: 2. Of the stars in the heavens, their nature and properties; the doctrine of these is called Astrology.

units.la: 3. De Stœcheiologia vulgari, & primum de elemento IGNIS.
units.tr: 3. Of the common Stoicheiology, and first of the element of FIRE.

units.la: 4. De AERE, ejusq; regionibus & qualitatibus, secundum Vulgus & Theologos.
units.tr: 4. Of AIR, its regions and qualities, according to the common people and the theologians.

units.la: 5. De Aqua, ubi de Mari & affectionibus ejus.
units.tr: 5. Of Water, where also of the Sea and its affections.

units.la: 6. De Terra, ejusq; affectionibus generatim.
units.tr: 6. Of Earth and its affections in general.

units.la: 7. MIXOLOGIA, ubi de Mixtione & Temperamentis.
units.tr: 7. MIXOLOGY, where of Mixture and Temperaments.

units.la: 8. Meteorologia, & quidem primò de Meteororum materia, HALITIBUS.
units.tr: 8. Meteorology, and first of the matter of meteors, the EXHALATIONS.

units.la: 9. De METEORIS Aqueis ex Vapore genitis, Nubibus & inde genitis.
units.tr: 9. Of the watery meteors produced from vapour, and of clouds and the things generated from them.

units.la: 10. De Meteoris Ignitis, secundum vulgus Physicorum, vere existentibus & apparentibus; Illis quidem simplicibus aut mixtis.
units.tr: 10. Of the fiery meteors, according to the common opinion of the natural philosophers, both those truly existing and those that only appear; and of these, both the simple and the mixed.

units.la: 11. De Meteoris ex utroq; halitu genitis, ubi de Ventis, Terræ motu, Item Observatio Libaviana.
units.tr: 11. Of the meteors generated from both kinds of exhalation, where also of winds and earthquakes; likewise the Libavian observation.

units.la: 12. ORYCTICE peripatetica, seu, de Metallis ex doctrina peripateticorum.
units.tr: 12. Peripatetic ORYCTICE, or, of metals according to the doctrine of the Peripatetics.

units.la: 13. Oryctica Chymica, de Metallis & Metallicis ex doctrina & experientia Chymicorum.
units.tr: 13. Chemical Oryctics, of metals and metallic things from the doctrine and experience of the Chemists.

units.la: Cap.14. De Lapidibus regularibus &anomalis+
units.tr: Chapter 14. On Regular and Irregular Stones

units.la: 15. De Animato corpore, ejusq; Vita & Morte.
units.tr: 15. On the animate body, and its life and death.

units.la: 16. De Anima vegetante, nutrice, auctrice, procreatrice.
units.tr: 16. On the vegetative soul, which nourishes, increases, and procreates.

units.la: 17. Phytologia, de Plantis & stirpibus, earumque partibus.
units.tr: 17. Phytologia, on plants and stocks, and their parts.

units.la: 18. De variis Plantarum affectionibus.
units.tr: 18. On the various affections of plants.

units.la: 19. Dendrographia, quæ est arborum doctrina generalis, & Botanologia, quæ est Herbarum.
units.tr: 19. Dendrographia, which is the general doctrine of trees, and Botanologia, which is that of herbs.

units.la: 20o+ De plantarum viribus ac facultatibus paulo specialius ad Medicos spectantibus.
units.tr: 20. On the powers and faculties of plants, pertaining somewhat more specifically to physicians.

units.la: 21. Zoographia, de anima sentiente, & animalium sensu in genere.
units.tr: 21. Zoographia, on the sentient soul and the sense of animals in general.

units.la: 22. De sensibus exterioribus, Visu, gustu, tactu olfactu & auditu.
units.tr: 22. On the external senses: sight, taste, touch, smell and hearing.

units.la: 23. De sensibus interioribus, sensu communi, Phantasia, Memoria, ubi de Somno.
units.tr: 23. On the internal senses: common sense, phantasy, and memory, where also on sleep.

units.la: 24. De motu animalium & affectibus.
units.tr: 24. On the motion and affections of animals.

units.la: 25. De animalium corpore generatim.
units.tr: 25. On the body of animals in general.

units.la: 26. De Brutorum distinctione. THERIOLOGIA, Anthropologiæ pars prima, scilicet.
units.tr: 26. On the distinction of brutes. THERIOLOGIA, namely the first part of Anthropology.

units.la: 27. PSYCHOLOGIA Humana, seu de anima hominis rationali: Ubi de Intellectu.
units.tr: 27. PSYCHOLOGIA of man, or on the rational soul of man, where on the intellect.

units.la: 28. De voluntatis humanæ affectione & actione.
units.tr: 28. On the affection and action of the human will.

units.la: 29. De facultate loquendi & ridendi.
units.tr: 29. On the faculty of speaking and laughing.

units.la: 30. Altera pars Anthropologiæ, Somatotomia Corporis humani, spiritu, calore, & humido innato.
units.tr: 30. The second part of Anthropology: Somatotomia of the human body, spirit, heat, and innate moisture.

units.la: 31. De partibus & conjunctione ossium.
units.tr: 31. On the parts and conjunction of bones.

units.la: 32. Osteologia, seu Humanorum ossium Sceleton. Constat hoc caput 14. Sectionibus+
units.tr: 32. Osteologia, or the skeleton of human bones. This chapter consists of 14 sections.

units.la: 33. De Cartilagine & Ligamento.
units.tr: 33. On cartilage and ligament.

units.la: 34. De Cute, Adipe & membrana Carnosa.
units.tr: 34. On skin, fat, and the fleshy membrane.

units.la: 35. De Membranis nominatis & innominatis.
units.tr: 35. On named and unnamed membranes.

units.la: 36. De Semine humano, & sanguine Menstruo generationis principiis.
units.tr: 36. On human seed and menstrual blood, the principles of generation.

units.la: 37. De communibus generationis membris.
units.tr: 37. On the parts common to generation.

units.la: 38. De propriis Maris & Fœminæ genitalibus.
units.tr: 38. On the proper genitals of male and female.

units.la: 39. De Fibris.
units.tr: 39. On fibres.

units.la: 40. De Ventriculo.
units.tr: 40. On the stomach.

units.la: 41. De Oesophago & intestinis gracilioribus.
units.tr: 41. On the gullet and the slender intestines.

units.la: 42. De Chymo, Sanguine & Pituita.
units.tr: 42. On chyme, blood, and phlegm.

units.la: 43. De Bile flava & atra, item de Vesicula fellis & Liene.
units.tr: 43. On yellow and black bile, likewise on the gall bladder and spleen.

units.la: 44. De Epate.
units.tr: 44. On the liver.

units.la: 45. De Venis.
units.tr: 45. On the veins.

units.la: 46. De organis tertiæ concoctionis.
units.tr: 46. On the organs of tertiary concoction.

units.la: 47. De membris expulsioni excrementorum inservientibus.
units.tr: 47. On the parts serving the expulsion of excrements.

units.la: 48. De Cerebro & Cerebello.
units.tr: 48. On the cerebrum and cerebellum.

units.la: 49. De Medulla spinali & Nervis.
units.tr: 49. On the spinal marrow and nerves.

units.la: 50. De organis sensus, tactus & gustus. Ubi Lingua.
units.tr: 50. On the organs of touch and taste, where the tongue.

units.la: 51. De visus organo, Oculo.
units.tr: 51. On the organ of sight, the eye.

units.la: 52. De organo auditus exteriori & interiori.
units.tr: 52. On the external and internal organ of hearing.

units.la: 53. De organo olfactus interiori & exteriori.
units.tr: 53. On the internal and external organ of smell.

units.la: 54. De membris Respirationis.
units.tr: 54. On the parts of respiration.

units.la: 55. De Corde & Arteriis.
units.tr: 55. On the heart and arteries.

units.la: 56. De Musculis.
units.tr: 56. On the muscles.

units.la: OTHONIS CAS-MANNI PHYSIOLOGIÆ NUCLEUS seu CORPORUM NA-TURALIUM PÆDAGOGI-CUM ET METHODICUM Systema. LIBER PRIMUS. CAPUT PRIMUM. DE CORPORE NA-TURALI.
units.tr: OTHO CASMANN'S NUCLEUS OF NATURAL PHYSIOLOGY, or a Pedagogical and Methodical System of Natural Bodies. BOOK ONE. CHAPTER ONE. ON NATURAL BODY.

units.la: PHYSICA seu PHYSIOLO-GIA est doctrina corporum naturalium.
units.tr: Physics, or physiology, is the doctrine of natural bodies.

units.la: CORPUS NATURALE est, quod sua constat Naturâ.
units.tr: A natural body is one that consists by its own nature.

units.la: Corpus est substantia materiata, sensilis, mobilis, quantitate continua per se terminata.
units.tr: A body is a material, sensible, mobile substance, continuous in quantity and terminated in itself.

units.la: Hæc substantia, si habet sibi à Deo inditam Naturam, qua est efficax ad sibi delegatas functiones obeundas, adeoq; est instructa agendi patiendiq; qualitatibus, dicitur Natu-rale corpus.
units.tr: When this substance has a nature implanted in it by God, by which it is effective in discharging the functions assigned to it, and so is equipped with qualities of acting and being acted upon, it is called a natural body.

units.la: NATURA est vis corpori naturali à Deo insita.
units.tr: Nature is the power implanted in a natural body by God.

units.la: Hæc vis est internum rerum naturalium principium, quo naturales motus & actiones cientur.
units.tr: This power is the internal principle of natural things, by which natural motions and actions are set in motion.

units.la: Natura hic duo significat: facultatem nimirum activam & passivam.
units.tr: Here nature signifies two things, namely an active and a passive faculty.

units.la: Activa facultas seu potentia est, qua ipsum corpus est actuosum & efficax ad motus & actiones sibi à Deo commissas edendas.
units.tr: The active faculty or power is that by which the body itself is active and effective in carrying out the motions and actions entrusted to it by God.

units.la: Passiva potentia seu facultas hic est nativa corporis habilitas, qua aptum est & propendet ad aliquem motum recipiendum.
units.tr: The passive power or faculty here is the body's innate aptitude, by which it is fitted and inclined to receive some motion.

units.la: Natura itaq; tripliciter se habere potest ad corpus.
units.tr: Nature therefore can relate to the body in three ways.

units.la: I. Ut forma, qua corpus naturale est natu-rale.
units.tr: I. As the form by which a natural body is natural.

units.la: II. Ut Adjuncta qualitas, scilicet habilitas & aptitudo, qua propendet ad motum.
units.tr: II. As an accompanying quality, namely readiness and aptitude, by which it tends towards motion.

units.la: III. Ut principium internum agens & efficiens mutationum, & actionum naturali-um.
units.tr: III. As the internal principle that acts and brings about changes and natural actions.

units.la: NB. Hinc Physicus in Analysi corporis naturalis spectat tria:
units.tr: NB. Hence the natural philosopher, in analysing a natural body, considers three things:

units.la: 1. οὐσίαν[?] seu essentiam corporalem, quâ est. Hanc comitatur corporis existentia.
units.tr: 1. Substance [οὐσία], or corporeal essence, by which it is. Bodily existence accompanies this.

units.la: 2. Δύναμιν seu potentiam ac facultatem, qua naturaliter tum habile, tum efficax est. Hæc igitur & habilitatem naturalem, & operosam efficaciam includit.
units.tr: 2. Power [δύναμις], or potency and faculty, by which it is naturally both able and effective. This therefore includes both natural aptitude and active efficacy.

units.la: 3. ἐνέργειαν[?] seu actionem, quæ procedit ab essentia per potentiam.
units.tr: 3. Energy [ἐνέργεια], or action, which proceeds from the essence through the power.

units.la: Omne itaq; corpus naturale est ex materia sua, à quâ quantitas corporis, per formam suam, à qua quantitas terminata, seu termini quantitatis. Idem habile & efficax est, per naturam sibi inditam, & suis qualitatibus instructam.
units.tr: Every natural body, therefore, is made up of its matter, which gives the quantity of the body, and of its form, which terminates the quantity or sets its limits. The same body is able and effective through the nature implanted in it and equipped with its qualities.

units.la: Idem vero operatur & efficit, aut per emanationem, aut per transmutationem.
units.tr: The same body, moreover, operates and produces effects either by emanation or by transmutation.

units.la: Emanatio hic est, interior effecti seu motus à virtute corporis naturali consecutio & productio.
units.tr: Emanation here is the internal consequence and production of an effect or motion from the natural power of the body.

units.la: Transmutatio hic est exterior agentis & moventis naturalis transitio in subjectum patiens.
units.tr: Transmutation here is the external passage of the natural agent and mover into a passive subject.

units.la: Hinc Actio corporis naturalis est Immanens vel transiens.
units.tr: Hence the action of a natural body is either immanent or transient.

units.la: Immanens remanet in corpore naturali, ab ejus interiore forma & actu profecta.
units.tr: Immanent action remains in the natural body, proceeding from its internal form and act.

units.la: Transiens ab agente foras ad externum procedit patiens, sive illud subjectum patiens sit contrarium, sive simile.
units.tr: Transient action goes forth from the agent outwards to an external patient, whether that passive subject is contrary or similar to it.

units.la: Actio autem transiens ut ab agente naturali fiat in patiete, requiruntur quatuor.
units.tr: For transient action to pass from a natural agent into the patient, four things are required:

units.la: I. Ut sit proportio agentis ad patiens, seu ut virtus agentis & subjectum patiens, quod eius actionem recipit, rationem inter se habeant.
units.tr: I. There must be proportion between agent and patient, that is, the power of the agent and the subject receiving its action must stand in some relation to each other.

units.la: II. Ut subjectum patiens sit idoneum & habile ad efficaciam & actionem agentis excipiendum.
units.tr: II. The passive subject must be suitable and apt to receive the efficacy and action of the agent.

units.la: III. Ut mora & justum tempus concedatur actioni. Omnis motus fit successive.
units.tr: III. Delay and due time must be allowed for the action, since all motion occurs successively.

units.la: IV. Ut fit contactus agentis & patientis, quo se contingant, & simul sint, vel saltem fit remotio impedimentorum.
units.tr: IV. There must be contact between agent and patient, so that they touch and are together, or at least the removal of hindrances.

units.la: Contactus autem Scholasticis duplex dicitur, Corporalis vel Virtuosus.
units.tr: Contact, however, is called twofold by the Scholastics: corporeal or virtual.

units.la: Contactus corporalis, qui proprius & verus est, quando duorum corporum superficies simul sunt. Ut tangens ignitum carbonem laedit manum. Contactu hoc agunt corpora, aut μεταβολικῶς [?] transitivè, ut flamma transiens incendit ædes, aut μεταδοτικῶς [?] distributivè, ut ignis ferrum igniens.
units.tr: Corporeal contact, which is proper and true, occurs when the surfaces of two bodies are together. For example, touching a glowing coal injures the hand. By this contact bodies act either metabolically [μεταβολικῶς], that is transitively, as a passing flame sets a building on fire, or distributively [μεταδοτικῶς], as fire heats iron.

units.la: Virtualis contactus est, cum non superficies, sed virtus unius corporis ad superficiem alterius pervenit. Hæc autem virtus ita agens, vel est manifesta, ut Solis terram calefacientis, vel occulta, ut Magnetis ferrum trahentis.
units.tr: Virtual contact occurs when not the surface but the power of one body reaches the surface of another. This power acting in this way is either manifest, as the sun warming the earth, or hidden, as the magnet drawing iron.

units.la: REGVLA.
units.tr: RULE.

units.la: Verum Physicum agens non potest agere in extrema, nisi prius agat in medium.
units.tr: A true physical agent cannot act upon extremes unless it first acts upon the medium.

units.la: Actio Physica sæpenumero cohibetur, manente potentia seu facultate actionis: Seu, Actus rei secundus sæpe cohibetur, manente actu primo.
units.tr: Physical action is often hindered while the power or faculty of acting remains; in other words, the second act of a thing is often hindered while its first act remains.

units.la: Et: Facultate seu potentia interna salva, res Physica nonnunquam sustinet ei contrariam ἐνέργειαν [?] seu actionem.
units.tr: And: with its internal faculty or power intact, a physical thing sometimes bears an action contrary to it.

units.la: Notandum & hoc: Omne agens in agendo ἀντιπάσχειν [?].
units.tr: This also is to be noted: every agent, in acting, is also acted upon [ἀντιπάσχειν].

units.la: 1. Si actio est transiens ac fit per transmutationem, ut cum cibus alteratur à naturali calore, cibus vicissim immutat naturalem calorem. Tale agens oportet patienti esse contrarium.
units.tr: 1. If the action is transient and occurs by transmutation, as when food is altered by natural heat, the food in turn changes the natural heat. Such an agent must be contrary to the patient.

units.la: 2. Si virtus agens patientis excedat resistentiam agentis. Actio enim fit à valentiori.
units.tr: 2. If the agent's power exceeds the resistance of the patient, for action is done by the stronger.

units.la: 3. Si resistentia agentis nullo externo juvetur.
units.tr: 3. If the resistance of the agent is not aided by anything external.

units.la: 4. Si agens ita vicinum sit patienti, ut hoc in illud agere possit. Non tamen omne patiens tantum patitur, quantum agens agit. Nam idem movens eadem vi vario motu saepius movet diversa[?].
units.tr: 4. If the agent is so near the patient that it can act upon it. Yet not every patient suffers as much as the agent acts, for the same mover, with the same force, often moves different things with varying motion.

units.la: Naturæ porrò peccatum dicitur MONSTRUM, quod est vitium naturæ deficientis ob aliquod impedimentum.
units.tr: Moreover, a fault of nature is called a MONSTER, which is a defect of a nature falling short because of some impediment.

units.la: Vitium hoc Naturæ fit 1. A qualitate[?] justæ proportionis limites excedente. 2. A virtute formatrice seminibus insita. 3. Vel ex materia redundantia, vel penuria, vel confusione & permixtione. 4. Vel deniq;[?] perversitate subjecti loci.
units.tr: This defect of nature arises: 1. from a quality exceeding the limits of due proportion; 2. from a formative power implanted in the seeds; 3. either from matter in excess, or in deficiency, or in confusion and mixture; 4. or finally from the perversity of the place of the subject.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM. DE CORPORUM NATURA-LIUM PRINCIPIIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 2. ON THE PRINCIPLES OF NATURAL BODIES.

units.la: PHysicæ partes duæ sunt : COM-MUNIS & PROPRIA. Communis ex Aristotele dici potest quodammodo ACROAMATICA,
units.tr: Physics has two parts: the common and the particular. The common part may be called, after Aristotle, in a sense the acroamatic part,

units.la: [Footnote-free page: no foot notes printed.] quæ communia rerum naturalium principia & communes affectiones explicat.
units.tr: [Footnote-free page: no footnotes printed.] It explains the common principles of natural things and their common affections.

units.la: Acroamaticæ partis membra duo sunt. 1. Doctrina principiorum Physicorum. 2. Doctrina affectionum Physicarum.
units.tr: The acroamatic part has two members. (1) The doctrine of the principles of physics. (2) The doctrine of the affections of physical things.

units.la: PRINCIPIA PHYSICA sunt, quorum vi effectus & res naturalis est. Suntq; externa & interna.
units.tr: The physical principles are those by whose power a natural thing and its effect exist. They are either external or internal.

units.la: Externa, quæ manent extra corporum constitutam essentiam, Suntq; Efficiens & Finis.
units.tr: The external principles, which lie outside the constituted essence of bodies, are the efficient cause and the final cause.

units.la: Efficiens est principium externum, unde seu à quo est motus & quies rei Physicæ.
units.tr: The efficient cause is the external principle from which a physical thing has its motion and rest.

units.la: Ab hoc procedit motus per operationem, & quies per cessationem suam, opere completo. Efficiens principium interne agit per Emanationem, aut externe per Transmutationem.
units.tr: From it motion proceeds through its operation, and rest through its cessation once the work is finished. The efficient principle acts internally by emanation, or externally by transmutation.

units.la: Efficiens est primum vel secundum.
units.tr: The efficient cause is either first or secondary.

units.la: Primum est Vniversalis causa, nempe Deus, qui dicitur Philosophis propterea, Primus motor, prima causa, causa infinita, primum movens, cujus nutu omnia gubernantur.
units.tr: The first is the universal cause, namely God, who is called by the philosophers for this reason the first mover, the first cause, the infinite cause, the first moving thing, by whose nod all things are governed.

units.la: Deus est principium CREANS,
units.tr: God is the CREATING principle,

units.la: ideoque Creator, qui res naturales creando, idque optimè produxit, productasq; providendo adhuc gubernat.
units.tr: and therefore the Creator, who by creating produced natural things, and produced them very well, and having produced them still governs them by providence.

units.la: Creatio autem est immediata vel mediata.
units.tr: Creation is either immediate or mediate.

units.la: Immediata est entis ex nonsimpliciter ente facta productio, (verbo divinæ potentiæ) ait Scaliger.
units.tr: Immediate creation is the production of a being from what is not simply a being, effected by the word of divine power, as Scaliger says.

units.la: Mediata est entis ex ente eductio, formatio, & distinctio facta per transformationem Naturæ inimitabilem, (ideoque ex ente inhabili & indispositio.)
units.tr: Mediate creation is the drawing out, forming and distinguishing of a being from a being, effected through a transformation of nature that cannot be imitated (and so from an unfit and undisposed being).

units.la: Creata providendo Deus gubernat.
units.tr: God governs the things created by providence.

units.la: Providentia est, qua creator res à se productas perpetim, sed absque molestia & liberè curat.
units.tr: Providence is the care by which the Creator continually looks after the things he has produced, yet without trouble and freely.

units.la: Hujus decretum dicitur Philosophis Fatum.
units.tr: The decree of this providence is called by the philosophers Fate.

units.la: Fatum est verum vel commentitum.
units.tr: Fate is either true or feigned.

units.la: Verum est divinum seu Hyperphysicum vel Physicum.
units.tr: True fate is either divine (or hyperphysical) or physical.

units.la: Divinum est hoc, de quo loquimur, divinæ scilicet providentiæ decretum.
units.tr: Divine fate is the one we are speaking of, namely the decree of divine providence.

units.la: Physicum fatum à divino dependet, tanquam instrumentum:
units.tr: Physical fate depends on the divine as an instrument does.

units.la: Estq; series & ordo causarum naturalium, quæ nisi impediantur, vi & natura sua, certum eundemque producunt esse-ctum.
units.tr: It is the series and order of natural causes which, unless they are hindered, by their power and nature produce a certain and single effect.

units.la: Ementitum est Chaldaicum, seu Astrologicum, & Stoicum.
units.tr: Feigned fate is Chaldean, or astrological, and Stoic.

units.la: Chaldaicum & Astrologicum ligat actiones & eventus omnes ad vim & positum stellarum.
units.tr: The Chaldean and astrological fate binds all actions and events to the power and position of the stars.

units.la: Stoicum dicitur ab æterno fluens talis causarum series, ut nec Deus aliter, quàm secundæ causæ feruntur, nec voluntas aliter, quàm ut cogitur à causis præcedentibus, possit agere.
units.tr: The Stoic fate is a series of causes flowing from eternity in such a way that neither God can act otherwise than secondary causes are carried along, nor the will otherwise than as it is compelled by preceding causes.

units.la: Fati consequens est Necessitas. Unde omnia, quæ fato fiunt, necessario fiunt, & fatalia sunt necessaria.
units.tr: The consequence of fate is necessity. Hence all things that happen by fate happen necessarily, and fated things are necessary.

units.la: Secundum efficiens est causa particularis, à Deo creata, à Deo dependens, vi à Deo accepta agens. Est quasi tanquam Dei organum & συνεργον, ut ipsa Natura. Hæc non agit, nisi virtute causæ primæ.
units.tr: The secondary efficient cause is a particular cause, created by God, dependent on God, acting by a power received from God. It is, as it were, an organ and co-worker of God, just as nature itself is. It acts only by the power of the first cause.

units.la: FINIS est alterum externum principium, cujus gratia sunt res Physicæ.
units.tr: The FINAL cause is the other external principle, for whose sake physical things exist.

units.la: Omnis enim Natura propter finem agit; adeoque à fine omnes naturæ operationes reguntur.
units.tr: For every nature acts for the sake of an end, and so all the operations of nature are governed by the end.

units.la: Natura igitur nihil frustrà facit.
units.tr: Nature therefore does nothing in vain.

units.la: Finis universalis, cujus gratia omnis Natura est, est Gloria Dei. Particularis seu naturalis est, ad quem tanquam ad suum bonum & commodum, unaquæq; res Physica, in suo genere, ex natura præscripto, tendit.
units.tr: The universal end, for whose sake all nature exists, is the glory of God. The particular or natural end is that to which each physical thing, in its own kind, tends as to its own good and advantage, as prescribed by its nature.

units.la: Internum principium est Essentiale, quod internam essentiam corporum naturalium ingreditur & constituit.
units.tr: The internal principle is the essential one, which enters into and constitutes the internal essence of natural bodies.

units.la: Estque materia & forma Physica.
units.tr: This is physical matter and form.

units.la: Materia est internum & essentiale principium, ex quo corpus naturale est.
units.tr: Matter is the internal and essential principle from which a natural body is.

units.la: Dicitur Principium Passivum, quia patiturse præparari ac informari. Dicitur item Potentia, eò quod δύναμις παθητικὴ [?] fit necessarium ejus adjunctum.
units.tr: It is called the passive principle, because it is by nature suited to be prepared and informed. It is also called potency, because the passive power [δύναμις παθητική] becomes its necessary attribute.

units.la: Dicitur item subjectum transmutationis & formæ.
units.tr: It is also called the subject of transmutation and of form.

units.la: Dicitur causa & principium corruptibilitatis; At Scaliger expressè negat materiam meditari corruptionem, & maleficium.
units.tr: It is called the cause and principle of corruptibility; but Scaliger expressly denies that matter contrives corruption and harm.

units.la: A materia corporis Physici proma-nat quantitas corporea, qua corpus mathematica quantitate informatum constat trinis dimensionibus.
units.tr: From the matter of a physical body flows corporeal quantity, by which the body, informed with mathematical quantity, consists in three dimensions.

units.la: Omne itaque Physicum corpus est quantum, habetque longitudinem, latitudinem & profunditatem.
units.tr: Every physical body is therefore extended, and has length, breadth and depth.

units.la: Materia Physica est Prima vel Secunda.
units.tr: Physical matter is either first or second.

units.la: Prima est, ex qua tanquam subjecto primo omnia corpora naturalia fiunt, & in quam corrupta ad extremum resolvuntur.
units.tr: First matter is that from which all natural bodies are made, as from a primary subject, and into which, when corrupted, they are at last resolved.

units.la: Materia itaq; hæc est primum subjectum transmutationis, & variarum formarum; habetq; ad has recipiendas facultatem.
units.tr: This matter, therefore, is the first subject of transmutation and of various forms, and it has the capacity to receive them.

units.la: Materiæ necessario adjungitur Privatio, scilicet formarum, cujus quasi occasione nova introducitur forma, seu Materiæ accidit forma vacuitas, privatio. Hæc conjuncta est, cum forma quadam certa antecedente formam introducendam.
units.tr: Privation is necessarily joined to matter, namely the privation of forms; on the occasion of which a new form is introduced. Or, emptiness of form, privation, befalls matter. This is conjoined with a certain form that precedes the form to be introduced.

units.la: Nunquam autem nuda & absq; omni forma actuq; materia prima extitit, sed sub quadam forma. Contradictorium est, id, quod non est actu, esse actu.
units.tr: Prime matter, however, has never existed bare and without all form and actuality, but always under some form. It is a contradiction for that which is not actual to be actual.

units.la: Privatio dicitur absentia formæ in subjecto habili ad eam recipiendam. Non est principium constitutionis, sed potius transmutationis rerum naturalium.
units.tr: Privation is the absence of a form in a subject able to receive it. It is not a principle of the constitution, but rather of the transmutation of natural things.

units.la: Materia prima Mosaica est materia, primo die à DEO ex nihilo solo verbo condita, expressâ appellatione cœli & terræ, abyssi & aquarum, ex qua tanquam rudi, fatiscente, & informi materia. Deus postea finxit distinctas corporum species. Sunt enim, qui Prima verba, capitis primi Geneseos, ita explicant; Primum omnium creavit Deus massam quandam, & quasi Chaos, unde coelum & terram, ceterasque res omnes efformaret.
units.tr: Moses' prime matter is matter, created by God on the first day out of nothing by his word alone, expressly named heaven and earth, the abyss and the waters, out of which, as from a raw, crumbling and formless matter, God afterwards fashioned the distinct species of bodies. Some explain the first words of the first chapter of Genesis in this way: God first of all created a certain mass, as it were a Chaos, out of which he would form heaven and earth and all the other things.

units.la: Quam constituit deinde, ut esset reliquarum rerum condendarum materies & seminarium.
units.tr: He then constituted it so as to be the material and seed-plot of the other things to be created.

units.la: Materia prima Aristotelica, est primum cujusq; rei subjectum, ex quo insito per se, & non secundum accidens, gignitur, & si interit, in hoc postremum interit.
units.tr: Aristotelian prime matter is the first subject of anything, from which, as something inherent in itself and not accidentally, a thing is generated, and if it perishes, it perishes into this last matter.

units.la: Haec dicitur neque generabilis, neque corruptibilis, informis, indefinita, & omnis qualitatis expers.
units.tr: This is said to be neither generable nor corruptible, formless, indefinite, and without any quality.

units.la: Secunda materia est, quae per transmutationem est effecta; estq; subjectum secundum transmutationis & formarum.
units.tr: Second matter is that which has been made by transmutation, and it is the subject of transmutation and of forms.

units.la: Haec pendet a prima, certo videlicet ordine naturae, ut Materia prima Creatione extitit: ita secunda generatione. Omnis materia secunda determinata est necessario in certa materia ad certam & unicam formam. Ut materia Muscae tantum determinata ad formam muscae, nec possibile est eam recipere formam Elephanti, aut alicujus alius animalis. Sic materiæ individu-ales ad certas formas individuales ejusdem spe-ciei ita sunt determinatæ, ut nullam ejusdem speciei aliam possint recipere. Unde certitudo resurrectionis ea, qua quilibet dicuntur idem numero corpus & animam recepturi.
units.tr: This depends on the first, by the fixed order of nature: as prime matter came into being by creation, so second matter by generation. Every second matter is necessarily determined to a certain matter, for a certain and single form. Thus the matter of a fly is determined only to the form of a fly, and it is not possible for it to receive the form of an elephant or of any other animal. So individual matters are determined to certain individual forms of the same species in such a way that they cannot receive any other of the same species. Hence the certainty of the resurrection, by which each is said to receive back the same body and soul in number.

units.la: Forma Physica est principium inter-num maximè essentiale, quod dat corpori naturali suum esse; & per quod corpus naturale est id quod est.
units.tr: Physical form is the most essential internal principle, which gives the natural body its being, and through which a natural body is what it is.

units.la: Forma naturalis est actus primus naturalis corporis & modus essendi.
units.tr: Natural form is the first actuality of a natural body and its mode of being.

units.la: Estq; potissima pars corporis ex materia per formam compositi, qua constituitur, & ab aliis essentialiter distinguitur.
units.tr: It is the chief part of a body compounded of matter through form, by which it is constituted and essentially distinguished from others.

units.la: 1. Forma enim corporis Physici materiam suam informat, & informando perficit & determinat. Hinc ἐντελέχεια[?] dicitur.
units.tr: 1. For the form of a physical body informs its matter, and by informing it perfects and determines it. Hence it is called actuality [ἐντελέχεια].

units.la: 2. Forma hæc corpus compositum constituit in entium certo gradu. Dat corpori essentiam, dat corpori quod est, & actualem existentiam, dat operationes. Unde à Forma proficiscuntur potentiæ, & facultates agendi, à potentiis operationes.
units.tr: 2. This form constitutes the compound body at a certain grade of beings. It gives the body its essence, gives the body what it is, and actual existence, and gives it its operations. Hence from the form proceed the potencies and faculties of acting, and from the potencies the operations.

units.la: 3. Forma igitur Physicæ proprie debentur o-perationes corporis Physici. Materia, inquit Aristoteles, quatenus materia, est passivum, ejus est moveri & pati: movere autem & operari est forma.
units.tr: 3. Therefore the operations of a physical body are properly owed to its physical form. Matter, says Aristotle, insofar as it is matter, is passive; to be moved and to be acted upon belong to it; but to move and to operate belongs to form.

units.la: Forma itaque est activum principium. Unde posita forma corporis Physici ponuntur tria, Essentia corporis, distinctio ejus, & operatio ejus.
units.tr: Form, therefore, is the active principle. Hence, when the form of a physical body is posited, three things are posited: the essence of the body, its distinctness, and its operation.

units.la: 4. Forma proinde in corpore Physico est principium distinguens ab aliis primario & essentialiter.
units.tr: 4. Form, accordingly, in a physical body is the principle that distinguishes it from others primarily and essentially.

units.la: 5. Ut a Materia quantitas emanat: ita a forma corporis termini quantitatis prascribuntur.
units.tr: 5. As quantity emanates from matter, so the limits of quantity are prescribed to a body by its form.

units.la: Forma item prima est aut secunda.
units.tr: Form too is either first or second.

units.la: Prima Physica forma est, propria primae materiae, & ordine reliquas omnes antecedit.
units.tr: The first physical form is proper to first matter, and in order precedes all the rest.

units.la: Secunda est, quae primam sequitur, quocunque in gradu: estque materiae secundae propria.
units.tr: The second is that which follows the first, at whatever grade it may be, and it is proper to second matter.

units.la: Haec aut educitur ex materia, vel inducitur in materiam.
units.tr: This is either educed from matter, or introduced into matter.

units.la: Haec naturaliter non unitur materiae, nisi recte dispositae & praeparatae.
units.tr: This does not naturally unite with matter unless the matter is rightly disposed and prepared.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM. DE MOTU ET QVIETE.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE. ON MOTION AND REST.

units.la: ADhuc fuerunt principia natu-ralia : Affectiones sunt, quæ corpo-ribus naturalibus essentialiter constitutis, adjunguntur naturaliter, e-isque vel insunt vel adsunt.
units.tr: There are also natural principles. Affections are those things which are naturally joined to natural bodies that are essentially constituted, and which either inhere in them or are present to them.

units.la: Affectio corporis naturalis est communis vel propria. Cōmunis affectio est Mu-tabilitas & Finitas corporis.
units.tr: An affection of a natural body is either common or proper. A common affection is mutability and finitude of body.

units.la: Mutabilitas est, qua corpus mutati-oni est obnoxium.
units.tr: Mutability is that by which a body is liable to change.

units.la: Omne enim Physicum corpus est Mutabile, Mutari potest.
units.tr: For every physical body is mutable; it can be changed.

units.la: A mutabilitate Naturæ pendet Motus. Cum enim natura mutatur, moveri dicitur.
units.tr: Motion depends on mutability. For when a nature is changed, it is said to be moved.

units.la: Motus Physicus est affectio corporis naturalis, est [?]ἐντελέχεια corporis mobilis, qua mobile à movente profecta. Seu: Est ἐνέργεια moventis in mobile. Per motum tanquam per medium itur ad perfectionem: adeoque est itio, progressio, contentio ad rem, non res ipsa.
units.tr: Physical motion is an affection of a natural body. It is the actuality [ἐντελέχεια] of a mobile body, by which the mobile is set in motion from a mover. Or: it is the activity [ἐνέργεια] of the mover in the mobile. Through motion, as through a means, one proceeds towards perfection; hence motion is a going, a progress, a striving towards a thing, not the thing itself.

units.la: Motus dupliciter consideratur, 1. Ratione moventis, à quo fit motus, & est ἐνέργεια & effectus moventis in mobili.
units.tr: Motion is considered in two ways. 1. In relation to the mover, from which the motion comes; and it is the activity and effect of the mover in the mobile.

units.la: Effectus, inquam, id est, naturalis effectio & actio, non autem ἐνέργημα[?] seu res effecta, producta & motu facta.
units.tr: I say "effect", that is, a natural effecting and action, and not the thing effected, produced and made by motion.

units.la: 2. Ratione Mobilis, quod motum recipit, seu movetur, & tum est corporis mobilis adjunctum πάθῳ[?], & adjunctum.
units.tr: 2. In relation to the mobile, which receives the motion, or is moved; and then it is an accident of the mobile body, and an accident of the passive condition.

units.la: In motu concurrunt Quinque.
units.tr: Five things concur in motion.

units.la: 1. Movens. Omne enim quod movetur, ab alio scilicet movente movetur. Inter movens & motum debet esse quaedam proportio, sed in movente inaequalis & virtute major.
units.tr: 1. The mover. For everything that is moved is moved by another, namely a mover. There must be some proportion between the mover and the motion, but in the mover it is unequal and greater in power.

units.la: 2. Mobile; quod motum ab agente excitatu excipit.
units.tr: 2. The mobile, which receives the motion excited by the agent.

units.la: Hoc esto affectum, & praeparatum ad actum perfectum suscipiendum: sit habile & dispositum.
units.tr: This must be disposed and prepared to receive the perfect act: it must be apt and fitted.

units.la: 3. Terminus a quo; Unde motus initium sumit, seu unde res moveri incipit.
units.tr: 3. The terminus from which; whence the motion takes its beginning, or whence a thing begins to be moved.

units.la: 4. Terminus ad quem est; in quo desinit motus. Haec forma quaedam est, unde imponuntur nomina motibus.
units.tr: 4. The terminus to which; where the motion ends. This is a certain form, from which motions are given their names.

units.la: 5. Tempus. Omnis enim motus fit in tempore. Hinc motus est momentaneus, qui in puncto temporis perficitur: Vel successivus, cum aperta est partium successio. Hinc motus tardus, qui magno tempore perficit parum: Vel velox, qui parvo tempore perficit multum.
units.tr: 5. Time. For every motion takes place in time. Hence a motion is momentary, when it is completed in a point of time; or successive, when there is a manifest succession of parts. Hence a motion is slow, which completes little in a long time; or swift, which completes much in a short time.

units.la: Motus porrò est Substantialis vel Accidentalis.
units.tr: Further, motion is either substantial or accidental.

units.la: Substantialis est, qui ipsam substantiam immutat, (scilicet eam aut procreando, aut corrumpendo.)
units.tr: Substantial motion is that which changes the substance itself (namely, by either generating or corrupting it).

units.la: Estque Generatio & corruptio.
units.tr: And this is generation and corruption.

units.la: Generatio seu Ortus est Motus (aliis mutatio; at distingue inter generans, & quod generatur, inter mutans & mutabile) substantialis, quo nova forma substantialis producitur, ut cum ex femine fit homo.
units.tr: Generation or origin is a substantial motion (some call it change, but distinguish between the generating and what is generated, between the changing and the changeable) by which a new substantial form is produced, as when a human being comes from seed.

units.la: Corruptio seu Interitus est motus, quo in materia abjicitur forma substantialis, ut cum ovum, quod ante erat, nascente pullo corrumpitur, & ovum esse desinit.
units.tr: Corruption or perishing is a motion by which a substantial form is cast off from matter, as when an egg, which existed before, is corrupted when the chick is hatched, and the egg ceases to be an egg.

units.la: Corruptio est destructio formæ; Materia manet, destruitur forma, sed ita, ut alia succedat. Unde Regula: Generatio unius est corruptio alterius, & vicissim: Corruptio unius est generatio alterius.
units.tr: Corruption is the destruction of a form. The matter remains; the form is destroyed, but in such a way that another succeeds. Hence the rule: the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, and conversely: the corruption of one thing is the generation of another.

units.la: Nota 1. Creatio non est generatio. Creatio non requirit aut omninò materiam, aut materiæ præjacentis naturalem habilitatem ad rei productionem, sed virtutem omnipotentē. DEI.
units.tr: Note 1. Creation is not generation. Creation requires neither matter at all, nor the natural capacity of a pre-existing matter for producing the thing, but the omnipotent power of God.

units.la: At Generatio materiam, & materiæ natura-lem lem potentiam & habilitatem, per quam unum ex altero posset procreari.
units.tr: But generation requires matter, and the natural power and capacity of the matter, through which one thing could be produced from another.

units.la: 2. Aliud corruptio hominis Theologica, haec accidentalis: aliud corruptio ejus Physica, haec substantialis.
units.tr: 2. Another thing is the theological corruption of man, which is accidental; another is his physical corruption, which is substantial.

units.la: {a}Accidentalis motus est, qui mutat corporis naturalis accidentia.
units.tr: {a} An accidental motion is one which changes the accidents of a natural body.

units.la: Accidentia haec vel inhaerent vel adhaerent.
units.tr: These accidents either inhere or adhere.

units.la: Inhaerent, Quantitas & Qualitas.
units.tr: Inherent accidents are quantity and quality.

units.la: Motus in quantitate est duplex: Augmentatio & Diminutio.
units.tr: Motion in quantity is twofold: increase and decrease.

units.la: Augmentatio est motus accidentalis, quo corpus naturale salva essentia majorem quantitatem acquirit.
units.tr: Increase is an accidental motion by which a natural body acquires a greater quantity while its essence is preserved.

units.la: Diminutio est motus, quo corpus naturale minorem quantitate acquirit.
units.tr: Decrease is a motion by which a natural body acquires a smaller quantity.

units.la: Motus in qualitate est Alteratio, quae est motus accidentalis, quo nova qualitas acquiritur, ut si ex frigido fiat calidum.
units.tr: Motion in quality is alteration, which is an accidental motion by which a new quality is acquired, as when what is cold becomes hot.

units.la: Adhaeret corpori Locus (scilicet Aristotelice definitus.)
units.tr: Place (namely, as defined by Aristotle) adheres to a body.

units.la: Motus in loco dicitur Latio, quae est motus de uno loco in alium, ut cum cibus ex ore & faucibus in ventriculum descendit.
units.tr: Motion in place is called transfer, which is a motion from one place to another, as when food descends from the mouth and throat into the stomach.

units.la: Nota alias motus distinctiones obiter: 1. Motus est insitus, aut externus. Insitus à principio interno est.
units.tr: Let us note in passing other distinctions of motion: 1. A motion is either innate or external. An innate motion comes from an internal principle.

units.la: Estq; Naturalis vel Animalis.
units.tr: It is also either natural or animal.

units.la: Naturalis est, cujus principium est natura (opposita scilicet sensitivo appetitui & voluntati.) Hic uniformis esse solet, & uno modo agere, scilicet in non diversis subjectis.
units.tr: A natural motion is one whose principle is nature (as opposed, namely, to the sensitive appetite and the will). This is usually uniform, and acts in one way, namely on non-diverse subjects.

units.la: Animalis est, cujus principium est anima. Hic in voluntariis varius & dissimilis est.
units.tr: An animal motion is one whose principle is the soul. This is varied and dissimilar in voluntary things.

units.la: Externus est Paraphysicus vel Hyperphysicus.
units.tr: An external motion is either paraphysical or hyperphysical.

units.la: Paraphysicus fit à principio externo, praeter naturam rei, ut tractio, item mors violenta.
units.tr: A paraphysical motion arises from an external principle, beyond the nature of the thing, as dragging, and likewise a violent death.

units.la: Hyperphysicus fit à principio externo divi-niore[?], ut motus ferri natantis.
units.tr: A hyperphysical motion arises from an external and more divine principle, as the motion of a floating iron.

units.la: 2. Omnis motus vel est naturalis, vel violentus, vel mixtus.
units.tr: 2. Every motion is either natural, or violent, or mixed.

units.la: Naturalis fit ab interno principio, Natura, vel inanimata vel animata. De hoc supra.
units.tr: A natural motion arises from an internal principle, nature, whether in inanimate or animate things. Of this we spoke above.

units.la: Violentus oritur à principio externo. Hic uni corpori potest accidere multiplex. Hic motus, si localis, 1. Est Pulsio, cum aliquis à se dispellit mobile. 2. Tractio. 3. Vectio, 4. Vertigo.
units.tr: A violent motion arises from an external principle. To one body there may happen many kinds of it. If this motion is local, it is: 1. a pushing, when someone drives a mobile away from himself; 2. a dragging; 3. a carrying; 4. a whirling.

units.la: Mixtus motus fit partim à Natura, partim Violentia.
units.tr: A mixed motion arises partly from nature and partly from violence.

units.la: Quies est affectio corporum naturalium, quae per motum acquiritur. Scaligero dicitur Motus perfectio & finis.
units.tr: Rest is an affection of natural bodies, which is acquired through motion. By Scaliger rest is called the perfection and end of motion.

units.la: At Quies, si est privatio motus in subiecto, ad eum ex natura sua apto, potest esse naturalis à principio interno: à principio externo violen-tus.
units.tr: But rest, if it is the privation of motion in a subject apt for it by its nature, can be natural from an internal principle, and violent from an external principle.

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM. DE LOCO ET TEMPORE.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR. CONCERNING PLACE AND TIME.

units.la: Entitas & circumscriptio est affectio corporis communis, 'qua corpus suis continetur terminis, (scilicet Loci aut temporis.
units.tr: Finitude and circumscription are an affection common to body, by which a body is contained within its own limits (namely, of place or of time).

units.la: Omne enim corpus naturale est finitum & circumscriptum.
units.tr: For every natural body is finite and circumscribed.

units.la: Nota. Ut quaedam mutabilitas & motus tribui potest mentibus ac Spiritibus creatis: ita etiam finitum esse, competit omni creaturae tam spirituali, quam corporeae. Ideoq; mutabilitas & finitas latius patent corpore naturali.
units.tr: Note. Just as a certain mutability and motion can be attributed to created minds and spirits, so too being finite belongs to every creature, spiritual as well as corporeal. Hence mutability and finitude extend more widely than natural body.

units.la: Omne quippe corpus est quantum. Quanti vero affectio est corporea finitudo, & circumscriptio.
units.tr: Indeed every body is extended, and finitude and circumscription are the bodily affection of extension.

units.la: Est vero corpus Physicum finitum & circumscriptum tùm Loco, tùm Tem-pore.
units.tr: A physical body is finite and circumscribed both by place and by time.

units.la: Locus aliter à doctis, aliter à vulgo accipitur.
units.tr: Place is understood one way by the learned and another way by the common people.

units.la: A doctis vel Platonicè vel Aristoteli-cè consideratur.
units.tr: By the learned it is considered either in the Platonic or in the Aristotelian manner.

units.la: Platonicè locus generatim est spatium locati cujusvis.
units.tr: In the Platonic sense, place is generally the space of whatever is located.

units.la: Speciatim&Physicè est spatium corporis Physici locati.
units.tr: In particular and physically, it is the space of a located physical body.

units.la: Adeoq; (ut non nemo describit) est situs partium corporis naturalis certa dimensionis τάξει & συμμετρίᾳ[?] ita determinatarum, ne extra aut supra seipsas & distantiam suam extendantur.
units.tr: And so (as someone describes it) it is the position of the parts of a natural body, determined in a certain dimension, order and proportion, so that they do not extend beyond themselves or their distance.

units.la: N. Omne corpus quia finitum & quantum, ideo est circumscriptum. Circumscribitur autem primò propriæ essentiæ terminis, extra quos nunquam est, dum est. Et hoc quidem necessitate definitionis & demonstrationis, quæ absolutè & simpliciter immutabilis est. Hoc est, terminari & comprehendi propriis finibus, de natura & essentia corporis est quanti, quia sine propriis terminis corpus non est finitum.
units.tr: Note: since every body is finite and extended, it is therefore circumscribed. It is circumscribed first by the limits of its own essence, beyond which it is never while it exists. This holds by the necessity of definition and demonstration, which is absolutely and simply unchangeable. That is, to be bounded and comprehended by its own limits belongs to the nature and essence of an extended body, since without its own limits a body is not finite.

units.la: A loco hoc Locatio est, quæ est affectio corporis naturalis, nempe ipsa mensuratio partium quantarum ad se invicem certa τάξει & συμμετρίᾳ[?] determinatarum ad certam distantiam, extra quam se nō extendentes, suis locantur terminis.
units.tr: From this place comes location, which is an affection of natural body, namely the very measurement of extended parts relative to one another, determined in a certain order and proportion at a fixed distance, beyond which they do not extend, and are located by their own limits.

units.la: Aristotelicè locus est superficies ultima corporis continentis, adeoque est externum contiguum certa partium ad partes applicatione, & coordinatione corpus aliud mensurans.
units.tr: In the Aristotelian sense, place is the ultimate surface of the containing body, and so it is the external thing contiguous with the body, measuring another body by the application and coordination of part to part.

units.la: Hic igitur locus complectitur extremam corporis partem cum ordine & applicatione ad aliud, quod continetur.
units.tr: Thus this place embraces the outermost part of the body together with its order and application to that which is contained.

units.la: Omne enim deinde corpus, si sit intra cœli complexum, circumscribitur & circumdatur termino alieno, alicujus corporis, quod extra & circum ipsum est. Atq; id quidem tum necessitate ex hypothesi, Et physica seu ordinaria, quæ Naturæ quidem est immutabilis, sed divina potentia potest mutari, salva corporis natura; tum accidentaliter, quòd terminari terminis alienis accidat, extrinsecus naturæ corporeæ & finitæ.
units.tr: For then every body, if it is within the compass of heaven, is circumscribed and surrounded by the alien limit of some body which lies outside and around it. This happens both necessarily, from the hypothesis and by physical or ordinary law, which is indeed unchangeable by nature but can be altered by divine power while the nature of the body is preserved; and accidentally, in that it happens to be bounded by alien limits, which is extrinsic to a corporeal and finite nature.

units.la: Ab hoc loco est etiam Locatio, quæ est affectio corporis Physici seu mundani, quâ pars est mundi, & aliis ejusdem partibus contigua.
units.tr: From this place also comes location, which is an affection of a physical or worldly body, by which it is a part of the world and contiguous with other parts of the same.

units.la: Estq; corporis jam ante in se locati & mensurati commensuratio ad aliud corpus contiguum, orta ex applicatione utriusq; ad se invicem τάξει[?] & mutua determinatione.
units.tr: It is the commensuration of a body, already located and measured in itself, with another contiguous body, arising from the application of each to the other in order and by mutual determination.

units.la: Hinc liquet, Esse in Loco, dupliciter dici eruditis: Platonicis est certam habere trinâ dimensione ordinatarum collocationem & situm. Aristotelicis est partibus suis trina dimensione inter se determinatis ad alterius corporis ambientis partes itidem quantas ordinari, & per applicationem commensurari.
units.tr: Hence it is clear that "to be in a place" is said in two ways by the learned: for the Platonists it is to have a fixed collocation and position in the threefold dimension of ordered things. For the Aristotelians it is for the parts of a body, determined among themselves in threefold dimension, to be likewise ordered to the parts of the surrounding body, which are also extended, and to be commensurated by application.

units.la: A vulgo accipitur Locus etiam dupliciter: 1. Pro spacio ac certa proportione sensili corporis subjacentis, ad quod aliud corpus adjacens suis partibus visibilibus est coordinatum.
units.tr: Among the common people place is also understood in two ways: 1. As the space and certain sensible proportion of the underlying body, to which another adjacent body is coordinated by its visible parts.

units.la: 2. Pro corporis naturalis parte extrema, quatenus ad aliud corpus terminandum, & sustinendum certa positionis τάξει[?] refertur. Sed hæc plebi relinquamus.
units.tr: 2. As the outermost part of a natural body, insofar as it is referred, for the purpose of bounding and supporting another body, to a certain order of position. But let us leave these things to the common people.

units.la: Tempus est affectio corporis naturalis exterior, qua corporis essentia & ex-istentia, potentia item & actio durare dicitur. Adeoque corpus naturale est finitum tempore, nempe sua duratio-ne.
units.tr: Time is an external affection of a natural body, by which the essence and existence of the body, and likewise its power and action, are said to endure. Hence a natural body is finite in time, namely in its duration.

units.la: Tempus item accipitur dupliciter à Physicis.
units.tr: Time is likewise understood in two ways by the physicists.

units.la: 1. Platoni & Ramo est duratio corporis poris Physici, mensurata per successio-nem, & fluxum à determinato principio ad determinatum finem.
units.tr: 1. For Plato and Ramus, time is the duration of a physical body, measured by succession and flow from a determinate beginning to a determinate end.

units.la: Estque duratio hæc, præterita, præ-sens & futura: unde tempus corporis Physici est præteritum, præsens aut futurum.
units.tr: And this duration is past, present and future; whence the time of a physical body is past, present or future.

units.la: 2. Aristoteli est Mensura motus secun-dum prius & posterius, adeoque non tam ipsum tempus, quam temporis accidens est, nimirum, Durationis & ordinatæ successionis mensuratio, facta ad aliquod externum, nempe motum cœli seu stellarum.
units.tr: 2. For Aristotle, time is the measure of motion according to before and after, and so it is not so much time itself as an accident of time: namely the measurement of duration and ordered succession, made by reference to something external, namely the motion of the heavens or the stars.

units.la: Hæc mensuratio accidit tempori extrinsecus; Nam motus stellarum non efficit tempus, quâ tempus, sed tempus seu durationem distinguit. Neq; motus est causa temporis, sed subjectum ejus. Motus enim dicitur fieri in tempore.
units.tr: This measurement belongs to time extrinsically; for the motion of the stars does not produce time as time, but distinguishes time or duration. Nor is motion the cause of time, but its subject. For motion is said to happen in time.

units.la: Tempus per successionem & fluxum semper est continuum: licet partes ratione discernantur in præteritum & futurum, quam utramq; partem intersecat & continuat præsens.
units.tr: Time by succession and flow is always continuous: although its parts are distinguished by reason into past and future, and the present intersects and connects each of these parts.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM. DE QUALITATIBUS PHYSICIS POTENTIALIBUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 5. ON POTENTIAL PHYSICAL QUALITIES.

units.la: Hactenus de communibus Physicorum corporum affectionibus: Propriæ sunt, quæ solis corporibus Physicis insunt.
units.tr: So far concerning the common affections of physical bodies. The proper ones are those that belong only to physical bodies.

units.la: Mutabilitas enim & finitas quodammodo creaturæ spirituali & corporatæ conveniunt: at qualitates hæ, quæ sequuntur, tales sunt affectiones, quas naturalia corpora sibi solis proprie vendicant.
units.tr: Mutability and a kind of finitude belong in some way both to spiritual and to embodied creatures; but the qualities that follow are such affections as natural bodies claim for themselves alone.

units.la: Propriæ hæ affectiones dicuntur Qualitates Physicæ, quæ sunt corporum naturalium ministræ in agendo facultates, quibus corpora illa, eorumq; forma ac natura, tanquam instrumentis utuntur, ut sint actuosa & efficacia ad id agendum, ad quod à Deo sunt ordinata.
units.tr: These proper affections are called physical qualities. They are the powers of natural bodies that serve them in acting, and by which those bodies, with their form and nature, are used as instruments, so that they are active and effective for the purpose for which God has ordained them.

units.la: Qualitates Physicæ sunt Potentiales vel actuales.
units.tr: Physical qualities are either potential or actual.

units.la: Potentiales dicimus à potentia & facultate naturali, quæ magis in intimis naturæ latent viribus.
units.tr: Potential qualities we call those that derive from a natural potency and faculty, which lie more hidden in the inner powers of nature.

units.la: Suntq; primæ vel secundæ.
units.tr: And they are either first or second.

units.la: Primæ qualitates potentiales sunt à prima potentia naturali.
units.tr: First potential qualities derive from a first natural potency.

units.la: Prima potentia naturalis est, quæ proximè emanat ex forma naturalis corporis. Estq; manifesta vel occulta.
units.tr: The first natural potency is that which flows most immediately from the form of a natural body. It is either manifest or occult.

units.la: Manifesta, cuius causa manifesta est in natura.
units.tr: It is manifest when its cause is manifest in nature.

units.la: Hinc potentialis qualitas prima manifesta est, quæ pervestigabilis & explicabilis est, ut potentia ad motum in Physico proximè fluens ab ejus natura. Sic in animali est potentia sentiendi emanans ab anima sentiente. In homine est potentia intelligendi, loquendi, ridendi, proximè fluens ab anima rationali. In gemmis, plantis, metallis, suæ cuique naturæ sunt congruentes vires. Hæc potentia est perfectè propria cuiusq; naturæ, ideoq; impossibile est, Eam à suo naturali subjecto tolli.
units.tr: Hence the first manifest potential quality is one that can be investigated and explained, as a power for motion flowing immediately from the nature of a physical thing. Thus in an animal there is the power of sensing, flowing from the sentient soul. In man there is the power of understanding, speaking and laughing, flowing immediately from the rational soul. In gems, plants and metals there are powers congruent with the nature of each. This power is wholly proper to each nature, and therefore it is impossible for it to be removed from its natural subject.

units.la: Etenim sunt suo subjecto absolutè propria, quæ ut fluunt à principiis essentialibus sui corporis: ita fieri non potest, ut perfectè propria potentia vel ad momentum temporis à suo naturali corpore re ipsa separetur. Quia cum proximè à forma corporis Physici manent, & vero causâ proximâ positâ effectus ponatur; item effectu sublato, causa illa proxima tollatur: Ideo perfectè propria separari nequeunt, quin ipsa essentia subjecti corporis dissolvatur. Hinc dicitur: Qui tollit proprietates, tollit naturas.
units.tr: For those things which are absolutely proper to a subject, since they flow from the essential principles of its body, cannot be separated in reality from its natural body, not even for a moment of time. For since they remain immediately with the form of the physical body, and the effect is posited when the immediate cause is posited, and likewise the immediate cause is removed when the effect is removed, therefore wholly proper powers cannot be separated without the very essence of the bodily subject being dissolved. Hence it is said: he who takes away the properties takes away the natures.

units.la: Occulta potentia est cuius causa obscura est.
units.tr: An occult power is one whose cause is obscure.

units.la: Ideoque potentialis qualitas prima occulta est, cujus in effectu ratio vix reddi potest. Est q; fere impervestigabilis & inexplicabilis.
units.tr: Therefore a first occult potential quality is one whose reason can hardly be given in its effect. It is also almost unexplorable and inexplicable.

units.la: Vulgo hæ qualitates occultæ dicuntur Tertiæ, virtuales, specificæ, aliàs etiam formales. Etsi autem virtutum & facultatum occultarum rationes ex temperamentis evidenter & manifestè reddi non possint: non tamen dubium est, quin ex peculiari & singulari temperamento, quæ ἰδιοσυγκρασία nuncupatur, vel à forma substantiali, cuiq; individuo propria, proficiscantur. Ideoq; vulgò tribuuntur corporibus aut per ἰδιοσυγκρασίαν, aut per συμπάθειαν, aut per ἀντιπάθειαν. Nos ita cum nonnullis distinguemus.
units.tr: Commonly these occult qualities are called tertiary, virtual, specific, and at other times formal. Although the reasons for occult virtues and faculties cannot be given clearly and manifestly from the temperaments, there is nonetheless no doubt that they proceed from a peculiar and singular temperament, which is called idiosyncrasy [ἰδιοσυγκρασία], or from a substantial form proper to each individual. Therefore they are commonly attributed to bodies either through idiosyncrasy, or through sympathy, or through antipathy [ἰδιοσυγκρασίαν, συμπάθειαν, ἀντιπάθειαν]. We shall distinguish them thus, with some others.

units.la: Potentialis qualitas occulta est <bl>συμπαθητικὴ</bl> vel <bl>ἀντιπαθητικὴ</bl>.
units.tr: An occult potential quality is either sympathetic or antipathetic [συμπαθητικὴ or ἀντιπαθητικὴ].

units.la: <bl>Συμπαθητικὴ</bl>, quæ <bl>συμπάθειαν</bl> præ se fert.
units.tr: Sympathetic [συμπαθητικὴ] is that which bears sympathy [συμπάθειαν].

units.la: <bl>Συμπάθεια</bl>, est naturalis quædam amicitia inter res naturales, ex peculiari & occulta affectione orta, quæ facit, ut ea se invicem amplectantur.
