units.tr: Sympathy [συμπάθεια] is a certain natural friendship between natural things, arising from a peculiar and hidden affection, which causes them to embrace one another.

units.la: Johan. Bapt. Porta dicit consensum, quo res Physicæ mutuo quasi connubio sibi asso-ciantur, ciantur, & tanquam fœdere devinciuntur. Ut Helitropium cum Sole circumagitur, Tri-polium floris colorem ter in die mutat ad solem. Ulmus gaudet cohabitare vitibus.
units.tr: Johann Baptist Porta speaks of an agreement by which physical things are joined to one another as if in a mutual marriage, and are bound as if by a covenant. Thus the heliotrope turns with the sun, and tripolium changes the colour of its flower three times a day according to the sun. The elm delights to live together with the vine.

units.la: ᾿Αντιπάθεια, quæ ἀντιπάθεια præ se fert.
units.tr: Antipathetic [ἀντιπαθητικὴ] is that which bears antipathy [ἀντιπάθεια].

units.la: ᾿Αντιπάθεια est naturalis quædam inimicitia & discordia inter res naturales, ex peculiari & nos latente affectione orta, quæ facit, ut quædam sese aversentur & refugiant.
units.tr: Antipathy [ἀντιπάθεια] is a certain natural enmity and discord between natural things, arising from a peculiar and hidden affection, which causes some things to shun and flee from one another.

units.la: Aliis dicitur dissensus; haud placet hoc Scaligero. Ut ut sit, per hanc nonnullæ res cæcis laborant discordiis. Ut notum est, Ovium & Luporum dissidium, in vivis & post mortem; Sic Kitis & Brassica: Homines & Serpentes, ut & Crocodilus: Elephas & Aries: Aquila & Draco: Alauda & Vulpes, & c. nunquam componendum inter se alunt odium.
units.tr: Others call it dissent; Scaliger does not like this. However that may be, some things suffer from blind discords through it. As is well known, there is the hostility of sheep and wolves, both while alive and after death; likewise of cabbage and brassica; of men and serpents, and also of the crocodile; of the elephant and the ram; of the eagle and the dragon; of the lark and the fox, etc. They nourish a hatred between themselves that can never be reconciled.

units.la: Secundæ qualitates potentiales sunt à secunda potentia naturali. Est autem potentia secunda, dispositio quædam temperamenti & organorum, in corpore naturali, per quam prima illa in actum producitur.
units.tr: Second potential qualities derive from a second natural potency. The second potency is a certain disposition of temperament and organs in a natural body, through which the first potency is brought into act.

units.la: Estq; communis, vel singularis.
units.tr: It is either common or singular.

units.la: Communis est naturalis instrumentorum in corpore dispositio, qua eget potentia quævis prima, si debeat in actum produci. Ut in animali non tantum est prima potentia Videndi, proximè fluens ab anima sensitrice, quam retinet perpetuò, sed etiam est certa dispositio oculi, per quam alius alio clarius videt. Hæc potest amitti.
units.tr: The common one is the natural disposition of the instruments in the body, which any first potency requires if it is to be brought into act. For example, in an animal there is not only the first power of seeing, flowing immediately from the sensitive soul, which it always retains, but also a certain disposition of the eye, by which one animal sees more clearly than another. This can be lost.

units.la: Singularis est orta ex temperamento singulorum individuorum, quo aliud alii naturæ dotibus antecellit.
units.tr: The singular one arises from the temperament of individuals, by which one surpasses another in natural endowments.

units.la: Huc itaq; pertinent Virtutes & dotes Natu-ræ, Generositas scilicet & Nobilitas na-turæ, quatenus accipitur pro evidenti dispositione animi & corporis ad virtutem omnem.
units.tr: To this belong the virtues and natural gifts, namely generosity and nobility of nature, insofar as it is taken to mean an evident disposition of mind and body toward every virtue.

units.la: Huc refertur Ingenium & εὐφυΐα[?] ad doctrinam facilè apprehendendam, & dijudicandam. Item Judicii nativa dexteritas: Robur item corporis nativum. Huc item referri possunt συργαὶ φυσικαί[?], &c.
units.tr: To this is referred talent, and [εὐφυΐα?] aptitude for grasping and judging teaching easily. Likewise a natural dexterity of judgement; likewise natural bodily strength. To this may also be referred natural [συργαὶ φυσικαί?], etc.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM. DE QUALITATIBUS ACTU-ALIBUS, SENSIBILIBUS, TAC-TILIBUS, PRIMIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX. CONCERNING THE ACTUAL, SENSIBLE AND TACTILE QUALITIES, THE PRIMARY ONES.

units.la: Valitas actualis est, quæ actu afficere sensum apta est. Ideoq; sensibilis dici potest, quia sensu percipitur.
units.tr: An actual quality is one that is apt to affect the sense when it is actually present. It may therefore be called sensible, because it is perceived by the sense.

units.la: Omne itaq; corpus per qualitates sensum afficientes est sensibile, seu,sen-su aliquo percipi potest.
units.tr: Every body, then, through qualities that affect the sense, is sensible, or can be perceived by some sense.

units.la: Sensu percipitur, vel Tactu, vel a-lio.
units.tr: It is perceived by the senses, either by touch or by another sense.

units.la: Tactu percipitur qualitas tactilis.
units.tr: The tactile quality is perceived by touch.

units.la: Eaque est Prima vel Secunda.
units.tr: And this is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Prima est, per quam natura corpo-ris primario & principaliter agendo assi-cit sensum tactus.
units.tr: The primary is that by which the nature of a body, acting primarily and principally, affects the sense of touch.

units.la: Estq; fortior, vel imbecillior.
units.tr: And it is either stronger or weaker.

units.la: Fortior est, quæ efficacius & fortius agendo afficit.
units.tr: The stronger is that which affects by acting more effectively and forcefully.

units.la: Fortior qualitas prima, est Calor & frigus.
units.tr: The stronger primary quality is heat and cold.

units.la: Calor est qualitas fortior prima, ca-lefaciendo heterogenea segregans, & homogenea congregans.
units.tr: Heat is the stronger primary quality which, by warming, separates unlike things and gathers like things together.

units.la: Caloris consideratur tum Actio, tum Distinctio.
units.tr: Two things are considered in heat: its action and its distinctions.

units.la: Actio caloris est Immediata vel me-diata.
units.tr: The action of heat is either immediate or mediate.

units.la: Immediata est calefacere & dispel-lere frigus.
units.tr: The immediate action is to warm and to drive away cold.

units.la: Mediata fit per calefactionem. Ea-que est primi vel secundi generis.
units.tr: The mediate action takes place through warming, and this is of the first or second kind.

units.la: Primi generis est heterogeneorum disgregatio & homogeneorum congregatio.
units.tr: The first kind is the separation of unlike things and the gathering together of like things.

units.la: Illa segregat calor, cum sunt diversæ & dissimilis naturæ, ut in unam naturam converti possint.
units.tr: Heat separates those things which are of different and dissimilar nature, so that they may be converted into one nature.

units.la: Hæc congregat, cum sunt ejusdem & similis naturæ, ut uniri possint.
units.tr: It gathers those which are of the same and similar nature, so that they may be united.

units.la: Secundi generis actio variat pro materiæ diversitate, in quam agit calor. Sic a caloris calefactione ut plurimum est attenuatio, dissolutio, digestio, coctio, maturatio, meatuü[?] apertio, rarefactio, eliquatio, fusio, & quæ per has rursum fiunt, ut exsiccatio, &c.
units.tr: The action of the second kind varies according to the diversity of the matter on which the heat acts. Thus from the warming produced by heat there usually follow thinning, dissolving, digesting, cooking, ripening, opening of the passages, rarefaction, melting, fusing, and those things which in turn come about through these, such as drying out, and so on.

units.la: Distinctio præcipuè est, vel è gradibus, vel è subiectis.
units.tr: The distinctions of heat are drawn chiefly either from its degrees or from its subjects.

units.la: E gradibus calor est moderatus & remissus, aut summus.
units.tr: By degrees heat is either moderate and mild, or intense.

units.la: Moderatus calor benignè fovet & conservat. Summus calor urit & consumit. Urens calor & summus est ignis, qui subiectum sibi pabulum utile depascit & absumit.
units.tr: Moderate heat gently cherishes and preserves; intense heat burns and consumes. Burning and intense heat is fire, which devours and consumes the useful fuel that is its subject.

units.la: E subiectis calor omnis aut est Universalis seu cœlestis, aut particularis seu Elementaris.
units.tr: By subjects, all heat is either universal or heavenly, or particular or elemental.

units.la: Universalis est corporum cœlestium, universè agentium, & calorem in hæc inferiora diffundentium. Hic excitator & promotor est particularis caloris, in singularibus corporibus, si benignus & moderatus sit.
units.tr: Universal heat belongs to the heavenly bodies, which act universally and diffuse heat into these lower things. This universal heat is the exciter and promoter of particular heat in individual bodies, if it is benign and moderate.

units.la: Particularis calor est, elementarium corporum particulariter pro sua natura agentium, & sibi proprium calorem insitum habentium, per quem pro suo ingenio sunt efficaces.
units.tr: Particular heat is that of elemental bodies, which act in particular according to their own nature and have their own innate heat, through which they are effective according to their character.

units.la: Frigus seu frigiditas est qualitas primaria fortior, calori contraria refrigerando, tum homogenea, tum heterogenea congregans, hoc est, quæ refrigerat, & cogit, congregatque, tàm ea quæ similis & ejusdem naturæ sunt, quàm quæ dissimilis & diversæ naturæ.
units.tr: Cold, or coldness, is the stronger primary quality, contrary to heat by cooling; it gathers together both like and unlike things, that is, it cools and constrains and gathers together those things which are of similar and the same nature as well as those of dissimilar and different nature.

units.la: Actio frigoris immediata & primaria est frigefacere, & dispellere calorem.
units.tr: The immediate and primary action of cold is to chill and to drive away heat.

units.la: Mediata & secundaria fit frigefactione interveniente, eaq; vel sola simpliciter, vel cum alia mediata conjuncta.
units.tr: The mediate and secondary action takes place when chilling intervenes, and this either alone by itself or joined with another mediate action.

units.la: Mediatæ actioni frigoris subjicitur, 1. Adstrictio, qua partes corporis propius uniuntur.
units.tr: Subject to the mediate action of cold are: (1) contraction, by which the parts of a body are drawn more closely together;

units.la: Hanc excipit Condensatio, qua prohibetur humiditas, ne diffluat; quam prohiprohibitionem sequitur Exsiccatio frigoris vi facta. Item,si materia patitur, Corrugatio, qualis in ventriculo cernitur, quae ciet appetentiam.
units.tr: This is followed by condensation, by which moisture is prevented from flowing away; and this prevention is followed by drying out brought about by the force of cold. Likewise, if the matter allows it, (3) shrivelling, such as is seen in the stomach, which stirs up appetite.

units.la: Deinde astrictione & densatione, potest quandoq; fieriCoactio & contentio caloris interioris, quae fit ambiente frigore per Antiperistasin & circumstentiam ejus:
units.tr: Then, by contraction and condensation, there can sometimes arise a constraint and tension of the inner heat, which takes place when the surrounding cold, by antiperistasis and encircling of it,

units.la: Est autem frigoris Antiperistasis, qua frigus undique circumstens & concludens calorem corporis cujusdam cogit & continet, quo minus disipetur, & ita contentus & unitus fortius calefaciat.
units.tr: Now antiperistasis of cold is this: the cold, surrounding and enclosing on every side, compels and holds back the heat of some body, so that it is not dissipated, and thus contained and united it warms more strongly.

units.la: Denique huc pertinet Obstructio, qua corporum meatus & pori obstruuntur: Strupefactio, qua stupor & hebetudo sensibus inducitur, & alia frigoris effecta.
units.tr: Finally, to this belong obstruction, by which the passages and pores of bodies are blocked; numbness, by which stupor and dullness are induced in the senses; and the other effects of cold.

units.la: Sic fuit primaria qualitas fortior: Imbecillior est, quae imbecillius & languidius agit, Estq; Humiditas & Siccitas.
units.tr: Thus far the stronger primary quality. The weaker is that which acts more feebly and languidly; and these are moisture and dryness.

units.la: Humiditas est qualitas primaria imbecillior, quae facile diffluit. Vel: quae propriis terminis difficulter, alienis vero facilius statuitur, & clauditur.
units.tr: Moisture is the weaker primary quality, which flows away easily; or: which is with difficulty held within its own limits, but more easily is contained and enclosed by foreign ones.

units.la: Humiditatis actio primaria est Diffluere & Humectare: Secundaria fit per Diffluxum & Humectationem, ut emollire, partes conglutinare, &c.
units.tr: The primary action of moisture is to flow away and to wet; the secondary action comes about through flowing and wetting, such as softening, binding parts together, and so on.

units.la: Humor porrò seu fluor duplex est: Aëreus vel Aqueus.
units.tr: Moreover, humour or flux is twofold: aerial or aqueous.

units.la: Aëreus, est tenuissimus, & sua liquiditate in omnes partes facilimè diffluens, penetransque. Estque igni amicus.
units.tr: The aerial is very thin, and by its fluidity flows and penetrates very easily into all parts. It is friendly to fire.

units.la: Aqueus est crassior, diutius rei humectandæ resistens: estqj igni inimicus, quem scilicet extinguit.
units.tr: The aqueous is thicker and resists wetting the thing for a longer time; it is hostile to fire, which indeed it extinguishes.

units.la: Siccitas est qualitas primaria imbecillior, quæ facilè terminis propriis statuitur.
units.tr: Dryness is the weaker primary quality, which is easily held within its own limits.

units.la: Actio ejus primaria est Exsiccare: Secundaria Indurare, Exasperare, &c.
units.tr: Its primary action is to dry out; its secondary action is to harden, to roughen, and so on.

units.la: Siccitas, quæ aliundè affertur corporibus, vel à calore est vel à frigore.
units.tr: Dryness that is brought to bodies from elsewhere comes either from heat or from cold.

units.la: A calore siccitas allata fit humido resoluto & extracto.
units.tr: Dryness brought about by heat arises when the moist is dissolved and drawn out.

units.la: A frigore inducitur, humido condensato & compresso.
units.tr: It is induced by cold when the moist is condensed and compressed.

units.la: Caput Septimum. De Qualitatibus Tactilibus Secundis.
units.tr: Chapter 7. On the Secondary Tactile Qualities.

units.la: Secundæ qualitates tactiles sequuntur, quæ è primarium mixtura oriuntur, earumque sunt quasi comites & soboles.
units.tr: The secondary tactile qualities follow. They arise from the mixture of the primary qualities, and are as it were their companions and offspring.

units.la: Negare hoc videtur Scaliger, & Fernelius secundas esse dictas existimat, non tam, quod aliis posteriore ortum acceperint, quàm quod minus validæ sint, minusq; effectrices. Variæ hæ sunt & multiplices, ita ut earum doctrina difficilior & obscurior, ac vix integra adhuc inveniatur.
units.tr: Scaliger seems to deny this, and Fernelius thinks they are called secondary not so much because they arise later than others, but because they are weaker and less effective. They are various and manifold, so that their doctrine is more difficult and obscure, and is scarcely found complete as yet.

units.la: Secundæ qualitates comitantur primas, aut fortiores aut imbecilliores.
units.tr: The secondary qualities accompany the primary ones, some stronger and some weaker.

units.la: Fortiores comitantur, aut colorem, aut frigus: Caloris comites & propagines quasi sunt, Raritas & Levitas.
units.tr: The stronger ones accompany either colour or cold. The companions and offspring of heat are, as it were, rarity and lightness.

units.la: Raritas est qualitas caloris comes, propter quam corporis partes rarefactę, extenuatæ, diductæ & porosæ sunt, ei adversatur Densitas.
units.tr: Rarity is a quality that accompanies heat, by reason of which the parts of a body are rarefied, thinned, spread out and porous. Density is opposed to it.

units.la: Raritas duplex est: una est in sub-stantiæ tenuitate, altera in distantia partium inter se.
units.tr: Rarity is twofold: one lies in the fineness of the substance, the other in the distance of the parts from one another.

units.la: Corpus igitur rarum est, cujus partes sunt extenuatæ, aut diductæ seu porosæ.
units.tr: A body is therefore rare when its parts are thinned out, or spread apart, or porous.

units.la: Rarefactio est actio, qua in corpore partes extenduntur, & diducuntur, aliis partibus magis subtilibus subeuntibus.
units.tr: Rarefaction is the action by which, in a body, the parts are stretched and spread apart, while more subtle parts enter among them.

units.la: Levitas est qualitas caloris plerumque comes & soboles, per quam corpus naturaliter sursum evehi potest, ei adversatur Gravitas.
units.tr: Lightness is a quality that for the most part accompanies and is the offspring of heat, through which a body can be naturally carried upwards. Heaviness is opposed to it.

units.la: Corpus igitur leve est, quod furfū facile per fe movetur: Et suo motu tedit furfū.
units.tr: A body is therefore light when it is easily moved upwards of its own accord, and by its motion tends upwards.

units.la: Frigoris comites sunt ut plurimum Densitas & Gravitas.
units.tr: The companions of cold are for the most part density and heaviness.

units.la: Densitas est qualitas frigoris comes & soboles, per quam partes corporis constringuntur, & compactae redduntur, seu:
units.tr: Density is a quality that accompanies and is the offspring of cold, through which the parts of a body are drawn together and made compact; or:

units.la: Est qualitas sub parva quantitate multum constringens & continens materiae.
units.tr: It is a quality that, under a small quantity, strongly binds and contains much matter.

units.la: Ei adversatur Raritas, sub magna quantitate parvam continens materiam.
units.tr: Rarity is opposed to it, containing little matter under a large quantity.

units.la: Densum itaq; corpus est, quod partes habet constrictas, & solide cohaerentes seu compactas.
units.tr: A dense body, therefore, is one whose parts are constricted and solidly cohering, or compact.

units.la: Densatio vero est partium in corpore appropinquatio, compactio, & propior unitio; Eftq; humidi, ne diffluat, in corpore cohibitio & constrictio.
units.tr: Densification, indeed, is the drawing near, compaction and closer union of the parts within a body; and it is the restraining and constriction, within the body, of what is moist, lest it flow apart.

units.la: Gravitas est qualitas frigoris comes & soboles, qua corpus deorsum vergit, moveturque.
units.tr: Heaviness is a quality that accompanies and is the offspring of cold, by which a body tends downwards and is moved.

units.la: Grave igitur corpus est, quod cum multis densisque constet partibus deorsum sine difficultate, suopte ingenio, ferri aptum natum est.
units.tr: A heavy body, therefore, is one that, consisting of many dense parts, is naturally fitted to be carried downwards without difficulty, by its own nature.

units.la: Sic fuerunt qualitates primas fortiores insequentes: sequuntur, quae primas imbecilliores comitantur: Et quidem vel Humiditatem vel Siccitatem.
units.tr: Thus the stronger secondary qualities that follow the primary ones have been set out. There follow those that accompany the weaker primary qualities, namely either moistness or dryness.

units.la: Humiditatis comites qualitates sunt aut Aereae, aut Aquae.
units.tr: The companions of moistness are qualities either of air or of water.

units.la: Humiditatis aerea comites qualitates secundae sunt Mollities & Tenuitas, quibus adjungimus Lentorem.
units.tr: The secondary qualities that are companions of moistness in its airy form are softness and thinness, to which we add viscosity.

units.la: Mollities est qualitas quae tactui facit cedere corpus, & impressionem recipere. Seu: propter quam corpus corpori, alii nonnihil cedendo lene contactu praebet.
units.tr: Softness is the quality that makes a body yield to touch and receive an impression; or: the quality by which a body, yielding a little to another body, offers a gentle contact.

units.la: Molle itaque corpus est, quod tactui cedit, & superficiem comprimentis corporis non circumdat.
units.tr: A soft body, therefore, is one that yields to touch and does not surround the surface of the body pressing upon it.

units.la: Tenuitas est qualitas, per quam corporum partes sunt subtiles & tenues. Hinc etiam dicitur Subtilitas.
units.tr: Thinness is the quality by which the parts of bodies are fine and slender. Hence it is also called subtlety.

units.la: Tenue seu subtile est id corpus, quod partes sui habet subtiles & exiles: Ideoque facile penetrat in corporum poros.
units.tr: A thin or subtle body is one whose parts are fine and slight, and which therefore easily penetrates the pores of bodies.

units.la: Corpus tenue est quandoque pellucidum, quod radiis transitum praebet.
units.tr: A thin body is sometimes transparent, allowing rays a passage.

units.la: Lentor seu lentitia est qualitas numi-dum insequens, corporis partes reddens tenaces, viscosas & glutinosas: Lentori adversatur Friabilitas.
units.tr: Viscosity, or stickiness, is a quality that follows what is moist, rendering the parts of a body tenacious, clammy and glutinous. Friability is opposed to viscosity.

units.la: Lentum Scaligero est, quod tractu & compressione dissipari facile nequit, cessione vincens, non resistentia. Vel: cujus partes sunt tenaces, viscosæ & glutinosæ.
units.tr: According to Scaliger, a viscous body is one that cannot easily be dissipated by drawing or pressure, yielding rather than resisting. Or: one whose parts are tenacious, clammy and glutinous.

units.la: Humiditatis aquosæ comites qualitates sunt Levitas & Lubricitas: Utraq; Asperi-tati adversatur.
units.tr: The secondary qualities that are companions of watery moistness are lightness and slipperiness; both are opposed to roughness.

units.la: Levitas est qualitas, per quam corpus redditur in superficie æquale & planum: seu: propter quam corpus (durum) æqualis est superficiei.
units.tr: Lightness is the quality by which a body is rendered even and level on its surface; or: by reason of which a body (being hard) is equal to its surface.

units.la: Leve igitur Scaligero, in quo tangendo fit motus continuus, & æqualis: Hoc dum contingitur tactum oblectare solet.
units.tr: A light body, according to Scaliger, is one in which, when touched, the motion is continuous and even; this usually delights the sense of touch when it is handled.

units.la: Lubricitas est qualitas humoris aquo-sisoboles[?], faciens ut corpora tactum facile effugiant, & elabantur.
units.tr: Slipperiness is a quality of watery humour, causing bodies to escape the touch easily and to slide away.

units.la: Omne itaq; corpus lubricum, facile tangentis tactu effugit, & sua lubricitate elabitur dum comprehenditur.
units.tr: Every slippery body, therefore, easily eludes the touch of one who touches it, and slips away by its slipperiness when it is grasped.

units.la: Qualitates secundariæ siccitatis co-mites & sociæ sunt duorum generum.
units.tr: The secondary qualities that accompany and are companions of dryness are of two kinds.

units.la: Primi generis sunt Durities & Crassities.
units.tr: Of the first kind are hardness and coarseness.

units.la: Durities est qualitas secunda, siccita-tis comes, faciens corpora, in quibus in-est, solidè compacta, ut tactui resistant & renitantur.
units.tr: Hardness is a secondary quality, a companion of dryness, which makes the bodies in which it is present solidly compact, so that they resist touch and push back against it.

units.la: Durum ergo corpus dicitur, quod be-nè densum & compactum, difficulter ce-dit tactui. Estq; vel flexile vel fragile.
units.tr: A body is therefore called hard when it is well dense and compact, and yields with difficulty to touch. It is either flexible or brittle.

units.la: Crassities est qualitas secunda, siccita-tis socia, partes corporū reddens terrestres ac solidas, ut non facile penetrent.
units.tr: Coarseness is a secondary quality, a companion of dryness, which renders the parts of bodies earthy and solid, so that they do not easily penetrate.

units.la: Crassum ergo corpus est, quod sub-stantiæ est terrestris ac solidæ, nec facile penetrat. Estq; opacum.
units.tr: A coarse body, therefore, is one whose substance is earthy and solid, and which does not easily penetrate. It is also opaque.

units.la: Opacum est, quod radiis transitum negat, eosq; reflectit.
units.tr: Opaque is that which denies a passage to rays and reflects them back.

units.la: Secundi generis sunt Asperitas & Fri-abilitas.
units.tr: Of the second kind are roughness and friability.

units.la: Asperitas est qualitas secunda siccita-tis comes & soboles, quæ facit corporum partes inæqualiter prominere.
units.tr: Roughness is a secondary quality, a companion and offspring of dryness, which causes the parts of bodies to stand out unevenly.

units.la: Ideoq; corpus asperum dicitur, quod habet partes prominentes & inæquales, & tactum, dum contrectatur, offendit.
units.tr: Hence a body is called rough when it has projecting and unequal parts, and offends the touch when it is handled.

units.la: Friabilitas est qualitas secunda, siccita-tis comes, partes corporum minus cohæ-rentes faciens, ut ita teri facilius possint. Corpus itaq; Friabile Scaligero dici-tur continuum, quod facile discretum fieri potest, seu cujus partes facile absi-stunt.
units.tr: Friability is a secondary quality, a companion of dryness, which makes the parts of bodies less cohering, so that they can be rubbed away more easily. Hence, according to Scaliger, a friable body is called a continuous body that can easily be made discrete, or whose parts easily part from one another.

units.la: His additur Ariditas, quæ est qualitas à siccitate orta, quæ partes corporis, ab-sorpto humido, arefacit. Opponitur qualitati multum humidi habenti.
units.tr: To these is added aridity, which is a quality arising from dryness, drying up the parts of a body by absorbing its moisture. It is opposed to the quality of having much moisture.

units.la: Aridum igitur hoc corpus æstimatur, quod partes habet humoris ferè exper-tes.
units.tr: A body is therefore judged arid when it has parts almost free of moisture.

units.la: OBSERVATIO.
units.tr: Observation.

units.la: Hæc de secundis qualitatibus tactilibus, quarum doctrina ut varia est, ita multis difficultatibus implicita, nec hic quisquam definiendo & dividendo accuratè sibi satisfecerit. Multa hic desidero, præsertim quoad ortum se-cundarum. Videntur quædam habere sim-plicem, quædam conjunctum ortum. Manca hæc doctrina est, & vix voces sufficiunt rebus.
units.tr: These things have been said about the secondary tactile qualities. Their doctrine, as it is varied, so it is entangled in many difficulties, and no one here has fully satisfied himself by defining and dividing them accurately. I miss much here, especially concerning the origin of the secondary qualities. Some seem to have a simple origin, others a compound one. This doctrine is incomplete, and words hardly suffice for the things.

units.la: I. Sunt enim quædam qualitates, quæ ad corporum dispositionem, ejusq; mutationem pertinent, vel Humiditatis, vel Siccitatis ratione.
units.tr: I. There are certain qualities which pertain to the disposition of bodies and their change, either with respect to moisture or to dryness.

units.la: Humiditatis beneficio insunt cor-poribus, (sit fas mihi non versanti in Comitio Romano, sed sub oculis Philosophicæ Veritatis, ita loqui) Concretilitas, Liquabilitas, Tenacitas, & Pressatilitas.
units.tr: By the benefit of moisture there belong to bodies (may I be allowed to speak thus, not as one taking part in the Roman assembly but under the eyes of philosophical truth): Concretility, Liquability, Tenacity, and Pressability.

units.la: Concretilitas est qualitas per quam corpus facile concrescere potest. Partim à Frigore, partim à Calore.
units.tr: Concretility is the quality by which a body can easily congeal, partly from cold, partly from heat.

units.la: A frigore per Congelationem, ut id corpus, cui multa inest humiditas, & aliquis calor, qui superveniente frigore repressus concretionem parum admodum repugnans admittit. Ut in Bitumine, Cera, Resina, Sævo, Pinguedine, &c.
units.tr: From cold, through freezing, as with a body in which there is much moisture and some heat, which, when cold supervenes and holds it back, admits concretion with very little resistance. As in bitumen, wax, resin, tallow, fat, and so on.

units.la: Hæc facile diffluunt, quia pauca siccitate terrea, multa vero aquea humiditate prædita, habent aliquid humidi aërei cum calore conjuncti, hunc si externus adjuvat, fit diffluxio. Concrescunt vero facile represso calore hoc propter frigus externum & internum, aqueum & terreum.
units.tr: These things flow apart easily, because, being endowed with a little earthy dryness and much watery moisture, they have something of airy moisture joined with heat; if external heat helps it, dissolution occurs. They congeal readily, however, when this heat is repressed by external and internal cold, watery and earthy.

units.la: A calore concrescunt ea, quæ multas partes terreas, cum humiditate quadam aquea acceperunt. Et quidem per Exsiccationem, ut Lutum, argilla, &c. Hic enim calor humorem educit & desiccat, adeoque firmam compingit massam.
units.tr: Things congeal from heat which have taken on many earthy parts together with a certain watery moisture. And indeed this happens through drying out, as with mud, clay, and so on. For this heat draws out the moisture and dries it, and so binds the mass firm.

units.la: Concretilitati adversatur inconcretilitas, propter quam corpus omnem respuit concretionem, Ut i. id corpus, quod maxima ex parte aërea humiditate, cum pauco terreo probè attenuato conflat, ut Mel. 2. Id, quod humiditatem habet aquea, aëream tamen & forti calore temperatam, ut Oleum.
units.tr: Opposed to concretility is inconcretility, on account of which a body rejects all concretion; for example, a body which is composed for the most part of airy moisture with a little earthy matter finely attenuated, as honey (Mel. 2.). That which has watery moisture, yet tempered by airy moisture and strong heat, as oil.

units.la: Liquabilitas est qualitas, propter quam corpus liquefieri potest.
units.tr: Liquability is the quality on account of which a body can be made liquid.

units.la: Omnia, quae frigore concrescunt, liquabilia sunt, si internus illorum calor debilis, externo excitatus adjuvetur, ut actu se exerere, & beneficio aërea humiditatis, solam substantiam fluidam reddere possit, Ut in Cera, Adipe, Bitumine &c. videre est.
units.tr: All things which congeal by cold are liquable, if their weak internal heat, roused by external heat, is helped so that it can exert itself in action, and by the benefit of airy moisture can render the substance alone fluid. As may be seen in wax, fat, bitumen, and so on.

units.la: Liquabilitati adversatur Illiquabilitas, per quam corpus se tuetur contra liquefactionem, Ut id corpus, quod ex multa siccitate terrea, & frigiditate aquea conflatum est.
units.tr: Opposed to liquability is illiquability, by which a body protects itself against liquefaction, as a body which is composed of much earthy dryness and watery coldness.

units.la: Tenacitas est, per quam corpus est lentum. Vide supra. Cui ea qualitas contraria, propter quam corpus omnem viscositatem, & extensionem aversatur. Huc referri possunt, Tractilitas & Ductilitas, illa in Coriis, haec in Metallis.
units.tr: Tenacity is that by which a body is tough. See above. Contrary to it is the quality on account of which a body shuns all viscosity and extension. To this may be referred tractility and ductility: the former in hides, the latter in metals.

units.la: Preffatilitas est, propter quam corpus pressiopressionem admittit, & partes suas ad interiora colligere potest, Ut omne corpus, in quo raritas substantiæ, seu multitudo meatuum ratione humiditatis, ut Spongia.
units.tr: Pressability is that on account of which a body admits pressure and can gather its parts inward; as every body in which there is rarity of substance, or a multitude of pores, by reason of moisture, as a sponge.

units.la: Huc referri potest, Formabilitas & Densatilitas.
units.tr: To this may be referred formability and densifiability.

units.la: Formabilitas facit corpus ad varias dispositiones & figuras aptum, ut Cera, Argilla mollita, Gypsum, &c.
units.tr: Formability makes a body apt for various dispositions and figures, as wax, softened clay, gypsum, and so on.

units.la: Huic Informabilitas adversatur, qua corpus ineptum, formas, quæ impressione fiunt, recipere, idque propter duritiem crassam.
units.tr: Opposed to this is informability, by which a body, unfit, does not receive the forms that are made by impression, and that on account of its coarse hardness.

units.la: Densatilitas, est qualitas, propter quam corpus stabilem retinet figuram, quam impressione accepit. Ut illud, in quo humidum aqueum, cum terreo cretoso est conjunctum, ut Argilla, &c.
units.tr: Densifiability is the quality on account of which a body keeps a stable shape which it has received by impression; as that in which watery moisture is joined with chalky earth, as clay, and so on.

units.la: Huic adversatur Indensatilitas, propter quam corpus figurâ acceptam statum relinquit, post impressionem sese attollendo & dilatando.
units.tr: Opposed to this is indensifiability, on account of which a body, having received a shape, leaves no lasting state after the impression, rising up and expanding again.

units.la: Ratione Siccitatis corpori inest qualitas, dicta Humectabilitas, propter quam illud humore admittere & imbibere potest. Huic multū inest sicci terrei & porosi, ut Spongia, Lana, Panis, Pu-mices.
units.tr: By reason of dryness there belongs to a body the quality called humectability, on account of which it can admit and soak up moisture. In this there is much dry, earthy and porous matter, as in sponge, wool, bread, pumice.

units.la: Contraria huic est Inhumectabili-tas, quae inest ei, quod licet sit siccum, nullum tamen in se humorem recipit, ut Metalla.
units.tr: Contrary to this is inhumectability, which belongs to that which, though dry, receives no moisture into itself, as metals.

units.la: II. Sunt qualitates quaedam spectantes ad corporis dissolutionem, vel partialem, vel totalem.
units.tr: II. There are certain qualities relating to the dissolution of a body, either partial or total.

units.la: Partialem : ut Fractilitas, Friabili-tas, Secabilitas, Fissilitas.
units.tr: Partial: as fractility, friability, sectility, fissility.

units.la: Fractilitas, propter quam corpus in partes majores divelli potest. Ut illud, quod ratione humidi cum terreo pingui-ore permixti longos ordinatos, & per rectum extensos poros habet, ut ligna, stipulae, &c. Infractilitas est contrariae conditionis.
units.tr: Fractility, on account of which a body can be torn apart into larger parts. As that which, by reason of moisture mixed with a fatter earthy matter, has long, ordered pores extended in a straight line, as wood, straw, and so on. Infractility is of the contrary condition.

units.la: Friabilitas, propter quam corpus in partes minutas, & quasvis comminui potest. Hoc habet plurimum terrei cretosi, cum pauco humido. De hac supra. Contraria est Infriabilitas.
units.tr: Friability, on account of which a body can be crumbled into small parts and into any parts whatever. This has much chalky earth with a little moisture. Concerning this see above. Its contrary is infriability.

units.la: Secabilitas est qualitas, propter quam corpus secando in partes est divisibile, in quo pori in latum diducti[?], & materia quodammodo humida, cum sicco terreo compacta.
units.tr: Sectility is the quality on account of which a body is divisible into parts by cutting, in which the pores are spread out widthwise, and the matter is in some way moist, compacted with dry earthy matter.

units.la: Contraria est Infecabilitas propter duritiem vel fluorem.
units.tr: The contrary is incectility, on account of hardness or fluidity.

units.la: Fissilitas, propter quam corpus in partes longas divisibile est, ut in quo est pororum longitudo, mediocris ariditas, & lentoris vacuitas: Contraria infissilitas.
units.tr: Fissility, on account of which a body is divisible into long parts, as in that which has length of pores, moderate dryness, and absence of viscosity. Its contrary is infissility.

units.la: Totalem corporis dissolutione spectat Flammabilitas & Exhalabilitas.
units.tr: Total dissolution of a body concerns flammability and exhalability.

units.la: Flammabilitas est, propter quam corpus flammae recipiendae capax est, & bustile. In hoc vel sicci terrei copia est, ut in lignis: vel aërei humidi, cum sicco terreo, & humido aqueo permistio, ut in bitumine. Contraria est Inflammabilitas.
units.tr: Flammability is that on account of which a body is capable of receiving flame and is combustible. In this either there is an abundance of dry earthy matter, as in wood, or a mixture of airy moisture with dry earthy and watery moisture, as in bitumen. Its contrary is inflammability.

units.la: Exhalabilitas est, propter quam corpus aliquod in vapores resolvi potest, ut quod plurimum habet humiditatis.
units.tr: Exhalability is that on account of which a body can be resolved into vapours, as that which has very much moisture.

units.la: Caput Octavum. DE VISIBILIBVS QVALITATIBVS, LVCE ET Coloribus.
units.tr: Chapter 8. ON VISIBLE QUALITIES: LIGHT AND COLOURS.

units.la: Actenus de qualitatibus quæ ta-ctu percipiuntur: sequuntur alio sensu perceptibiles & sensiles qualitates: Eæ sunt duorum generum.
units.tr: So far we have treated the qualities perceived by touch. Next come the qualities perceptible to another sense, the sensible and visible qualities. These are of two kinds.

units.la: Primi generis, quę sensu nobiliori percipiuntur, suntq; vel VISIBILES, vel AUDIBILES.
units.tr: The first kind are those perceived by the nobler sense, and they are either VISIBLE or AUDIBLE.

units.la: Corpus itaq; est per qualitatem visibilem visibile, hoc est, Omne corpus Visibile est per visibilem qualitatem.
units.tr: Therefore a body is visible through a visible quality: that is, every body is visible through a visible quality.

units.la: NB.
units.tr: NB.

units.la: At non simpliciter omne corpus, qua corpus, est aspectabile. Distinguenda sunt corpora. DENSA enim corpora sunt vel opaca, in quorum superficie radii & species fluxus cohibentur: vel pellucida, quæ visibilibus speciebus transitum præbent: hæc sunt tenuis sub-stantiæ & à sece depurgatæ. Hæc omnia sunt visibilia propter densitatem, licet cum puritate & subtilitate conjunctam, Ut Aqua, Cristallus, Vitrum; Etsi sunt διαφανῆ[?] & radiis non invia: tamen quia habet densitatem, efficaciter radiant, & conspiciuntur.
units.tr: But not every body, simply as a body, is visible. Bodies must be distinguished. Dense bodies are either opaque, where rays and the flow of species are checked at the surface, or pellucid, which give passage to visible species; these are of thin substance and purged of dregs. All of these are visible on account of their density, although it is joined with purity and subtlety, as water, crystal and glass are. Although they are [diaphanē] and not impervious to rays, nevertheless, because they have density, they effectively radiate and are seen.

units.la: Scaliger Exer. 325. Sect. 8. docet densitatem facere colorem actu videri (non tamen absente luce) qui erat in potestate principiorum ineptus, ut videretur.
units.tr: Scaliger, Exercitationes 325, section 8, teaches that density makes a colour actually seen (though not with the light absent), which, in the power of the principles, was unfit to be seen.

units.la: Rara etiam, quæ habent aliquid feculen-tiæ & impuritatis, sunt aspectabilia. Maxi-mè rara à sece depurata, summa substantia tenuitate, & subtilitate constantia, solent o-culi aciem fugere, ut Aër, & subtilissimi Halitus. De crassis corporibus, quin videantur, dubium est nullum. Maximè verò tenui-um, subtilium & rararum partium corpora, Pellucida videri non possunt.
units.tr: Rare bodies too, which have some dregs and impurity, are visible. Very rare bodies, purged of dregs, constant in the utmost thinness and subtlety, tend to escape the eye's sight, as air and the finest vapours do. There is no doubt that thick bodies can be seen. But bodies of very thin, subtle and rare parts cannot be seen as transparent.

units.la: Quædam igitur corpora natură suâ sunt invisibilia, nempè summa subtilitate, tenuita-te, puritate & raritate prædita.
units.tr: Some bodies, therefore, are by their nature invisible, namely those endowed with the utmost subtlety, thinness, purity and rarity.

units.la: Corpora verò quæ densa sunt, licet per-spicua, crassa item & impura omnia omninò sunt visibilia.
units.tr: Bodies, however, which are dense, even if transparent, and likewise thick and impure, are altogether visible.

units.la: Quicquid enim est luminosum vel colora-tum, est aspectabile.
units.tr: For whatever is luminous or coloured is visible.

units.la: Omnia ejusmodi corpora densa & crassa, sunt aut luminosa, aut colorata. Si sunt lu-minosa, certè non solum per se radiant & vi-dentur, sed etiam alia, ut colorata videri fa-ciunt. Si sunt colorata, lucis præsentia & o-pera radios coloris sui, de se diffundunt. O-mnia ergò densa & crassa corpora sunt visibilia. At axioma illud: Omne corpus est aspectabi-le, neq; est κατὰ πάντως, neq; καθ' ὅλα πέων.
units.tr: All such bodies that are dense and thick are either luminous or coloured. If they are luminous, they not only shine and are seen by themselves, but also make other things appear coloured. If they are coloured, the presence and working of light diffuses the rays of their colour from themselves. Therefore all dense and thick bodies are visible. But that axiom, "every body is visible," is neither [kata pantōs] (absolutely) nor [kath' hola] (in every respect) true.

units.la: Corpus enim, non quâ corpus, est visibile. Locale esse quippiam poterit, licet sit inspectabile: Quantū & definitum aliquod potest aspectum fugere. Deinde Visibilitas de corpore dicitur per aliud, nempe corporis lucem & colorem, hoc est, Quia corpus est lucidum, & radius lucis ab illo speciem lucis defert ad visum. Et quia corpus est coloratum, & radius coloris ab illo speciem coloris offert visui, ideò visibile.
units.tr: For a body is visible not as a body. Something can be local and yet be non-visible, since what is quantified and defined can escape sight. Further, visibility is predicated of a body through something else, namely the body's light and colour: that is, because the body is luminous and a ray of light conveys the species of light from it to the sight, and because the body is coloured and a ray of colour presents the species of colour from it to the sight, therefore it is visible.

units.la: Visibilitas, est affectio corporis, solidi, densi, sive pellucidi, sive opaci, ut & impurè rari necessaria: Modo visionis requisita adsint. Si enim non cernitur, necesse est vel in organo, medio, & ipso visu impedimentum aut vitium esse: vel densum extenuando & expandendo summè rarefieri, & ita rarefactum, tenuissimum mumq; instar aeris ab impuritate & crassitie purgari. Atq; sic fiet transmutatio quaedam corporis. Lux à luminoso quâ tale, non abest, aut mutatur in non luminosum. Quod si coloratum, quâ tale, iterum per colorem illuminato Medio est visibile. Si non coloratum, nec lucidum, non amplius corpus solidum & densum. Et color, ut postea, est in tota corporis soliditate, aut saltem in superficie. Tolle superficiem & soliditatem corporis illius, & tolles visibilitatem. Aliud autem est corpus esse vel fieri invisibile. visibile in se, aliud in alio, scilicet organovisionis, vel medio.
units.tr: Visibility is an affection of a body that is solid, dense, whether transparent or opaque, and also of what is impurely rare, provided the requisites of vision are present. For if it is not seen, there must be an impediment or defect either in the organ, the medium, or the sight itself; or the dense body is made very rare by thinning and expanding, and so rarefied, it is purged of impurity and thickness, becoming as thin as air. And so a certain transformation of the body takes place. Light does not leave the luminous body as such, nor is it changed into non-luminous. But if it is coloured as such, then again it is visible through its colour, when the medium is illuminated. If it is neither coloured nor luminous, it is no longer a solid and dense body. And colour, as will be said later, is in the whole solidity of the body, or at least on its surface. Take away the surface and solidity of that body, and you take away its visibility. However, it is one thing for a body to be or to become invisible in itself, and another for it to be invisible in another, namely in the organ of vision or in the medium.

units.la: Visibiles qualitates sunt, quae visu percipiuntur.
units.tr: Visible qualities are those perceived by sight.

units.la: Suntq; vero Lux & Color.
units.tr: These are light and colour.

units.la: Lux est qualitas visibilis primo & per se in corpore lucido lucens ac fulgens, radiorum ac luminis fons.
units.tr: Light is the visible quality that primarily and of itself shines and glows in a luminous body, the source of rays and of illumination.

units.la: Corpus igitur Lucidum est luce plenum, tenebris impervium, radios & lumen spargens.
units.tr: Therefore a luminous body is full of light, impervious to darkness, and sends out rays and brightness.

units.la: Corpus distinguitur naturale, in Lucidum, quod lucem de se diffundit, in Pellucidum, quod radios transmittit, & Opacum, quod radios cohibet.
units.tr: A natural body is distinguished as luminous, which diffuses light from itself; as pellucid, which transmits rays; and as opaque, which checks rays.

units.la: Lux est Coelestis, vel Elementaris.
units.tr: Light is either celestial or elemental.

units.la: Coelestis est lux in corporibus coelestibus lucentibus purior.
units.tr: Celestial light is the purer light in the shining heavenly bodies.

units.la: Estq; prima, vel à prima orta.
units.tr: It is either the first light or light derived from the first.

units.la: Prima, quae à Deo primo die est creata.
units.tr: The first light is that created by God on the first day.

units.la: A prima orta condita est quarto creationis die, seu, ut creditur, in sidera relata est.
units.tr: The light derived from the first was made on the fourth day of creation, or, as is believed, was transferred into the stars.

units.la: Elementaris est in corporibus ignis impurior.
units.tr: Elemental light is the more impure light in bodies of fire.

units.la: A Luce porrò emanat tum Radius, tum Lumen.
units.tr: From light emanate both ray and lumen.

units.la: Radius est fulgor à sola luce in rectum & acutum exiliens & promicans.
units.tr: A ray is a flash of light darting and shooting forth in a straight and sharp line from light alone.

units.la: Lumen est fulgor à luce & radiis quaquà versum emanans.
units.tr: Lumen is a brightness emanating from light and rays on every side.

units.la: Estq; vel Primarium, vel Secundarium.
units.tr: It is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Primarium, quod rectâ in oppositum sibi subjectum incidit, per rectam radiorum incidentiam.
units.tr: Primary lumen is that which falls directly on an object opposite it, by the straight incidence of rays.

units.la: Secundarium, quod à latere obliquè extra radiorum incidentiam se diffundit.
units.tr: Secondary lumen is that which spreads obliquely from the side, outside the incidence of the rays.

units.la: Luce fiunt omnia colorata visibilia.
units.tr: All coloured things become visible through light.

units.la: Luci opponuntur Tenebrae, ut plenum & integrum lucis contrarium; Et Um-bra, ut disparatum, quae diminutio lucis opaco interposito.
units.tr: Opposed to light are darkness, as the full and complete contrary of light, and shadow, as its partial absence, which is a diminution of light caused by an interposed opaque body.

units.la: COLOR sequitur, qui est qualitas corporis colorati, per lumen in superficie visibilis.
units.tr: COLOUR follows; it is the quality of a coloured body, visible on its surface through light.

units.la: Estq; Apparens vel Realis.
units.tr: It is either apparent or real.

units.la: APPARENS seu Intentionalis color, Zabarellæ spiritalis, pendet ab agente, à quo producitur, nec ad motum subjecti, in quo recipitur, movetur. Talis color est imaginis in speculo, Tales colores sunt apparentes in Iride.
units.tr: APPARENT or intentional colour, which Zabarella calls spiritual, depends on the agent by which it is produced, and does not move with the motion of the subject in which it is received. Such is the colour of an image in a mirror; such colours appear in a rainbow.

units.la: Realis seu verus pendet à corpore subjecto, in quo est, & ad ejº motū movetur.
units.tr: Real or true colour depends on the subject body in which it is, and moves with that body's motion.

units.la: Realis autem color consideratur dupliciter, absolutè vel relativè.
units.tr: Real colour, however, is considered in two ways, absolutely or relatively.

units.la: Absolutè, secundum suam naturam, sive videatur, sive non. Color enim sua natura visibilis est, etsi nunquam videatur.
units.tr: Absolutely, according to its own nature, whether it is seen or not. For colour is by its nature visible, even if it is never seen.

units.la: Non enim tollitur potentia (scilicet Visibilitas) per objecti (scilicet rei coloratæ, seu coloris) ablatione (i.e. remotione à visu) quia fluit ab internis principiis essentialibus.
units.tr: For the power (namely visibility) is not taken away by the removal of the object (namely the coloured thing, or the colour), that is, by its removal from sight, because it flows from internal essential principles.

units.la: Hoc respectu dicitur qualitas ex ipsa corporis qualitate & dispositione ac luce conflata, quatenus Lux est.
units.tr: In this respect the quality is said to be compounded from the quality and disposition of the body itself and from light, insofar as light is light.

units.la: Lux enim est quidam actus visibilitatis.
units.tr: For light is a certain act of visibility.

units.la: Relatè consideratur, quatenus aspectui est subjectus, & facit corpus aspectabile.
units.tr: It is considered relatively insofar as it is subject to sight and makes the body visible.

units.la: Hoc respectu est qualitas (Scaligero) in toto suo corpore subjecto, sua specie, quæ à luce elicitur, pingens aërem ad visionem faciendam.
units.tr: In this respect colour is (according to Scaliger) a quality in its whole subject body, by its species, which is drawn out by light, painting the air so that vision may take place.

units.la: Color non est ipsa superficies seu extremitas corporis, sed quiddam in illa. Est quidem tantum in exteriore superficie corporis, quatenus est aptus ad visum afficiendum. Nusquam enim cernitur, nisi in extremitate. At nec per se colore destituuntur interiora corporis, sed is color potentia tantum aspectabilis est, & actu fit visibilis cum corpus dissecatur.
units.tr: Colour is not the surface or extremity of the body itself, but something in it. It is indeed only on the outer surface of the body, insofar as it is apt to affect sight. For it is never discerned except at the extremity. Yet the interior parts of a body are not for that reason destitute of colour; rather, that colour is visible only potentially, and becomes actually visible when the body is cut open.

units.la: Color Realis est Simplex, qui & primus & extremus dicitur: vel Mixtus, ex duorum primorum commixtione ortus, qui & Medius dicitur.
units.tr: Real colour is either simple, which is called both first and extreme, or mixed, arising from the mixture of two first colours, which is also called middle.

units.la: Simplex seu extremus, est primi & simplicis ortus, non ex aliorum commistione contemperatus. Estque Albedo & Nigredo, seu Albor & Nigror.
units.tr: The simple or extreme colour arises from the first and simple origin, not tempered by mixing with others. These are whiteness and blackness, or whitishness and blackishness.

units.la: Albedo est color extremus seu simplex, multum habens luciditatis, visum disgregans.
units.tr: Whiteness is the extreme or simple colour, having much brightness, dispersing sight.

units.la: Corpus itaq; Album plurimum habet luminositatis, eaq; si magna fuerit, visum dissipat[?] & offendit.
units.tr: Therefore a white body has very much luminosity, and if this is great, it dazzles and offends the sight.

units.la: Nigredo est color extremus seu simplex, multum habens obscuritatis, parum luciditatis, visum contrahens.
units.tr: Blackness is the extreme or simple colour, having much obscurity and little brightness, contracting sight.

units.la: Nigrum itaq; Corpus plurimum continet opacitatis, & obscuri, ideoque visum contrahit & congregat.
units.tr: Therefore a black body contains a great deal of opacity and darkness, and so it contracts and gathers the sight.

units.la: Mixtus seu Medius color est, ex permixtione extremorum conflatus: seu, ex simplicium contemperatione produ-ctus.
units.tr: A mixed or intermediate colour is one compounded from the blending of the extremes, or produced from a tempering of the simple colours.

units.la: Et quidem vel Æquabiliter, vel inæ-quabiliter.
units.tr: And this is either evenly or unevenly so.

units.la: Æquabiliter, qui ex æquabili extremorum contemperatione, tanquam exactè Medius gignitur.
units.tr: It is evenly mixed when it is generated from an even tempering of the extremes, as an exactly intermediate colour.

units.la: Estque color ruber vel rubeus, qui est medius, ex æquali albedinis & nigredinis contemperatione ortus: seu ex utroque extremorum luminis habens mediocritatem.
units.tr: And there is the colour red (ruber or rubeus), which is intermediate, arising from an equal tempering of whiteness and blackness: that is, it has a mean between the two extremes of light.

units.la: Inæquabiliter, qui ex inæquabili extremorum contemperatione ortus, uni propius, alteri longinquius accedit: vel ex alterutro extremorum & rubedine gignitur.
units.tr: Unevenly mixed is that which arises from an uneven tempering of the extremes, approaching one more closely and the other more distantly; or it is generated from one of the extremes together with redness.

units.la: Hic vel propius ad alborem, vel propius ad nigrorem accedit, ita ut vel plus alboris, quàm ruboris, vel minus alboris, & plus ruboris habeat: Ille flavus hic croceus dicitur.
units.tr: This colour either comes closer to white or comes closer to black, so that it has either more whiteness than redness, or less whiteness and more redness. The former is called yellow (flavus), the latter saffron (croceus).

units.la: Flavus color ex albedine minus intensa, aliquantulum ad rubedinem accedente generatur.
units.tr: Yellow (flavus) is generated from a whiteness less intense, approaching somewhat towards redness.

units.la: Croceus color ex rubedine minus intensa, aliquantulum ad albedinem accedente gignitur.
units.tr: Saffron (croceus) is generated from a redness less intense, approaching somewhat towards whiteness.

units.la: Ad nigrorem propius accedit, conflatus ex nigrore & rubore: Et quidem ita, ut vel plus nigroris quam ruboris, vel minus nigroris & plus alboris habeat. Ille viridis, hic purpureus color dicitur.
units.tr: Those which come closer to black, compounded of blackness and redness, are of two kinds: either they have more blackness than redness, or less blackness and more whiteness. The former is called green (viridis), the latter purple (purpureus).

units.la: Viridis color est Medius, cui plus nigroris, minus vero ruboris in contemperatione est admistum.
units.tr: Green (viridis) is an intermediate colour in whose tempering there is mingled more blackness and less redness.

units.la: Purpureus color est Medius, cui plus rubedinis, minus vero nigredinis est admistum.
units.tr: Purple (purpureus) is an intermediate colour in which more redness and less blackness is mingled.

units.la: Hae praecipuae sunt colorum Intermediorum & Mixtorum species: plures sunt pro varia mixtione.
units.tr: These are the principal kinds of intermediate and mixed colours; there are more, according to the varying mixture.

units.la: Caput Nonum. DE QUALITATE AUDIBILI, SCILICET SONO.
units.tr: Chapter 9. ON THE AUDIBLE QUALITY, NAMELY SOUND.

units.la: Qualitas audibilis est, quae sensu auditus percipitur. Dicitur Sonus.
units.tr: The audible quality is that which is perceived by the sense of hearing. It is called sound.

units.la: Sonus est qualitas audibilis, in corpore sonante, quae ex corporis (praesertim duri:) collisione aut fractura, aeris potissimum refractione motuque peracta, ad aures delata, afficit auditum.
units.tr: Sound is an audible quality in a sounding body, which, produced chiefly by the collision or breaking of a body (especially a hard one) and by the refraction and motion of the air above all, is carried to the ears and affects the sense of hearing.

units.la: Durum requiritur corpus. Mollia enim sua commissione sonum excitare non possunt, quia unum alteri cedit. Non autem opus est bina ad omnem sonum corpora dura concurrere.
units.tr: A hard body is required. For soft bodies cannot excite sound by their meeting, because one gives way to the other. Yet it is not necessary that two hard bodies come together for every sound.

units.la: Tribus enim modis fieri solet Sonus; Ictu, Impulsu, & Ruptura.
units.tr: For sound is usually produced in three ways: by a blow, by an impulse, and by a rupture.

units.la: Ictu, quando dura corpora inter se colliduntur, sive vere dura sint, ut ferrum, aes, &c. sive ex parte quidem mollia, duriora tamen renixu & extensione, ut Chordae extensae, & pelles expansae in tympanis.
units.tr: By a blow, when hard bodies strike one another, whether they are truly hard, like iron or bronze, or in part soft but made harder by their resistance and stretching, like stretched strings and skins spread over drums.

units.la: Impulsu, quando corpus flabile ad durum vel ejus ratione habens impellitur: quo modo aer vel adactus & trajectus per fenestrarum, caminorum, platearum ac sylvarum angustias: vel attractus ab animantibus, vel e pulmone in asperam arteriam expressus, vel in fistulas spiratus sonum edit.
units.tr: By an impulse, when a yielding body is driven against a hard body, or against something that has a relation to one: in this way air, driven and forced through the narrow passages of windows, chimneys, streets and woods, or drawn in by living creatures, or expelled from the lungs into the windpipe, or breathed into pipes, produces sound.

units.la: Ruptura, cum durum corpus frangitur, ut, cum lignum frangitur, sonus excitatur in aere, non collisione corporis duri ad durum, non impulsu, sed ruptura.
units.tr: By a rupture, when a hard body is broken, as when wood is split and sound is produced in the air, not by the collision of a hard body against a hard one, nor by impulse, but by breaking.

units.la: Distinctio sonorum potest esse varia.
units.tr: The distinction of sounds may be of various kinds.

units.la: I. Sono accidit vel esse simplicem seu rectum, vel reflexum.
units.tr: I. A sound is either simple or straight, or reflected.

units.la: Sonus SIMPLEX, qui simpliciter editus nec reflexus multiplicatur.
units.tr: A SIMPLE sound is one which, uttered plainly and not reflected, is not multiplied.

units.la: REFLEXUS sonus est, qui ex refractione aëris in aliquo cavo opposito reciprocatur & multiplicatur: diciturque Echo.
units.tr: A REFLECTED sound is one which, through the refraction of the air against some opposing hollow, is thrown back and multiplied; it is called an echo.

units.la: 2. Sono accidit acumen & gravitas, propter pulsum & motum: Unde alius est acutus, alius gravis.
units.tr: 2. Sounds have sharpness and gravity, on account of the pulse and motion: hence one is sharp, another grave.

units.la: Cum sonus ut ad auditum referatur non fiat sine pulsu: Pulsus autem non sine motu: Motus autem alii sint crebriores & velociores, alii sint rariores & tardiores: ita & sonus fit varius.
units.tr: Since a sound, so far as it is referred to hearing, does not come about without a pulse, and a pulse not without motion, and since some motions are more frequent and swifter, others rarer and slower, so too the sound becomes varied.

units.la: Sonus Acutus est, qui crebrioribus & velocioribus constat motibus. Alii: Qui breviori tempore longius conficit intervallum, & diutius permanet.
units.tr: A sharp sound is one that consists of more frequent and swifter motions. Others say: one that covers a longer interval in a shorter time, and lasts longer.

units.la: Gravis sonus est, qui ex rarioribus & tardioribus conflatur motibus. Alii: Qui longo tempore longum conficit intervallum, sero excluditur, & cito evanescit.
units.tr: A grave sound is one that is made up of rarer and slower motions. Others say: one that covers a long interval in a long time, is slow to be released, and fades quickly.

units.la: 3. Accidit sono suavitas & insuavitas: unde sonus est gratus vel ingratus.
units.tr: 3. Sound also has pleasantness and unpleasantness: hence a sound is either agreeable or disagreeable.

units.la: Gratus sonus est, qui certam cum organo auditus servat proportionem, ita ut illud quadam cum suavitate attingat, & sensum auditus suaviter demulceat.
units.tr: An agreeable sound is one that keeps a certain proportion with the organ of hearing, so that it touches it with a certain sweetness and gently soothes the sense of hearing.

units.la: Ingratus sonus est, qui ob inconvenientiam suam & inaequabilitatem sensum auditus infuaviter & molestè afficit.
units.tr: A disagreeable sound is one that, because of its discordance and unevenness, affects the sense of hearing unpleasantly and painfully.

units.la: Sonus porrò est vel animatorum vel inanimatorum.
units.tr: Moreover, sound is either of animate or of inanimate things.

units.la: Inanimatorum corporum sonus est, qui ab illis editur: cujus species sunt variae, pro varia corporum inanimatorum affectione & concussione: varia item sortiuntur nomina.
units.tr: The sound of inanimate bodies is that which is produced by them; its kinds are various, according to the various states and shocks of inanimate bodies, and it likewise receives various names.

units.la: Animatorum sonus dicitur Vox, quae est sonus excitatus aere per respirationem vi pulmonum tracto in guttur, & cum impetu concusso ad gutturis latera, & vocalem arteriam: Estq; vel Inarticulata, vel Articulata.
units.tr: The sound of animate beings is called voice: it is a sound produced when air, drawn into the throat by the force of the lungs through breathing, is struck with force against the sides of the throat and the vocal windpipe. It is either inarticulate or articulate.

units.la: Inarticulata vox est brutorum, quae fit non distinctis rerum significandarum notis, nec ad certi quid distinctè significandum: Instinctu tamen naturae, ad aliquam sensus passionem judicandam fit. Estque aliquando in homine, ut in infante ploratus, infirmorum gemitus, dolentium suspirium.
units.tr: The inarticulate voice belongs to the brutes; it is made without distinct marks of the things to be signified, nor to signify anything definite in a distinct way, yet by the impulse of nature it arises to indicate some passion of the senses. In man it is sometimes present, as in the wailing of an infant, the groaning of the sick, the sighing of those in pain.

units.la: Articulata vox est, quae res certas distinctis rerū symbolis effert: Estq; rationis & mentis nuntia & interpres in solis hominibus.
units.tr: The articulate voice is that which expresses definite things by distinct signs of things; it is the messenger and interpreter of reason and mind, and is found in men alone.

units.la: Sic est sonus, qui cum aer, qui sonum vehit, fractus & percussus efficit gyros, gyri alterando aerem successivè deferuntur ad aures, internus etiam aurium aer gyrorum similitudinem assu-mit, & vibrat panniculos, auditu percipitur.
units.tr: Thus sound is produced when the air that carries it, broken and struck, forms circles; these circles, by alternately moving the air, are successively conveyed to the ears, and the air within the ears likewise takes on the likeness of these circles and sets the small membranes vibrating, and it is perceived by hearing.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM. DE QVALITATE GVSTATILI, scilicet SAPORE.
units.tr: CHAPTER TEN. CONCERNING THE GUSTATORY QUALITY, namely FLAVOUR.

units.la: Actenus primi generis qualita-tes, quae alio quam tactu nempe sensu nobiliori percipiuntur: Secundi generis sunt qualitates sensu ignobi-liori perceptibiles: Estq; vel Gustatilis vel Odorabilis qualitas.
units.tr: Hitherto we have dealt with the qualities of the first kind, which are perceived by some sense other than touch, namely the nobler sense. The qualities of the second kind are those perceptible to the baser sense; and these are either gustatory or odorous qualities.

units.la: Gustatilis qualitas gustu percipitur & dicitur Sapor.
units.tr: The gustatory quality is perceived by taste and is called flavour.

units.la: Sapor est qualitas gustatilis corporis sapidi ex humiditatis per siccum terre-um percolatione, virtute caloris genita, & gustu perceptibilis.
units.tr: Flavour is the gustatory quality of a flavoursome body, produced by the percolation of moisture through dry earthy matter, by the power of heat, and perceptible to taste.

units.la: Hinc omne corpus aut est Sapidum, aut Insipidum.
units.tr: Hence every body is either flavoursome or flavourless.

units.la: Sapidum corpus, sapore quodam imbutum. Insipidum saporis expers ineptum est ad gustum afficiendum.
units.tr: A flavoursome body is imbued with some flavour. A flavourless body, lacking flavour, is unfit to affect the taste.

units.la: Materia igitur saporum est humidum cum sicco terrestri conjunctum & connexum. Forma est ipsa temperatura humidi cum sicco, ita ut humiditas siccitatem vincat, adeoq; sapore linguam imbuere possit.
units.tr: The matter of flavours, therefore, is moisture joined and connected with dry earthy matter. The form is the very tempering of moisture with dryness, such that the moisture overcomes the dryness and so can imbue the tongue with flavour.

units.la: Efficiens est calor, cujus vi humidum per siccum percolatur.
units.tr: The efficient cause is heat, by whose power the moisture percolates through the dry matter.

units.la: Haec autem qualitas, ex commixtione sicci terrei cum humido virtute caloris genita, est gustatilis, quia suam affectionem gustatui a lingua dissoluta imprimit.
units.tr: This quality, produced by the mixture of dry earthy matter with moisture through the power of heat, is gustatory, because it impresses its affection upon the taste by dissolving the tongue.

units.la: Est autem Sapor mediocris & tem-peratus, aut à mediocritate recedens.
units.tr: A flavour is either moderate and tempered, or departs from moderation.

units.la: Mediocris sapor est, cujus humidum temperato seu mediocri calore per siccum terrestre percolatur.
units.tr: A moderate flavour is one in which the moisture percolates through dry earthy matter with a tempered or moderate heat.

units.la: Est�q; Dulcedo seu Sapor dulcis, graecè γλυκὺς[?]: hic ex temperato[?] & mediocri sicco terrestri & humido moderato productus lingua lenit, & cum suavitate applanat, qualis est in lacte, melle, & saccaro, &c.
units.tr: There is also sweetness, or the sweet flavour, in Greek glykys [γλυκὺς]: this, produced from tempered and moderate dry earthy matter and moderated moisture, soothes the tongue and smooths it with gentleness, as is found in milk, honey and sugar, and so on.

units.la: Dulcedini autem sui sunt gradus secundum magis & minus. Unde quaedam corpora sunt insigniter, quaedam mediocriter, quaedam minus dulcia.
units.tr: Sweetness has its degrees according to more and less. Hence some bodies are notably sweet, some moderately, and some less sweet.

units.la: Hic sapor (Aristoteli extremus, cum amaro) quia maximè cum animantis sanguine convenit, inprimis nutrit, secundum regulam:
units.tr: This flavour (for Aristotle the extreme one, along with bitterness) agrees most of all with the blood of living creatures, and above all nourishes, according to the rule:

units.la: Nutrimentum hominū oportet esse dulce, aut dulci permixtum.
units.tr: The food of men ought to be sweet, or mixed with sweet.

units.la: Non tamen omnis dulcedo nutrit: cum in quibusdam venenis mortem afferat.
units.tr: Yet not every sweetness nourishes, since in some poisons it brings death.

units.la: Excellenter etiam dulcia interdum nocent, quia cum sint valdè calida & aërea, citò in igneam naturam vertuntur, ut mel & saccarum celerrimè vertuntur in flavā bilem. Cum dulces cibi eduntur intemperantius, ob humoris copiam putrefactiones gignunt.
units.tr: Excellently sweet things also sometimes do harm, because, being very hot and airy, they quickly turn into a fiery nature, as honey and sugar very quickly turn into yellow bile. When sweet foods are eaten too immoderately, they generate putrefactions because of the abundance of moisture.

units.la: Est autem potior vis in nutriendo, si mediocris fuerit.
units.tr: Yet its power in nourishing is greater if it is moderate.

units.la: Hactenus fuit Sapor temperatus & moderatus: succedit Sapor à mediocritate recedens, cujus calor terminū mediocritatis deserit.
units.tr: So far we have had a tempered and moderate flavour; there follows a flavour departing from moderation, whose heat forsakes the limit of moderation.

units.la: Eum autem vel excedit nimia vehementia, vel deficit nimia debilitate.
units.tr: This heat either exceeds it through excessive vehemence, or falls short of it through excessive weakness.

units.la: Est ergo sapor à mediocritate recedens, aut valdè vehemens, aut nimis debilis calore, seu Caloris vel excedentis vel deficientis.
units.tr: A flavour departing from moderation is therefore either very vehement or too weak in heat, that is, of heat either excessive or deficient.

units.la: Vehementia caloris à mediocritate recedens est in essentia, vel tenuiore vel crassiore.
units.tr: A vehemence of heat departing from moderation exists in the substance either thinner or thicker.

units.la: In essentia tenuiore vehemens calor si fuerit, Acrimonia gignitur.
units.tr: If the heat is vehement in a thinner substance, sharpness is produced.

units.la: Acrimonia est sapor vehementis calo-ris linguam mordicans, erodens, penetrans, & valdè dissolvens exsiccando, qualis est in Pipere, Zinzibere, Allio, Cœ-pis, &c.
units.tr: Sharpness is a flavour of vehement heat that bites, corrodes and penetrates the tongue, and dissolves it very much by drying, as is found in pepper, ginger, garlic, onions, and so on.

units.la: Hinc Medici Physici docent acria attenu-are & incidere: incidendo separare serosum humorem à sanguine, digerere halitus, & lapides ex materia pituitosa compactos disjicere.
units.tr: Hence physicians teach that sharp things thin and cut: by cutting they separate the serous humour from the blood, disperse vapours, and break up stones compacted from phlegmatic matter.

units.la: In essentia crassiore est Salsedo & Amaritudo.
units.tr: In a thicker substance there is saltiness and bitterness.

units.la: Salsedo est sapor abundantis caloris congregando & desiccando linguam detergens & abluens, ac gustui gratiam præbens, qualis est in Sale & paucis Plantis, quæ locis proveniunt salsis.
units.tr: Saltiness is a flavour of abundant heat, which cleanses and washes the tongue by gathering and drying it, and gives pleasantness to the taste, as is found in salt and in a few plants that grow in salt places.

units.la: Hic igitur sapor, abstergendi, abluendi, exsiccandi, & putrefactionem prohibendi facultate pollet. Hinc falsa dicuntur exsiccare, & absumere humiditates. Hinc est, quod mollem indurant carnem, & duram reddunt molliorem. In illa enim absumunt superfluam hu[?]miditatem, in hac vero durum erosione quadam attenuant & relaxant. Hic sapor est in humido aqueo abundante, & in sicco terreo crasso. Hinc Sal igni injectus crepat, quia humoris in se plurimum continet, qui ab igne attenuatus spumosam induit naturam, violentoq; motu exsiliens rumpit salem ; Testibus Aristotele & Scaligero.
units.tr: This flavour, therefore, has the power of wiping clean, washing, drying up, and preventing putrefaction. Hence salt things are said to dry up and consume moistures. Hence it is that it hardens soft flesh and makes hard things softer: for in the former it consumes the superfluous moisture, while in the latter it thins and loosens the hardness by a certain erosion. This flavour is found in abundant watery moisture and in thick earthy dryness. Hence salt thrown into fire crackles, because it contains within itself a great deal of moisture, which, thinned by the fire, takes on a frothy nature and, leaping out with violent motion, bursts the salt; with Aristotle and Scaliger as witnesses.

units.la: Amaritudo est sapor abundantis caloris, linguam validius detergens ; & ad profundum penetrando , vehementer desiccans, omnium ingratissimus, qualis est in felle, aloë, absynthio, &c.
units.tr: Bitterness is a flavour of abundant heat, which cleanses the tongue more forcefully, penetrates deeply and dries vehemently; it is the most unpleasant of all.

units.la: In magno sicco terrestri & pauco humido aqueo fertur hic sapor esse. Amara item putredini dicuntur resistere, vermes ex materia putrida & cœnosa generatos enecare.
units.tr: This flavour is said to exist in a great deal of dry earthy matter and little watery moisture. Bitter things are also said to resist putrefaction and to kill worms generated from putrid and filthy matter.

units.la: Sic fuit sapor vehementis & excedentis caloris : Superest Sapor , nimis debilis & deficientis caloris, qui generatur à calore admodum debili , ideoque aliis nonnullis frigidus sapor dicitur, qui astringit.
units.tr: Thus much for the flavour of vehement and excessive heat. There remains the flavour of too weak and deficient heat, which is produced by a very weak heat, and therefore by some is called a cold flavour, which astringes.

units.la: Versatur hic in substantia vel tenuiore, vel crassiore.
units.tr: This flavour exists either in a thinner or in a thicker substance.

units.la: In substantia tenuiore sapida deprehenditur
units.tr: In a thinner substance the flavoursome is found

units.la: Aciditas ergo est sapor deficientis caloris in substantia sapida, tenuiore, mordicatione non urente, constringens, vellicans, & divides, qualis est in aceto, oxalide, fructibꝰ Poteru, & similibus multis.
units.tr: Acidity, then, is a flavour of deficient heat in a flavoursome, thinner substance, a biting that does not burn, constricting, pricking and cutting the tongue, as is found in vinegar, sorrel, the fruit of the Poteru, and many similar things.

units.la: Itaq; acida dicuntur ciere appetentiam: humores enim vitiosos in ventriculo dividunt & pellunt, & ventriculum ad alimoniam capessendam irritant.
units.tr: Hence acid things are said to stir up appetite: for they cut and drive out vicious humours in the stomach, and stimulate the stomach to take up nourishment.

units.la: In substantia crassiore sapida est Austeritas & Acerbitas.
units.tr: In a thicker substance the flavoursome is astringency and sourness.

units.la: Austeritas est sapor valdè deficientis & debilis caloris in substantia crassiore, asperitatem quandam in summa lingua, eam remissius contrahendo, efficiens & leniter desiccans.
units.tr: Astringency is a flavour of very deficient and weak heat in a thicker substance, producing a certain roughness on the upper tongue, contracting it rather loosely, and gently drying.

units.la: Austera quædam Ventriculo grata sunt, quia corrugando & uniendo Ventriculi partes, appetitum excitant, & calore ejus congregant.
units.tr: Certain astringent things are pleasing to the stomach, because by contracting and uniting the parts of the stomach they excite appetite and gather its heat.

units.la: Acerbitas est sapor nimis debilis & deficientis caloris in substantia crassiore, linguam fortiter contrahens, & introrsum pellens, ita ut velut humorem ex ea exprimere videatur, qualis est in pyris sylvestribus, & pomis immaturis.
units.tr: Sourness is a flavour of too weak and deficient heat in a thicker substance, which strongly contracts the tongue and drives it inwards, so that it seems to squeeze out moisture from it, as is found in wild pears and unripe apples.

units.la: Itaq; acerba constipandi & condensandi vim habent.
units.tr: Hence sour things have the power of compacting and condensing.

units.la: CAPUT UNDECIMUM. DE QVALITATE ODORABILI, SEU ODORE.
units.tr: CHAPTER 11. ON THE ODOROUS QUALITY, OR ODOUR.

units.la: Ualitas odorabilis, quæ odoratu percipitur, diciturq; Odor.
units.tr: An odorous quality, which is perceived by the sense of smell, is called odour.

units.la: Odor est qualitas corporis odorabilis, ex sicco superante, cum humido sapido contemperato per calorem orta & deducta.
units.tr: Odour is an odorous quality of a body, arising and derived from a dry element predominating over a moist sapid element, the two being tempered by heat.

units.la: Efficiens ergo odoris est calor, & quidem cùm Internus, tùm Externus.
units.tr: The efficient cause of odour is heat, both internal and external.

units.la: Internus est tanquam artifex odoris coquens, alterans, & miscens humidum sapidum cum sicco.
units.tr: Internal heat is, as it were, the craftsman of odour: it cooks, alters and mixes the moist sapid element with the dry.

units.la: Externus est calor odorata corpora laxans, odorem q; ex iis educens & extrahens, ut Solis & Ignis calor.
units.tr: External heat loosens odorous bodies and draws out and extracts their odour, as the heat of the sun and of fire does.

units.la: Materia odoris est siccum, cum humido sapido mixtum & contemperatum.
units.tr: The matter of odour is the dry, mixed and tempered with the moist sapid element.

units.la: Unde Forma odoris in temperatura, & miscella utriusq; certa & determinata consistit.
units.tr: Hence the form of odour consists in a certain and determined temperature and blend of both.
