units.la: Mixtio autem utriusq; est talis, ut humor sapidus à sicco superetur, & tamen tantum humidi maneat, ut sapor constare possit.
units.tr: The mixture of both is such that the sapid moisture is overcome by the dry, yet enough moisture remains for flavour to subsist.

units.la: Siccum, quod humidum complectitur, à calore interno concoquitur. Finis odoris ratione brutorum, est alimentum a non alimento discernere, cujus signum est, quod animalia non capiantur odoribus.
units.tr: The dry, which embraces the moist, is digested by internal heat. In regard to animals, the purpose of odour is to distinguish food from non-food, and the sign of this is that animals are not caught by odours.

units.la: Ratione hominum est delectatio, & sanita-tis conservatio confirmatioq;
units.tr: In regard to humans, it is delight, and the preservation and strengthening of health.

units.la: Inde omne corpus est odoriferum, aut odoris expers. Odoriferum est, vel bene, vel male olens.
units.tr: Hence every body is either odoriferous or devoid of odour. An odoriferous body is either sweet-smelling or foul-smelling.

units.la: Odores cum in sicco sapido, contemperato singulari ratione cum humido insint, Saporibus plerumq; suam distin-ctionem acceptam referunt.
units.tr: Since odours inhere in the dry sapid element, tempered in a singular way with the moist, they mostly derive their distinction from the tastes.

units.la: Esto igitur Odor alius Extremus, a-lius Medius.
units.tr: Let there therefore be one odour that is extreme and another that is middle.

units.la: Extremus habet genera duo: prius est Εὐώδης, posterius δυσώδης.
units.tr: The extreme has two kinds: the first is euodes [εὐώδης], the second dysodes [δυσώδης].

units.la: Εὐώδης est odor gratus, seu fragrantia, ex sicci in humido congrue temperati resolutione orta, suaviter odoratum afficiens.
units.tr: Euodes is a pleasant odour, or fragrance, arising from the dissolution of the dry, suitably tempered in the moist, and agreeably affecting the sense of smell.

units.la: Hic odor cum ad delectationem, tum ad sanitatis custodiam, ad instaurandos & reficiendos spiritus, ad cerebri frigidam & humidam intemperiem corrigendam, memoriamq; stabiliendam, & sensus confirmandos multum confert.
units.tr: This odour contributes much both to delight and to the keeping of health, to restoring and refreshing the spirits, to correcting the cold and moist intemperance of the brain, to strengthening the memory, and to confirming the senses.

units.la: Δυσωδὴς[?] est odor ingratus, graveolentia & fœtor, ex sicci in humido crasso, & plerumq; putrefacto temperati resoluti-one ortus, olfactum molestia afficiens.
units.tr: Dysodes [δυσώδης] is an unpleasant odour, a stench and fetor, arising from the dissolution of the dry tempered with the thick and mostly putrefied moist, and affecting the sense of smell with discomfort.

units.la: Hic spiritus & cerebrum infuaviter affici-endo, nonnunquam infert insignem noxam.
units.tr: This odour, by disagreeably affecting the spirits and the brain, sometimes brings serious harm.

units.la: Utriq; odori sui sunt gradus, ut odo-rata quædam odorem magis suavem, vel insuavem: quædam minus suavem vel insuavem spirent: Hinc Plinio odores quidam sunt acuti, quidam ignavi.
units.tr: Each of these odours has degrees: some scented things give off a sweeter or more unpleasant odour, others a less sweet or less unpleasant one. Hence Pliny says some odours are sharp and some sluggish.

units.la: Acuti possunt dici, qui ex longinquo cito, prompte, & acriter feriunt odo-ratum.
units.tr: Those may be called sharp which strike the sense of smell quickly, promptly and keenly from a distance.

units.la: Ignavi, qui etiam in propinquo tar-de & languidè afficiunt sensum.
units.tr: Those are sluggish which affect the sense slowly and feebly even at close range.

units.la: Medii odores sunt, qui pro diversa sicci in humido affectione oriuntur, & saporum nomina sortiuntur.
units.tr: Middle odours are those which arise from the varying disposition of the dry in the moist, and receive the names of tastes.

units.la: Deinde odores alii sunt Alimentosi, alii Medicamentosi. Alimentosi, quia alimentis insunt, quatenus alimenta sunt, ut ex iis animal eminus dignosceret alimenta sibi convenientia: Hoc commune genus odorum animalibus.
units.tr: Further, some odours are nourishing and others medicinal. Nourishing odours are present in foods insofar as they are foods, so that an animal may recognise from afar the foods suited to it; this common kind of odour belongs to animals.

units.la: Medicamentosi, qui Medicum præstant usum, & insunt medicamentis,un-guentis, aromatis, &c. hoc genus odo-rum dicitur proprium esse hominis.
units.tr: Medicinal odours, which afford a medicinal use and are present in medicines, ointments, spices, and so on, are said to be a kind of odour proper to man.

units.la: Varietatem quoque odoribus affer-re solent proprietates naturarum singu-lares, quibus odorantes sunt praediti, ut quod mihi suave, alii non est suave.
units.tr: The singular properties of natures, with which odorous things are endowed, also tend to bring variety to odours, so that what is pleasant to me is not pleasant to another.

units.la: Odorem Stercoris nemo bene fert, at in hoc Scarabei & Sues delitias suas quaerunt. Satis de qualitatibus corporum.
units.tr: Nobody bears the smell of dung well, yet beetles and pigs seek their delights in it. Enough on the qualities of bodies.

units.la: Finis Libri primi Nuclei Physici.
units.tr: End of the first Book of the Nucleus Physicus.

units.la: OTHONIS CASMANNI NVCLEI PHYSICI LIBER SECVNDVS. CAPUT PRIMVM. DE ΟΥΡΑΝΟΓΡΑΦΙΑ SEU DE COELO.
units.tr: OTHONIS CASMANNI NUCLEUS PHYSICUS, BOOK TWO. CHAPTER ONE. ON URANOGRAPHY [ΟΥΡΑΝΟΓΡΑΦΙΑ], OR ON THE HEAVEN.

units.la: Hactenus exposita est Physicæ pars prior, in communibus principiis & affectionibus: Se-quitur pars altera quæ PRO-PRIA dicitur, quippe quæ propria singulorum corporum naturalium natura scru-tatur & distincte explicat.
units.tr: So far the first part of physics has been set out, dealing with common principles and affections. There follows the second part, called proper, since it examines the proper nature of each natural body and explains it distinctly.

units.la: Universum corporum naturalium ordinatum Systema dicitur MUNDUS, qui est, Aristoteli, compages constans è Cœlo & Terra, & Naturis, quæ in eis continentur.
units.tr: The orderly system of all natural bodies is called the WORLD, which, according to Aristotle, is a structure made up of Heaven and Earth and the natures contained in them.

units.la: Hinc distinctio corporum mundanorum est in Continentia & Contenta: Eaq. Scriptu-ris non ignota, quæ mundum seu corpora omnia complectitur Cælo & Terra, & omnibus quæ sunt in Cælo & in Terra. Illa Continentia, hæc Contenta.
units.tr: Hence the distinction of worldly bodies into Containing and Contained: a distinction not unknown to Scripture, which embraces the world, that is all bodies, under Heaven and Earth, and all things that are in Heaven and in Earth. The former are the Containing, the latter the Contained.

units.la: Est itaque Mundus legitimè dispositum & ordinatum omnium, corporum naturalium, à Deo, & propter Deum in tempore factorum, & ad ultimum durationis in statu suo terminum conservandorum Systema.
units.tr: The world is therefore the system of all natural bodies, lawfully disposed and ordered by God and for God's sake, made in time, and to be preserved until the final term of their duration in their present state.

units.la: Corpora hæc mundana & naturalia, ut ex antecedentibus & sequentibus liquet tota sua natura quinq; potissimum fugiunt & aversantur.
units.tr: These worldly and natural bodies, as is clear from what precedes and follows, in their whole nature chiefly shun and avoid five things.

units.la: 1. Infinitam actu magnitudinem, quia omnis magnitudo figurata est, id est, certis terminis inclusa.
units.tr: 1. An actually infinite magnitude, since every magnitude is shaped, that is, enclosed within definite limits.

units.la: 2. Multitudinem locorum, ne videlicet unum numero corpus in diversis locis simul existat. Necesse est enim dimensiones esse distinctas ex situ.
units.tr: 2. A multiplicity of places: namely, that one body in number should not exist in different places at the same time. For dimensions must necessarily be distinct by position.

units.la: 3. Hinc Penetrationem dimensionum, ne duo corpora sint in uno, eodemq; loco proprio. Nam si simul essent, judicarentur esse unum corpus
units.tr: 3. Hence penetration of dimensions: that two bodies should not be in one and the same proper place. For if they were together, they would be judged to be one body.

units.la: 4. Natura aversatur vacuum, quod antequam admittatur, res loca sua mutant. Natura amans est copulationis seu conjunctionis.
units.tr: 4. Nature abhors a vacuum; before one is admitted, things change their places. Nature loves joining and conjunction.

units.la: §. Deniq non datur accidentium per se subsistentia: nec eorum eadem numero de subjecto in subjectum migratio. Accidentis enim esse est turpe.
units.tr: §. Finally, there is no subsistence of accidents on their own, nor any numerically identical migration of an accident from subject to subject. For it is shameful for an accident to exist on its own.

units.la: Corpus vero Mundanum & Naturale est Inanimatum, aut Animatum. Corpus itaque omne est aut vita praeditum, aut vitae est expers.
units.tr: A worldly and natural body is either inanimate or animate. Every body therefore either has life or lacks life.

units.la: Inanimatum est expers animae, adeoque vitae.
units.tr: The inanimate lacks soul, and so lacks life.

units.la: Inanimatum corpus est Æthereum vel Sublunare.
units.tr: An inanimate body is either ethereal or sublunary.

units.la: Æthereum est corpus inanimatum à Deo Creatore in suprema, eaque Extrema mundi parte, tanquam loco proprio collocatum.
units.tr: The ethereal is an inanimate body placed by God the Creator in the highest and outermost part of the world, as in its proper place.

units.la: Æthereum corpus est simplex, quia in se est ὁμοιομερὴς, ideoque nullius per se concretione mixtum.
units.tr: The ethereal body is simple, because it is homoeomerous [ὁμοιομερὴς] in itself, and therefore not mixed by any concretion of its own.

units.la: Est pars mundi major, excedens quantitate sua inferiora, & sublunaria corpora.
units.tr: It is the greater part of the world, exceeding the lower and sublunary bodies in its quantity.

units.la: Æthereum corpus est Coelum, vel Stella coeli.
units.tr: The ethereal body is the Heaven, or a star of heaven.

units.la: Coeli doctrinam explicat Ουρανογραφία[?].
units.tr: Uranography [?] explains the doctrine of heaven.

units.la: At coelum hic specialius accipiemus, pro sidereo & astrifero coelo: Empyreum ac beatorum cœlum ac sedem jam aliis discutiendum relinquemus. λόγον σοίας illius sciemus, cum in patriam cœlestem, ad quam duce Servatore aspirabimus, pervenerimus.
units.tr: But here we shall take heaven more specifically, as the starry and star-bearing heaven; the Empyrean and the heaven and seat of the blessed we shall leave to be discussed elsewhere. We shall know the account [λόγον σοίας] of that when we have arrived in the heavenly fatherland, to which we shall aspire with the Saviour as our guide.

units.la: Aereum cœlum jam cum vulgo Physicorum in Stœcheologia tractabimus.
units.tr: We shall now treat the aerial heaven in the Stoicheology, along with the common view of the physicists.

units.la: Cœlum est corpus simplex æthereū, secundo creationis die à Deo extensum seu expansum, subtile, continuum pervium, immobile, omnium maximum, sphæricum, suo ambitu sublunaria omnia complectens, in quo sidera suum conficiunt cursum.
units.tr: Heaven is a simple ethereal body, extended or expanded by God on the second day of creation, subtle, continuous, pervious, immobile, the greatest of all, spherical, embracing all sublunary things with its circuit, in which the stars complete their course.

units.la: 1. Cœlum (scilicet siderium) est corpus simplex, quia in se cœlum est ὁμοιομερὲς, non concretum ex diversis partibus.
units.tr: 1. Heaven (namely the starry heaven) is a simple body, because in itself heaven is homoeomerous, not compounded of different parts.

units.la: 2. Est Æthereum, quippe in parte mundi superiore collocatum & expansum.
units.tr: 2. It is ethereal, since it is placed and extended in the upper part of the world.

units.la: 3. Cœlum aliis est ex aqua in tenuissimum halitum diffusum. Aliis est naturæ aereæ: aliis est quinta quædam essentia, ratione elementorum quatuor, quinta dicta. Vide disputationes P.P. Landgravii, Et Tychonis Brahe.
units.tr: 3. Some hold that heaven is water diffused into the thinnest vapour; others that it is of an airy nature; others that it is a certain fifth essence, called fifth with respect to the four elements. See the disputations of P. P. Landgravius and of Tycho Brahe.

units.la: 4. Cœlum est substantia tenue & subtile, non solidum, durum, adamantinum.
units.tr: 4. Heaven is a substance thin and subtle, not solid, hard, or adamantine.

units.la: I. Quia si dura & ferrea effet instar materiæ, stellarum radii per duo diversa transirent diaphana, ideoq; duplici refractione essent ob-noxii, & proinde semper extra locum suum conspicerentur, totamq; scientiam Astronomicam perpetui erroris & inconstantia argueret. Sed constat sidera debitis suis locis esse observata, nec ab ullo unquam Artifice gemina ejusmodi siderum animadversa est refractio, nec duo diversa deprehensa sunt diaphana. Cœ-lum igitur nō constat ex dura & impervia quadam materia, sed tenuissima & subtilissima.
units.tr: I. For if it were hard and iron-like in the manner of matter, the rays of the stars would pass through two different transparent media, and so would be subject to double refraction, and consequently would always be seen out of their place, and would prove all astronomical science to be marked by perpetual error and inconstancy. But it is established that the stars have been observed in their due places, and no astronomer has ever noticed such a double refraction, nor have two different transparent media been detected. Heaven therefore does not consist of a hard and impervious matter, but of one most thin and subtle.

units.la: Propositio est bimembris: Primum sic pro-batur; Quacunq; corpora pellucida, tum ipsa substantia, tum qualitatibus, præsertim luci-ditate ac raritate inter se differunt, ea perspi-cuitate quoq; differant, & diversa diaphana constituant, necesse est. Sed cœlum, si solida compactum effet materia, & aër, non tantum ipsa substantiâ, sed etiam qualitatibus differ-rent.
units.tr: The proposition has two parts. The first is proved thus: whatever transparent bodies differ from one another both in substance and in qualities, especially in brightness and rarity, must also differ in transparency and constitute different diaphanous media; this is necessary. But heaven, if it were compacted of solid matter, and air would differ not only in substance but also in qualities.

units.la: Posterius sic ostenditur: Si cœlum & aër diversa essent diaphana, geminas quoq; efficerent refractiones: Quot enim sunt diversa, & transeuntes radios refrangentia media inter rem visam & oculum videntis, tot etiam mediorum refractiones erunt. Si ergo inter sidera cœlestia, & hominum sidera seu oculos duo interveniunt diversa media: alterum densum & pellucidum, ut cœlum; alterum tenue & variis exhalationibus refertum, ut aër: certè sidera duplici refractioni erunt obnoxia.
units.tr: The second is shown thus: if heaven and air were different diaphanous media, they would also produce a double refraction. For as many as there are different media refracting the passing rays between the seen object and the eye of the viewer, so many refractions there will be. If therefore two different media lie between the heavenly stars and the stars of men, that is, the eyes — one dense and transparent, like heaven, the other thin and filled with various exhalations, like air — then certainly the stars will be subject to double refraction.

units.la: 2. Deinde, Si cometæ in ipso cœli firmamento inter planetarum sphæras progignuntur, & peculiari motu non secus ac perennia cœli sidera, in quorum orbibus resident, progrediuntur, fieri sanè non potest, ut cœlum solida & dura quapiam materia sit compactum, quod sic demonstratur:
units.tr: 2. Further, if comets are born in the very firmament of heaven among the spheres of the planets, and advance with a peculiar motion, just as the perennial stars of heaven, in whose orbs they reside, do, then it certainly cannot be that heaven is compacted of some solid and hard matter. This is shown thus:

units.la: Si hoc ita esset, 1. Cometæ, sive ex evaporatione terrestri, sive ex cœli materia nascantur, citra tamen dimensionum penetrationem in cœlo moveri non poterunt. Si ab exhalationibus gignantur Cometæ, ad cœlum usque nequaquam conscendere, nedum densissimos ac durissimos ejus parietes transcendere poterunt.
units.tr: If this were so: 1. comets, whether they arise from terrestrial evaporation or from the matter of heaven, could not move in heaven without penetration of dimensions. If comets are generated from exhalations, they could by no means climb up to heaven, much less pass beyond its very dense and very hard walls.

units.la: Deinde, si in ipso cœlo ex materia cælesti Cometæ prodeunt, moveri non poterunt, nisi orbi alicui sint alligati, vel magnetica quadam & spontanea concomitantia motum alicujus perpetui sideris æmulentur: vel deniq; nativo cursu circumducantur. Si orbi alicui annexi essent, is vel unus foret ex octo illis, quos fingunt, vel alius de novo creatus. Si unus ex octo illis eandem perpetuo distantiam à terris habe-rent, eundemq; motum, cum reliquis stellis. At neq; eandem distantiam, neq; eundem motum. Novos creari orbes absurdum est. Si duceretur Cometa à Planeta quopiam, cur ductorem su-um perpetuo non comitaretur, cur ipsum suo cursu anteverteret? Si ingenito motu fertur, liquidum erit cœlum & pervium.
units.tr: Again, if comets come forth in heaven itself from celestial matter, they could not move unless they were bound to some orb, or imitated the motion of some perpetual star by a certain magnetic and spontaneous sympathy, or were finally carried round by a native course. If they were attached to some orb, that orb would be either one of those eight which they feign, or another newly created. If it were one of the eight, they would always have the same distance from the earth and the same motion as the other stars. But they have neither the same distance nor the same motion. To create new orbs is absurd. If a comet were led by some planet, why would it not always accompany its leader, why would it outrun it in its course? If it moves by an innate motion, heaven must be fluid and pervious.

units.la: Sed Cometas in ipso cœlo gigni firmissimis demonstrationibus ostendunt, Mathematici & Astrologi nostri seculi peritissimi. Si planetæ nunc propius ad terram se dimittunt: nunc altius ab ea recedunt, cœlū ex materia impervia & dura non constistit. Si enim hoc, citra dimensionum penetrationem, aut cœli disruptionem, Cometa suum ita cursum non deflecterent. Sed propius nunc, nunc altius moventur Planeta, ut ostendunt eorum parallaxes & magnitudines.
units.tr: But that comets are generated in heaven itself is shown by the most solid demonstrations of the most skilled mathematicians and astrologers of our age. If the planets now let themselves down closer to the earth, and now recede higher from it, heaven does not consist of impervious and hard matter. For if it did, comets could not so deflect their course without penetration of dimensions or rupture of heaven. But the planets are moved now nearer, now higher, as their parallaxes and magnitudes show.

units.la: Huc accedit testimonium Iesaiæ 40.v. 22. Qui extendit cœlum sicut tenue quid, & cap. 51. Cœli, sicut fumus, liquescent.
units.tr: To this is added the testimony of Isaiah 40. v. 22, who stretches out the heaven like a thin thing, and of chapter 51, The heavens shall vanish away like smoke.

units.la: 5. Cœlum deinde est continuitate unum, non duris orbium machinis distinctum nec divisum: 1. Quia stante subtili & tenui cœli substantiâ, rigida & dura illa orbium compages admitti nequit. Qui enim id, & tenuissimâ praeditum substantiâ, & tamen rigidis ac densis Sphæris conflatum esse queat?
units.tr: 5. Heaven is then one in continuity, not distinguished or divided by hard machines of orbs. 1. For while the substance of heaven is subtle and thin, that rigid and hard structure of orbs cannot be admitted. For who could suppose that something endowed with a most thin substance is yet made up of rigid and dense spheres?

units.la: Deinde ipsa in cœlo sidera sponte sua conficiunt spatia, Gen. 1. v. 15. Deus sidera in ex-panso cœli collocavit, ut terram circumquaq; il-lustrent, & ratas temporum periodos definiant, 2. Movendi quoq; vim, qua hoc expedire pos-sunt, una iisdem insevit. 3. Ipsa stellæ oriri & occidere dicuntur, properare & circumire, Ec-cl. 1. 3. Luna substitisse narratur, Josu. 10. Ha-bac. 3. Summa, Ortus, occasus, statio, progressio, & reliqua quæ motum præsupponunt, non cœlo, sed stellis tribuuntur. 4. Si reales essent in cœlo orbes, tot essent, quot distincti motus in cœlo reperiuntur. At non hoc: Fixæ enim stellæ duplicem habere motum dicuntur. E. & geminos saltem orbes: Planetæ singuli variis motibus agitari videntur: Varios igitur rotabiles orbes habebunt. 5. Cum stellæ dicuntur densiores partes sui orbis, & clarè cernantur, certè etiam ipsæ duræ & vastæ machinæ præfulgidæ cernentur.
units.tr: Then the stars in heaven themselves complete their spaces of their own accord. Gen. 1. v. 15: God placed the stars in the expanse of heaven, to illuminate the earth all round and to define the fixed periods of times. 2. He also implanted in them one and the same power of moving, by which they can accomplish this. 3. The stars themselves are said to rise and set, to hasten and go round: Eccl. 1. 3. The moon is said to have stood still: Josh. 10. Hab. 3. In sum, rising, setting, station, progression, and the rest which presuppose motion are attributed not to heaven but to the stars. 4. If there were real orbs in heaven, there would be as many as there are distinct motions found in heaven. But this is not so: for the fixed stars are said to have a twofold motion, and so at least two orbs. Individual planets seem to be driven by various motions, so they will have various rotating orbs. 5. Since the stars are said to be the denser parts of their orb, and are clearly seen, certainly the hard and vast machines themselves would also be seen shining forth.

units.la: Expansio illa continua in S. literis celebratur, instar pellis, utris, vesicæ, vel Tapetis, Psal. 104. v. 2. Jesa. 40. v.22. & 42. v.5.
units.tr: That continuous expanse is celebrated in Holy Scripture, likened to a skin, a bellows, or a curtain: Psal. 104. v. 2. Jesa. 40. v.22. & 42. v.5.

units.la: Huc accedit Augustin.lib.2.de Gen. ad literam. Ambr.lib.2. Hexam.cap.4. Basil.Homil. 3. Notetur & vox Hebræa, Rakia, expansum.
units.tr: To this add Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 2; Ambrose, Hexameron, book 2, ch. 4; Basil, Homily 3. Note also the Hebrew word rakia [רקיע], meaning "expanse."

units.la: 6. Est item cœlum immobile, quia tenuissimum & subtilissimum, ut quippiam rapido & jugi motu circumrotetur, densioris & solidioris sit natura necesse est.
units.tr: 6. Again, the heaven is immovable. Whatever is turned around by a swift and continual motion must necessarily be of a denser and more solid nature, and the heaven is most thin and subtle.

units.la: 7. Deniq; quia est tenuissimæ & subtilissimæ essentiæ, humanis conspici oculis nequit: Quia quæcunq; ita videntur, ea per radios videri necesse est: Sed subtilissima per radios videri non possunt: quia radii visibiles à denso corpore, non à tenuissimo producuntur: Omne quippe visibile medium in densitate transcendere debet: Et nihil potest esse per se elaboratum aut luminosum, nisi densum.
units.tr: 7. Finally, because it is of the most thin and subtle essence, it cannot be seen by human eyes. Whatever is seen is seen through rays, but the most subtle things cannot be seen through rays, because visible rays are produced by a dense body, not by a most tenuous one. Every visible medium must surpass others in density, and nothing can be luminous or illuminated in itself unless it is dense.

units.la: Expansum porro hoc distinguitur in duo stellifera spatia, vulgò Sphæras & Orbes appellant, Superius & Inferius.
units.tr: This expanse is further divided into two starry spaces, which are commonly called spheres and orbs: the Superior and the Inferior.

units.la: Superius est cœlo summo proximum, in quo sunt & feruntur stellæ fixæ, dicitur Græce ἀπλανὴς, specialiter Firmamentum; Orbis seu Sphæra octava.
units.tr: Superior lies nearest the highest heaven, and in it the fixed stars are and move. In Greek it is called aplanes [ἀπλανὴς], and specifically it is the Firmament, the eighth orb or sphere.

units.la: Hujus partes itidem duæ constitui possunt, Media & Extrema.
units.tr: Its parts too can be reckoned as two: the Middle and the Extreme.

units.la: Media est pars firmamenti, seu superioris spatii, à septentrione in meridiem patens, continens signa Zodiacalia & astra.
units.tr: The Middle is the part of the firmament, or upper space, extending from north to south, containing the signs of the Zodiac and the stars.

units.la: Extrema mediæ partis seu Zodiaci latera utrinq; claudit, reliquarum stel-larum spatium & receptaculum.
units.tr: The Extremes close off the two sides of the middle part, or Zodiac, on each side; they are the space and receptacle of the remaining stars.

units.la: Inferius cœli stelliferi spatium est proximum aëreo cœlo infra firmamentum constitutum, in quo sunt & feruntur Planetæ, unde Sphæræ & orbes Planeta-rum in hoc spatio comprehendi dicuntur.
units.tr: Inferior is the starry space of heaven nearest the aerial heaven, set below the firmament, in which the planets are and move; hence the spheres and orbs of the planets are said to be contained in this space.

units.la: Hujus item partes possunt esse duæ; Una planetarum superiorum, continens orbes Saturni, Jovis & Martis: Altera Inferiorum, continens sphæras Solis, Veneris, Mercurii & Lunæ*.
units.tr: Its parts also can be two: one of the upper planets, containing the orbs of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars; the other of the lower planets, containing the spheres of the Sun, Venus, Mercury and the Moon.

units.la: N B.
units.tr: N.B.

units.la: De orbium systasi & hyparxi multa sunt hactenus dicta, scripta; Extructa autem est duabus rationibus. 1. Quia stellæ octavæ Sphæ-ræ seu firmamenti eandem semper situs diffe-rentiam observant, 2. Quia omnes ab Oriente per Meridiem in Occidentem feruntur: idcirco eas orbibus affixas ad eorum motum moveri, ceu clavus ad motum rotæ, seu nodus ad motum tabulæ movetur.
units.tr: Much has been said and written so far about the systasis and hyparxis of the orbs, and it rests on two grounds. 1. The stars of the eighth sphere, or firmament, always keep the same relative positions. 2. All of them move from east through south to west. Therefore they are thought to be fixed to the orbs and moved by their motion, as a nail is moved by the motion of a wheel, or a knot in a board by the motion of the board.

units.la: Respondetur autem: hæc quidem apparen-tias, hanc ab ortu per meridiem ad occasum siderum lationem, æquabilemq; semper distanti-am, negari non posse. Verum quod motus horum ab orbibus, non verò à principio sibi in creatione indito dependeat, nondum est probatum. Numeramus certè in octava Sphæra, Æquatorem, numeramus duos Tropicos, aliosq; circulos parallelos, quos à Sole describi docent Astrologi. Hi autem Solem sibi præsentem non circumagunt, sed is pro natura suæ conditione incedit; ad motum enim stellarum excogitati sunt orbes, & postea his substrati.
units.tr: But it is answered that these appearances cannot be denied: this motion of the stars from rising through the south to setting, and their always equal distance. But it has not yet been proved that the motions of these stars depend on orbs, and not on the principle implanted in them at creation. Certainly in the eighth sphere we count the equator, we count two tropics and other parallel circles, which astrologers teach are described by the Sun. But these do not carry the Sun around with them; rather it advances according to the nature of its own condition. For the orbs were devised to account for the motion of the stars, and were afterwards placed beneath them.

units.la: Sed ἐξ ὑποθέσεων[?] agemus & rem absurdo demonstrabimus. In confesso est, Sphæras æthereas mutuo sese ad modum tunicarum in cepis, vel in ovorum Gallinaceorum Vitelli, albuminis & putaminis ambire: esse item solidas, perspicuas instar Cristalli purissimi.
units.tr: But we shall proceed from hypotheses [ἐξ ὑποθέσεων] and show the matter to be absurd. It is agreed that the ethereal spheres embrace one another, like the tunics of an onion, or the yolk, white and shell of a hen's egg. They are likewise solid and transparent, like the purest crystal.

units.la: Jam verò Planeta ἐπιφέρεται ἐπικύκλου[?] superat, eamq; dimidio corporis sui modo egreditur, non secus ac Sol contrarius existens in alterutro puncto tropico superat medietate sua parallelum, per Solis centrum transeuntem.
units.tr: Now the planet, carried on an epicycle [ἐπιφέρεται ἐπικύκλου], surpasses the contiguous orb and goes out beyond it only by half its body, just as the Sun, being opposite, at either tropical point surpasses by half its own body the parallel that passes through the centre of the Sun.

units.la: In quocunq; igitur loco ἐκκέντρως[?] existit ἐπι-κύκλῳ[?], ibi Planeta medietate sua corporis, in contiguum orbem fertur, eumq; aut penetrat, aut ab eodem impeditur.
units.tr: Wherever, then, the planet is situated eccentrically [ἐκκέντρως] on the epicycle [ἐπικύκλῳ], there with half its body it is carried into the contiguous orb, and either penetrates it or is impeded by it.

units.la: Non impediri eundem docent observationes: E. frangit Planeta orbem contiguum.
units.tr: The observations show that it is not impeded; therefore the planet breaks through the contiguous orb.

units.la: Sed nec frangit eundem: repullulant enim duo ἀπόπα ȝ vacuum, quia solidi in solidum nulla remeatio: aut penetratio: quia duo corpora uno esse nt loco. Utrum mḕ ἀφιλόσοφον. E. nulli orbes.
units.tr: But neither does it break through it. For two absurdities follow: a vacuum, since there is no return of solid into solid, nor any penetration, because two bodies cannot be in one place. Both of these are unphilosophical [μὴ ἀφιλόσοφον]. Therefore there are no orbs.

units.la: Obganniunt autem hic nobis orbium conglomeratores, & dicunt: I. Totum corpus Planetæ recondi intra orbem ἐπικύκλε, non secus ac ille intra eccentricum, hicq; inter utrumq; deferentem conditur.
units.tr: Here the compilers of orbs object to us and say: 1. The whole body of the planet is hidden within the orb of the epicycle, just as that is hidden within the eccentric, and this is placed between the two deferents.

units.la: II. Si stella in cælo moveretur, corpus cœleste ejusmodi esset, ut cedere posset corporibus stellarum. E. & in motæ stellæ subire locum. Scal. Exerc. 76. Sect. 1.
units.tr: 2. If a star moved in heaven, the heavenly body would have to be such that it could yield to the bodies of the stars; therefore a star in motion would have to enter the place of another. Scaliger, Exercitations 76, section 1.

units.la: Ad prius respondemus, I. Ptolomæum Astrologorum principem observationes cœlestes, non per extremos siderum margines, sed per centra, ut eo modo ἐκκέντρως & ἐπικύκλως deprehenderet, instituisse.
units.tr: To the first we reply: 1. Ptolemy, the prince of astrologers, made his heavenly observations not through the outer margins of the stars but through their centres, so that he might detect the eccentric and epicyclic motions in that way.

units.la: II. Ex ipsis Planetarum Theoriis constat Astrologos in Theoricarum χρήματα, non intra ἀπεφέρειαν, sed in ipso ambitu ἐπικύκλε, quod ibi Planeta centro suo infixus hæreat, lineas extendere, ut locum in Zodaico, ut regressiones, ut progressiones, ut omnium motuum eventus exemplo demonstrent.
units.tr: 2. From the very theories of the planets it is evident that astrologers extend their lines not within the deferent, but in the very circuit of the epicycle, on the ground that the planet, fixed at its centre, stays there. They use this to demonstrate by example the place in the Zodiac, the retrogradations, the progressions, and the outcome of all the motions. The uses of the theories are these.

units.la: III. Ut maximè concedamus, Planetas & Orbes intra orbes invicè condi, nō tamē adhuc res caret absurdo: Eo enim ipso penetratio solidi per solidum statuitur, quia utrinque Planeta in Epicyclo, & ἐκκεντρ[?]ῳ in eccentrico, eccentricus vero in deferentibus moveri dicitur.
units.tr: 3. Even if we concede most fully that planets and orbs are contained within orbs, reciprocally, the matter is still not free of absurdity. For by that very fact the penetration of solid through solid is posited, since on both sides the planet is said to move in an epicycle and the eccentric [ἐκκεντρ] in an eccentric, and the eccentric in the deferents.

units.la: Ad posterius dicimus, eo ipso hos totum orbium σύστημα destruere, dum eam partem, quam permeat Planeta, liquidam asserunt: quod enim illi particulatim admittunt, idem nos ad integram orbium σύστασιν transferre commodè quimus.
units.tr: To the latter we say that by this very fact they destroy the whole system of the orbs, while they assert that the part which the planet passes through is liquid. For what they admit part by part, we can conveniently apply to the whole constitution of the orbs.

units.la: Rectius ergo sentit Plinius libr. 2. Hist. Mund.cap.6. Sidera illa inter hanc caelum, eodem spiritu pendere certis discreta spatiis.
units.tr: More rightly, therefore, Pliny thinks (Natural History, book 2, ch. 6): those stars hang by the same breath, separated by fixed intervals between this heaven and that.

units.la: Secundo: Si caelum hoc septem siderum est solidum, est quoque densum: si densum, obscurum: idque maxime in orbium ista profunditate fuerit immensa: refractè igitur videntur a nobis sidera.
units.tr: Second: if this heaven of the seven planets is solid, it is also dense; if dense, it is dark; and this would be especially so given the immense depth of those orbs. Therefore the stars are seen by us refracted.

units.la: Non hoc: per tot enim media tam late fusa, tot superficiebus distincta, alibi quam in Horizontis polo visa, nunquam pro loco cernentur, nec eorum vera quantitas cognoscetur, nec distantiae verae mensura comprehendi poterit: Frangentur enim a perpendiculo, propter mediorum, ex rariore scilicet in densius, varietatem: Juxta 45.47. prop. 2. & 4. p. 10. Vitell. Sed satis: Veritati peritorum magis accedamus, quam speculationibus ociosorum.
units.tr: Not so. For through so many media, so widely spread and divided by so many surfaces, they would never be seen in their true place except at the pole of the horizon; their true magnitude would not be known, nor could the measure of their true distance be grasped. For they would be refracted from the perpendicular, on account of the variety of the media, passing from rarer into denser. According to Vitell. 45.47, prop. 2 and 4, p. 10. But enough: let us give more weight to the truth of the experts than to the speculations of idlers.

units.la: Caput Secundum. DE ASTROLOGIA, SEV Stellarum Natura Et Proprietatibus.
units.tr: Chapter 2. ON ASTROLOGY, OR THE NATURE AND PROPERTIES OF THE STARS.

units.la: Actenus de Cœlo : sequitur Stella, cujus doctrinam explicat Astrologia Physica. Stellæ autem consideratur, tùm Essentia, tùm affectio.
units.tr: So far concerning the heaven: there follows the star, whose doctrine is explained by physical astrology. The star is considered both in its essence and in its affections.

units.la: Essentia: Stella enim est corpus æthereum, adeoque simplex, quarto creationis die à Deo conditum, in se collectam conglobatamq; lucem habens, eamque pro insita sibi vi ac demenso suo diffundens, in media Cœli expansione (seu expanso astrifero) collocatum, & in ea jussu Creatoris suos conficiens cursus ac motus.
units.tr: Essence: the star is an ethereal body, and therefore simple, created by God on the fourth day of creation, having light gathered and condensed within itself, which it diffuses according to the power and measure implanted in it; placed in the expanse of the heavens (or the starry firmament), and there, at the Creator's command, carrying out its courses and motions.

units.la: Stella itaq; quarto Creationis die condita, ex substantia lucida, coacta, & quasi (ut quidam ex Orthodoxis Patribus loquuntur) in vase collecta, & in cælo, seu expanso illo, de quo supra, positaest. Tycho Brahe ad Rothmannum ait; Exististimo omnia, quæ in cælo volvuntur corpora, è cælesti & æterna constare materia, quæ qualis sit, vix exprimi potest : Supra tamen omnem Elementarem qualitatem graduatam necesse est.
units.tr: Thus the star, created on the fourth day of creation, was made from a luminous substance, compacted, and, as some of the orthodox Fathers put it, gathered as if into a vessel, and set in the heaven, or that expanse of which we spoke above. Tycho Brahe, writing to Rothmann, says: "I think all the bodies that revolve in the heavens consist of celestial and eternal matter, of which the quality can scarcely be expressed; yet it must be above every graded elementary quality."

units.la: Videtur autem Essentia stellarum consistere, 1. In interiore corporis globosi purissima luciditate, qua tota interior substantia, plena lucis congregatione perfusa, apta est, lucem suam lumen & radios diffundere. 2. In lucida essentia in globum compactione & efformatione, qua per insitam Virtutem motricem est apposita ferri motu orbico, suasque conficere periodos.
units.tr: The essence of the stars seems to consist: (1) in the most pure luminosity of the inner globular body, by which the whole inner substance, suffused with a gathering of light, is fitted to diffuse its light, its brightness and its rays; (2) in the compaction and shaping of the luminous essence into a globe, by which, through its implanted motive power, it is fitted to be carried in a circular motion and to complete its periods.

units.la: Quidam excipiunt a prima parte Lunam, quae videtur aliquid impuritatis obtinere, quam maculae ejus ostendere dicuntur. Deinde dictante Spiritu Veritatis, stellae lucis gloria sunt impares.
units.tr: Some exclude the Moon from the first part, since it is thought to have some impurity, which its spots are said to show. Then, the Spirit of truth speaking, the stars are unequal in the glory of their light.

units.la: Stellarum affectio est Interior, vel Exterior.
units.tr: The affection of the stars is either interior or exterior.

units.la: Interior ab ipsa magis dimanat & dependet stellarum essentia.
units.tr: The interior is that from which the essence of the stars flows and depends more directly.

units.la: Estq; Lux & Motus.
units.tr: There is Light and Motion.

units.la: Lux stellarum est interior & formalis earum affectio, seu proprietas visibilis, primo & per se in stellis lucens, radiorum ac luminis coelestis inferiori mundo communicati fons.
units.tr: The light of the stars is their interior and formal affection, or visible property, shining first and of itself in the stars, the source of the rays and of the heavenly light communicated to the lower world.

units.la: Hujus vis est, omnia lucem apta recipere in mundo collustrare, & tenebras dispellere.
units.tr: Its power is to make all things apt to receive light, to illuminate the world, and to dispel darkness.

units.la: A Luce stellarum emanat Radius & Lumen cœleste.
units.tr: From the light of the stars there emanates the ray and the heavenly light.

units.la: Radius sidereus est fulgor à sola luce stellarum in rectum & acutum exiliens & promicans.
units.tr: The starry ray is a brightness springing and darting straight and sharp from the light of the stars alone.

units.la: Lumen cœleste est fulgor à luce & radiis stellarum quaqua versum emanans.
units.tr: The heavenly light is a brightness emanating on every side from the light and rays of the stars.

units.la: Harum affectionum interventu & efficientia Cœlestis calor gigni dicitur, qui est calor universalis, insitum inferiorum corporum calorem pro sua natura efficiens, excitans, fovens, frigus discutiens, & alia multa efficiens.
units.tr: By the intervention and efficacy of these affections, heavenly heat is said to be produced, which is a universal heat, bringing about, exciting, fostering, dispelling cold according to its nature, the inborn heat of lower bodies, and effecting many other things.

units.la: Cœlestis hic Calor, si moderatur & benignus est, fovet. Sin vero intensus & immoderatus, potest etiam comburere.
units.tr: This heavenly heat, if it is moderate and kindly, fosters. But if it is intense and immoderate, it can also burn.

units.la: Hic calor origo caloris inferioris: at ita, ut si primarium agens spectes & formam, cui ut instrumentum servit, duplex nihilominus sit calor, Cœlestis & Elementaris, pro duplici forma Elementari, nimirum, qua rebus inanimatis aliquid largitur, & anima seu virtute vitali, qua animata informat. Calor, quo forma Elementaris utitur, dicitur Elementaris. Huic maxima ex parte debetur terminatio humidi cum sicco. Calor, quo cælum vel anima utitur, in animatorum, tum Univoca, tum Æquivoca generatione dicitur quibusdam Cœlestis. Est autem unus numero calor, conflatus ex duo-bus in uno subjecto, ut ex duabus candelis, no-stu in eodem cubiculo splendentibus, unum nu-mero Lumen conficitur.
units.tr: This heat is the origin of the lower heat; yet, although one regards the primary agent and the form, which it serves as an instrument, there is nonetheless a twofold heat, heavenly and elementary, corresponding to the twofold form: the elementary form, by which it bestows something on inanimate things, and the soul or vital power, by which it forms animate things. The heat which the elementary form uses is called elementary. To this is owed for the most part the termination of the moist with the dry. The heat which the heavens or the soul use, in the generation of animals, both univocal and equivocal, is called by some heavenly. Yet the heat is one in number, compounded of two in one subject, just as one light in number is made from two candles shining in the same room.

units.la: Motus seu motrix facultas est interior & formalis affectio, indita à Creatore stellis, qua unaquæq; stella pro sua natu-ra apta & promta est ad jussum Creato-ris motari, & sibi delegatos conficere cursus.
units.tr: Motion, or the motive faculty, is an interior and formal affection, implanted by the Creator in the stars, by which each star, according to its nature, is apt and ready at the Creator's command to move and to complete the courses assigned to it.

units.la: Ab hac facultate interiore est exte-rior Ἐνέργεια & motus stellarum, quo in pura tenuiq; ætheris ac expansi substan-tia actu feruntur, & suas absolvunt peri-odos.
units.tr: From this interior faculty comes the exterior energy [ἐνέργεια] and motion of the stars, by which they are actually carried through the pure and thin substance of the ether and the expanse, and complete their periods.

units.la: Motus stellarum est Diurnus vel Pe-riodicus.
units.tr: The motion of the stars is either daily or periodic.

units.la: Motus diurnus est, qui rapidissimo circumactu intra spatium diurnum, seu 24. horarum, communiter ab omnibus stellis conficitur: Estq; communis stel-lis omnibus & singulis.
units.tr: Daily motion is that which is completed by all the stars in common, by a most rapid revolution within the space of a day, that is, of 24 hours; and it is common to all the stars, both individually and collectively.

units.la: Nostri respectu motus hic vel est ortus vel occasus stellarum: & quidem uterq; distingui-tur in Astronomicum & Poeticum.
units.tr: With respect to us, this motion is either the rising or the setting of the stars; and each of these is distinguished into astronomical and poetical.

units.la: Poeticus dicitur, vel verus, vel apparens, uterq; tum ortus & occasus, tum verus & apparens dicitur, vel matutinus, vel vespertinus, de quibus in libellis Sphæricis.
units.tr: It is called poetical or true, or apparent; each of rising and setting is called true or apparent, and either matutinal or vespertine, concerning which see the books on the sphere.

units.la: Externam affectionem stellarum dicimus Figuram & Quantitatem.
units.tr: We call the exterior affection of the stars their figure and quantity.

units.la: Figura est rotunda & sphærica. Quantitas est continua vel discreta. Continua rursus est Simplex vel Comparata.
units.tr: Figure is round and spherical. Quantity is continuous or discrete. The continuous in turn is simple or compared.

units.la: Simplex magnitudo stellarum ut varia est; ita nondum satis explorata; licet vulgò sextuplici magnitudine distin-guantur.
units.tr: The simple magnitude of the stars, as it varies, is not yet sufficiently explored; although they are commonly distinguished into six magnitudes.

units.la: Comparata est distantia & altitudo stellarum à terra, quæ certè in multis incerta, licet certis instrumentis depre-hensa dicatur.
units.tr: The compared quantity is the distance and height of the stars from the earth, which indeed is uncertain in many cases, although it is said to have been ascertained by certain instruments.

units.la: Distantia hæc inter stellas fixas, & inter terram, in firmamento semper eadem est: distantia à terra Planetarum, continuò mutatur.
units.tr: This distance between the fixed stars and the earth, in the firmament, is always the same; the distance of the planets from the earth is continually changing.

units.la: Discreta quantitas est numerus seu multitudo Stellarum, nobis innumera-bilis, in se tamen non infinita.
units.tr: Discrete quantity is the number or multitude of the stars, innumerable to us, yet not infinite in itself.

units.la: Hactenus de affectionibus commu-nibus stellarum; Distributio est in Plane-tas, & Fixas.
units.tr: So far concerning the common affections of the stars; the distribution is into planets and fixed stars.

units.la: NB.
units.tr: NB.

units.la: Stella nonnullis latè & popularitèr sumta, Vel vera seu ordinaria, constans, & perpetua est; Vel nova, extraordinaria & inconstans. Hi enim Cometas qui in æthere supremo generantur, appellant etiam stellas, ut stellam novã dicunt, quæ in signo Cassiopeæ anno 1572. apparuit.
units.tr: A star, taken broadly and popularly, is either true or ordinary, constant and perpetual; or new, extraordinary and inconstant. For they also call the comets, which are generated in the highest ether, stars, as they say of the new star which appeared in the sign of Cassiopeia in the year 1572.

units.la: Planeta est stella, quæ mutabilibus spatiis in citeriore parte siderei cœli comeans cursus sui vestigia inflectit.
units.tr: A planet is a star which, moving through variable spaces in the nearer part of the starry heaven, bends the traces of its course.

units.la: Ideoq; sub firmamento, vulgo dicto, seu Zodiaco laxioribus quasi habenis, & cursu liberiore, sed tamen certo lapsu, certoq; spatio, nunc in hac, nunc in alia expansi ætherei parte consistere cernuntur: nunc his, nunc aliis stellis propinquiores: nunc obscuriores, nunc fulgentiores apparent.
units.tr: Therefore, beneath the firmament commonly called the Zodiac, as if with looser reins and a freer course, yet with a certain gliding and a certain space, they are seen now to stand in this part of the expanse of the ether, now in that; now nearer to these stars, now to those; now they appear dimmer, now brighter.

units.la: Planetarum tùm est Affectio, tùm Distributio.
units.tr: The planets have both affection and distribution.

units.la: Affectio dépendet ex eorum motu: ut Primò, est aspectus seu positus eorū in Zodiaco, quo se invicè quasi respiciunt; cujus species sunt Conjunctio & Oppositio.
units.tr: The affection depends on their motion: first, there is their aspect or position in the Zodiac, by which they, as it were, look upon one another; the kinds of which are conjunction and opposition.

units.la: Ad Conjunctionem pertinet aspectus sextans, quadrantalis & trientalis.
units.tr: To conjunction belong the sextile, quadrate and trine aspects.

units.la: Secundò ad affectiones pertinent alia φαινόμενα, quæ vel omnibus absolutè, vel solo excepto Sole, Planetis coveniút.
units.tr: Secondly, to the affections belong other phenomena, which apply either to all the planets absolutely, or to all except the Sun.

units.la: Omnibus absolutè Planetis conve-niunt, Altitudo, humilitas, & directio. Excepto Sole Planetis conveniunt, regressio, statio, & latitudo.
units.tr: To all the planets absolutely belong altitude, humility and direct motion. To the planets except the Sun belong retrogression, standing still, and latitude.

units.la: Distributio Planetarum est in duo genera: Prioris generis sunt Luminaria: quæ sunt Planetæ, distinguentes diem & noctem, lucem & tenebras, in cœlo omnium maximi apparentes.
units.tr: The distribution of the planets is into two kinds. Of the first kind are the luminaries, which are planets that distinguish day and night, light and darkness, and appear greatest of all in the heaven.

units.la: Luminaribus quandoq; accidit Ecli-psis, quæ est radiorum præcipuè solarium aversio seu exclusio, quæ fit interposito corpore opaco.
units.tr: Sometimes an eclipse happens to the luminaries, which is the aversion or exclusion of the rays, chiefly the solar rays, brought about by the interposition of an opaque body.

units.la: Eclipsis omnis fit in Zodiaco, & quidem in nodis, vel propè nodos, intra tamen terminos Eclipticos.
units.tr: Every eclipse occurs in the Zodiac, and indeed at the nodes, or near the nodes, yet within the limits of the ecliptic.

units.la: Nodi dicuntur hic puncta, in quibus se interse-cant via Solis & Lunæ, eorumque figura dicitur Draco.
units.tr: The nodes here are called the points at which the path of the Sun and that of the Moon intersect one another; and their figure is called the Dragon.

units.la: Nodus Draconis est Superior, vel Inferior.
units.tr: The node of the Dragon is either upper or lower.

units.la: Superior seu caput Draconis, est punctū illud, ubi Luna ab Ecliptica digrediens ad verticè nostrū versꝰ Septètrioné ascédit.
units.tr: The upper or head of the Dragon is that point where the Moon, departing from the ecliptic, ascends towards the north, toward our zenith.

units.la: Inferior seu cauda Draconis est punctum illud, ubi Luna ab Ecliptica digrediens Austrum versus descendit.
units.tr: The lower or tail of the Dragon is that point where the Moon, departing from the ecliptic, descends towards the south.

units.la: Eclipsis est totalis vel partialis.
units.tr: An eclipse is either total or partial.

units.la: Totalis est totius diametri nobis apparentis in luminari.
units.tr: Total is when the whole diameter apparent to us is covered in the luminary.

units.la: Partialis est unius vel aliquot partium, seu Digitorum.
units.tr: Partial is when one or several parts, or digits, are covered.

units.la: Digitus hoc loco est duodecima luminaris pars.
units.tr: A digit here is the twelfth part of the luminary.

units.la: Luminare est Majus vel Minus.
units.tr: The luminary is either greater or lesser.

units.la: Majus est Planeta, qui praeest diei, diciturq; Sol, ac est luminare majus, seu Planeta omnium maximus & lucidissimus, calorem vivificum cum luce mundo impertiens, motu communi seu diurno diem, proprio & periodico annum & vices temporum efficiens.
units.tr: The greater luminary is the planet that presides over the day, and is called the Sun. It is the greatest and brightest of all the planets, bestowing on the world its life-giving heat together with its light. By its common or daily motion it produces the day, and by its own periodic motion it produces the year and the changes of the seasons.

units.la: Sol dicitur Lucis sedes & vehiculum, luce lucens propria & nativa. Magnitudo lucis est tanta, ut Universum mundum repleat, & radios ad mundi extrema mittat; Copia tanta est, ut alia sidera obscuret.
units.tr: The Sun is called the seat and vehicle of light, shining with its own native light. The magnitude of its light is so great that it fills the whole universe and sends its rays to the farthest limits of the world. Its abundance is so great that it obscures the other stars.

units.la: Motus solis periodicus est, quo Sol anno vertente, scilicet dies 365. civiles & unius quaquadrantem continente, suam absolvit periodum.
units.tr: The periodic motion of the sun is that by which the Sun, as the year turns, completes its period, which contains 365 civil days and a quarter of one day.

units.la: Solis Eclipsis est aversio seu impeditio radiorum solarium, ab aliqua parte Hemisphaerii terrae, interposito corpore Lunae inter Solem & aspectum nostrum.
units.tr: A solar eclipse is the turning away or hindrance of the sun's rays from some part of the hemisphere of the earth, the body of the Moon being interposed between the Sun and our view.

units.la: Fit hæc Eclipsis in novilunio sive conjun-ctione, non quidem vera, sed apparente seu visibili, & ab iis tantùm cernitur, quibus Sol est supra Horizontem, non tamen omnibus, neque uno & eodem modo: quibusdam apparet totalis, quibusdam partialis.
units.tr: This eclipse happens at new moon or conjunction, not indeed a true one but an apparent or visible one. It is seen only by those for whom the Sun is above the horizon, though not by all, nor in one and the same way: to some it appears total, to others partial.

units.la: Minus luminare est Planeta, qui praeest nocti, dicitur; LUNA, quae est Planeta substantiae difformis, terrę citimus, adeoque omnium insim°, mutabiliter lucens, suo motu (27. dierum & septem horarum spatio) tempus menstruum seu mensem describens.
units.tr: The lesser luminary is called the planet that presides over the night, the Moon. It is a planet of unlike substance, nearest to the earth and therefore lowest of all, shining with changing light. By its motion, over a space of 27 days and seven hours, it describes a monthly period, or month.

units.la: Eclipsis Lunæ est solaris luminis in luna privatio, quæ fit interposita terra, inter Solem & Lunam. Lunæ accidit luminis mutatio, qua ejus hemisphærium, pro motus varietate à Solis luce variè affectum nobis mutabiliter lucet.
units.tr: A lunar eclipse is the privation of solar light in the Moon, which happens when the earth is interposed between the Sun and the Moon. The Moon undergoes a change of light: its hemisphere, variously affected by the sunlight according to the variety of its motion, shines to us in changing fashion.

units.la: Hinc Lunæ figura alia est invisibilis, alia visibilis:
units.tr: Hence the figures of the Moon are of two kinds: one invisible, another visible.

units.la: Invisibilis est vel κρύψις vel σύνοδος@[?].
units.tr: The invisible is either kryphis [κρύψις] or synodos [σύνοδος].

units.la: Κρύψις est Lunæ sub radiis solaribus recta occultatio.
units.tr: Kryphis [κρύψις] is the direct concealment of the Moon under the sun's rays.

units.la: Σύνοδος cum Luna centro Solis recta est subjecta.
units.tr: Synodos [σύνοδος] is when the Moon lies directly beneath the centre of the Sun.

units.la: Visibilis apparet vel non plena, vel plena.
units.tr: The visible appears either not full or full.

units.la: Non plena est Crescens vel Decrescēs.
units.tr: Not full is either waxing or waning.

units.la: Crescens, quæ Lumine augetur.
units.tr: Waxing: that which is increased in light.

units.la: Decrescens, quæ minuitur. Utraq; est vel Falcata, vel διχότομος, vel ἀμφίκυρος.
units.tr: Waning: that which is diminished. Each is either crescent-shaped, or dichotomous [διχότομος], or amphikyros [ἀμφίκυρος].

units.la: Falcata, cum primum e radiis Solis emergere apparet.
units.tr: Crescent, when it first appears to emerge from the sun's rays.

units.la: Διχότομος est, cum per medium quasi dissecta quadrante circuli à Sole distat.
units.tr: Dichotomous [διχότομος] is when it is, as it were, cut through the middle, a quarter of a circle distant from the Sun.

units.la: Ἀμφίκυρος[?] est, cum à Sole quatuor signis distat.
units.tr: Amphikyros [ἀμφίκυρος] is when it is four signs distant from the Sun.

units.la: Plena Lunæ figura est πανσέληνος[?], cum Soli diametraliter oppositā totam medietatem irradiatam terræ ostentat.
units.tr: The full figure of the Moon is panselene [πανσέληνος], when, diametrically opposite the Sun, it shows the whole irradiated half to the earth.

units.la: Secundi generis Planetæ sunt vel Heterodromi, vel Homodromi.
units.tr: Planets of the second kind are either heterodromi or homodromi.

units.la: Heterodromi sunt, qui diverso motu, impariq; tempore, sua conficiunt spatia, Ut sunt.
units.tr: The heterodromi are those which, with different motion and unequal time, complete their courses. They are:

units.la: I. Saturnus omnium supremus, 30. annis periodum suam absolvens.
units.tr: 1. Saturn, highest of all, completing its period in 30 years.

units.la: 2. Jupiter Saturno proximus, 12. annorum spatio circulum suum conficiens.
units.tr: 2. Jupiter, nearest Saturn, completing its circuit in the space of 12 years.

units.la: 3. Mars Jovi vicinus, 2. annis spatium suum conficiens.
units.tr: 3. Mars, near Jupiter, completing its course in 2 years.

units.la: Homodromi simul currentes fere pari tempore suum conficiunt iter, ut sunt.
units.tr: The homodromi, running together, complete their journey in nearly the same time. They are:

units.la: 1. Venus matutino tempore antecedens Solem, dicituq; Lucifer, vesperti-no subsequens Solem, dicitur q; Hesperus, cursum suum anni spatio conficiens.
units.tr: 1. Venus, going before the Sun in the morning and called Lucifer, and following the Sun in the evening and called Hesperus, completing its course in the space of a year.

units.la: 2. Mercurius Venere inferior, itidem annuo spatio cursum suum conficiens.
units.tr: 2. Mercury, lower than Venus, likewise completing its course in a year's space.

units.la: Hactenus de Planetis: Fixæ Stellæ sunt, quæ æqualibus inter se spatiis & locorum intervallis perpetuò differunt, & abiunt, adeoq; nullum unquam cursus sui vestigium inter se inflectunt: Sedes earum est superior pars expansi, seu firmamentum. Ex harum varia compositione, qua in aliquod signum efformantur, existit varium sidus.
units.tr: So much for the planets. Fixed stars are those which, at equal intervals and distances, are always separating and moving apart from one another, and so never bend any trace of their course among themselves. Their seat is the upper part of the expanse, or firmament. From the varied combination of these, by which they are formed into some sign, a varied constellation arises.

units.la: Sidera hæc vel sunt in Zodiaco, vel extra Zodiacum.
units.tr: These stars are either in the Zodiac, or outside the Zodiac.

units.la: In Zodiaco sunt sidera[?], & constellationes 12. quas signa vocant: Ut Sunt Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra[?], Scorpius, Arcitenens, Caper, Amphora, Pisces.
units.tr: In the Zodiac are the stars and the 12 constellations which are called signs, namely: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces.

units.la: Extra Zodiacum sidera vel sunt Bore-alia, vel Australia.
units.tr: Outside the Zodiac, the stars are either northern or southern.

units.la: Borealia sunt versus Aquilonem conspicua Septentrionalibus populis: sunt-que 21.
units.tr: The northern are those visible to northern peoples towards the north; there are 21 of them.

units.la: Australia sunt ultra Æquinoctialem versus Meridiem, Meridionalibus populis conspicuae: suntq; 15. De quibus singulis in Astrologia.
units.tr: The southern are those beyond the equator towards the south, visible to southern peoples; there are 15. Each of these is treated in astrology.

units.la: His fixis stellis à quibusdam annumeratur Circulus Lacteus, qui putatur esse extensa compactura multarum minutissimarum stellarum, ob parvitatem visum effugientium.
units.tr: Some count among the fixed stars the Milky Way, which is thought to be an extended compacting of very many very small stars, escaping sight because of their smallness.

units.la: Hactenus stellarum doctrina breviter comprehensa est. Sunt autem hae conditae, in tempora, dies, & annos: Ergo motus astrorum dimetitur tempora, quorum doctrina dicitur ἀστρονομία[?].
units.tr: So much of the doctrine of the stars has been briefly summarised. These stars, moreover, were made for times, days and years. Therefore the motion of the stars measures out times, and the doctrine of this is called astronomy [ἀστρονομία].

units.la: Astrorum motus non tempus, id est, durationem efficit, sed temporum dimensiones & distinctiones. Tempus distinctū, qua distinctum, est effectus quidam motus : adjunctum vero est rerum durabilium.
units.tr: The motion of the stars does not produce time, that is, duration, but the measurements and distinctions of times. Time, insofar as it is distinguished, is a certain effect of motion; but as attached to things, it belongs to durable things.

units.la: Temporis tum sunt Partes, tum Species, quatenus distinguitur astrorum motu.
units.tr: Time has both parts and kinds, insofar as it is distinguished by the motion of the stars.

units.la: Partes sunt Dies & Annus.
units.tr: The parts are day and year.

units.la: Dies est pars temporis motu stellarum diurno dimensa: Ejus partes sunt Horae.
units.tr: A day is a part of time measured by the daily motion of the stars; its parts are hours.

units.la: Annus est pars temporis, motu stellarum periodico numerata.
units.tr: A year is a part of time counted by the periodic motion of the stars.

units.la: Estq; Usitatus vel Inusitatus.
units.tr: It is either customary or uncustomary.

units.la: Usitatus est Solaris, vel Lunaris.
units.tr: The customary is solar or lunar.

units.la: Solaris motu periodico solis definitur.
units.tr: The solar is defined by the periodic motion of the sun.

units.la: Lunaris Lunae periodico, vulgo Menses.
units.tr: The lunar is defined by the periodic motion of the Moon; commonly called months.

units.la: Inusitatus est reliquarum stellarum, tum Planetarum, tum fixarum.
units.tr: The uncustomary is that of the other stars, both planets and fixed stars.

units.la: Planetarum, ut Saturninus, qui est Solarium annorum triginta: Jovialis 12. Martius dierum 687. Venereus & Mercurialis est fere solaris.
units.tr: Of the planets: Saturn's year is of thirty solar years; Jupiter's is 12; Mars's is 687 days; Venus's and Mercury's is nearly solar.

units.la: Fixarum stellarum annus dicitur Mundanus, Magnus, Verteus: Estq; incognitus.
units.tr: The year of the fixed stars is called the mundane, great or Platonic year, and it is unknown.

units.la: Species sequuntur. Tempus enim vel est Naturale, vel Civile. Naturale, quod ad motus cœlestes exacte describitur.
units.tr: Kinds follow. For time is either natural or civil. Natural time is that which is exactly described by the heavenly motions.

units.la: Estque DIES & ANNUS.
units.tr: There are the DAY and the YEAR.

units.la: Naturalis Dies est tempus ab oriente Sole ad occasum: sicut nox ab occasu ad Solis ortum.
units.tr: The natural day is the time from sunrise to sunset, just as the night is the time from sunset to sunrise.

units.la: Naturalis dies est vel noctis æqualis, vel inæqualis: Ab æquali dicitur Æquinoctium, idq; vel Vernale, vel Autumnale.
units.tr: The natural day is either equal to the night or unequal. From the equal one it is called the equinox, and this is either vernal or autumnal.

units.la: Æquinoctium vernum est, quod fit tempore Veris, Solis ad nos appulsu, in principio Arietis.
units.tr: The vernal equinox is the one that occurs in the season of spring, when the sun draws near to us, at the beginning of Aries.

units.la: Æquinoctium autumnale est, quod fit tempore Autumni, Solis à nobis abscessu, in principio Librae.
units.tr: The autumnal equinox is the one that occurs in the season of autumn, when the sun withdraws from us, at the beginning of Libra.

units.la: Inæquales dies sunt noctibus vel longiores vel breviores.
units.tr: Unequal days are either longer or shorter than the nights.

units.la: Longiores nobis sunt Sole signa Septentrionalia percurrente, in locis cis Æquatorem sitis.
units.tr: Longer days occur for us when the sun passes through the northern signs, in places on this side of the equator.

units.la: Breviores sunt, Sole in Meridionalibus signis constituto.
units.tr: Shorter days occur when the sun is in the southern signs.

units.la: Naturalis porro diei & noctis partes sunt Communes, vel propriæ.
units.tr: The parts of the natural day and night are either common or proper.

units.la: Communes sunt partes duodecim, quæ vocantur horæ naturales eæq; inæquales & temporales, quia tempore mutabiles sunt, & pro dierum longitudine vel brevitate modò crescunt, modò decrescūt. Cujusmodi horæ inæquales ferè omnes intelliguntur, quæ in sacris literis & prophanis, ad annum Christi 3oo. usq;, aut circiter occurrunt:
units.tr: Common parts are twelve in number, and are called natural hours; they are also unequal and temporal, because they change with the season, and now grow and now shrink as the days lengthen or shorten. Almost all the hours that occur in sacred and profane writings, up to about the year 300 of Christ, are understood to be of this unequal kind.

units.la: Propriæ partes diei naturalis sunt pars Antemeridiana & Pomeridiana. Noctis sunt vigiliæ quatuor.
units.tr: The proper parts of the natural day are the morning and afternoon portions. The night has four watches.

units.la: Annus naturalis est vel Solaris vel Lunaris.
units.tr: The natural year is either solar or lunar.

units.la: Solaris est Tropicus vel Sidereus.
units.tr: The solar year is either tropical or sidereal.

units.la: Tropicus quadripartitas anni tempe-rat vicissitudines, quæ sunt Ver, & Æstas, Autumnus & Hyems.
units.tr: The tropical year marks out the four changes of the year: spring, summer, autumn and winter.

units.la: VER est prima pars anni tropici ab Æquinoctio Arietis ad Solstitiū in Cancro numerata.
units.tr: SPRING is the first part of the tropical year, counted from the equinox of Aries to the solstice in Cancer.

units.la: ÆSTAS est ejus pars secunda à Solstitio Cancri ad Æquinoctium Librę numerata.
units.tr: SUMMER is its second part, counted from the solstice of Cancer to the equinox of Libra.

units.la: AUTUMNUS est hujus anni pars tertia ab Æquinoctio Librae ad Solstitium Capricorni.
units.tr: AUTUMN is the third part of this year, from the equinox of Libra to the solstice of Capricorn.

units.la: HYEMS est pars quarta à Solstitio Capricorni ad Æquinoctium Arietis, Sydereus annus est spatium temporis, quo toto Zodiaco peragrato Sol revertitur ad eandem stellam fixam.
units.tr: WINTER is the fourth part, from the solstice of Capricorn to the equinox of Aries. The sidereal year is the span of time in which the sun, having travelled through the whole zodiac, returns to the same fixed star.

units.la: Uterque Tropicus & Sidereus est aequalis vel inaequalis.
units.tr: Each of the tropical and sidereal years is either equal or unequal.

units.la: Lunaris annus periodico Lunae decursu est Simplex vel Compositus.
units.tr: The lunar year, measured by the periodic course of the moon, is either simple or compound.

units.la: Simplex unica periodo Lunae describitur: Estq; proprie Mensis: qui triplex est, Periodicus, Synodicus, & Apparitionis.
units.tr: The simple lunar year is measured by a single period of the moon, and is properly a month. There are three kinds of month: periodic, synodic, and of apparition.

units.la: Periodicus est, quo Luna pervagata Zodiacum redit ad idem principium: Estq; 27. dierum & horarum 7.
units.tr: The periodic month is that in which the moon, having wandered through the zodiac, returns to the same starting point. It lasts 27 days and 7 hours.

units.la: Synodicus est lunae a Sole profectae ad eundem reditus: Estque dierum 29. & horarum 12.
units.tr: The synodic month is the time in which the moon, having set out from the sun, returns to the same conjunction. It lasts 29 days and 12 hours.

units.la: Apparitionis mensis est tempus a primo conspectu Lunae prodeuntis a coitu, usq; ad momentum evanescentis ex oculis: Estq; fere 28. dierum.
units.tr: The month of apparition is the time from the first sight of the moon emerging from conjunction until the moment it vanishes from our eyes. It lasts about 28 days.

units.la: Compositus Lunaris annus 12. menses synodicos complectitur.
units.tr: The compound lunar year comprises twelve synodic months.

units.la: Sit fuit tempus naturale: Civile est, quod unaquaevis gens suo quodam instituto ad politica negotia accommodatu observat.
units.tr: So much for natural time. Civil time is what each nation observes by its own established custom, adapted to political affairs.

units.la: Civilis tùm Dies est, tùm Annus est.
units.tr: Civil time is both day and year.

units.la: Dies civilis est tempus, quo dies verus & nox continetur: Estq; æqualis vel in-æqualis, & quidem hic vel major vel minor est.
units.tr: The civil day is the period that contains a true day and night. It is either equal or unequal, and this civil day is either longer or shorter than the natural day.

units.la: Partes porrò diei civilis sunt Homogeneæ, vel Heterogeneæ.
units.tr: The parts of the civil day are either homogeneous or heterogeneous.

units.la: Homogeneæ sunt horæ civiles, quæ sunt partes diei civilis vicesimæ quartæ.
units.tr: The homogeneous parts are the civil hours, which are the twenty-fourth parts of the civil day.

units.la: Heterogeneæ sunt 1. Gallicinium, cum galli canere incipiunt. 2. Conticinium, cum conticuerunt. 3. Diluculum, cum Sole nondum orto jam lucet. 4. Mane, cum lux videtur Solis. 5. Ad meridiem. 6. Ipsa meridies. 7. A meridie. 8. Suprema tempestas. 9. Vespera. 10. Crepusculum. 11. Prima fax. 12. Concubium. 13. Intempesta nox. 14. Ipsa nox media. 15. A media nocte.
units.tr: The heterogeneous parts are: (1) cockcrow, when the cocks begin to crow; (2) the hush, when they have fallen silent; (3) daybreak, when it is already light before the sun has risen; (4) morning, when the light of the sun appears; (5) toward midday; (6) midday itself; (7) after midday; (8) the final part of the day; (9) evening; (10) dusk; (11) first torch; (12) bedtime; (13) the unseasonable night; (14) midnight itself; (15) after midnight.

units.la: Species dierum civilium, vel à quotidianis actibus, vel ab æquatione annui temporis nominantur.
units.tr: The kinds of civil days are named either from daily activities or from the equalizing of the annual time.

units.la: Ab actibus quotidianis dies civiles, alii sunt Festi, alii Profesti, alii Intercisi.
units.tr: From daily activities, some civil days are festal, some working, and some divided.

units.la: Festi, qui Deo consecrati sunt.
units.tr: Festal days are those consecrated to God.

units.la: Profesti, qui hominibus dicati, iisq; concesi ad administranda publica vel privata negotia.
units.tr: Working days are those given over to men and granted to them for conducting public or private business.

units.la: Intercisi sunt, qui sacris & profanis negotiis suint dicati: Vide Macrobium.
units.tr: Divided days are those given both to sacred and to secular business. See Macrobius.

units.la: Ab æquatione annui temporis dies alii sunt Tralatitii, Infititii alii, sive intercalares, alii Epactæ, alii Epagomenæ, alii Concurrentes.
units.tr: From the equalizing of the annual time, some days are transferred, some inserted or intercalary, some epact days, some epagomenal, and some concurrent.

units.la: Tralatitii, qui ex causa Religionis transferuntur.
units.tr: Transferred days are those moved from their place for reasons of religion.

units.la: Infititii seu intercalares, qui propter æquationem temporum anno inferuntur. Græcis ἐμβολισμοί, Bissexti.
units.tr: Inserted or intercalary days are those added to the year on account of the equalizing of the times. The Greeks call them embolismi; they are the bissextile days.

units.la: Epactæ sunt dies undecim, qui anno Lunari adjecti, æquant illum Solari.
units.tr: Epact days are the eleven days which, added to the lunar year, make it equal to the solar year.

units.la: Epagomenæ sunt, quicunq; explendis anni spatiis adjiciuntur.
units.tr: Epagomenal days are those added to fill out the spans of the year.

units.la: Concurrentes, quorum ope Characteres dici, cujusque Mensium inveniuntur.
units.tr: Concurrent days are those by whose help the dominical letters of each month are found.

units.la: Hactenus de diebus civilibus: Annus civilis est, quem quæque natio & civitas sibi statuit: Estque Solaris vel Lunaris.
units.tr: So much for civil days. The civil year is the one that each nation and state has established for itself; it is either solar or lunar.

units.la: Solaris vel est Simplex, vel Periodicus.
units.tr: The solar civil year is either simple or periodic.

units.la: Civilis Simplex, qui una alicujus stellæ conversione conficitur: estq; perfectus vel imperfectus.
units.tr: The simple civil year is the one completed by a single revolution of some star; it is either perfect or imperfect.

units.la: Perfectus est spatium dierum 365[?]. cum quadrante diei, qui quarto quoq; anno intercalatur : dicituṙq; Julianus, à J. Cæsare primo publicatus.
units.tr: The perfect year is a span of 365 [?] days together with a quarter of a day, which is intercalated every fourth year. It is called Julian, after Julius Caesar, who first published it.

units.la: Imperfectus est spatium dierum 365. sine quadrante diei.
units.tr: The imperfect year is a span of 365 days without the quarter of a day.

units.la: Periodicus civilis annus est, qui certo annorum orbe, interventu ut plurimum embolismorum, recurrit.
units.tr: The periodic civil year is one that recurs within a fixed cycle of years, usually with the insertion of embolismic months.

units.la: Annus civilis Lunaris seu Menses civiles est numerus quidam dierum, quem unaquæq; civitas suo observat instituto: numeraturq; vel à conjunctione, vel ab apparitione Lunæ prima. Romanorum mensium dies notati sunt hisce versic.
units.tr: The civil lunar year, or civil months, is a certain number of days which each community observes by its own custom. It is reckoned either from the conjunction or from the first appearance of the moon. The days of the Roman months are noted in these verses:

units.la: Triginta Aprilis, Junius, Septemq, Novemq, Uno plus reliqui, viginti Februus octo.
units.tr: Thirty days have April, June, September and November; the rest have one more, February has twenty-eight.

units.la: Partes mensis Romani sunt, Calendæ, Nonæ, & Idus.
units.tr: The parts of the Roman month are the Kalends, the Nones and the Ides.

units.la: Calendæ sunt dies, quo subducta hominum conspectui Luna latet, apud Solem radiis ejus tecta.
units.tr: The Kalends are the day on which the moon, withdrawn from human sight, lies hidden, covered by the rays of the sun.

units.la: Nonæ sunt dies, quo rursus nova conspicitur Luna.
units.tr: The Nones are the day on which the new moon is seen again.

units.la: Idus vocarunt plenilunium. Hinc versus :
units.tr: The Ides they called the full moon. Hence the verse:

units.la: Sex Nonas Majus, October, Julius & Mars, Quatuor at reliqui, dabit Idus quilibet octo, Inde dies reliquos omnes dic esse Calendas.
units.tr: Six Nones have May, October, July and March; the rest have four, and each gives eight Ides; all the remaining days are called Kalends.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM. De ΣΤΟΙΧΕΙΟΛΟΓΙΑ VULGARI, ET PRIMO de Elemento Ignis.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE. On common stoicheiology [ΣΤΟΙΧΕΙΟΛΟΓΙΑ], and first on the element of fire.

units.la: Dhuc fuit Corpus inanimatum aethereum in Coelo & Stellis: Inanimatum corpus Sublunare sequitur, quod sub aethereo corpore Mundi à Deo conditore collocatum subsistit: adeoq; aetheris ambitu continetur.
units.tr: Thus far we have treated the inanimate, ethereal body in the heavens and the stars. There follows the inanimate sublunary body, which was placed by God the Creator beneath the ethereal body of the world and so subsists, enclosed by the circuit of the aether.

units.la: Est hoc aut Primarium, aut Secundarium.
units.tr: This is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Primarium Sublunare inanimatum corpus est principium quoddam secundarii, & sequentium animatorum corporum. Diciturq; Elementum.
units.tr: A primary sublunary inanimate body is a certain principle of the secondary and of the animate bodies that follow. It is called an element.

units.la: ELEMENTA sunt corpora inanimata sublunaria primaria, dicta Simplicia, ex quibus corpora secundaria sublunaria & animata reliqua, quæ mixta dicuntur, componuntur, & in quæ pri-mo resolvuntur.
units.tr: Elements are the primary sublunary inanimate bodies, called simple, out of which the secondary sublunary bodies, and the remaining animate bodies, which are called mixed, are composed, and into which they are first resolved.

units.la: Elementa sunt & partes mundi in-tegrantes, & omnium mixtorum princi-pia. Zabarellæ lib. de Nat. Scient. Const. sunt duo munera Elementorum; unum, integrare hanc machinam. Alterum, ut sit materia mixti. Piccol. lib. 2. de Elem. Elementa ut suo ordine mundum constituunt, sui conservatione illum servant; suaq; ordinata partium vicissitudine, varietatum innumerarum sunt origo: ita sui cognitione & splendore cætera cuncta ex iis prodeuntia patefaciunt, & illustrant.
units.tr: Elements are also the integrating parts of the world and the principles of all mixed things. Zabarella, On the Nature of the Sciences, says there are two offices of the elements: one, to make up this machine; the other, to be the matter of a mixed body. Piccolomini, Book 2 On the Elements: the elements, by their own order, constitute the world and preserve it by their own conservation; and by the orderly interchange of their parts they are the origin of innumerable varieties. So by their own knowledge and brilliance they reveal and illuminate all the other things that come forth from them.

units.la: Simplicia dicuntur corpora, respectu Mixtorum, non quod simpliciter sint simplicia; ex materia enim & forma constant, & sic sunt composita. At non sunt ita composita, ut mixta: Elementa respiciunt Elementata, seu mixta.
units.tr: Bodies are called simple in relation to mixed bodies, not because they are simple in an absolute sense. For they consist of matter and form, and so are composite. But they are not composed in the way mixed bodies are: elements stand in relation to the things made from them, or mixed bodies.

units.la: Ex Elementis componuntur mixta. Ait enim Scaliger 275. omnes substantiæ, quibus tanquam principiis corpora constant, sunt Elementa. At principia illa sint essentialia & constituentia.
