Resolvuntur mixta in Elementa, prima resolutione, non extrema, quæ fit in materiam & formam. Ubicunq; enim mixtum resolvitur, ibi fit resolutio in Elementa: Si jam ulterius fiat progressus, & elementa ipsa rursus resolvantur, resolutio fit in materiam & formam. Hic jam subsistendum.
units.tr: Mixed bodies are composed of elements. For Scaliger, in 275, says that all the substances of which bodies consist, as their principles, are elements. But those principles are essential and constituent. Mixed bodies are resolved into elements by the first resolution, not the last, which goes into matter and form. For wherever a mixed body is resolved, there a resolution into elements occurs. If now one proceeds further, and the elements themselves are resolved again, the resolution goes into matter and form. Here one must stop.

units.la: Elementa vulgo numerantur quatuor, quæ ad hanc διχοτομίαν[?] referuntur: Elementa sunt duplicia: Levia seu Subtiliora, & Gravia seu Crassiora.
units.tr: The elements are commonly counted as four, which are referred to this division [διχοτομίαν]. The elements are of two kinds: light or finer, and heavy or grosser.

units.la: LEVIA dicuntur, quæ sursum feruntur, scilicet innata sua vi & raritate.
units.tr: LIGHT elements are those that are carried upward, namely by their innate force and rarity.

units.la: Levia Elementa & Subtiliora sunt Ignis & Aër.
units.tr: The light and finer elements are fire and air.

units.la: IGNIS dicitur Elementum leve vel subtilius, calidissimum, siccissimum, & omnium supremum.
units.tr: FIRE is called the light or finer element, the hottest, the driest, and the highest of all.

units.la: Ignis nonnullis distinguitur in Pu-rum seu simplicem; & Impurum seu den-satum, & materiæ mixtum.
units.tr: Some distinguish fire into pure or simple fire, and impure or condensed fire, which is mixed with matter.

units.la: Purus ignis dicitur, qui per se & sua natura habet calorem blandissimum a-lentem, & fovendam ad naturam cra-sinvè[?] constituendam & tuendam aptis-simum.
units.tr: Pure fire is said to be that which of itself and by its nature has a most gentle warmth, most suited to nourishing and fostering the constitution and preservation of nature.

units.la: Hic Elementaris Ignis est & dicitur per se & sua natura, quâ simpli-citer ignis, non comburere, non lucere, eò, quòd careat corpulentiâ, adeòque non esse conspicuus.
units.tr: This elemental fire is, and is called, such by itself and by its nature, by which it is simply fire: it does not burn and does not shine, because it lacks bulk and so is not visible.

units.la: Ignis impurus seu densatus, & materiae mixtus est, qui habet calorem propter partium propinquitatem, edacem, comburentem & consumentem.
units.tr: Impure fire, or condensed fire mixed with matter, is that which has a heat, arising from the nearness of its parts, that is corrosive, burning and consuming.

units.la: Sic ignis nostras & διαχοντικὸς[?] ex aliorum corporum densiorum admissione hunc calorem edacem sibi comparat, ut validior est ignis in ferro, in flamma est valde dilutus, ut manum sine laesione traducamus.
units.tr: Thus our [διαχοντικὸς] fire acquires for itself this corrosive heat from the admixture of other denser bodies. Hence fire is stronger in iron, but in a flame it is very diluted, so that we can pass a hand through it without injury.

units.la: Flamma enim Aristoteli dicitur, fumus ardens, seu, spiritus succi ardor. Alexand. Aphrod. Flamma minus calida est ferro ignito, non frigidi missione, sed propter materiae solidi-tatem & resistentiam. Et cum sit fumus ardens, minime perspicua est, terrestre enim in se permixtum habet.
units.tr: For Aristotle calls flame "burning smoke," or the glow of the moisture of a juice. Alexander of Aphrodisias: flame is less hot than red-hot iron, not from the admission of cold, but because of the solidity and resistance of the matter. And since it is burning smoke, it is least transparent, for it has earthy matter mixed into it.

units.la: Ustionis autem in hoc nostrate igne duplex fertur ratio:
units.tr: Now two explanations are offered for burning in this fire of ours:

units.la: 1. Est alienae materiae, seu alieni solidi corporis admissio.
units.tr: (1) It is the admission of alien matter, that is, of an alien solid body.

units.la: 2. Si ipse purus ignis condensetur.
units.tr: (2) It is the condensing of pure fire itself.

units.la: Utriusque rursus una ratio, partium scilicet propinquitas, quarum coactione in minori spatio, substantia major, ac sic major vis est.
units.tr: Both have one explanation, namely the nearness of the parts, by whose compression into a smaller space the substance is greater, and so the force is greater.

units.la: Ignis porro hic noster, tu generatur & conservatur, tu corrumpitur & extinguitur,
units.tr: Further, this fire of ours is generated and preserved, and it is corrupted and extinguished.

units.la: Ignis gignitur & confervatur iisdem de causis. Conservatio enim ignis nihil aliud est, quàm continua generatio. I-gnis enim hic non est stabile, sixum & durabile quiddam, sed continuè fluit & gignitur.
units.tr: Fire is begotten and preserved for the same reasons. For the preservation of fire is nothing other than continual generation. For this fire is not a stable, fixed and lasting thing, but flows and is begotten continuously.

units.la: Ad generationem & conservationem Ignis requiruntur quatuor:
units.tr: Four things are required for the generation and preservation of fire:

units.la: Aër,Pabulum, Ventilatio,&Focus.
units.tr: Air, fuel, ventilation, and a hearth.

units.la: 1. Opus est aere ambiente: Nam ignis ex pabulo idoneo gignitur per rarefactio-nem, per quam, quicquid in ignem converti potest, resolvitur. Quod autem rarefit, locum majorem requirit, in quem se diffundat.
units.tr: 1. Surrounding air is needed. For fire is begotten from suitable fuel by rarefaction, through which whatever can be turned into fire is resolved. What is rarefied, however, requires a larger place into which it may spread.

units.la: Aëre igitur opus est, in que[?] non modo flamma & fumus sese explicent, sed & ea, quæ ab ignitis carbonibus exhalant.
units.tr: Therefore air is needed, into which not only the flame and smoke spread out, but also those things that exhale from the glowing embers.

units.la: Cum enim continuò gignatur ignis, continua etiam dabitur resolutio. Exhalatio autem prior subsequenti locum cedit. Hoc autem fieri nequit, nisi in aërem ambientem diffundatur. Nec potest hanc ob causam ignis aëre egere, 1. Ut in aërem sua excrementa expuat, qualia sunt flammæ, fuligo, et favilla. Videre hoc est in fornace occlusa, & paulo post aperta.
units.tr: For since fire is continually begotten, a continual resolution will also occur. But the earlier exhalation gives way to the following one. This cannot happen unless it is diffused into the surrounding air. Nor can fire, for this reason, do without air: first, so that it may spit its excrements into the air, such as flame, soot and ash. This can be seen in a furnace that is closed and a little later opened.

units.la: 2. Ignis videtur ex materia in qua succen-sus est non solum ali, sed etiam vicinum aërem lambere, tanquam sibi cognatum, eoq; foveri.
units.tr: Second, fire seems not only to be fed by the material in which it has been kindled, but also to lick the neighbouring air, as if it were akin to it, and so to be fostered.

units.la: 2. Necessarium est Pabulum seu fomen-tum, ex quo continuo gignatur & reparetur, quia continuè fluit, & ab ambiente aëre absorbetur.
units.tr: 2. Fuel or tinder is necessary, from which it may be continually begotten and renewed, because it flows continuously and is absorbed by the surrounding air.

units.la: Pabulum autem hoc oportet esse igni idoneum, quod scilicet cum igne proportionem habet, quod tale & tantum est, ut ab igne superetur.
units.tr: Now this fuel ought to be suitable for fire, that is, it ought to have a proportion with fire, being such and of such an amount that it is overcome by the fire.

units.la: Pabuli itaq; proportio est in Quantitate vel Qualitate.
units.tr: The proportion of the fuel therefore lies in quantity or quality.

units.la: Quantitas ea est, ut neq; nimia alimenti copia obruatur flamma, neq; ob defectum pabuli marcescat.
units.tr: The quantity is such that the flame is neither overwhelmed by too great an abundance of nourishment, nor withers for lack of fuel.

units.la: Qualitas ea est, ut sit aëreum & terreum pabulum. Aër enim ratione caloris, terra ratione siccitatis, igni cognata dicitur. Ut ligna arida, conveniens sunt igni pabulum, quia & rara sunt, & aërea, & terrea.
units.tr: The quality is such that the fuel is airy and earthy. For air, by reason of its heat, and earth, by reason of its dryness, are said to be akin to fire. As dry wood is a fuel suitable for fire, because it is both rare and airy and earthy.

units.la: 3. Moderata Ventilatio & agitatio requi-ritur, quocunq; modo ista fiat. Obscura haud est ratio. Videtur enim aër, qui afflatur, veluti in sinum ipsius flammæ receptus, statim in ignem converti, suaq; accessione ignem augere, & sopitum resuscitare. Alii putant, motu dilatari flammam, ut plures materiæ partes occupet, & ex ea augmentum capiat, non ex aere.
units.tr: 3. Moderate ventilation and agitation are required, however they are brought about. The reason is not obscure. For the air that is blown on seems, as if received into the bosom of the flame itself, at once to be turned into fire, and by its addition to increase the fire and revive it when it is dormant. Others think that the flame is dilated by motion, so that it occupies more parts of the matter, and receives its increase from that, not from the air.

units.la: 4. Focus requiritur. Etsi enim ubique posit[?] accendi ignis, non tamen ubique æque bene & diu conservari potest. Carbones si in liberiore aere ponas, multò citius expirat ignis, quàm si in fornace conclusa, aut si sub cineribus asservetur.
units.tr: 4. A hearth is required. For although fire can be kindled anywhere, it cannot be preserved equally well and for equally long everywhere. If you place coals in freer air, the fire expires much more quickly than if they are in a closed furnace, or if they are kept under ashes.

units.la: Ignis corrumpitur, aut per se ipsum, aut ab alio.
units.tr: Fire is corrupted either by itself or by something else.

units.la: Prior corruptio per se ipsum facta dicitur μάρανσις.
units.tr: The former corruption, brought about by itself, is called withering [μάρανσις].

units.la: Μάρανσις porro est naturalis vel violenta.
units.tr: Moreover, withering [μάρανσις] is either natural or violent.

units.la: Μάρανσις naturalis est, per quam sensim & justo tempore conficitur. Ignis enim paulatim absumto pabulo suo tandem ob defectum pabuli marcescit.
units.tr: Natural withering [μάρανσις] is that by which fire is consumed gradually and in due time. For when its fuel is gradually used up, the fire at last withers for lack of fuel.

units.la: Μάρανσις violenta, per quam ignis ante justum tempus corrumpitur.
units.tr: Violent withering [μάρανσις] is that by which fire is corrupted before its due time.

units.la: Hæc fit propter sublatam ignis cum materia proportionem, aut ex parte materiæ, aut ex parte ipsius ignis.
units.tr: This happens because the proportion of fire to matter has been destroyed, either on the side of the matter or on the side of the fire itself.

units.la: Ex parte materiæ, quæ non servat proportionem vel in qualitate vel in quantitate.
units.tr: On the side of the matter, which does not keep the proportion either in quality or in quantity.

units.la: In qualitate, cum materia fovendo igni inepta est, ut ligna viridia.
units.tr: In quality, when the matter is unsuitable for fostering the fire, as green wood is.

units.la: In quantitate, cum ignis nimia materiae copia obruitur.
units.tr: In quantity, when the fire is overwhelmed by too great an abundance of matter.

units.la: Ex parte ipsius ignis, fit μαρανσις[?] violenta, cum vel excedit, vel deficit.
units.tr: On the side of the fire itself, violent withering [μάρανσις] occurs when it either exceeds or falls short.

units.la: Excedit mediocritatem, & praeter modum augetur, aut ex sese, propter frigidi aëris defectum: aut accessione majoris flammae.
units.tr: It exceeds the mean and is increased beyond measure, either of itself, through the lack of cold air, or by the addition of a greater flame.

units.la: Deficit à mediocritate & minuitur aut sua sponte paulatim expirans: aut per vim à materia avellitur.
units.tr: It falls short of the mean and is diminished, either by gradually expiring of its own accord, or by being torn away from the matter by force.

units.la: Avellitur autem vel motu & agitatione nimia: vel majoris flammae appro-pinquitate[?].
units.tr: It is torn away, however, either by excessive motion and agitation, or by the approach of a larger flame.

units.la: Ignis si ab alio corrumpitur, dicitur σβέσις[?] extinctio, quę fit à frigore contrario.
units.tr: If fire is destroyed by another agent, it is called σβέσις [sbesis], extinction, which comes about from a contrary cold.

units.la: Hoc modo extinguitur vel saltem imminuitur Ignis, aut à nimio gelu: aut ab humore balnei, & aëris nebulosi: aut ab aquae effusione.
units.tr: In this way fire is extinguished, or at least diminished: either by excessive frost, or by the moisture of a bath and of misty air, or by the pouring on of water.

units.la: Sed satis de Igni, cujus effectus in re-rum natura sunt mirabiles, unde in ge-nere nata est Pyrotechnia, & in specie variae artes <bl>Feuerfunst.</bl>
units.tr: But enough about fire, whose effects in the nature of things are wonderful; from it in general has arisen pyrotechnics, and in particular the various arts <bl>Feuerfunst.</bl>

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM. DE AERE.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR. ON AIR.

units.la: ALterum leve & subtilius elemen-tum sequitur, nempe Aër, cujus explicatio hodie est duplex: Peripatetica, & magis Theologica.
units.tr: The next element, light and more subtle, is air. Its explanation today is twofold: the Peripatetic, and the more theological.

units.la: I. Peripatetici aërem definiunt in suis scholis, Elementum leve, calidum, & summe humidum, complens omnem locum nullo alio corpore repletum.
units.tr: I. The Peripatetics define air in their schools as a light, warm and extremely moist element, filling every place not occupied by another body.

units.la: Forma ejus in remissione constituitur, ideo quia neq; ignis est, neq; ab ignis subsistantia [?] valde alienus videtur: Deinde in humiditatis excellentia, quia aquæ Elemento debeat opponi, eamq; conservare. Argumenta, quibus calor & humiditas illa probatur, videris & examina-veris in Peripato.
units.tr: Its form is established by a certain moderation, because it is neither fire, nor does it seem far removed from the substance of fire. Then, in its excess of moisture, because it ought to be set against the element of water and preserve it. The arguments by which that heat and moisture are proved you may see and examine in the Peripatetics.

units.la: Fines & usus aëris sunt innumerabiles, in animalibus tamen præcipui observantur, ad refrigerationem, ad humorum eductionem, ad humectationem, ad spiritum generationem, ad substituendos alios eorum loco, qui consumti sunt. Et-enim non est Spiritus aër: tamen adfert aliquid naturæ spiritibus ipsis. Commistus enim frigidus aër, spiritibus internis excalefactis, temperat ipsos frigore convenienti. Hinc refrigeratio contingit, & purificatio: Unde à Cicerone aer dicitur anima. Ad cordis igitur & aliorum éstuantium membrorum temperandum calorem conducit; Ad respirationem pulmonum, ad corporis mobilitatem facit, adfert enim tenuitatem, ne legnitie torpeant; Adfert itèm corporibus raritatem.
units.tr: The ends and uses of air are innumerable, yet in animals the chief ones are these: for cooling, for drawing off humours, for moistening, for generating spirit, and for supplying others in place of those that have been used up. For air is not itself spirit, yet it contributes something to the nature of the spirits themselves. For the cold air, mixed in with the internal spirits when they have grown heated, tempers them with a suitable coolness. Hence comes cooling and purification; whence Cicero calls air the soul. It therefore helps to temper the heat of the heart and of the other seething members. It serves the breathing of the lungs and the mobility of the body, for it brings fineness, so that the body may not grow sluggish from heaviness. It also gives bodies rarity.

units.la: Ab aëre non corrupto conservatur aqua. Aër quoque est visionis medium.
units.tr: Water is preserved by air that is not corrupted. Air is also the medium of sight.

units.la: Aër quò purior & tenuior fuerit, eò quoque nobis salubrior; quò impurior, eò perniciosior.
units.tr: The purer and finer the air, the more wholesome it is for us; the more impure, the more harmful.

units.la: Purus autem aër an alicubi invenia-tur, dubitant Peripatetici, ob Elementorum & aliorum corporum mutuam inter se conjunctionem : unde impuritas quædam contrahitur.
units.tr: Whether pure air is found anywhere, the Peripatetics doubt, on account of the mutual conjunction of the elements and other bodies, from which a certain impurity is contracted.

units.la: Crassus igitur existit aër è commixtione Ignis, aquæ, & terræ. Insalubris aër est, qui montibus inclusus non diffatur, & qui animalium, olerum, aut leguminum putredine, aut fimo coinquinatur. Insalubris quoqi nimis humidus, qui Stagni aut Paludis habitu inficitur, vel inde nebulosus est.
units.tr: Air is therefore thick, arising from the mixture of fire, water and earth. Unwholesome is the air shut in among mountains where it is not dispersed, and that is polluted by the putrefaction of animals, herbs or pulses, or by dung. Also unwholesome is air that is too moist, which takes on the character of a pool or marsh, and for that reason is misty.

units.la: Aëris partes seu regiones tres distinguuntur: Suprema, Media, & Infima.
units.tr: Three parts or regions of the air are distinguished: the Upper, the Middle, and the Lower.

units.la: Suprema pars aëris dicitur, quae à summitatibus montium incipit, & definit in ignis concavo.
units.tr: The upper part of the air is that which begins at the peaks of the mountains and ends at the concave surface of fire.

units.la: Media inter supremam & infimam collocatur.
units.tr: The middle is placed between the upper and the lower.

units.la: Infima initium sumit à superficie ter-rae, & eò protenditur, quousque radii à terra resiliunt. Differunt hae regiones in-ter se, Quantitate & Qualitate.
units.tr: The lower takes its beginning from the surface of the earth, and extends thither as far as the rays reflect from the earth. These regions differ from one another in quantity and in quality.

units.la: 1. Quantitate differt suprema à duabus inferioribus: Haec enim omnium maxi-ma est, eandemque semper & immutabi-lem quantitatem servat, initium à sum-mitatibus montium sumens, ad princi-pium usque ignis definens.
units.tr: 1. In quantity, the upper region differs from the two lower ones. For it is the greatest of all, and always keeps the same and unchanging quantity, beginning at the peaks of the mountains and ending at the beginning of fire.

units.la: Duae inferiores sunt minoris quanti-tatis, neque quidem ejusdem semper. Modo enim sunt majoris, modo minoris.
units.tr: The two lower regions are of smaller quantity, and not always the same. For sometimes they are larger, sometimes smaller.

units.la: Æstivo tempore infima major, me-dia vero minor: Hyeme infima minor, media major est. In causa est Solis in ae-state sublimitas, punctoque nostro verti-cali propinquitas: Hyeme vero ejusdem depresio, & à puncto nostro verticali remotio.
units.tr: In summer the lower is larger and the middle smaller; in winter the lower is smaller and the middle larger. The cause is the sun's height in summer and its nearness to our zenith point, but in winter its depression and remoteness from our zenith point.

units.la: Quo fit, ut in æstate radii terram percutiant angulis rectis, vel rectis propioribus: proinde etiá vehementius percutiant, & ad sublimiorem locum resilien-tes ascendant; Contrà vero hyeme obtu-siores angulos faciant, & obliquè admo-dum terram percutiendo, debilem faci-ant ictum & reflexionem, eoque parum sublimem locum ascendant.
units.tr: Hence it comes about that in summer the rays strike the earth at right angles, or at angles nearer to right, and therefore strike more violently and rise up by reflection to a higher place. On the other hand, in winter they make blunter angles, and striking the earth very obliquely, they make a weak blow and reflection, and so rise to a place not very high.

units.la: 2. Qualitate differunt regiones. Suprema enim dicitur omnium calidissima, tùm à motu coelesti, nullis eum montibus impedientibus, tū à propinquitate ignis, ad cujus natură etiá videtur magis vergere, respectu inferioris aeris magis humidi.
units.tr: 2. In quality the regions differ. The upper is said to be the hottest of all, both from the heavenly motion, no mountains impeding it, and from the nearness of fire, to whose nature it also seems more inclined, compared with the lower air, which is more moist.

units.la: Hujus regionis summam caliditatem videntur probare Exhalationes calidæ & siccæ, ex quibus ignita fiunt meteora.
units.tr: The great heat of this region seems to be proved by hot and dry exhalations, from which fiery meteors are made.

units.la: Media regio frigida est ob defectum utriusque causæ calorem producentis. Nō enim ad illam partem perveniunt radii à terra repercusi, neq; ita à coelo circumfertur & movetur, ut motus hic calorem gignere possit. Nō autē est aer ille frigidissimus. Nec quidem frigidus propter Antiperistasin proprie dicta. Eum enim ante Antiperistasin dixeris calidum aut frigidū. Si calidum, nullum locum habebit Antiperistasis, quia ubi frigus nō est, constipari nō potest. Sin frigidum, quæritur a quonam fit factus frigidus, cum suapte natura sit calidus, nec potest hujus frigoris causa statui Antiperistasis, cum prius frigidus statuatur, quàm Antiperistasis adveniat. Sed de his alibi.
units.tr: The middle region is cold because of the lack of both causes that produce heat. For the rays reflected from the earth do not reach that part, nor is it carried round and moved by the heavens in such a way that this motion could generate heat. Yet that air is not most frigid. Nor is it cold on account of antiperistasis properly so called. For if you call it warm or cold before antiperistasis: if warm, antiperistasis will have no place there, because where there is no cold it cannot be compressed. But if cold, the question is by what it has been made cold, since by its own nature it is warm, and the cause of this cold cannot be set down as antiperistasis, since it is supposed to be cold before antiperistasis arrives. But of these things elsewhere.

units.la: Infima regio Calida est & Humida.
units.tr: The lower region is warm and moist.

units.la: Calida dicitur reddi tùm per motum, tùm maximè per lumen à terra reflexū: à motu debilissimum, à radiis verò validiorem calorem accipiens.
units.tr: It is said to be made warm both by motion and especially by the light reflected from the earth: receiving from motion a very weak heat, but from the rays a stronger one.

units.la: Non autem hæc regio ubiq; est æque calida, sed modò magis, modò minus, pro temporum ac locorum diversitate.
units.tr: Yet this region is not everywhere equally warm, but sometimes more, sometimes less, according to the diversity of times and places.

units.la: Humida dicitur, tùm propter propriam naturam, tùm quia defert continuè vapores humidos, qui ab aqua & terra exhalantur, attractiqué diutius in ea commorantur.
units.tr: It is said to be moist, both on account of its own nature and because it continually carries moist vapours, which are exhaled from water and earth, and, being drawn up, remain in it for a long time.

units.la: 2. Theologicè magis ita explicatur Aëris natura.
units.tr: 2. Theologically, the nature of air is explained more in this way.

units.la: Aër est corpus expansum continuoque diffusum à siderio cœlo ad terræ & aquæ superficiem usque patens. Vel: Est pars cœli infima, à terræ convexo ad cœlum usque stellarum se extendens, a-quarum cœlestium reliquorumque Me-teororum receptaculum.
units.tr: Air is a body spread out and continuously diffused, extending from the starry heaven down to the surface of the earth and water. Or: it is the lowest part of heaven, reaching from the convex surface of the earth up to the heaven of the stars, the receptacle of the heavenly waters and of the other meteors.

units.la: Qui ita considerant aërem negant supra ipsum esse ignem Elementarem, & statuunt a-quas cœlestes, quarum mentio in sacris literis fit, esse de aquosis nubibus intelligendas.
units.tr: Those who consider air in this way deny that elemental fire lies above it, and they hold that the heavenly waters, of which mention is made in the sacred writings, are to be understood as watery clouds.

units.la: Aëris huius considerantur, tùm asse-ctiones, tùm regiones.
units.tr: Two things about this air are considered: its affections, and its regions.

units.la: Affectiones aëris, tùm sunt internæ, tùm externæ.
units.tr: The affections of the air are either internal or external.

units.la: Interna ab interna aëris essentia promanant, ut sunt, tenuitas, raritas, fluiditas, perspicuitas, & mobilitas.
units.tr: The internal ones arise from the inner essence of air, such as: fineness, rarity, fluidity, transparency, and mobility.

units.la: Tenuitas est, qua aëris partes valdè sunt subtiles, & in poros corporum penetrabiles.
units.tr: Fineness is that by which the parts of air are very subtle and able to penetrate into the pores of bodies.

units.la: Raritas, qua aëris partes subtiliter inter se sunt contextæ.
units.tr: Rarity is that by which the parts of air are finely woven together.

units.la: Fluor est, quo ejus partes continuè & facilè diffluunt, subtili liquiditate influunt, crassioribus cedunt, sparguntur, dividuntur. A tenuitate & liquiditate hac rarâ, est tùm aëris invisibilitas, quæ ob substantiæ tenuitatem, cum defæcata puripuritate conjunctam visus nostri aciem fugit: tum permeabilitas, qua fe in meatus corporum insinuat, poros permeat, & fe ipso implet.
units.tr: Fluidity is that by which its parts continually and easily flow apart, flow in with a subtle liquidity, yield to thicker things, are scattered and divided. From this fineness and this rare liquidity comes both the invisibility of air, which, because of the fineness of its substance joined with a purity freed from dregs, escapes the keenness of our sight, and its permeability, by which it insinuates itself into the passages of bodies, passes through their pores, and fills them.

units.la: Perspicuitas aeris est, qua radiis & lumini tenuis ejus substantia est pervia.
units.tr: Transparency of air is that by which its fine substance is open to rays and light.

units.la: Mobilitas aeris est, qua multis & magnis permutationibus, & commotionibus, variisque impressionibus agitari & turbari aptus est.
units.tr: Mobility of air is that by which it is apt to be stirred and disturbed by many and great changes, movements and varied impressions.

units.la: Externae affectiones extrinsecus & mutabiliter accidunt: funtq; trium fere generum. 1. Aer jam calidus, jam frigidus est, quippe sua natura utriusq; qualitatis capax ab interno principio aut incalescens aut frigescens. 2. Aer est humidus, vel siccus. Humidus, cum ipse in se liquidus & fluidus imbibit aqueam humiditatem, vel pluviosam, vel vaporosam. Siccus est aer, cum a radiis & calore Solis, vel a quorundam ventorum perseverantia siccatur. 3. Aer aut est luminosus, aut tenebricosus. Luminosus, cum aer per se pellucidus recepto lumine illustratur; Tenebricosus, cum absente lumine obscuratur. Aëris ita fuerunt affectiones; Regiones ejus sequuntur.
units.tr: External affections happen from without and in a changeable way, and they are of roughly three kinds. 1. Air is now warm, now cold, since by its nature it is capable of either quality, becoming warm or cold from an internal principle. 2. Air is moist or dry. It is moist when, being itself liquid and fluid, it takes in watery moisture, either rain or vapour. Air is dry when it is dried by the rays and heat of the sun, or by the persistence of certain winds. 3. Air is either luminous or dark. It is luminous when air, transparent of itself, is illuminated by received light; it is dark when, with light absent, it is obscured. Such were the affections of the air; its regions follow.

units.la: Earum alia est superior, alia inferior.
units.tr: Of these, one is upper, another lower.

units.la: Superior regio est, quæ supra aquas cœlestes & meteora ad cœlum usque sidereum expansa est. Eaque subtilior, quippe ab exhalationum terrestrium fœculenta irrigatione immunis, per quam radii luminum cœlestium irrefractè & impeditè permeant.
units.tr: The upper region is that which is spread out above the heavenly waters and the meteors, up to the starry heaven. It is finer, being free from the foul watering of earthly exhalations, through which the rays of the heavenly lights pass unbroken and unimpeded.

units.la: Inferior est aquarum præcipuè cœlestium receptaculum, & meteororum plerorumque generandorum matrix & officina.
units.tr: The lower is especially the receptacle of the heavenly waters, and the womb and workshop of most of the meteors to be generated.

units.la: Hæc ob exhalationes continuas, quæ tamen ultra 12. aut 13. Miliaria in aërem, ut demonstrant Opticæ probationes, non ascendunt, crassior & spissior nonnihil: Ideoque radios siderum cœlestium, non nisi aliquantulum præpeditos & refractos per suam actionem transfire patitur.
units.tr: This region, on account of the continual exhalations which, however, as optical proofs demonstrate, do not rise into the air above twelve or thirteen miles, is somewhat thicker and denser; and so it allows the rays of the heavenly stars to pass through its action only when they are somewhat hindered and refracted.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM. DE AQUA:
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE. CONCERNING WATER:

units.la: Actenus Levia & subtiliora Elementa fuerunt: Gravia & crassiora, quorum substantia crasior & densior est, sunt duo, Aqua & Terra.
units.tr: Thus far we have dealt with the light and finer elements. The heavy and grosser ones, whose substance is thicker and denser, are two: water and earth.

units.la: AQUA est Elementum crassius, sed tamen fluidum, quodammodo pellucidum, & humidum, suapte vi & inclinatione deorsum tendens, terram interluens vel ambiens.
units.tr: WATER is a grosser element, yet fluid, somewhat transparent and moist, tending downward by its own force and inclination, and flowing around or surrounding the earth.

units.la: Aqua verum est constituens corporum principium & Elementum, quo tanquam glutino sicca in corpore conjunguntur; & non so-lum materia mixtorum, sed etiam nutrix. Nu-tritur quodq;eo[?], ex quo constat. Constant ex a-qua mixta. Frigidum putatur, quod longius distet à fonte & principio caloris: & quia habeat naturam densiorem, & quidem densitas sit à frigore, frigidum Elementum concluditur. Vide Zabarel. 2. de Elem. Qual.
units.tr: Water is truly the principle and element that constitutes bodies, the element by which dry things are joined together in a body, as if by glue. It is not only the matter of mixed bodies but also their nurse. Each thing is nourished by that out of which it is made. Things are made of mixed water. It is thought to be cold because it is farther from the source and origin of heat, and because it has a denser nature; and since density comes from cold, it is concluded that water is a cold element. See Zabarella, On the Elemental Qualities, book 2.

units.la: Humidum dicitur, quia non facile suo termino continetur, sed semper diffluit; alieno fa-cile. Deinde palam est aquam humectare & madefacere.
units.tr: It is called moist because it is not easily contained within its own boundaries but always flows apart, and readily takes on what is foreign to it. Moreover, it is plain that water wets and moistens.

units.la: Ex frigiditate & humiditate inter se jun-ctis oritur Gravitas. Aqua igitur gravis, quia densa: ad sedem gravium sua sponte fertur, quod densum est.
units.tr: From the combination of cold and moisture arises heaviness. Water is therefore heavy because it is dense: it moves of its own accord to the seat of heavy things, as everything dense does.

units.la: Ascendit autem in montium jugis, vbi non raro fontes scaturiunt, item in tubis nostris, quibus egeritur aqua in puteos: quia ut habet Scal. Exerc. 46. Instat vis premens, quæ cum & ipsa mole graviore prematur, antecedentem protrudit, quæ cum exitum non inveniat, naturæ convenientem, ad eum etiam locum conscendere cogitur quem minimè appetebat.
units.tr: Water rises, however, on the ridges of mountains, where springs often gush forth, and likewise in our pipes, through which water is conveyed into wells. This happens, as Scaliger holds (Exercises 46), because a pressing force presses on, and being itself pressed by a heavier mass, it pushes forward the water in front; and since that water cannot find an exit, it is forced, though it is contrary to its natural tendency, to climb even to a place it did not at all seek.

units.la: Aquarum collectio dicitur Mare, quod est aquarum omnium, quæ sub cœlo sunt, receptaculum salsum, thesaurus & promtuarium, perpetuo æstu fluens, refluens, & intra alveum suum se continens.
units.tr: A gathering of waters is called the sea. It is the salty receptacle of all the waters that are under heaven, a storehouse and treasury, flowing and ebbing in constant tide, and keeping itself within its own bed.

units.la: Quamvis mare sit omnium aquarum receptaculum, singularum item origo: nunquam tamen fluviis abundat, nec iisdem est defectum, quia sufficit fluminibus mutua gratia dependione. Accipit, quod dat, & idem quod ab iis accipit, iisdem refundit; Ut Scaliger docet.
units.tr: Although the sea is the receptacle of all waters, and likewise the origin of each, it never overflows the rivers, nor is it deficient to them, because by a mutual dependence of grace it suffices for the rivers. It receives what it gives, and again gives back to them what it receives from them, as Scaliger teaches.

units.la: Maris considerantur tùm Partes, tùm Affectiones.
units.tr: Two things are considered in the sea: its parts and its affections.

units.la: Ex partium consideratione, marium aliud est Universale, aliud Particulare.
units.tr: From the consideration of its parts, one sea is universal and another particular.

units.la: Universale, quod totum terrarum orbem suo circuitu circundat, diciturque Oceanus. Particulare, quod per terras diffusum eas distribuit in certas partes, idq; in nostro orbe est vel Mediterraneum vel Caspium.
units.tr: The universal sea, which encircles the whole globe of the earth in its circuit, is called the Ocean. The particular sea is that which, spread through the lands, divides them into certain regions; in our world it is either the Mediterranean or the Caspian.

units.la: Mediterraneum mediam terram nostram illuit, ab Occasu versus Meridiem ex Oceano prorumpit, & Europam, Asiam, Africam, à se maximè disterminat, soletq; dici Magnum; ratione reliquorum, quæ in comparatione hujus Minora sunt.
units.tr: The Mediterranean lies in the middle of our land, breaks out from the Ocean from the west towards the south, and sharply separates Europe, Asia and Africa from one another; it is commonly called the Great Sea, in comparison with the rest, which are smaller than it.

units.la: Caspium sive Hircanum est mare inter Caspios & Hircanos montes, peculiari ambitu, propemodum rotundo sed oblongo, definitum, ex Oceano nō fluens.
units.tr: The Caspian, or Hyrcanian, is a sea lying between the Caspian and Hyrcanian mountains, bounded by its own circuit, nearly round but elongated, and not flowing from the Ocean.

units.la: Scriptores Oceanum distinguere solent in Atlanticum, Hyperboreum, Indicum, & Meridionalem.
units.tr: Writers are accustomed to distinguish the Ocean into the Atlantic, the Hyperborean, the Indian, and the Southern.

units.la: Affectiones præcipuè considerantur hic tres: 1. Quantitas maris: Quæritur enim an mare capiat incrementum & decrementum? A doctis & probatis viris improbatur: 2. Salsedo maris unde sit? nos à Deo einsitam sentimus, causis externis eam conservari & augeri non negamus: 3. Æstus seu reciprocatio maris, quo mare apud nos 24. horarum spatio bis affluit & refluit: Causa hujus disquiritur; Plerique eam Soli tribuunt, alii aliis: nos cum Patricio partim internae maris proprietati, quae est in salsugine ejus, spiritibus, & calore: partim viribus Lunae & Solis, illius quidem augentis humorem, hujus vero excitantis calorem, eam tribuimus.
units.tr: Three affections of the sea are considered here especially: 1. The quantity of the sea. For it is asked whether the sea receives increase and decrease; this is rejected by learned and approved men. 2. The saltiness of the sea: whence does it come? We perceive that it was implanted by God, yet we do not deny that it is preserved and increased by external causes. 3. The tide or reciprocation of the sea, by which, with us, the sea flows in and out twice in a space of twenty-four hours. The cause of this is disputed. Most attribute it to the Sun, others to other things. We, with Patricius, attribute it partly to the sea's own inner property, which lies in its saltiness, its spirits and its heat, and partly to the forces of the Moon and the Sun: the Moon indeed increasing the moisture, and the Sun stirring up the heat.

units.la: Alii sic argumentantur: Motus ille regressionis & progressionis motorem habeat necesse est. Motor ille vel est internus vel externus. Non internus: Esset enim mare animal, cum sola anima contrariorum motuum causa sit. (Sed hac de re vide Problemata Marina:)
units.tr: Others argue thus: That motion of ebb and flow must necessarily have a mover. That mover is either internal or external. Not internal: for the sea would then be an animal, since the soul alone is the cause of contrary motions. (But on this matter see the Marine Problems.)

units.la: Et plures motus interni in corpore simplici essent. Motus autem maris simplex internus est deorsum.
units.tr: Moreover, there would be several internal motions in a simple body. But the motion of the sea is a simple internal motion, downward.

units.la: Externus vero. Ille igitur est Sublunaris vel Aethereus.
units.tr: But it is external. That external mover is therefore either sublunary or ethereal.

units.la: Non sublunaris: Nec enim Elementum, nec Elementatum.
units.tr: Not sublunary: for it is neither an element nor something compounded of elements.

units.la: Aethereus igitur. Hic autem agit vel per Motum, vel Lumen, vel Utrumq;
units.tr: Therefore ethereal. This mover acts either by motion, or by light, or by both.

units.la: Non per motū tantū, nec per lumen tantū.
units.tr: Not by motion alone, nor by light alone.

units.la: Per utrumq; igitur.
units.tr: Therefore by both.

units.la: Motor autem ille, qui per lumen & motum mare trahit, est Luna.
units.tr: Now that mover which draws the sea by light and motion is the Moon.

units.la: Motu diurno attrahit aquas ab Oriente, easq; suspendendo ducens donec ad littora per- uentum fuerit, quorum obiectu repulsa prius iter retro legunt. Hæc attractatio sex horis per- ficitur, cui totidem attributæ sunt horæ ad re- pedandum, quod secutum est mare, iter.
units.tr: By its daily motion it draws the waters from the east, and, lifting them up, leads them until they come to the shores; when they are repelled by the shore's obstacle, they retrace their course backward. This drawing is completed in six hours, and an equal number of hours is assigned for the sea to return by the path it followed.

units.la: Lumine, eoq; menstruo inflat aquas, easq; pro ratione temporis, nunc turgidiores, nunc remissiores efficit. At hic multa sunt perplexa & obscura, de quibus in Marinis.
units.tr: By its light, and so by its monthly phases, it swells the waters, making them now more swollen, now more subdued, according to the proportion of time. But many things here are perplexing and obscure; these are treated in the Marine Problems.

units.la: Porro à mari sunt tùm Fontes, tùm Fluvii.
units.tr: Furthermore, from the sea come both springs and rivers.

units.la: Fons est principium aquæ in terra jussu divino nascentis & scatentis, hoc est, ebullientis, & successivè emanantis.
units.tr: A spring is the origin of water that rises and gushes forth in the earth by divine command, that is, that boils up and flows out successively.

units.la: Ipsa ebullitio aquæ è terra ebullientis dicitur Scatebra & scaturigo: Unde fons definiri potest, scaturigo aquæ è meatibus terræ erumpentis.
units.tr: The very boiling of water rising out of the earth is called a welling up and a spring-head. Hence a spring may be defined as a spring of water breaking forth from the passages of the earth.

units.la: Fluvius est aqua fontis perennis, continuè magna mole decurrens; Si parva aquarum copia è fonte fluit, rivus est, vel rivulus.
units.tr: A river is the water of a perennial spring, flowing continuously with a great volume. If a small quantity of water flows from a spring, it is a brook or a rivulet.

units.la: Perennitate, sicut & modo cursus Fluvius differt à Torrente: hic enim non habet perennem fontem, nec continuè, sed per quædam temporis intervalla fluit, & venit cum impetu.
units.tr: A river differs from a torrent in its perennial spring and in the manner of its flow, as the course of a river is continuous, whereas a torrent does not have a perennial spring, and does not flow continuously but at certain intervals of time, and comes with violence.

units.la: In fluviis[?] considerantur duo: Origo eorum, & Affectio, seu Quantitas & Qualitas.
units.tr: In rivers two things are considered: their origin, and their affection, that is, their quantity and quality.

units.la: Origo fluviorum est mare, quod non tantum aquarum receptaculum, sed & thesaurus, penu, & promtuarium. Subit autem ex mari aqua per internos terrae meatus, ex quibus in unum tandem locum confluit.
units.tr: The origin of rivers is the sea, which is not only the receptacle of waters but also their treasury, store and storehouse. Water passes up from the sea through the inner passages of the earth, from which it finally flows together into one place.

units.la: Affectio fluviorum est tum quantitas, tum qualitas.
units.tr: The affection of rivers is both their quantity and their quality.

units.la: Quantitas hoc loco est incrementum eorum, quod sumunt duplici de causa, intra terram, & extra terram.
units.tr: Here quantity means the increase they receive, which comes from two causes: from within the earth, and from outside the earth.

units.la: In terrae sinu vapores inclusi, & in aquam commutati, per easdem cavernas ad scatebras prolabuntur, & fontes efficiunt auctiores.
units.tr: Vapours enclosed in the bosom of the earth, changed into water, slip through the same caverns to the springs and make them fuller.

units.la: Extra terram augentur flumina, imbribus & liquefactis nivibus.
units.tr: Rivers are increased from outside the earth by showers and melted snows.

units.la: Qualitas aquarum est hic affectio earum, propter diversimodam locorum, per quos transeunt, constitutionem, eis accidens: Estque praecipue tactilis, gustatilis, odorabilis.
units.tr: The quality of waters here is their affection, which accrues to them from the varied constitution of the places through which they pass. It is chiefly perceptible to touch, taste and smell.

units.la: Tactilis qualitas aquarum est frigus & calor: Aquae igitur quaedam insigni frigiditate[?] prædita sunt, ut videantur etiam nonnullæ commutare quædam corpora injecta, ut lapidescant.
units.tr: The tactile quality of waters is cold and heat. Some waters are therefore endowed with a remarkable coldness, so that they appear even to change certain bodies placed in them into stone.

units.la: Plinius & Seneca frigus illud lapidibus adscribunt.
units.tr: Pliny and Seneca ascribe that coldness to the stones.

units.la: In pluribus etiam locis scaturit calida aqua, alibi tepida, alibi plane effervescés: Caloris causa est subjecta terra præcalida & æstuans, per quā aquarū transcursus est: Terræ enim in quibus illi defluxus visuntur, abundant ignis fomite, ut sulphure & bitumine, aliquando interius æstuant & inardescunt. Hinc sunt aquæ thermales.
units.tr: In many places warm water springs up, elsewhere tepid, and elsewhere plainly boiling. The cause of the heat is the very hot and seething ground beneath, through which the water's course runs; for the lands in which such outflows are seen abound in fuel for fire, such as sulphur and bitumen, and sometimes glow and burn inwardly. Hence come thermal waters.

units.la: Gustatilis qualitas est varius isq; adventitius aquarū sapor, qui iis accidit è terra, per quam percolantur: vel enim. 1. Mixtæ cum terra insipida aliquantulū vi caloris excoquuntur. 2. Vel terram sapidam, lapidemve, aut metallum, aut concretum succum lambunt. 3. Vel ebibunt liquidū succū cuiuscunq; saporis. 4. Vel expirationes recipiūt: Hinc dulces fontes & fluvii, purarum terrarum & arenarum percolatione: acerbi reddunt per loca aluminosa: amari per loca nitrosa: salsi vel è mari retinent originem, vel per loca salsuginea, &c.
units.tr: The gustatory quality is the varied and adventitious taste of waters, which they acquire from the earth through which they percolate. For either: 1. mixed with insipid earth, they are somewhat cooked by the force of heat; 2. or they lick a savoury earth, stone, metal, or concreted juice; 3. or they drink in any liquid juice of whatever flavour; 4. or they take in exhalations. Hence sweet springs and rivers arise from the percolation through pure earth and sand; they become sour through aluminous places, bitter through nitrous places, and salty, either retaining their origin from the sea or through salty places, and so on.

units.la: Odorabilis qualitas est varius itidem odor aquarum: vel enim lambunt terram olidam, vel in se halitus adustos, aut succum odoratum recipiunt: vel quia nonnihil sunt coctæ: vel quia in locis cavis detentæ putrescunt, &c.
units.tr: The odorous quality is likewise the varied smell of waters: either they lick up foul-smelling earth, or they take into themselves scorched vapours or odoriferous juice; or because they are somewhat cooked; or because, held in hollow places, they putrefy, etc.

units.la: Ingens est aquarum varietas, quæ breviter ita possunt constringi: Aquæ scilicet fluidæ, sunt Simplices vel Minerales.
units.tr: The variety of waters is vast, and can briefly be classed thus: liquid waters are, namely, either simple or mineral.

units.la: Simplices, quæ simplicem suam & nativam vulgaremq; retinent naturam: ut aqua fontana, Mera.
units.tr: Simple waters are those which keep their simple, native and common nature, pure: such as spring water.

units.la: Minerales dicuntur, quæ à simplici, vulgari & mera discedentes, cum aliqua subterraneorum minera conspirarunt, et aut spiritaliter sunt tinctæ, aut mistæ corporaliter.
units.tr: Mineral waters are said to be those which, departing from the simple, common and pure state, have joined with some quality of the subterranean ores, and are either tinctured spiritually or mixed corporeally.

units.la: Mineralis appellari generaliter quoq; posset Sabulosa, glareosa, & similis. At specialiter dicta Mineralis est, quæ ex minera mutationem quandam patitur.
units.tr: Sandy and gravelly waters, and the like, could also be called mineral in a general sense. But in the specific sense, mineral is the water that undergoes some change from an ore.

units.la: Est autem Minera matrix subterranea, in qua aliquid fossilium efficacium ex genere mistorum exoriri solet, sive id metallum sit, sive lapis, sive succus, sive gleba, terrave minera-lis. De quibus infra.
units.tr: A minera is an underground matrix, in which some effective fossil of the class of mixed bodies is usually generated, whether it be a metal, a stone, a juice, a clod, or mineral earth. Of these more below.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM. DE TERRA.
units.tr: CHAPTER 6. OF THE EARTH.

units.la: TERRA restat Elementum grave, crassissimum, siccum, aridum, opacum, firmum & stabile in medio Universi libratum.
units.tr: Earth is the remaining element: heavy, very dense, dry, arid, opaque, firm and stable, poised in the middle of the universe.

units.la: Geographis terra est medium & unum totius Universitatis, rotunda, immobilis.
units.tr: For geographers, the earth is the centre and one unit of the whole universe, round and immobile.

units.la: Fallopio terra est omne illud, quod effoditur, & addito humido primò emollescit, fitq; lutum, mox aucto humido eliquatur dissolvitur-ve.
units.tr: For Fallopius, the earth is everything that is dug up; when moisture is added it first softens and becomes mud, and then, with more moisture, it melts or dissolves.

units.la: Peripato Terra est simplex corpus, seu ut Casparus Contarenus ait, terra est nullibi & nulla sui parte simplex, præterquàm circa centrum.
units.tr: For the Peripatetics, earth is a simple body, or, as Caspar Contarenus says, earth is nowhere and in no part simple, except near the centre.

units.la: Patricio Terra vera est Compositissima.
units.tr: For Patrizi, true earth is most compound.

units.la: S. Scriptura vocat Aridam. Sicca est, quia affusum humorem combibens suapte natura exsiccat.
units.tr: Holy Scripture calls it dry land. It is dry because, by its own nature, it soaks up whatever moisture is poured on it and so dries out.

units.la: Hac tametsi partibus constet solidis, intrinsecus tamen suos habet meatus, sinus & cavernas, quæ recipiunt fumum quasi spiritum, aquam & humores quasi sanguinem.
units.tr: Although it consists of solid parts, it nevertheless has within itself passages, hollows and caverns, which receive smoke as if it were spirit, and water and humours as if they were blood.

units.la: Vulgò fertur esse frigida, at ita esse terram frigidam, ut omnis caloris sit expers, rectè negatur, & quidem rationibus evidentissi-mis.
units.tr: It is commonly said to be cold; but that the earth is so cold as to have no share of heat at all is rightly denied, and indeed on the clearest grounds.

units.la: Terra est in medio mundi librata, adeoq; centrum mundi. Et quidem in medio mundi quiescit, neq; circa medium, neq; in medio circa suum axem, neq; motu recto movetur, scili-cet secundum se, & tota considerata in suo loco. Sed partes quaedam terrae moventur, ut per accidens.
units.tr: The earth is poised in the middle of the world, and so it is the centre of the world. Indeed it rests in the middle of the world, neither moving around the middle nor turning in the middle about its own axis, nor moving in a straight line, that is, in itself, and taken as a whole in its own place. But certain parts of the earth move, but only accidentally.

units.la: Terra deinde est rotunda, & globosa figu-ra praedita, & non sola, sed juncta aquae. Sola enim terra rotundum corpus non efficit: interim corpus terrenum, propter vallium rimas, & montium tubercula est rudis & minus po-litus globus.
units.tr: Next, the earth is round and endowed with a spherical shape, and it is not alone but joined to water. For earth alone does not make a round body; meanwhile the earthly body, because of the clefts of valleys and the bumps of mountains, is a rough globe and less smooth.

units.la: Terra 1. Ratione suae qualitatis varias recipit distinctiones: Est enim alia Sa-bulosa, alia mineralis, alia cretosa, alia arenosa, alia argillosa, alia rubra, alia al-ba, alia nigra, & aliis praedita qualitatibus.
units.tr: The earth, (1) by reason of its quality, receives various distinctions. For one kind is sandy, another mineral, another chalky, another gritty, another clayey, another red, another white, another black, and it is endowed with other qualities.

units.la: 2. Exterior terrae superficies vulgo di-stinguitur in Zonas: sed distemperata Zona inprimis torrida, hactenus præfer-vore inhabilis æstimata, per Experien-tiam habitabilis inventa est, proinde terrae superficiem alii in quatuor partes dispescunt, Asiam, Africam, Europam, Americam. Alii in tres partes melius videntur distinguere. 1. Continet terram nostram, seu Europam, Asiam, & Africam comprehendit. 2. Continet terram occiduam, seu Indiam novam, quam Americam dicunt. 3. Dicitur Australis ea, cujus littora late pervagata à Lufitanis perhibentur.
units.tr: (2) The outer surface of the earth is commonly divided into zones; but the torrid zone, which was formerly judged uninhabitable on account of its heat, has been found habitable by experience. Accordingly, some divide the surface of the earth into four parts: Asia, Africa, Europe and America. Others seem to divide it better into three parts: (1) the first contains our earth, that is Europe, and comprises Asia and Africa; (2) the second contains the western land, that is the New India, which they call America; (3) the third is called the southern land, whose coasts are said to have been widely explored by the Portuguese.

units.la: 3. Terra respectu aquarum & marium distinguitur in continuam & solutam seu liberam: Continua dicitur quæ continuatis partibus etiam in fundo marium cohæret: libera vero quæ soluta à reliquis terræ partibus mari incumbit, ut Insulæ quædam feruntur in mari sustentari & fluctuare.
units.tr: (3) The earth, with respect to waters and seas, is divided into continuous and separated or free. That is called continuous which, by its continuous parts, also clings together on the bed of the seas; but free land is that which, separated from the other parts of the earth, lies on the sea, as some islands are said to be held up and float in the sea.

units.la: 4. Terra distinguitur in planam & montosam: ubi Terræ & montes nonnulli perpetuo & evidenti igne ardent.
units.tr: (4) The earth is divided into level and mountainous; and some mountains and lands burn perpetually with a clear fire.

units.la: Temperamentum terræ non est frigidissimum, quippe quæ non est caloris vivifici expers. Hunc enim arguit. 1. Ejus fertilitas, quæ omnis generis germina producit: calorem hunc Sol excitat, promit & auget. 2. Metallorum productio in visceribus terræ, quæ non fit sine calore innato. 3. Metallorum, lapidum-que & salium Fossores sub terra continuē calorem sentire dicuntur. 4. Sapores diversos in terra caloris ope confici necesse est. 5. Frigus hybernum terrae calorem cohibet & auget per ἀντιπερίστασιν[?]. 6. Alicubi etiam ignem inveniri testantur montes, & subterranea incendia.
units.tr: The temperature of the earth is not extremely cold, since it is not without vivifying heat. For it proves this: (1) by its fertility, which produces every kind of growth; this heat the sun stirs up, brings forth and increases; (2) by the production of metals in the bowels of the earth, which does not occur without innate heat; (3) miners of metals, stones and salts are said to feel constant heat under the earth; (4) diverse flavours in the earth must necessarily be made by means of heat; (5) winter cold holds in the heat of the earth and increases it by antiperistasis [ἀντιπερίστασιν]; (6) they also bear witness that fire is found in some places, in mountains and in subterranean conflagrations.

units.la: Quantitas terrae vix videtur exactè scire, cum tot anfractibus divisa, tot aquis operta jaceat: Quantacunque tamen simul cum aqua est, si in longitudinem & latitudinem per 360. gradus secetur, gradus autem quilibet, ut ex Lusitanorum navigationibus est observatum, 17. & mediam Leucas continet: quaelibet autem Leuca quatuor Italicis miliaribus respondeat, 70. miliaria cuilibet gradui respondebunt: totus itaque terrae circuitus continebit 25200. miliaria Italica.
units.tr: The quantity of the earth can hardly be known exactly, since it lies divided by so many inlets and covered by so many waters. Yet however much it is, together with the water, if it is cut lengthwise and crosswise into 360 degrees, and each degree, as has been observed from the Portuguese voyages, contains 17 and a half leagues, and each league corresponds to four Italian miles, then 70 Italian miles will correspond to each degree; the whole circuit of the earth will therefore contain 25,200 Italian miles.

units.la: CAPUT SEPTIMUM, De ΜΙΞΟΛΟΓΙΑ.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN, On Mixology.

units.la: HActenus fuit primarium sublunare inanimatum corpus, in Elementis explicatum : sequitur Secundarium corpus sublunare inanimatum, in mixtis inanimatis explicandum.
units.tr: Hitherto the primary sublunary inanimate body has been explained among the Elements; there follows the secondary sublunary inanimate body, to be explained among the inanimate mixed bodies.

units.la: Mixtum seu concretum corpus est per mixtionem.
units.tr: A mixed or compound body is one produced by mixture.

units.la: Mixtio est miscibilium alteratorum unio, cuius doctrina dicitur, μιξολογία.
units.tr: Mixture is the union of miscible things that have been altered; its doctrine is called mixology [μιξολογία].

units.la: Miscibilia dicuntur, quorum natura est habilis & idonea ad agendum & patiendum invicem, quae terminum alienum fusilem admittunt, atq; minutim dividi possunt.
units.tr: Miscible things are those whose nature is apt and fitted to act and be acted upon by one another, which admit a foreign fluid term, and can be divided into minute parts.

units.la: Alterata mixtilia dicuntur, quae mutua per contrarias facultates facta actio-ne & passione, fortem alterationem cum substantiae permutatione conjun-ctam subeunt.
units.tr: Altered mixables are those which, by mutual action and reaction through contrary powers, undergo a strong alteration joined with an exchange of substance.

units.la: Unio est hoc loco quaedam συνέχεια & concordia, qua mixtilia nunc unum sunt facta specie, ac in unam transmigrave-runt naturam.
units.tr: Union here is a certain cohesion [συνέχεια] and concord, by which the mixables now become one in kind and pass over into one nature.

units.la: Mixtionis, tum Requisita, tum Con-sequens, & Oppositum videbimus.
units.tr: We shall consider the requisites of mixture, both its consequence and its opposite.

units.la: 1. Requisita mixtionis sunt quatuor.
units.tr: 1. The requisites of mixture are four.

units.la: Miscibilia sint activa & passiva inviinvicem, id est, ut mutuo agant & patiantur, utq; tangant, & tangantur, & tota alterentur, & ut habeant eandem materiam.
units.tr: The miscible things must be active and passive towards each other, that is, they must mutually act and be acted upon, and touch and be touched, and be altered throughout, and have the same matter.

units.la: 2. Ut sint aliquo modo adæquata in potentiis, id est, ut sint quodammodo viribus paria: sic enim fiet, ut quodlibet agat in aliud, illudq; alteret, ipsumque vicissim alteretur ab aliis, neq; ullum penitus convertatur in alterius naturam. Agentis & patientis oportet debitam esse proportionem, ita ut agens sit aliquando fortius: Si sunt æqualia viribus, non sequitur actio, adeoque nec talis mixtio.
units.tr: 2. They must be in some way equal in powers, that is, they must be somewhat matched in strength: for in this way each will act on the other and alter it, and be in turn altered by the others, and none will be wholly converted into the nature of another. There must be a due proportion between agent and patient, so that the agent is sometimes the stronger. If they are equal in strength, no action follows, and so no such mixture.

units.la: 3. Sint divisibilia, id est, ut possint se invicé dividendo facilé penetrare. Cum enim Elementa tota totis sint permiscenda, talis aptitudo & dispositio ad penetrationem necessaria erit.
units.tr: 3. They must be divisible, that is, able to penetrate one another easily by dividing themselves. For since the Elements as wholes must be mixed with wholes, such aptitude and disposition for penetration will be necessary.

units.la: 4. Ad facilitatem mixtionis requiritur etiam, ut miscibilia sint, in minimas partes redacta: sic enim facilius sese invicem transmutabunt.
units.tr: 4. For ease of mixture it is also required that the miscible things be reduced into the smallest parts: for in this way they will more easily transmute one another.

units.la: II. Consequens mixtionis est Temperamentu, quod est qualitas corporis mixti, ratione mixtionis ei proximè inhærens, à qua sunt reliquæ ejus qualitates.
units.tr: II. The consequence of mixture is the temperament, which is the quality of a mixed body, lying closest to it by reason of the mixture, from which its other qualities arise.

units.la: Temperamentum in corpore mixto est Simplex & Compositum.
units.tr: The temperament in a mixed body is simple or compound.

units.la: Simplex, quando unum & idem totius & partium est temperamentum, ut in corporibus homogeneis, auro, argento, quorum substantia & in toto & in partibus, unius & ejusdem generis est & naturæ.
units.tr: It is simple when one and the same temperament belongs to the whole and to the parts, as in homogeneous bodies, such as gold and silver, whose substance, both in the whole and in the parts, is of one and the same kind and nature.

units.la: Compositum, quando aliud totius, aliud partium est temperamentû, ex peculiari mixtione genitum, ut in animalibus, quibus peculiare est cordis, cerebri, carnis, sanguinis, ossium &c. temperamentum.
units.tr: It is compound when the temperament of the whole is one thing and that of the parts another, produced by a peculiar mixture, as in animals, which have a peculiar temperament of the heart, brain, flesh, blood, bones, and so on.

units.la: Deinde Temperamentum est Æquale, vel Inæquale.
units.tr: Again, the temperament is either equal or unequal.

units.la: Æquale, quod æquè potentibus qualitatibus primis constat; quod fit, quando qualitates quasi ad æquilibrium misceantur, sic ut nulla aliam superet.
units.tr: Equal is that which consists of the primary qualities in equal strength; this happens when the qualities are mixed as it were in equilibrium, so that none surpasses another.

units.la: Inæquale, quod inæqualiter potentibus qualitatibus primis constat, quando scilicet vel una, vel duæ qualitates excedunt: ut cum calidum excedit frigidum, humidum siccum. Æquale est perfectissimum: facile externa aliqua causa ad inæqualitatem reduci potest.
units.tr: Unequal is that which consists of the primary qualities in unequal strength, that is, when either one or two qualities predominate: as when the hot exceeds the cold, or the moist the dry. The equal is the most perfect: some external cause can easily reduce it to inequality.

units.la: Utrumq; Temperamentum vel pluribus constat diversorum Elementorum qualitatibus, vel paucioribus.
units.tr: Either temperament consists of the qualities of several Elements or of fewer.

units.la: Si pluribus: ad plures quoq; & magis diversas actiones mixtum propendet.
units.tr: If of several, the mixed body inclines also to several and more diverse actions.

units.la: Sin paucioribus, ad pauciores. Animal quoniam temperamentum ejus est ex pluribus conflatu qualitatibus, quàm temperamentum vel lapidis vel plantæ, pluribus actionibus subeundis est ido-neum.
units.tr: If of fewer, to fewer. Since the temperament of an animal is compounded of more qualities than the temperament of a stone or a plant, it is fit to undergo more actions.

units.la: Actiones enim & passiones mixtorum magna ex parte ex temperamentis dependent, Ut: Vinum sublimatum ratione calidi & aerei temperamenti facile Epar & sanguinem inflammat. Vinum nativum ratione calidi & humidi calefacit & in vapores aereos facile convertitur.
units.tr: For the actions and passions of mixed bodies depend to a great extent on their temperaments. Thus: wine, distilled, by reason of its hot and airy temperament, easily inflames the liver and blood. Native wine, by reason of its hot and moist nature, warms, and is easily converted into airy vapours.

units.la: Ergo ex crebris actionibus corporis mixti facile in Temperamenti illius cognitionem devenire possumus.
units.tr: Therefore, from the frequent actions of a mixed body we can easily arrive at knowledge of its temperament.

units.la: III. Oppositum mixtionis est Natu-ralis corruptio seu putrefactio, quae est innati caloris in humido proveniens ab alieno sive externo, & non naturali calore corruptio.
units.tr: III. The opposite of mixture is natural corruption or putrefaction, which is a corruption of the innate heat in moisture, arising from a heat that is foreign or external and not natural.

units.la: Putrefactio est corruptio, corrumpit enim mixtum, ne fit amplius, quod fuerat. Est corruptio nativi caloris non qualiscunq;, sed naturalis, qui congregat homogenea, &sic partium facit concretionem, & est vinculum, quasi concretarum in unum quasi mixtū partium, quo victo & dissoluto corrumpitur.
units.tr: Putrefaction is corruption; for it corrupts the mixed body, so that it is no longer what it had been. It is the corruption of native heat, not of any kind but natural, which gathers together like things and so makes the concretion of parts, and is the bond, as it were, of the parts concreted into one mixed whole; when this is overcome and dissolved, the body is corrupted.

units.la: Corruptio autem provenit ab alieno calore, qui est aëris ambientis. Nulla enim res sui causa putrescit, sed propter alienum.
units.tr: Corruption, moreover, arises from a foreign heat, which is that of the surrounding air. For nothing putrefies on account of itself, but on account of something foreign.

units.la: Fit putredo in humido, quod est caloris pabulum, in quo proprius calor conservatur. Hinc Regula: Calor & humiditas pater & mater est putredinis. Medici dicunt: Humiditas diffluens est putredinis mater.
units.tr: Putrefaction occurs in moisture, which is the food of heat, in which the proper heat is preserved. Hence the rule: Heat and moisture are the father and mother of putrefaction. The physicians say: Diffluent moisture is the mother of putrefaction.

units.la: Ergo; Quæ abundant multo & excrementitio humido, facilè putrescunt.
units.tr: Therefore: those things which abound in much moisture that is excrementitious putrefy easily.

units.la: Est autem putrefactio aut Totalis, qua totum mixtum in omnibus suis partibus corrumpitur & dissolvitur: aut Partialis, vel secundum quid, & determinata, qua non ex toto, sed ex parte putrescit mixtum.
units.tr: Putrefaction is either total, by which the whole mixed body is corrupted and dissolved in all its parts; or partial, or in a certain respect and limited, by which the mixed body putrefies not wholly but in part.

units.la: Caput Octavum. METEOROLOGIA, & quidem primò de Meteororum Materia, HALITIBUS.
units.tr: Chapter 8. METEOROLOGY, and first of the matter of meteors, HALITUSES (EXHALATIONS).

units.la: [?]E[?]cundarium fublunare inanimatum corpus est, quod è primario conflatum concretumve constat.
units.tr: A secondary sublunary inanimate body is one that is compounded or concreted from the primary.

units.la: Animata corpora ab hac concretione & constitutione non excluduntur.
units.tr: Animate bodies are not excluded from this concretion and constitution.

units.la: Estque Meteorum aut Nerterum. Μετέωρον[?] latinis sonat sublime, ἀ[?] μετὰ & ἀείρω, quasi sursum feratur: Eftq; corpus inanimatum sublunare, secundarium, quod ex halituum materia, coelesti calore in aere vel terra effectum.
units.tr: There are meteors and [Nerterum]. The Latin word means "sublime" and corresponds to the Greek meteoron, from meta and aeiro, as if it were carried upward. A meteor is a secondary, sublunary, inanimate body, made from the matter of exhalations, produced in air or earth by celestial heat.

units.la: Meteororum doctrina dicitur Meteoria vel Meteorologia, in qua multa obscura & obstrusa. In Meteoria multa sunt meteora, multa esse videntur.
units.tr: The doctrine of meteors is called Meteoria or Meteorologia. In it many things are obscure and hidden. Among the meteors there are many that are meteors only in appearance.

units.la: Meteororum igitur Materia est Halitus, quem ex corporibus elicit Calor externus, vel internus.
units.tr: The matter of meteors, therefore, is an Halitus (exhalation), which external or internal heat draws out of bodies.

units.la: Externus calor halitum educens est Elementaris vel Coelestis.
units.tr: The external heat that draws out an exhalation is either elemental or celestial.

units.la: Internus est corpori congenitus calor.
units.tr: The internal heat is innate to the body.

units.la: Externus calor Elementaris est igneus, qui efficit duplices halitus, 'Ἀτμίδα[?] seu vaporem & Θυμίασιν.
units.tr: External elemental heat is fiery, and it produces two kinds of exhalation: atmis [ἀτμίδα], or vapour, and thymiasis [θυμίασιν], or fume.

units.la: 'Ἀτμὶς est halitus quidam calidus, tenuis, (ideoq; levis & sursum tendens) & humidus, humectans ea quæ attingit. Hic educitur ab igni urgente, ex corporibus humidis tantum ἀκαυστοις[?], quæ nihil sicci terrei, aut perparum habent, aut in quibꝰ simul humor aut terreum dominatur.
units.tr: Atmis is a certain hot, thin exhalation (and therefore light and tending upward), and moist, wetting whatever it touches. It is drawn out by urging fire from moist bodies alone that are non-combustible [ἀκαυστοις], which have little or no dry earthy matter, or in which moisture and earth are present in equal measure.

units.la: Sic aqua ab igne urgente in halitus resolvitur: terra etiam madefacta, & lutum humidum, humorem solum resolutum in vaporem exhalant, terreo remanente.
units.tr: So water is resolved by urging fire into exhalations. Earth too, when moistened, and damp clay give off only their moisture, resolved into vapour, while the earthy part remains.

units.la: Θυμίασις est halitus calidus & siccus, a terreis potissimum partibus, humore aliquo præditis cremabili attenuatus, qui propter siccitatem non humectat, sed calore tantum inficit id, quod attingit.
units.tr: Thymiasis is a hot and dry exhalation, rarefied chiefly from earthy particles endowed with some combustible moisture, which because of its dryness does not wet what it touches but only tinges it with heat.

units.la: Hujus halitus genera Sex numerantur.
units.tr: Six kinds of this exhalation are counted.

units.la: Primum dicitur Θυμίαμα, estq; odora quædam θυμίασις, eorum scilicet, quæ suffitibus idonea sunt. Θυμίαματα non reddunt suffitum nisi succensa: habent enim humorem in se cremabilem, sed ita cum siccis & terreis partibus continuum, ut non accenda-tur humor separatim, & sine siccis terre-isq; partibus exhalare nequeant: & tota fere consumuntur ab igne.
units.tr: The first is called thymiama [Θυμίαμα], and it is a certain fragrant thymiasis, namely of those things suited to fumigation. Thymiamata give off fume only when they are set alight. For they have combustible moisture in them, but this is so bound up with dry and earthy parts that the moisture cannot catch fire separately, and cannot exhale without the dry earthy parts; and they are almost entirely consumed by the fire.

units.la: Secundum Aristoteli dicitur καπνὸς, qui est halitus ab igne de ligno expressus: hic tamen non habet θυμιαματικὴν, licet sit inflammabilis. Corpus ligneum habet plus terrae, quam aquae. Hic halitus vulgo dicitur fumus, qui tamen non est omnis φλογιστὸς, id est, inflammabilis, sed ille qui moderate siccus & humidus, & quidem humore aereo superante.
units.tr: The second, according to Aristotle, is kapnos [καπνὸς], which is an exhalation pressed out of wood by fire. Yet this does not have the fragrance of incense, although it is inflammable. Wood has more earth than water. This exhalation is commonly called smoke, which, however, is not all flammable, that is, inflammable, but only that which is moderately dry and moist, and in which airy moisture predominates.

units.la: Lignum putridum non facile ardet propter nimiam siccitatem; Spongia propter raritatem; Hebenum propter densitatem.
units.tr: Rotten wood does not burn easily on account of its excessive dryness; a sponge, on account of its rarity; ebony, on account of its density.

units.la: Tertium dicitur λιγνὺς, qui est halitus suffitus opimi, alias fuligo, ex pinguire, qualis est Cera, Pix, Gummi, Resina, expressus.
units.tr: The third is called lignys [λιγνὺς], which is an exhalation of rich incense, otherwise soot, pressed out of fatty substances such as wax, pitch, gum and resin.

units.la: Quartum genus est Nidor, ex iis rebus, quae pinguedinem habent madidam & evidentem, eductus, ut est oleum, leum, lardum, adeps, butyrum, quae sunt aereae & aqueae naturae. Graeci λιπαρά[?], id est, unctuosa vocant.
units.tr: The fourth kind is nidor (savour), drawn out of those things which have a moist and evident fatness, such as oil, lard, bacon fat, suet, butter, which are of an airy and watery nature. The Greeks call them λιπαρά [lipara], that is, unctuous things.

units.la: Quintum est id, quod ex fumo & fuligine in furno caminis aut vaporariis adhaerens colligitur.
units.tr: The fifth is that which is collected from smoke and soot adhering in ovens, chimneys or hothouses.

units.la: Sextum deniq; genus dicitur Aristotelis Πνεῦμα, spiritus halitui illi, quem Sol è terra educit, similimus, qualis est Chymicorum spiritus, quem è multis rebus, per tenerum & tenue extrahunt.
units.tr: The sixth kind, which Aristotle calls pneuma [Πνεῦμα], is a spirit most like that exhalation which the sun draws out of the earth. It is like the spirit of the chemists, which they extract from many things through fine and delicate channels.

units.la: Externus calor Cælestis eliciens halitus est Solis, qui cum multo major sit terra, hanc à lumine & calore ejus affici necesse est.
units.tr: The external celestial heat that draws out exhalations is that of the Sun. Since the sun is much greater than the earth, the earth must be affected by its light and heat.

units.la: Haec è terra halituum eductio adjuvatur & augetur calore terrae insito. Coelesti calore eductus halitus dicitur Ἀνα-θυμίασις. Haec duplex est: Humida & Sicca. Humida Ἀναθυμίασις dicitur Vapor. Sicca consuevit vulgo dici Exhalatio.
units.tr: This drawing out of exhalations from the earth is aided and increased by the heat inborn in the earth. An exhalation drawn out by celestial heat is called anathymiasis [Ἀνα-θυμίασις]. This is twofold: moist and dry. The moist anathymiasis is called vapour; the dry one is commonly called exhalation.

units.la: Vapor est halitus calidus, humidus, qui est naturae inter aquam & aerem mediae: in alterum enim horum duorum facilius transit.
units.tr: Vapour is a hot, moist exhalation, of a nature intermediate between water and air, for it passes more easily into one of these two.

units.la: Exhalatio est halitus calidus & siccus, qui fertur naturae mediae inter terram & ignem, quod facilem in alterutrum transitum habeat.
units.tr: Exhalation is a hot and dry exhalation, which is carried in a nature intermediate between earth and fire, because it has an easy passage into either of them.

units.la: Congenitus corporibus calor educit è corporibus halitum medium inter eos, quos sol & ignis educunt, quia leniori multò calore, quàm Solis, aut ignis exprimitur.
units.tr: The innate heat of bodies draws out of bodies an exhalation intermediate between those which the sun and fire draw out, because it is pressed out by a much milder heat than that of the sun or of fire.

units.la: Huc pertinent Flatus, quos color internus in animantium & stirpium corporibus excitat.
units.tr: To this belong the blasts which the internal heat stirs up in the bodies of animals and plants.

units.la: CAPUT NONUM. DE METEORIS AQUEIS ex vapore genitis.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. ON WATERY METEORS GENERATED FROM VAPOUR.

units.la: METEORORUM genera duo sunt: Prius est eorum quæ ex halitu quopiam generatur: Et quidem ex alterutro: aut ex utroq; simul.
units.tr: There are two kinds of meteors. The first is of those generated from some exhalation, and these arise either from one of two sources or from both together.

units.la: Ex alterutro nimirum vel vapore, vel fumosa exhalatione.
units.tr: From one or the other, that is, from either vapour or smoky exhalation.

units.la: Ex vapore humido in aquam aut aërem facilè resolubili generantur meteora aquea.
units.tr: From moist vapour, watery meteors are generated, which are easily dissolved into water or air.

units.la: Aquea meteora sunt ex vapore humido vi caloris cœlestis, ex terra vel aqua excitato, concreta, & in aquam vel aërem facilè resolubilia. Causa efficiens horum est, vis caloris cae-lestis vapores ex terra extractos subigens, & pro ratione & affectione materia in varias meteororum species immutans.
units.tr: Watery meteors are formed from moist vapour, raised from earth or water by the power of heavenly heat and condensed, and they are easily dissolved into water or air. The efficient cause of these is the power of heavenly heat, which drives the vapours drawn up from the earth and changes the matter into the various kinds of meteor, according to its nature and condition.

units.la: Vapores autem illi tum non sint vehementer calidi, sed plurimum humidi & graves, ad supremam aeris regionem afferri, ibidemq; in meteora mutari non possunt, sed prout graves, vel minus graves sunt, aut in ventre terra manent, aut ad infimam, aut mediam regionem evolant, ubi amisso naturali calore, frigore condensantur, ac vicissim cum media sint natura in aerem vel aquam resolvuntur.
units.tr: Those vapours, however, are not violently hot but for the most part moist and heavy. They are carried to the highest region of the air, and there they cannot be changed into meteors. Instead, according as they are heavy or less heavy, they either remain in the bowels of the earth, or fly up to the lowest or middle region, where, having lost their natural heat, they are condensed by the cold, and in turn, since they are of a middle nature, they are resolved into air or water.

units.la: Ergo vel in aere, vel in terra generantur. In aere, vel media vel infima ejus in regione. In media fiunt, cum nubes, tum ex nubibꝰ orta.
units.tr: So they are generated either in the air or in the earth. In the air, either in its middle or its lowest region. In the middle region both clouds are formed, and things arising from clouds.

units.la: Nubes est meteoron aqueum, ex vapore copioso & crasso, in mediam aeris regionem sublato, qui ibi constrictus frigore & quasi congelatus pendet.
units.tr: A cloud is a watery meteor, made of copious, thick vapour raised into the middle region of the air, which, constricted there by the cold and as if congealed, hangs suspended.

units.la: Nubes tantum in media aeris regione generari hinc patet. In suprema generari nequeunt, propter calorem & motum coelestem, unde condensatio ibi fieri nequit. In infima nō. Quia in illa calor est à reflexione radiorum Solis. Ergo cogi non possunt vapores.
units.tr: That clouds are generated only in the middle region of the air is clear from this. They cannot be generated in the highest region, because of the heat and the motion of the heavens, so that condensation cannot take place there.
