Nor in the lowest, because there the heat comes from the reflection of the sun's rays. Therefore the vapours cannot be condensed.

units.la: Igitur in media-
units.tr: Therefore in the middle-

units.la: NB. Nubes alia à terra propius absunt alia remotius.
units.tr: NB. Some clouds are nearer to the earth, others farther away.

units.la: Ratio I. Diversi sunt vapores, rariores & densiores; quæ hi altius assurgunt, illi humi-liori in loco sunt.
units.tr: Reason 1. Vapours are of different kinds, rarer and denser. Those which rise higher are found in a lower place.

units.la: 2. Venti nubes hinc illinc agitant. Hinc quædam spatio dimidii miliaris germanici à terra absunt. Zabarel. & Scaliger. Quædam ulterius ad miliaria germanica 10. 13. 25. & c. ascendunt, alia altius.
units.tr: 2. The winds drive the clouds this way and that. Hence some are at a distance of half a German mile from the earth. Zabarella and Scaliger. Some rise further, to 10, 13, 25 and so on German miles, others higher still.

units.la: Est autem Nubes fertilis vel sterilis.
units.tr: A cloud is either fertile or sterile.

units.la: Fertilis est nubes nigra, densis vapo-ribus constans, ideoque in pluvias re-soluitur.
units.tr: A fertile cloud is dark, made of dense vapours, and therefore it dissolves into rain.

units.la: Sterilis est alba, tenuis, & lucida, à Sole exsiccata, ideoq; non dissolvitur, sed flatu ventorum dissipatur. Hæc serene-nitatis prænuncia esse solet.
units.tr: A sterile cloud is white, thin and bright, dried by the sun; therefore it does not dissolve but is dispersed by the blowing of the winds. It is usually a sign of fair weather.

units.la: Nubium porro sunt affectiones, Mo-tus scilicet, & Color.
units.tr: Further, clouds have affections, namely motion and colour.

units.la: Motus pendet à Dei moventis vo-luntate, quam sæpè per vim & motum ventorum, aliquando etiam, si non sint venti, per motum Solis exequitur: sic e-tiá detentio earū in aëre libero & liquido pendet à mirabili Dei virtute, & ordina-tione, licet alii causas secundas addant. Ajunt citra impietatem asseri[?] posse, nubes partim calore proprio & innato, partim calore solis & astrorum ad se attrahentium, partim motu aeris, & lucta materiarum contrariarum inter sese in media regione aeris detineri, donec in Elementum grauius resoluantur, & mole sua depressa in terram decidant.
units.tr: Motion depends on the will of God who moves them, which he often carries out through the force and motion of the winds, and sometimes, even when there are no winds, through the motion of the sun. So too their suspension in the free and fluid air depends on the wonderful power and ordering of God, although others add secondary causes. They say that without impiety it may be asserted that clouds are held in the middle region of the air partly by their own innate heat, partly by the heat of the sun and the stars drawing them upward, partly by the motion of the air, and by the struggle of contrary matters among themselves, until they are resolved into the heavier element and, their mass being weighed down, fall to the earth.

units.la: Colores nubium fiunt diversi, ex diversitate materiae vaporosae, & luminis solaris, & radiorum coelestium incidentia. Color in nubibus est vel simplex, vel mixtus.
units.tr: The colours of clouds become various, from the variety of the vaporous matter, of the sunlight, and of the incidence of the heavenly rays. The colour in clouds is either simple or mixed.

units.la: Simplex est albus, vel niger.
units.tr: Simple colour is white or black.

units.la: Albus color fit, quando in nubem tenuem & raram fit luminis immissio.
units.tr: White colour arises when light is admitted into a thin and rare cloud.

units.la: Niger color fit, quando in nube crassa & densa radiorum incidentium fit reflexio.
units.tr: Black colour arises when the incident rays are reflected from a thick and dense cloud.

units.la: Mixtus color in nubibus apparens est ruber, aut viridis.
units.tr: The mixed colour appearing in clouds is red or green.

units.la: Ruber color fit, quando in nubem humidam & fumosam terrestri adusto co-temperatam, radii immittuntur.
units.tr: Red colour arises when rays are admitted into a moist and smoky cloud tempered with terrestrial heat.

units.la: Hinc causa rubedinis matutina & pluviarum, quae eam consequi solent. Nubes ita deposita, & Sole illustrata, ruborem oculis exhibet: atque etiam cum crassa & humida sit, facilime, quando Sol supra Horizontem assurgit, in pluvias dissolvitur; sed cum motu ventorum saepe alio rejiciatur, non semper eundem effectum praestat.
units.tr: Hence the cause of the redness of morning, and of the rains that usually follow it. A cloud thus laid down and illumined by the sun presents a red appearance to the eyes. And since it is thick and moist, it very easily dissolves into rain when the sun rises above the horizon; but since it is often driven elsewhere by the motion of the winds, it does not always produce the same effect.

units.la: Contraria autem causa & effectus est rubedinis vespertina, quae fit in nube tenui & rara, aestu Solis exsiccata: quare nubes illa, cum omnis humor inde sit sublatus, facile dissipatur, ac in rorem convertitur, serenitatemque sequentis diei indicat.
units.tr: The opposite cause and effect is the redness of evening, which arises in a thin and rare cloud dried by the heat of the sun. Therefore that cloud, once all its moisture has been drawn away, easily disperses and turns into dew, and it indicates fair weather for the following day.

units.la: Viridis color nubis efficitur, quando in nubem aquosam & roridam jam destillare incipientem lumen infertur.
units.tr: The green colour of a cloud is produced when light is shed upon a watery and dewy cloud which is just beginning to drip.

units.la: Ad colores referimus Idola & Apparentias, quae varia efformantur in nubibus, a Sole, Luna, vel in aliis stellis clarioribus illustratis.
units.tr: To the colours we refer the phantoms and appearances which are formed in clouds in various ways, when they are illuminated by the sun, the moon, or other brighter stars.

units.la: Hae apparentiae seu imagines in nubibus fere densis ac roridis a Sideris luce superne incidente generantur. Non autem in tenuibus & omnino raris, quia cum hae radios transmittant, figuras impressas retinere, & visui nostro objicere nequeunt.
units.tr: These appearances or images in clouds are generated, for the most part, in dense and dewy clouds, by the light of a star falling from above. They do not arise in thin clouds, and altogether rare ones, because these transmit the rays and cannot retain the impressed figures and present them to our sight.

units.la: Idola autem haec conspiciuntur vel sub stellis illustrioribus, vel ex oppositionibus earum.
units.tr: These phantoms are seen either beneath the brighter stars or from their opposition.

units.la: {*} Praeterea Plerumque temporibus ut Halones. Sub stellis illustrioribus, utpote luminaribus, vel directè vel à latere apparent.
units.tr: {*} Moreover, they occur mostly at times such as halos. Beneath the brighter stars, as luminaries, they appear either directly or from the side.

units.la: Directè, ut Halo, qui est circulus in nube minus densa & æquabili, circa Solem, Lunam, aut aliam clariorem stellam lucidus, & in extremitate nigricans apparens. A Seneca dicitur Area, à Plinio Corona.
units.tr: Directly, as a halo, which is a circle in a cloud that is less dense and uniform, shining around the sun, the moon or another brighter star, and appearing dark at its outer edge. By Seneca it is called an area, by Pliny a corona.

units.la: Quod Halo in medio luminosior, in extremitate nigrior appareat, fit hoc ob radios reflectiores[?], mediam ejus partem fortius illuminantes, & attenuantes: illud fit ob radios obliquiores, & ad illuminandum minus efficaces. Halones sæpius sub Luna, quam Sole conspiciuntur. Nam Sol calore suo adurente facilius dissipat & absumit nubium vapores, quam humidum Lunæ lumen.
units.tr: That the halo appears brighter in the middle and darker at the edge happens because the rays are reflected and illuminate and thin out its middle part more strongly; the other happens because the rays are more oblique and less effective at illuminating. Halos are more often seen under the moon than under the sun. For the sun by its burning heat more easily dissipates and consumes the vapours of the clouds than the moist light of the moon does.

units.la: Eadem quoq; causa est, quod noctu sæpius, quàm interdiu videantur: die enim splendente Sole: calor est intensior[?], præsertim æstate, nocte vero remissior.
units.tr: For the same reason they are seen more often at night than by day. For when the sun shines by day, the heat is more intense, especially in summer, but at night it is milder.

units.la: Autumno creberrimè cernuntur, quia calor tunc temporis remissus, vapores dissipare nequit, sed frigus eo tempore moderatum leviter cogit & condensat eosdem.
units.tr: They are seen most frequently in autumn, because the heat at that time is weakened and cannot disperse the vapours, while the moderate cold at that season gently condenses and thickens them.

units.la: Halones plerumq; tempestatum mutatio-
units.tr: Halos usually announce changes in the weather.

units.la: Halonum pregnostica. nes pronunciant, si subito instar fumi evanes-cunt, significant serenitatem: Si parte aliqua franguntur, ventos ab eadem flaturos portendunt; Si nigrescunt, densioresq;[?] fiunt, pluviam designant, tunc enim materia earum altius assurgere, ad mediam aeris regionem, ibiq; magis ac magis cogi, ac in pluvialem nubem converti incipit.
units.tr: Prognostics from halos: if they suddenly vanish like smoke, they signify fair weather; if they are broken in some part, they foretell winds that will blow from that quarter; if they grow dark and become denser, they point to rain, for then their matter begins to rise higher, into the middle region of the air, and there to be compressed more and more and turned into a rain cloud.

units.la: A latere sunt Parelii, Parafelinæ, & Virga.
units.tr: From the sides come the parhelia, the paraselenae, and the virga.

units.la: Parelius est imago Solis, in nube aquosa æquabili, & mediocriter densa, justa proportione ad Solem collocata, à radiis reflexis expressa, adeoq; est imaginarius Sol, seu ejus simulacrum.
units.tr: A parhelion is an image of the sun, formed in a watery, uniform and moderately dense cloud, placed in due proportion to the sun, expressed by reflected rays; and so it is an imaginary sun, or its likeness.

units.la: Sicut in speculo fracto tot repræsentantur imagines, quot fractæ ejus partes: ita prout nubes apta & disposita est, interdum duo, interdum tres, interdum plures parelii apparent.
units.tr: Just as in a broken mirror as many images are represented as there are broken parts, so, according as the cloud is suitable and disposed, sometimes two, sometimes three, sometimes more parhelia appear.

units.la: Etsi vero nonnunquam plures Soles conspiciantur: revera tamen est unus verus Sol, reliqui omnes simulacra ejus. Apparent parelii ut plurimum oriente vel occidente Sole propter nubes eo tempore densiores, radiisque solaribus non-dissolutas. Rarò meridie, quia cum nubes calore solis tum fere exsiccatæ & rariores factæ sint, repercussio radiorum valdè est imbecillis.
units.tr: Although indeed several suns are sometimes seen, in truth there is only one real sun, and all the rest are its likenesses. Parhelia appear for the most part when the sun is rising or setting, on account of the clouds, which are then denser and not yet dissolved by the solar rays. They rarely appear at midday, because then the clouds have been almost dried up and made thinner by the heat of the sun, so that the reflection of the rays is very weak.

units.la: Quod autem in omnibus nubibus hæc idola Solis non exprimantur, ratio est, quod vel sint mobiles, vel rarę, aut non justa ratione ad Solem collocatæ. At verò hic peculiarem rationem habet diurna actio.
units.tr: The reason why these images of the sun are not formed in all clouds is that they are either mobile, or rare, or not placed in the right relation to the sun. But here the daily action has a particular reason.

units.la: Denunciatio Pareliorum partim est Physica, partim hyperphysica. Physicè, teste Seneca, denunciant pluvias. Nubes enim aquosa & rorida propè Solem posita, facilimè in pluvias resolvitur.
units.tr: The announcing of the Parelii is partly physical and partly hyperphysical. Physically, as Seneca reports, they announce rain: a cloud that is watery and dewy, placed near the Sun, very easily dissolves into showers.

units.la: Hyperphysicè denunciare dicuntur distractiones voluntatum, dissolutiones fœderum, & dissidia gubernatorum in imperiis, Unde sæpè tumultus & calamitates.
units.tr: They are said to announce hyperphysically the disruption of wills, the breaking of covenants, and the discord of rulers in kingdoms, whence often tumults and calamities.

units.la: Parafelinæ sunt idola eodem modo ad latus lunæ apparentia, seu imaginariæ Lunæ, in plenilunio apparentes. Dico in plenilunio: quia radii Lunares eo tempore sunt fortiores & efficaciores.
units.tr: The parhelia are images appearing in the same way at the side of the moon, or imaginary moons, seen at full moon. I say at full moon, because the lunar rays are then stronger and more effective.

units.la: Virgæ sunt radii Solares directè in nubem aquosam &dissimiliter raram incidentes, & formam virgarum seu funis protensi referunt; aliàs funes tentorii, seu : imperfectæ irides, arcus : Lineæ etiam perpendiculares.
units.tr: Rods are rays of the Sun falling directly on a watery cloud that is unevenly thin, and they resemble the shape of rods or a stretched cord. Otherwise they are cords of tents, or imperfect rainbows, arches; also perpendicular lines.

units.la: Ex opposito Luminarium apparens idolum dicitur Iris, quæ est arcus varicolor in nube cava & rorida, à reflexione radiorum luminarium nubi oppofitorû generatus, (Poëtis Thaumantias.)
units.tr: The image that appears opposite the luminaries is called the rainbow, which is a many-coloured arch formed in a hollow and dewy cloud, generated by the reflection of the rays of the luminaries from the cloud set opposite (by the poets, Thaumantias).

units.la: Iris apparet variis tincta coloribus, qui variant, 1. Ratione lucis & umbræ, 2. Pro ratione medii, per quod transfit. 3. Pro lucis distantia. 4. Ex oculi debilitate.
units.tr: The rainbow appears tinted with various colours, which vary (1) according to the light and shade; (2) according to the medium through which it passes; (3) according to the distance of the light; (4) according to the weakness of the eye.

units.la: Oritur hæc colorum varietas ex mixtura nubium, aëris, igniumq;, ut placet Plinio. Secundum quod enim radii reflexi plus vel minus nigredini umbrarum permiscentur, secundum hoc distribuunt actum sui luminis in varios colores, ut habet Vitell.
units.tr: This variety of colours arises from a mixture of clouds, air and fire, as Pliny thinks. For according as the reflected rays are more or less mingled with the blackness of shadows, so they distribute the action of their light into various colours, as Vitellio holds.

units.la: Colores autem Iridis præcipui sunt tres, qui ex reflexione radiorum Solariû, & mixtura lucis & umbræ generantur.
units.tr: The principal colours of the rainbow are three, which are generated from the reflection of the rays of the Sun and from the mixture of light and shade.

units.la: Primus color est Puniceus, qui in circumferentia arcus cernitur, & reliquos duos ambit:
units.tr: The first colour is purple, which is seen at the outer edge of the arch and surrounds the other two.

units.la: Hic fit à reflexione fortissima. Radii enim sub basi propinquiore ad visum nostrum resiliunt, Ergo sunt valentiores. Fit in nube densiore ; res enim lucida in atra visa puniceum refert colorem, ut ait Aristoteles.
units.tr: This arises from the strongest reflection. For the rays leap back to our sight from the nearer base, and so they are more powerful. It occurs in the denser cloud; for a bright thing seen against black takes on a purple colour, as Aristotle says.

units.la: Secundus color marinus est, qui inter convexum & concavum medius est.
units.tr: The second colour is sea-green, which lies between the convex and the concave.

units.la: Hic fit à reflexione sed debiliore. Radii enim altius ingrediuntur nubem, minusq; reflectuntur.
units.tr: This arises from a reflection that is weaker. For the rays penetrate the cloud more deeply, and are reflected less.

units.la: Fit in parte nubis aquosiore, & nonnihil remotiore: huic major in reflexione ad basin, ad visum minor existit angulus. Vis autem unita fortior dispersa, non enim ita facile congregari possunt radii. Hinc Regula Opticorum. In minore distantia, & materia spissiore radiatum fit viride.
units.tr: It occurs in the part of the cloud that is wetter and somewhat more distant: for this one the angle is greater at the base in reflection and smaller at the eye. Moreover, united force is stronger than dispersed force, for the rays cannot so easily be gathered together. Hence the rule of the optical writers: at a smaller distance and in denser matter, the radiance becomes green.

units.la: Tertius est cœruleus, qui in concavitate arcus apparet, eodé modo, quo superiores duo fiunt, sed reflexione infirmissima. Vergit hic color ad obscuritatē & nigredinē. Quia quando visus deficit, atrum apparet.
units.tr: The third is blue, which appears in the concavity of the arch, produced in the same way as the two above, but by the weakest reflection. This colour tends toward dimness and blackness, because when the sight fails, things look dark.

units.la: Quartum colorem addit Scaliger, non agnoscit Aristoteles. Fit enim non ex reflexione radiorum, sed tantùm ex collatione & contagio viridis inter se & punicei. Puniceus enim ad viridem positus flavum gignit.
units.tr: Scaliger adds a fourth colour, which Aristotle does not recognise. For it arises not from the reflection of rays but only from the juxtaposition and contact of green and purple with each other. For purple placed next to green produces yellow.

units.la: Iris porrò generatur in nube: quia generatur nō nisi in materia transparente. Transparens autem ex aduerso Solis collocetur, quae exceptos radios accipiat, recta tamen penetrare prohibeat.
units.tr: Moreover, the rainbow is generated in a cloud, because it is generated only in transparent matter. The transparent matter should be placed opposite the Sun, so that it receives the rays that have entered it, yet does not allow them to pass straight through.

units.la: Nubes autem illa oportet primum fit cava, deinde coagmentata ex rorantibus guttulis pluribus.
units.tr: That cloud must first be hollow, and then compacted from many dewy droplets.

units.la: Iris est Solaris tantum, vel Lunaris.
units.tr: The rainbow belongs only to the Sun or to the Moon.

units.la: Reliqua enim caelestia lumina ejusmodi exprimere figuram non possunt, propter imbecillitatem & obtusum lumen, respectu Solis, deinde propter maximam distantiam respectu Lunae.
units.tr: For the other heavenly lights cannot form such a figure, on account of their feebleness and dull light compared with the Sun, and then on account of their very great distance compared with the Moon.

units.la: Solares Irides potissimum fiunt hye-me, & maximè ab aequinoctio autumnali, quo rursus decrescente, ab aequinoctio verno non visuntur, Plinius.
units.tr: Solar rainbows occur above all in winter, and especially from the autumnal equinox, when it decreases again; from the vernal equinox they are not seen, as Pliny says.

units.la: Lunares Irides fiunt rarissimè, 1. Propter debilitatem luminis lunaris. 2. Propter noctis frigiditatem, quia nubes nimirum condensantur.
units.tr: Lunar rainbows occur very rarely: (1) on account of the weakness of the moonlight; (2) on account of the coldness of the night, because the clouds are of course condensed.

units.la: Differunt ambae Irides colore[?]. Lunaris colores candidiores sunt, & rariores, quàm Solaris.
units.tr: Both rainbows differ in colour. The colours of the lunar one are paler and rarer than those of the solar.

units.la: Finis iridum partim est Physicus, partim Hyperphysicus.
units.tr: The end of rainbows is partly physical, partly hyperphysical.

units.la: Physicus, quod significet modo pluvias, modo serenitatem.
units.tr: Physical, in that it signifies sometimes rain, sometimes fair weather.

units.la: Pluvias: quando colores sunt obscuriores in nube alia. Serenitatem: quando clariores apparent, & postea evanescunt. Hyperphysicus, ut sit signum fœderis di-vini, nunquam deinceps Mundum aquarum inundatione periturum.
units.tr: Rain: when the colours are darker in another cloud. Fair weather: when they appear brighter and afterwards fade away. Hyperphysical, that it may be a sign of the divine covenant that the world will never again perish by a flood of waters.

units.la: Hactenus de Nubibus. Ex nubibus orta meteora, aut liquida fiunt, aut denuo congelantur.
units.tr: So far concerning clouds. Meteors arising from clouds either become liquid or are again frozen.

units.la: Liquida quæ fiunt sunt Pluviæ, ortæ e nubibus densius remissiore frigore coactis, & sensim in guttas resolutis, quæ in terras decidunt, in commodum crescentium & animantium.
units.tr: The liquid ones that are formed are rains, arising from clouds condensed by a moderately lessened cold, and gradually resolved into drops, which fall to the earth for the benefit of growing things and living creatures.

units.la: Hæc si naturalis est, aut levis est, aut vehemens.
units.tr: These, if natural, are either light or violent.

units.la: Levis, cum levis guttarum sublime cadentium est dispersio.
units.tr: Light, when there is a fine scattering of drops falling from on high.

units.la: Vehemens est guttarum majorum: & quidem Imber aut Nimbus.
units.tr: Violent, when the drops are larger; and indeed this is either a heavy shower or a storm.

units.la: Imber fit densioribus & plenioribus guttis decidentibus.
units.tr: A heavy shower comes from drops falling thicker and fuller.

units.la: Nimbus fit cum impetu repentino, magnis & continuis guttis descendentibus.
units.tr: A storm comes with sudden violence, with large and continuous drops descending.

units.la: Diversitas harum pluviarum fit vel propter diversam nubium materiam, modo subtiliorem, modo crassiorem: vel propter diversam caloris efficaciam: vel propter diversum, unde pluviæ descendunt, locum.
units.tr: The difference between these rains arises either from the different matter of the clouds, now finer, now coarser, or from the different efficacy of heat, or from the different place from which the rains descend.

units.la: Prodigiosæ si pluviæ fuerint, res quædam aliæ præter pluvias decidunt quarum veræ causæ naturales vix à quoquâ mortalium reddi possunt. Ut frumentum, ferrum, sanguis, lac, lana, pili, lapides, ranæ, caro, &c.
units.tr: If the rains are prodigious, certain things other than rain fall, whose true natural causes can hardly be given by any mortal: such as grain, iron, blood, milk, wool, hairs, stones, frogs, flesh, etc.

units.la: Meteora è nubibus resolutis denuò congelata sunt Nix & Grando.
units.tr: Meteors resolved from clouds and again congealed are snow and hail.

units.la: Nix est meteorum è nubibus in pluviam resolutum, sed ante descensum denuò frigore intensiore constrictum, tenuiterq; quasi conglobatum, ac à flatu ventorum in floccos-instar lanæ carminatæ distractum descendens.
units.tr: Snow is a meteor resolved from clouds into rain, but before it falls constricted again by a more intense cold, and loosely gathered as it were into a ball, and descending, separated by the blowing of the winds into flakes like carded wool.

units.la: Mollis est nix & instar lanæ (ut est Psal. 147) quia adhuc humoris aliquid cum exiguo calore nondum à frigore profligato in ea reliquum est; ideoq; partes ejus cohærent, sed raræ, ut flocculi vellerum. Alba est nix, propter frigus materiam raram constringens. Frigus autem hoc fortius est in nive, quàm in pluviis.
units.tr: Snow is soft and like wool (as in Psalm 147), because some moisture with a little warmth, not yet overcome by the cold, remains in it; therefore its parts cohere, but loosely, like flakes of fleece. Snow is white because the cold constricts the thin matter. This cold, moreover, is stronger in snow than in rains.

units.la: Interdum in summis montibus ningit, in vallibus pluit.
units.tr: Sometimes it snows on the highest mountains while it rains in the valleys.

units.la: Calor enim in vallibus propter reflexionem intensus est, ideoq; ab illo antequam nix ad terram perveniat, resolvitur in aquam. In summis montibus majus frigus est.
units.tr: For the heat in the valleys is intense on account of reflection, and so before the snow reaches the ground it is resolved into water. On the highest mountains the cold is greater.

units.la: In alto mari etiam dicitur ningere propter spiritus quosdam calidos è mari expirantes.
units.tr: On the open sea it is also said to snow, on account of certain warm spirits breathing out from the sea.

units.la: Nix terrae optimi fimi loco est: fovet item & conservat fruges terrae mandatas eis incubans.
units.tr: Snow is in place of the best manure for the earth: it also cherishes and preserves the crops entrusted to the earth, by lying upon them.

units.la: Grando est meteoron aqueum ex pluvia guttatim descendente, in descensu vero densius frigore congelatum: Frigus, si minus intensum est, granula fiunt seu globuli, extrinsecus nive congelati, intrinsecus nive molliores.
units.tr: Hail is a watery meteor, falling drop by drop from the rain, but in its descent congealed more densely by the cold. If the cold is less intense, the grains or globules are formed, congealed outwardly like snow and softer inwardly than snow.

units.la: Grando Vere & Autumno frequentius ruit: Sol enim tempore aestatis omnem materiam absumit: hyeme vero pori a frigiditate constricti & occlusi manent, ut vapores egredi & in materiam grandinis converti non possint.
units.tr: Hail falls more often in spring and autumn: for in summer the Sun consumes all the matter; in winter, however, the pores remain constricted and closed by the cold, so that vapours cannot go out and be turned into the matter of hail.

units.la: Pro diversitate loci, ubi generatur grando, varia & diversa ejus est forma. Citius in aquam resolvitur atq; nix: Quia, quod naturâ aquae propius est, id facilius in aquam resolvitur, quàm illud, quod longius naturâ ab aqua abest. Grando propior est naturâ aquae, quia est aqua concreta. Nix longius abest, quia fit ex vapore.
units.tr: The form of hail is various and different according to the diversity of the place where it is generated. It is resolved into water more quickly than snow: because whatever is nearer to the nature of water is more easily resolved into water than that which is further from the nature of water. Hail is nearer to the nature of water, because it is concrete water. Snow is further away, because it arises from vapour.

units.la: Aquea meteora in infima regione aëris fiunt Ros, Pruina, Nebula.
units.tr: The watery meteors generated in the lowest region of the air are dew, hoar-frost, and mist.

units.la: Ros est vapor subtilis modicè, noctis frigofrigore parum condensatus, qui resolutus exiguis guttis descendens, graminibus, foliisq; arborum adhærescit.
units.tr: Dew is a subtle vapour, moderately, by the cold of the night only slightly condensed, which, resolved and falling in small drops, clings to the grasses and the leaves of trees.

units.la: Ros generatur locis ac temporibus tepidioribus & serenis, ut Vere & Autumno, flante vento Australi & Orientali: In altioribus locis ros non gignitur; Vapores enim frigiditate congelantur.
units.tr: Dew is generated in warmer and clear places and times, as in spring and autumn, when the south or east wind blows. In higher places dew is not produced, for the vapours are congealed by the cold.

units.la: Roris species sunt Manna & Ladanū.
units.tr: Species of dew are manna and ladanum.

units.la: Manna ex crasso & præpingui terræ vapore genitus, qui foliis arborum spicisq; frumentorū adhærescens, certis in terræ locis saccharū, aut farinā mellitam sapit.
units.tr: Manna is produced from a thick and very fatty vapour of the earth, which, clinging to the leaves of trees and to the ears of grain, in certain places of the earth tastes like sugar or honeyed flour.

units.la: Manna non generatur in quibusvis locis, sed in iis tantùm, in quibus temperatior est aër, propter æstus & frigoris successionem.
units.tr: Manna is not produced in just any places, but only in those where the air is milder, on account of the alternation of heat and cold.

units.la: Ladanum est vapor roris cadens super herbā ὁμώνυμον sudore foliorum permixtus.
units.tr: Ladanum is a dew-vapour falling upon a herb of the same name [ὁμώνυμον], mixed with the sweat of the leaves.

units.la: Pruina est vapor tenuis, fortiore frigore congelatus, & in salis forma quasi constrictus.
units.tr: Hoar-frost is a thin vapour, congealed by a stronger cold and, as it were, compressed into the form of salt.

units.la: Pruina albescit propter frigus: album enim plerumq; frigiditatis est indicium. Generatur hyeme, tempore sereno, flante vento Boreali. Eo die, quo discutitur, serenitatem promittit. Fœtet aliquando propter terram, cui admixta: aqua pruinæ est noxia.
units.tr: Hoar-frost looks white because of the cold, for whiteness is generally a sign of coldness. It is generated in winter, in calm weather, when the north wind blows. On the day it melts away, it promises fair weather. Sometimes it smells of the earth with which it is mixed; water from hoar-frost is harmful.

units.la: Nebula est vapor densus in proximo aëre, oriente vel occidente Sole excitatus, adspectum cœli prohibens.
units.tr: Mist is a dense vapour in the air close at hand, raised when the sun rises or sets, which blocks the view of the sky.

units.la: Nebula si calore Solis dissolvitur, & in terram deponitur, serenitatis est indicium: Si vero sursum evehitur, pluviam plerumq; portendit. Fœtet quandoq; propter exhalationes putridas vaporibus immixtas.
units.tr: If mist is dissolved by the heat of the sun and falls to the ground, it is a sign of fair weather; but if it is carried upwards, it usually portends rain. Sometimes it smells because of putrid exhalations mixed with the vapours.

units.la: Huc refertur Glacies quæ est aqua in Stagnis, paludibus, fluminibus, aliisque locis congelata.
units.tr: To this belongs ice, which is water congealed in pools, marshes, rivers, and other places.

units.la: Superstunt Aristoteli aquea meteora intra terram generata, quæ nos ad eundem remittimus: siquidem fontes, flumina, mare, nobis meteora sunt neutiquam, licet in cavernis terræ sit vapor aqueus, qui frigore condensatus potest destillare, & nonnihil augere aquam.
units.tr: There remain the watery meteors generated within the earth, which we refer back to Aristotle, since springs, rivers and the sea are by no means meteors to us, although in the caverns of the earth there is watery vapour which, condensed by cold, can drip down and somewhat increase the water.

units.la: CAPUT DECIMUM. DE METEORIS IGNITIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER TEN. ON FIERY METEORS.

units.la: Adhuc fuerunt meteora aquea ex vapore genita: succedunt ex fumo seu fumosa exhalatione producta [?]: dicunturq; Ignita meteora, quæ ex fumis accensis genita, instar ignis exardescunt : Suntq; vel verè existentia, vel ap-parentia: Verè existentia aut simplicia sunt aut mista: Simplicium materia simplex & pura est, minusque terrestris, aut viscosa.
units.tr: Still to be treated are the watery meteors generated from vapour. There follow those produced from smoke, or from a smoky exhalation [?]. They are called fiery meteors: generated from kindled smoke, they blaze up like fire. Some truly exist, others only appear. The truly existing ones are either simple or mixed. The matter of simple ones is simple and pure, and less earthy or viscous.

units.la: Hujus variæ sunt speciès & formæ ob multiplicem dispositionem habituum, secundum raritatem, densitatem, subtilitatem, crassitiem, magnitudinem, paucitatem, & majorem, minoremq; levitatem.
units.tr: These have various species and forms, owing to the manifold disposition of their qualities: rarity, density, subtlety, thickness, size, scantness, and greater or lesser lightness.

units.la: Accenduntur vero vel in aere, vel in terræ cavernis. Quod in aere inflammatur, est ascendens vel descendens. Ascendens ex fumis calidissimis, siccis & levissimis in supremum aerem evectis & accensis oritur.
units.tr: They take fire either in the air or in the caverns of the earth. That which ignites in the air is either ascending or descending. An ascending one arises from very hot, dry and light fumes, carried up into the highest air and kindled there.

units.la: Estq; Conjunctum vel Disjunctum. Conjunctum habet omnes partes continuas & cohærentes, ut sunt Fax seu candela accensa, Trabs seu ignis perpendicularis seu pyramidalis, & Bolis sive jaculum.
units.tr: It is either conjoined or disjoined. The conjoined has all its parts continuous and cohering, such as the lit torch or candle, the beam (a perpendicular or pyramidal fire), and the bolis or javelin.

units.la: Fax seu candela accensa, est fumus continuus, rarus & tenuis, & in longum & latum æquè distensus, qui superiore parte accensus instar facis inflammatæ ardet.
units.tr: The torch, or lit candle, is a continuous smoke, rare and thin, extended equally in length and breadth, which, kindled at its upper part, burns like a blazing torch.

units.la: Trabs est fumus longus & arctius com-pactus, qui æquabiliter accensus trabis repræsentat speciem.
units.tr: The beam is a long smoke, more closely compacted, which, kindled evenly, presents the appearance of a beam.

units.la: Bolis sive jaculum est fumus mediocriter longus, crassioribus partibꝰ æquabiliter cum subtilioribꝰ commixtis constans, qui accensus in summo aëre, sursumq; evolans, teli ardentis discurrentisq; formam refert.
units.tr: The bolis, or javelin, is a moderately long smoke, made up of thicker parts evenly mixed with finer ones, which, kindled in the highest air and flying upward, resembles a burning, darting missile.

units.la: Disjunctum habet partes magis dispersas, ut sunt Capræ saltantes, & Scintillæ volantes.
units.tr: The disjoined has its parts more widely scattered, such as the leaping goats and the flying sparks.

units.la: Capræ saltantes sunt fumi disjuncti in longum magis, quàm in latum porrecti, ac neutiquam interrupti, qui accensi motu & scintillatione in morem capra-rum saltare videntur.
units.tr: Leaping goats are disjoined smokes extended more lengthwise than breadthwise, and by no means interrupted, which, when kindled, seem to leap with motion and sparkling, in the manner of goats.

units.la: Scintillæ volantes sunt fumi, in multas minutasq; partes sparsi, quorum singuli instar stipularum inflammantur.
units.tr: Flying sparks are smokes scattered into many small particles, each of which catches fire like straw.

units.la: Descendens ex fumis minus calidis & siccis ortū, infra summū accéditur aëre: & quidem vel in medio, vel infimo aëre.
units.tr: The descending, arising from smokes less hot and dry, is kindled below the highest air, either in the middle air or in the lowest air.

units.la: In medio gignitur Stella cadens, & Lancea ardens.
units.tr: In the middle air is generated the falling star and the burning lance.

units.la: Stella cadens est fumus mediocriter compactus & globatus, qui supernè accensus à nube deorsum repellitur, & ita stellæ è Cœlo descendentis imaginem nobis exhibet.
units.tr: The falling star is a smoke moderately compacted and globular, which, kindled at its upper part, is driven downward by a cloud, and so shows us the image of a star falling from heaven.

units.la: Hujus motus cernitur aut rectus, aut obliquus.
units.tr: Its motion is seen either as straight or as oblique.

units.la: Rectus, cum exhalatio accensa recta deorsum tendit. Obliquus, quando exhalatio ad latus impellitur.
units.tr: It is straight when the kindled exhalation tends directly downward; oblique when the exhalation is driven sideways.

units.la: Lancea ardens est fumus oblongus bene compactus, qui accensus è medio aëre in mare vel terram instar titionis detruditur.
units.tr: The burning lance is a long, well-compacted smoke, which, once kindled, is thrust down from the middle air into sea or land like a firebrand.

units.la: In infimo aëre inflammantur, quæ ob caloris inopiam, altius evehi nequeunt, ideoq; imo in aëre inflammantur, qui modo calet, modo friget, Draco volans, & Ignis erraticus seu fatuus & lambens: Ille si unus & simplex est, dicitur Helena; si duplex, dicitur Castor & Pollux.
units.tr: In the lowest air are kindled those which, lacking heat, cannot be carried higher. Therefore in the lowest air, which now grows warm and now cold, there arise the flying dragon and the wandering, or foolish, and licking fire. If this is single and simple it is called Helena; if double, it is called Castor and Pollux.

units.la: Draco volans est fumus crassior, nec valdè compressus, qui in sublime evectus, & succensus impulsu frigidæ nubis curvatur & flectitur, ejusq; partes mediæ, ventrem, duæ autem extremæ, caput caudamq; Draconis referunt.
units.tr: The flying dragon is a thicker smoke, not very compressed, which, carried aloft and kindled by the push of a cold cloud, is bent and curved; its middle parts represent the belly of a dragon, and its two extreme parts the head and tail.

units.la: Ignis erraticus seu fatuus, est fumus crassior & tenacior, in imo aere per ἀν-ἡωθίσεων[?] nocturni frigoris accensus, qui vento agitatus decliviora loca petit, & viatores à via recta in praecipitia vel aquas plerumq; seducere solet.
units.tr: The wandering, or foolish, fire is a thicker and more tenacious smoke, kindled in the lowest air by the [ἀν-ἡωθίσεων?] of the night's cold. Agitated by the wind, it seeks lower ground and is wont to lead travellers from the straight road into precipices or, most often, into waters.

units.la: Crebrius apparet circa caemiteria, patibula, & ubi magna militum strages est facta, quod è cadaveribus viscosae exhalationes prodeant.
units.tr: It appears more often near cemeteries, gallows, and places where a great slaughter of soldiers has occurred, because viscous exhalations come forth from the corpses.

units.la: In magnis tempestatibus Malo aut antennis navium, propter materiam unctuositatem insidens conspicitur.
units.tr: In great storms it is seen clinging to the mast or yards of ships, on account of its oily matter.

units.la: Ignis lambens est fumus rarus & subtilis, qui accensus & per aerem dispersus, aliquando hominum vestimentis, eorumq; & equorum capillis sine ulla laesione inhaerescit. Quidam putant prodigiosum hoc meteoron, quidam è sudore animalium praecalidi temperamenti cum velociori agitatu incalescere.
units.tr: The licking fire is a rare and subtle smoke, which, kindled and dispersed through the air, sometimes clings to men's garments and to the hair of men and horses without any injury. Some think this a prodigious meteor; others think it arises from the sweat of animals of very hot temperament, heated by more rapid motion.

units.la: In terrae cavernis, ut in fodinis metallicis, hi accensi ignes nonnunquam conspiciuntur.
units.tr: In the caverns of the earth, as in metal mines, these kindled fires are sometimes seen.

units.la: Mixtum meteoron ignitum constat ex exhalatione ad admixtionem vaporis crassiore & viscosiore: Estq; Durans, vel Evanescens. Durans ob copiosiorem materiam diutius aliquando perdurat.
units.tr: The mixed fiery meteor consists of an exhalation combined with a thicker and more viscous vapour; it is either lasting or evanescent. The lasting one sometimes endures a long time because of its more abundant matter.

units.la: Estq; Cometa aereus, qui est meteoron igneum ortum ex exhalatione sicca, viscosa, copiosa, arcte compacta, in superiorem aerem evecta, ibidemque inflammata, ex se vel omnes vel aliquas in partes radios spargens, certaeq; alicujus stellae dominio subjectum.
units.tr: There is the aerial comet, which is a fiery meteor arising from a dry, viscous, abundant exhalation, tightly compacted, carried up into the higher air and kindled there, and scattering rays from itself in all or some directions, and subject to the dominion of some particular star.

units.la: Cometa interdum est immobilis, interdum mobilis: Ejusq; motus, vel simplex, vel varius est. Deinde ratione figurę Cometa aut est rotunda & crinitus, aut barbatus & oblongus. Deniq; ratione colorum aut est candidus, aut rubicundus seu sanguineus, & lucidus: & quidem in eo notatur tempus tum apparitionis, tum durationis. Postea plura de Cometis.
units.tr: A comet is sometimes motionless, sometimes mobile, and its motion is either simple or varied. Then, by reason of its shape, a comet is either round and hairy, or bearded and elongated. Finally, by reason of colour, it is either white, or reddish or blood-coloured, and bright; and in it is noted the time both of its appearance and of its duration. More on comets below.

units.la: Superest Evanescens meteoron, quod ob paucitatem materiae citius dissipatur, ut Fulmen, quod est exhalatio calida & sicca, crassior, magisq; viscosa in nube densa intercepta & conclusa, & per [illegible, ~8 letters] inflammata, atq; e nube magno impetu excussa & deorsum decidens. Fulminis adjuncta sunt Tonitru & Fulgur. Tonitru est sonus, quem sicca exhalatio, intra nubem magnam & den-sam conclusa, & ictu vehementi eam disrumpens, efficit. Fulgur seu coruscatio est flammae micatio, ab exhalationibus accensis & e nube erumpentibus exorta.
units.tr: There remains the evanescent meteor, which, because of the scantness of its matter, is quickly dissipated, such as lightning (fulmen). This is a hot and dry exhalation, thicker and more viscous, intercepted and enclosed in a dense cloud, [illegible], kindled, and hurled from the cloud with great force, falling downward. Thunder and lightning-flash are joined to the lightning. Thunder is the sound which a dry exhalation, enclosed within a great and dense cloud, produces when it bursts the cloud with a violent blow. The lightning-flash, or flashing, is a flicker of flame arising from exhalations kindled and bursting out of the cloud.

units.la: Fulmen porro Senecae triplex est, terebrans, discutiens (cum quo aliquando lapis seu telum fulmineum ex multis fuliginosis & conglutinatis exhalationibus coagulatum una ejicitur) et urens.
units.tr: Moreover, according to Seneca, lightning is threefold: boring, shattering (with which sometimes a stone or lightning-bolt, coagulated from many sooty and conglutinated exhalations, is cast out together), and burning.

units.la: Apparens ignitum meteoron est Chasma, quod speciem exhibet aperien-tis se & dehiscentis coeli, quando scili-cet exhalatio densa & viscosa, serena no-cte ad summam aeris oram evecta, in ex-tremis partibus, quae rariores sunt, in-flammatur, mediis vero densioribus non accensis; tunc enim propter album il-lum & luminosum partium extrema-rum, & nigrum seu caeruleum Medii colorem, coelum discedere videtur.
units.tr: The apparent fiery meteor is the chasm, which presents the appearance of heaven opening and gaping. This happens when a dense and viscous exhalation, carried on a clear night to the uppermost edge of the air, is kindled in its outermost parts, which are rarer, while the denser middle parts are not kindled. For then, because of the white and luminous colour of the outer parts and the black or blue colour of the middle, heaven seems to part.

units.la: CAPUT Undecimum. DE METEORIS EX UTROQVE, FUMO ET VAPORE, GENITIS, ubi de Ventis.
units.tr: CHAPTER 11. ON METEORS PRODUCED FROM BOTH, SMOKE AND VAPOUR, AND ON WINDS.

units.la: Actenus fuerunt meteora ex alterutro tantum halitu generata; ex utroq; simul, vapore & fumo, quæ fiunt, dicuntur aërea, quia aëris vehementius impulsi similitudinem quandam habent: suntque vel in aëre, vel in terræ viscéribus.
units.tr: Hitherto the meteors have been generated from only one of the two exhalations. Those produced from both together, vapour and smoke, are called aerial, because they have a certain likeness to air violently driven. They occur either in the air or in the bowels of the earth.

units.la: In aëre fit Ventus, qui dicitur exhalatio multa & copiosa, quæ à terra progressa, ab occurrente frigore repulsa & repressa, paulatim in obliquum retorquetur, & cum impetu per aërem ruit.
units.tr: In the air arises the wind, which is a large and abundant exhalation. It rises from the earth, is repelled and checked by the cold it meets, is gradually turned aside obliquely, and rushes through the air with force.

units.la: Ventus ab aëre differt. Aër dicitur tenuissimus spiritus, leni afflatu (si movetur) recreans; Ventus vero crassior & concitatior.
units.tr: The wind differs from the air. Air is called the most tenuous spirit, refreshing with a gentle breath when it is moved; but the wind is thicker and more violent.

units.la: Efficiens causa Ventorum Prima est vel Secunda.
units.tr: The efficient cause of winds is either first or second.

units.la: Prima seu Universalis est Deus, qui Elementarem regionem, harum impressionum domicilium, veluti materiam artifici, æthereæ subjecit. Ipse enim dixit, & facta sunt.
units.tr: The first, or universal, cause is God, who subjected the elementary region, the home of these impressions, to the heavenly region as clay to the craftsman. For he spoke, and they were made.

units.la: Secunda est Remota aut Proxima.
units.tr: The second cause is either remote or proximate.

units.la: De ventis. Remota, calor & virtus radiorum solari-um, aliorum̄ siderum, quorum virtute materies è terræ visceribūs extracta sublevatur, & ad percussionem aëris præparatur.
units.tr: The remote cause of winds is the heat and power of the rays of the sun and of the other stars, by whose power the matter is drawn up out of the bowels of the earth and made ready for the stirring of the air.

units.la: Proxima est, tùm frigus media aëris regionis materiam sursum intentem repercutiens & ad latera propellens, tùm alia multa exhalationes, priorem subsequentes, & infernè eam agitantes.
units.tr: The proximate cause is both the cold of the middle region of the air, which drives back the matter tending upward and pushes it sideways, and the many other exhalations that follow the earlier one and drive it from below.

units.la: Materia ventorum est item remota vel propinqua.
units.tr: The matter of winds is likewise remote or proximate.

units.la: Remota est, exhalatio calida & sicca, ex terra & aqua educta, & aëri conjuncta. Non vero omnis, sed moderatè calida & sicca.
units.tr: The remote matter is a warm and dry exhalation drawn out of earth and water and joined to the air. Yet not every such exhalation, but only one moderately warm and dry.

units.la: Propinqua est, exhalatio frigida & sicca. Etsi enim materia sit calida per vim Solis: tamen in nubem frigidam impingens, ipsa etiam frigefacta vi deprimitur, in infimam regionem, & lateraliter movetur.
units.tr: The proximate matter is a cold and dry exhalation. For although the matter is warmed by the force of the sun, when it strikes against a cold cloud it is itself chilled, is forced down by that force into the lowest region, and is moved sideways.

units.la: Forma ventorum consistit in tortuosa agitatione facta à conflictu halituum, in aëre lu-ctantium.
units.tr: The form of winds consists in a twisting agitation produced by the collision of vapours struggling together in the air.

units.la: Halitus enim cum sint sicci, naturaliter sursum ad locum germanum tendunt, sed aliquò usq; delati repelluntur, ut in proprio levitatis loco quiescere nò possint, sed violentia quadam contra naturā deorsum dejiciuntur, ut in contrarias partes ferantur, & sic inter se digladiantes aërem verberent & ventum faciant.
units.tr: For since the vapours are dry, they naturally tend upward to their proper place; but when they have been carried some way up they are repelled, so that they cannot rest in their own place of lightness, and by a certain violence, contrary to nature, they are thrown downward, so that they are borne in opposite directions; and so, fighting against one another, they beat the air and make the wind.

units.la: Cæterum Ventus est Regularis, vel Erraticus seu irregularis?
units.tr: Moreover, is the wind regular, or erratic and irregular?

units.la: Regularis, qui ex certa mundi regione oritur: Estq; indefinitus vel status.
units.tr: Regular winds are those that arise from a fixed region of the world. These are either indefinite or fixed.

units.la: Indefinitus, qui non spirat ad certum temporis terminum. Estq; hic vel princeps seu cardinalis, vel principi adjunctus, seu collateralis.
units.tr: Indefinite winds are those that do not blow for a fixed term of time. These are either principal or cardinal, or adjoined to a principal wind, that is, collateral.

units.la: Princeps seu cardinalis, à mundi cardine quopiam spirat, ejusq; qualitatem induit, ut ab ortu æquinoctiali spirat Subsolanus: Ab occasu æquinoctiali Zephyrus seu Favonius: A septentrione Aquilo: A meridie Auster.
units.tr: The principal or cardinal winds blow from some pivot of the world and take on its quality: the Subsolanus blows from the equinoctial east; the Zephyrus or Favonius from the equinoctial west; the Aquilo from the north; the Auster from the south.

units.la: Principibus adjuncti seu collaterales venti sunt, qui ad latera illorum tanquam socii adjiciuntur, & quidem singulis bini. Subsolano ab ortu solstitiali additus est Cæcias seu Hellespontus: ab ortu Brumali Eurus seu Vulturnus. Zephyrum ab occasu solstitiali comitatur Caurus seu Corus, qui & Olympias dicitur: ob occasu hyberno λύψ [?] seu Africus. Aquiloni versus ortum additus est Boreas; versus occasum Circeus. Austro versus ortum Brumalem Euronotus; versus occasum Libonotus.
units.tr: The winds adjoined to the principals, or collateral winds, are those added to their sides as companions, two to each of the principals. To the Subsolanus, from the solstitial east, is added the Caecias or Hellespontus; from the winter east, the Eurus or Vulturnus. The Zephyrus is accompanied from the solstitial west by the Caurus or Corus, which is also called Olympias; from the winter west, by Lips [λύψ] or Africus. To the Aquilo, toward the east, is added the Boreas; toward the west, the Circius. To the Auster, toward the winter east, the Euronotus; toward the west, the Libonotus.

units.la: Stati venti sunt, qui certo & stato anni tempore recurrunt, ut sunt Etesiae. Ornithiae, seu Chelidoniae. Etesiae sunt venti Aquilonares, qui circa caniculae ortum 40. dies perflant, & Syrii ardorem flatu suo mitigant. Chelidoniae verno tempore circa hirundinum adventum 9. diebus spirant.
units.tr: Fixed winds are those that return at a certain and settled time of the year, such as the Etesiae, the Ornithiae or Chelidoniae. The Etesiae are northerly winds that blow for forty days about the rising of the Dog Star and soften the heat of the Syrius by their breath. The Chelidoniae blow for nine days in spring, about the arrival of the swallows.

units.la: Erratici venti seu repentini uspiam videntur oberrare vel cum igne, vel sine igne: & quidem cum pluviis, vel sine pluviis. Cum pluviis, ut sunt Exhydriae, ventus scilicet impetuosissimus, qui e nube impulsa erumpens cum imbribus & grandinibus grassatur & omnia prosternit.
units.tr: Erratic or sudden winds seem to wander about anywhere, either with fire or without fire; and indeed, either with rain or without rain. Those with rain are such as the Exhydriae, namely a most violent wind which bursts out of a driven cloud and rages with showers and hail and levels everything.

units.la: Sine pluviis est Ecnephias & Turbo. Ecnephias seu procella est ventus repentinus & tumultuosus, qui ob materiae subtilitatem altius vagans terram elevat, aeremque obscurat.
units.tr: Without rain are the Ecnephias and the Turbo. The Ecnephias, or storm, is a sudden and tumultuous wind which, because of the fineness of its matter, roams higher and raises the earth and darkens the air.

units.la: Turbo est ventus repentinus, qui effracta nube erumpens, & in gyrum contortus obvia quaeque corripit, sursum attollit, & instar rotae versat.
units.tr: The Turbo is a sudden wind which, when a cloud is broken open, bursts out, is twisted into a whirl, seizes whatever lies in its way, lifts it up on high, and whirls it like a wheel.

units.la: Cum igne spirat Præster, qui est halitus ex repercussu ignem ex parte concipiens & inardescens depressæ nubis specu erumpens, proxima & prosternens & amburens.
units.tr: The wind that blows with fire is the Praester, a vapour which, by reflection, partly takes fire and catches flame, and bursts out from the hollow of a pressed-down cloud, and tears up and scorches whatever is nearby.

units.la: In terrę visceribus fit Terra motus, qui est agitatio seu concussio terræ, orta ex conflictu & impulsu spirituum in telluris cavernis compactorum, & obstructis meatibus erumpere pugnantium.
units.tr: In the bowels of the earth arises the earthquake, which is the agitation or shaking of the earth, arising from the collision and impact of spirits packed into the caverns of the earth, which, fighting to break out with their passages blocked, struggle to escape.

units.la: Causa ejus Prima Deus est; Secunda remota calor est cœlestis, proxima, spiritus in terra cavernosa constricti: De terræ motu videris Elegantem disputationem, Dn. Keckermanni.
units.tr: Its first cause is God; its remote second cause is the heavenly heat; its proximate cause is the spirit pent up in the hollow earth. On earthquakes you may consult the excellent disputation of Mr. Keckermann.

units.la: Hactenus meteororum fuit genus, ex halitibus conflatū[?]: Præterea ex quorundam sententia aëream & cœlestem quæ-dam meteora splendentia assumunt ma-teriā. Aëream dicunt, quia licet aër sua natura sit fluxus & rarus, ut per se fugiat visu, cogi tamē aliqua affectione potest, ut lumen finiat, coloréq; reddat: neq; id tantū ob mixtione cujusdam, sed aër in sua simplicitate & puritate cogi ita putatur. Quò purior est cū addensatur, eò propius accedit ad sidereā naturā & perspicuā, ac candidiore cū splendore exhibet colore: pura n. addensata sunt candida. Ætherem quoq; in morem puri aëris circumfluum, & spatia siderea explentem hujus sententiæ Patroni ponunt, & hunc alicubi se ipso densiorem ab externo aliquo principio evadere posse, atque exsplendere more stellæ, & visu occurrere, si vasta sit moles, illis nihil habet absurdi. Quod ita constitit conspicuú, motu alius causæ disgregari iterum potest: etsi cum disgregans non urgeat, satis diu quoq; in eo statu permanere potest: maximè tamen dissipatur in via stellarum, ubi motus & virtus disgregans major est.
units.tr: So far the kind of meteors formed from vapours. In addition, according to some opinions, certain shining meteors take their matter from the air and the heavens. They say they are aerial because, although air by its nature is fluid and rare, so that by itself it escapes the sight, it can nevertheless be condensed by some affection so as to terminate light and give colour. And they think air is condensed in this way not only by some mixture, but in its own simplicity and purity. The purer it is when condensed, the closer it comes to the starry and transparent nature and shows a whiter splendour of colour, since pure condensed things are white. The defenders of this opinion also hold that the ether, flowing around like pure air and filling the starry spaces, can, at some point, by some external principle, condense itself more densely than before, and shine out like a star and present itself to sight, if its mass is large. There is nothing absurd in this. Once it has become visible in this way, it can again be dispersed by the motion of another cause; yet, since the dispersing cause does not press on it, it can also remain in that state for a long time. It is, however, most of all dissipated in the path of the stars, where the motion and power of dispersion are greater.

units.la: Sidera perpetua nihilominus unde quaq; radios dispergunt, quanquam non appareant semper oculis, quod majoris luminis actus visum occupet, ne possit admitti minor. Quando itaq; lumen intra radiorum ambitum existens corpus tangit, ibiq; finitur, præsertim in summa concretione aerea vel ætherea[?], quod alias fit in nube per colores, parelia, iridessi, &c. id multo nobilius & præstantius fieri in superiore regione putandum est.
units.tr: Nevertheless, the perpetual stars scatter their rays on every side, although they do not always appear to the eyes, because the greater light occupies the sight, so that the lesser cannot be admitted. When therefore a light that exists within the circuit of its rays touches a body and is terminated there, especially in a very dense aerial or ethereal mass, which elsewhere happens in a cloud through colours, parhelia, rainbows, and so on, we must think this happens far more nobly and excellently in the higher region.

units.la: Huc referunt Cometas in regione superiore, ultra turbas aereas resplendentes instar stellæ: Etsi nubes candida, in altitudinem elevata, & divinitus excitata, & ad lumen stellę in modum repræsentandū dispositā, iisdem materia possit esse. Huc referunt etiam <bl>Ρ</bl> Trajectiones & Stellas cadentes: illa enim est & regio addensati ætheris perpetua: hæ vero non semper ardent, sed splendorem duntaxat trahunt, sicut & in muscis, similibus levibus & viscosis conspicimus. E cum prope terram venerint, extra refractionem videntur extingui, cum duntaxat splendor ob mutatum locum & dispositionem evanescat. Hæc ita Philosophi varie de sublimi meteororū, & non satis explicata materia. Scio alios aliter meteora tractare.
units.tr: To this they refer the comets, shining in the upper region beyond the aerial disturbances, like a star. Yet a white cloud, raised high and stirred up by divine power and arranged to represent the light of a star, could be the same matter. To this they refer also the Trajectiones and falling stars. The former belong to the region of the perpetually condensed ether; the latter do not always burn, but only draw a splendour, as we see also in the flies and similar light and viscous things. When they come near the earth they are seen to go out beyond refraction, since the splendour simply fades because of the changed place and arrangement. These things the philosophers have variously said about the lofty meteors, and about a matter not sufficiently explained. I know that others treat the meteors differently.

units.la: CAPUT DUODECIMUM. ORYCTICA PERIPATETICA, SEU DE METALLIS EX DOCTRINA PERIPATETICORUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 12. PERIPATETIC ORYCTICS, OR ON METALS ACCORDING TO THE DOCTRINE OF THE PERIPATETICS.

units.la: Actenus de Meteoria egimus, & Meteora explicavimus: Sequitur corpus Nerterum, quod subtus in terra generatur: diciturq; Fossile, quia è terra effoditur. Nεφλεφον, inferius, infra positum, à νέφε, vel νέφεν, subtus, infra. Nerterum igitur opponitur Meteoro, quod sublime sonat.
units.tr: Hitherto we have dealt with meteors and explained them. There follows the corpus Nerterum, which is generated beneath the earth. It is called Fossile because it is dug out of the earth. Nephlephon [Νεφλεφον] means lower, placed underneath, from nephe or nephen [νέφε, νέφεν], beneath, below. The Nerterum is therefore opposed to the meteor, a word that sounds of what is on high.

units.la: Corpus Nerterum ac fosile est Metallum vel Lapis.
units.tr: A Nerterum body, whether fossil or metallic, is either a metal or a stone.

units.la: Corporum fosilium & Nerterorum metallicorū doctrina dici potest Oryctice.
units.tr: The doctrine of fossil bodies and metallic Nerterums may be called Oryctics.

units.la: Hæc tùm Peripatetica est, tùm Chymica.
units.tr: This is both Peripatetic and Chymical.

units.la: Peripatetica ex Aristotelicorum placitis deducta, docet Metallū esse perfectè mixtū corpus, ex vaporibus aqueis magis quàm terreis, crassis tamen & viscosis à calore & frigore, fosile, & durum, quod ab igne liquescere & malleo diduci potest.
units.tr: The Peripatetic account, drawn from the tenets of the Aristotelians, teaches that a metal is a perfectly mixed body, made of watery vapours rather than earthy ones, yet thick and viscous through heat and cold. It is fossil and hard, and can be melted by fire and beaten out with a hammer.

units.la: Calor enim primum miscet bene, temperat, decoquit materiam, humorem viscosum. Hæc deinde à frigore condensata & consolidata in certum metallum efformatur.
units.tr: For heat first mixes the viscous moisture well, tempers it, and cooks the matter. Then this, condensed and solidified by cold, is shaped into a definite metal.

units.la: Peripatetica Schola duplicem halitum in terra visceribus latere statuit: unum aridum, hoc est, magis terreum quàm aqueum: alterum humidum & glutinosum, hoc est, magis aqueum quàm terreum: ex illo duriora fossilia, lapides nimirum, concrescere, ex hoc vero metalla proprie sic dicta produci.
units.tr: The Peripatetic school holds that two kinds of exhalation lie hidden in the bowels of the earth. One is dry, that is, more earthy than watery; the other is moist and glutinous, that is, more watery than earthy. From the former, harder fossils, namely stones, solidify; from the latter, what are properly called metals are produced.

units.la: Metallum vero est purum, adeoq; nobilius, aut impurū, adeoq; ignobilius.
units.tr: A metal is either pure, and so nobler, or impure, and so baser.

units.la: Purum in quo facta est materię decoctio magis exquisita, ut Aurum & Argen-tum.
units.tr: Pure, that in which the cooking of the matter has been more exquisite, such as gold and silver.

units.la: Aurum est metallum purum splendidissimum, tenuissimum, mollissimum & nobilissimum, partibus constans bene calore compactis, densis & flavis.
units.tr: Gold is a pure metal, most splendid, finest, softest and noblest, consisting of parts well compacted by heat, dense and yellow.

units.la: Nobilissimum est: quia uni auro ex-omnibus metallis praeter tenuitatem nihil deperit igne, (nisi venenum conjuncto:) imo igne sine detrimento sui fit purius & melius. 2.Purisi-mum est: quia minima ac pene nulla, dum li-quatur, exhalant incrementa: & neq; rubigo, neq; ærugo aurum conterit, aut ejus bonitatem vel pondus imminuit: usu etiam nihil deperit. 3. Mirum in modum ductile est, adeo etiam ut neri ac texile fieri possit. 4. Maxime suavem odorem habet inter metalla.
units.tr: Most noble: because of all metals gold alone loses nothing in fire except its thinness (unless poison is combined with it); indeed, by fire it becomes purer and better without loss of its own substance. 2. Most pure: because while it melts it gives off almost no waste at all, and neither rust nor verdigris wears away gold, nor diminishes its goodness or weight; it loses nothing even by use. 3. Wonderfully ductile, so much so that it can be drawn into thread and woven into cloth. 4. It has the sweetest smell among metals.

units.la: OBRYZUM aurum dicitur optimum: Quidam putant vocem corruptam, quasi Ophi-ryzum, id est, ex Ophir advectum.
units.tr: Obryzum is said to be the best gold. Some think the word is corrupted, as if it were Ophryzum, that is, brought from Ophir.

units.la: Argentum est Metallum purum ex vapore minus excalefacto, & qua-dantenus impuriore concretum, quàm aurum. Argentum non est ita purum, quàm aurum, quia cum funditur non ut aurum igni resistit, sed aliquid ex eo deperit. Ac laboris maximi est, ut igne expurgetur, adeò terræ sordibus est impactum. Firmitudine & tenuitate substantiæ argentum propè accedit ad aurum, eodemq; frigidius est.
units.tr: Silver is a pure metal, formed from vapour less heated and somewhat more impure than that of gold. Silver is not as pure as gold, because when it is melted it does not resist fire as gold does, but some of it is lost. It takes the greatest labour to be purged by fire, so much is it clogged with the dregs of earth. In firmness and fineness of substance silver comes close to gold, and it is also colder.

units.la: Impuriora adeoq; ignobiliora metalla sunt, quæ ex impuriore constant materia.
units.tr: Less pure, and therefore baser, metals are those which consist of more impure matter.

units.la: Ex his quædam plus humoris: quædam plus terræ habent.
units.tr: Of these, some have more moisture and some have more earth.

units.la: Plus humoris participant Plumbum & Stannum.
units.tr: Lead and tin partake of more moisture.

units.la: Plumbum est metallum impurius, ex humore crasso seculento, malè concocto, genitum.
units.tr: Lead is a more impure metal, produced from thick, foul moisture that is badly concocted.

units.la: Estq; pro materiæ diversitate & calore quo coquitur, nigrū aut candidum.
units.tr: According to the diversity of its matter and the heat by which it is cooked, it is either black or white.

units.la: Nigrum, nobis Bley/minus ex impuriore materia est elaboratum, ideoque vilioris pretii.
units.tr: Black, which we call Bley, is elaborated from more impure matter and is therefore of lower price.

units.la: Album seu candidum est plenius percoctum, ideoq; est levius & rarius; aliis dicitur Stannum.
units.tr: White or bright lead is more thoroughly cooked and therefore lighter and rarer. Others call it tin.

units.la: Stannum est metallum album, ex multo, neque ita puro humore, extrinsecus albo,intrinsecus vero rubro,& ex terreo non bene digesto, genitum.
units.tr: Tin is a white metal, produced from much moisture that is not so pure, white outwardly but red inwardly, and from undigested earthy matter.

units.la: Plus terræ habent Æs & Ferrum, quibus additur Orichalcum.
units.tr: Bronze and iron have more earth, and orichalc is added to them.

units.la: Æs est metallum impurius,mixtione terræ magis quàm humore concretum, medium quiddam inter ferrum & aurum, vel argentum.
units.tr: Bronze is a more impure metal, formed more by a mixture of earth than of moisture. It is a middle thing between iron and gold or silver.

units.la: Ejus species est æs cyprium,quod copiosè nascitur in Insula Cypro,unde Cuprum dicitur.
units.tr: Its species is Cyprian bronze, which grows plentifully on the island of Cyprus, whence it is called cuprum.

units.la: Ferrum est metallum impurissimum, firmissimum & durissimum,ex plurimo terreo crudo,& adurente & modico humore etiam impuro, generatum.
units.tr: Iron is the most impure metal, very firm and very hard, generated from a great deal of raw, burning earthy matter and a moderate moisture, also impure.

units.la: Licet sit durissimum, assiduo tamen usu conteritur, quoniam ad ejus generationem minus humoris, plus vero terræ concurrit. Ferrum rubiginescens crescit Mathematicè, sed corrumpitur Physicè, quia aliquid de meliore substantia decedit.
units.tr: Although it is very hard, it is nevertheless worn down by constant use, since less moisture and more earth go into its generation. Rusting iron grows mathematically but decays physically, because something of its better substance departs.

units.la: Ferrum igne sæpius expurgatum fit cha-lybs. Chalybs igitur est ferrum densissimum igne purgatum, & in aqua restinctum.
units.tr: Iron often purged by fire becomes steel. Steel, therefore, is very dense iron purged by fire and quenched in water.

units.la: Orichalcum est æs factitium & percolatum colore auri, sed magis flavescéte.
units.tr: Orichalc is artificial bronze, refined to the colour of gold but more yellowish.

units.la: Metallis porrò affinia sunt, Metallica quae dicuntur, funtq; mediae naturae in-ter metalla & lapides.
units.tr: Next, akin to metals are those called metallic substances, which are of an intermediate nature between metals and stones.

units.la: Horum alia liquari possunt: alia ut liquari nequeant, molliora tamen sunt, ut in lapides indurescant.
units.tr: Of these, some can be melted; others cannot be melted, yet they are softer, so that they harden into stones.

units.la: Primi generis sunt, succi concreti quidam: Secundi generis, terrae metallares.
units.tr: Of the first kind are certain concrete juices; of the second kind, metallic earths.

units.la: Succi concreti sunt Sal, Alumen, Bitumen, Vitriolum.
units.tr: Concrete juices are salt, alum, bitumen and vitriol.

units.la: Sal est corpus metallicum friabile, ex succo humido aqueo, & crasso terreo, mixtis & decoctis genitum.
units.tr: Salt is a friable metallic body, produced from a moist watery juice and thick earthy matter, mixed and cooked together.

units.la: Vim habet abstergendi, expurgandi, abstringendi, dissipandi, extenuandi.
units.tr: It has the power to cleanse, purge, astringe, dissipate and thin.

units.la: Estq; aut Naturalis aut Artificialis: Ille natura gignitur, & dicitur alias Fossilis: hunc ars facit, Factitiusque vel co-ctus nominatur.
units.tr: It is either natural or artificial. The former is generated by nature and is also called fossil; the latter is made by art and is called factitious or boiled.

units.la: Fossilis reperitur vel in terra, vel extra terram.
units.tr: Fossil salt is found either in the earth or outside the earth.

units.la: In terra repertus aut cædītur in montibus: vel e campis effoditur, arenis, quibus tegitur, prius remotis.
units.tr: Found in the earth is either cut in mountains, or dug out of plains, after the sands covering it have first been removed.

units.la: Hujus quamvis variae sint differen-tiae, diversisq; locis reperiantur, quatuor tamen potissimum hodie sunt cognitae: Sal Ammoniacus, Sal Gemmae, Sal Ni-trum, & Sal Indicus.
units.tr: Although there are various kinds of this, and it is found in diverse places, four are chiefly known today: ammoniac salt, rock salt, saltpetre and Indian salt.

units.la: Sal Ammoniacus est Sal fossilis, amarissimus, sub arena ardentissima in Cyrenaica erutus: unde etiam Cyrenaicus dicitur.
units.tr: Ammoniac salt is a fossil salt, very bitter, dug out from under the most scorching sand in Cyrenaica. Whence it is also called Cyrenaic.

units.la: Sal Gemma est Sal fossilis, e fodinis erutus, Cristalli in morem translucens & candidus.
units.tr: Rock salt is a fossil salt, dug out of mines, translucent like crystal and white.

units.la: Sal Nitrum seu Petrosum est, quod ex coagulato humore in locis subterraneis humidis instar stiriae salsae dependet, aut instar frigoris congelati in parietibus nitet. Hodie etiam arte Nitrum colligitur.
units.tr: Saltpetre, or stony salt, is that which hangs down like a salty stalactite from humour coagulated in damp subterranean places, or gleams on walls like congealed frost. Today saltpetre is also collected by art.

units.la: Sal Indicus est Sal quadantenus nigricans, vel subrufus, in India ex monte Oremeno excisus.
units.tr: Indian salt is a salt somewhat blackish or reddish, cut in India from Mount Oremenus.

units.la: Extra terram Sal repertus effoditur ex aquis, & dicitur vel Fontalis, quando fontis rivuli calore Solis siccati, in salem convertuntur: vel Fluvialis, quando fluvius aliquis ramenta fert, quae in salem densantur: vel Stagnalis a Stagnis, quae sale aestuant. vel denique Marinus, quando in extremis littoribus tenuis quidam Sal gignitur.
units.tr: Salt found outside the earth is dug out of waters. It is called fountain salt when the rivulets of a spring, dried by the heat of the sun, turn into salt; or river salt when some river carries sediment which thickens into salt; or pond salt, from ponds which seethe with salt; or finally sea salt, when a thin salt is generated on the outermost shores.

units.la: Sal coctus fit ex aquis, vel marinis, fluvialibus, lacustribus, salsis fontanis, putealibus, vel etiam ex muria nativa tiva fontium, ut in Hallis Saxoniæ, in Salinis Thuringiæ & Hafsiæ ad Altendor-phum & Niddam, &c.
units.tr: Boiled salt is made from waters, whether sea, river, lake, salty spring or well, or even from the natural brine of springs, as at the salt-works in Halle in Saxony, in Thuringia and Hesse at Altendorf and Nidda, and elsewhere.

units.la: Alumen definitore Plinio, est falsu-go, vel falsus sudor terræ, ex aqua limoque concrescens.
units.tr: Alum, according to Pliny's definition, is a salty efflorescence or salty sweat of the earth, condensed from water and mud.

units.la: Estq; candidum aut nigrum.
units.tr: It is either white or black.

units.la: Candidum, quod optimum censetur, aut est liquidum, aut spissum.
units.tr: White alum, which is judged best, is either liquid or thick.

units.la: Liquidum molle, pingue & limpidum existit, cui immersa charta etiam pesfi-ma & siccata, atramentum retinet, ne perfluat.
units.tr: Liquid alum is soft, oily and clear. A paper, even a very poor one, dipped into it and dried retains ink so that it does not run through.

units.la: Spissum vel Rotundum est vel scisi-le: illud formam habet sacchari: hoc in capillamenta quædam canescentia dehiscens videtur.
units.tr: Thick alum, or rounded alum, is either compact or fissile. The former has the form of sugar; the latter seems to split into greyish filaments.

units.la: Nigrum in Cypro invenitur, quo purgatur aurum.
units.tr: Black alum is found in Cyprus, and gold is purged with it.

units.la: Bitumen est succus terræ, lentus, te-nax, pici similis, facilime ignem concipiens.
units.tr: Bitumen is a juice of the earth, viscous, tenacious, like pitch, and very easily catching fire.

units.la: Estquè Durum aut Liquidum.
units.tr: It is either hard or liquid.

units.la: Durum quod fortius concretum & te-nax est, instar terreæ glebæ, & carbonü.
units.tr: Hard bitumen, which is more firmly set and tenacious, is like an earthy clod or charcoal.

units.la: Hujus generis sunt Asphaltus, Pissa-sphaltus, & Succinum.
units.tr: Of this kind are asphalt, pissasphalt and amber.

units.la: Asphaltus est bitumen nigricans, pici simile, sed durius & magis inspissatum, splendidius, & minus male olens.
units.tr: Asphalt is blackish bitumen, like pitch, but harder and more thickened, shinier, and less foul-smelling.

units.la: Pissaphaltus est bitumen quodammodo nigricans, magis terrenę cōcretionis.
units.tr: Pissasphalt is bitumen somewhat blackish, of a more earthy consistency.

units.la: Succinum est bitumen & pinguedo terræ, ex maris æstu; Colore reperitur, vel flavo, vel pellucidiore, vel candido & obscuro: candidum autem pretiosissimum est.
units.tr: Amber is bitumen and fat of the earth, produced from the surge of the sea. It is found in colour either yellow, or more transparent, or white and dark; white amber, however, is the most precious.

units.la: Liquidum bitumen est, quod ut oleo-sus liquor diffluit; cujus species præstantiores sunt Naphtha, & Ambra Arabica.
units.tr: Liquid bitumen is that which flows like an oily liquor. The more excellent kinds are naphtha and Arabian amber.

units.la: Naphtha est bitumen liquidum, olei lentore & crassitie, tantam vim ignis habens, ut ignes ex longinquo ad se tra-hat & inflammetur.
units.tr: Naphtha is a liquid bitumen, with the thickness and density of oil, and it has such a strength of fire that it draws flames to itself from a distance and catches fire.

units.la: E petris profluens dicitur Petroleum, quasi dicas, naphtha petrea.
units.tr: Petroleum, flowing out of rocks, is so called, as if you were to say "stone naphtha".

units.la: Ambra est bitumen fragrantissimum; utcum pretiosissimis conferatur mercibus.
units.tr: Amber is a very fragrant bitumen, and it is compared with the most precious wares.

units.la: Nascitur circa Sichrim Arabiæ felicis oppidum.
units.tr: It arises near Sichrim, a town of Arabia Felix.

units.la: Vitriolum est succus concretus perspicuitatem vitream obtinens; dicitur & Chalchantum. Nativum in terræ venis, aut saxorum commisturis concretum reperitur.
units.tr: Copperas is a concreted juice with a glassy transparency; it is also called chalcanthum. It is found native, concreted in veins of the earth or in mixtures of rocks.

units.la: Porro succi, qui liquari nequeunt, in lapides tamen non indurantur, sunt: Auripigmentum, Sandaraca, Calx, Gypsum, Creta, Argilla, Terra sigillata, Terra Armenica.
units.tr: Moreover, the juices which cannot be liquefied but do not harden into stones are these: orpiment, sandarach, lime, gypsum, chalk, clay, sealed earth, and Armenian earth.

units.la: Auripigmentum seu Arsenicum est succus concretus lutei coloris, in picturis aureum colorem referens · calidum est & siccum in 2. gradu, & venenum præsentissimum. Vid. Scal. exerc. 102. sect. 2. 2[?].
units.tr: Orpiment, or arsenic, is a concreted juice of yellow colour, which in paintings represents a golden colour; it is hot and dry in the second degree, and a most immediate poison. See Scaliger, Exercitation 102, section 2, [2?].

units.la: Sandaraca est terra rufa, Cinnabaris colore, nihil ad luteum vergens, in metallicis venis plerumque cum auripigmento nascens, redolens Sulphuris virus. De hac Scal. exerc. 102. sect. 2. 2[?].
units.tr: Sandarach is a reddish earth, in colour like cinnabar, not inclining to yellow, usually arising in metallic veins together with orpiment, and smelling of the fumes of sulphur. On this see Scaliger, Exercitation 102, section 2, [2?].

units.la: Calx est terra siccior, lapide cocta, quæ postquam arserit, aqua incenditur, oleo extinguitur: viva dicitur, quia intus occultū ignem continet. De hac Scal. Exerc. 102. sect. 17. Item exerc. f[?]. sect. 8 & 9.
units.tr: Lime is a drier earth, made from stone by burning, which, once it has been burned, is set alight by water and put out by oil; it is called quicklime, because it holds a hidden fire within. On this see Scaliger, Exercitation 102, section 17. Likewise Exercitation [f?], section 8 and 9.

units.la: Gypsum est terra candida, tenax & lævis, calci cognata, sed non ita calida, quæ ex summa tellure effoditur.
units.tr: Gypsum is a white, tough and smooth earth, akin to lime but not so hot, which is dug out of the highest part of the earth.

units.la: Creta est terra tenax, albissima, in Insula Creta fossilis.
units.tr: Chalk is a tough, very white earth, found fossil on the island of Crete.

units.la: Argilla est terra pinguis & lenta, è qua fiunt figulina vasa.
units.tr: Clay is a rich and sticky earth, from which potters' vessels are made.

units.la: Terra sigillata vel Lemnia, est portio terræ valdè rubens, in Infula Lemno effossa, & Dianæ sacerdotis sigillo obsignata. Effoditur hodie etiam in Silesia & Hafsia terra Lemnia non deterior: Venenis resistit. Scal. exerc.93.&33.sect.2.
units.tr: Sealed earth, or Lemnian earth, is a portion of very red earth, dug on the island of Lemnos and stamped with the seal of the priestess of Diana. Lemnian earth no worse than this is dug up today also in Silesia and Hesse; it resists poisons. See Scaliger, Exercitation 93 and 33, section 2.

units.la: Terra Armenica est portio terræ in Armenia effossa, colore pallido, egregiè siccans.
units.tr: Armenian earth is a portion of earth dug in Armenia, of pale colour, which dries excellently.

units.la: CAPUT XIII. DE ORYCTICA CHYMICA seu DE METALLIS ET METALLICIS, ex doctrina & experientia Chymicorum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. ON CHEMICAL ORYCTICS, OR ON METALS AND METALLIC THINGS, from the teaching and experience of the chemists.
