units.la: ORYCTICE[?] explicat natura Mineralium & Lapidum.
units.tr: Oryctics explains the nature of minerals and stones.

units.la: Mineralia sunt Metalla & Metallis affinia.
units.tr: Minerals are metals and things related to metals.

units.la: Metallum est corpus minerale vi virtutis metallorum seminariæ in terræ chalchantosæ minera è mercuriali succo sulphureoq; spiritu, caloris digerētis vehiculo constitutū, & in substantiâ fusile, malleoq; extensilem conformatum.
units.tr: A metal is a mineral body, formed in the veins of the earth by the power of the seminal virtue of metals, from a mercurial juice and sulphurous spirit, with heat as the vehicle of digestion, and it is fusible in substance and shaped so as to be extensible under the hammer.

units.la: Metallorū tùm sunt affectiones communes, tùm genera.
units.tr: Metals have both common properties and kinds.

units.la: Metallorum affectiones communes sunt, fundi à calore, duci, & malleo extendi; combibere item argentum vivum, commisceri mutuo, & maximè in plumbo nigro; præterea reduci posse ad Mercurialem formam, transmutari seu in aliud metallum, seu vitrum, seu liquorem, seu pulverem sui generis; ab aqua regia solvi & corrodi; solvi item ab hydrargyro; frigore concrescere, & ob soliditatem in laminis metallicum tinnire, chalchantum ex se promere, &c.
units.tr: The common properties of metals are these: they are melted by heat, drawn out, and extended by the hammer; they likewise absorb quicksilver and mix readily with one another, especially in black lead; moreover, they can be reduced to a mercurial form, and transmuted either into another metal, or into glass, or into a liquor, or into a powder of their own kind; they are dissolved and corroded by aqua regia; they are likewise dissolved by hydrargyrum; they harden in cold, and by their solidity they ring like metal when formed into plates, and they give off verdigris from themselves, and so on.

units.la: Genera metallorum sequuntur: Metallorum enim quædam sunt perfecta, quædam imperfecta.
units.tr: The kinds of metals follow. For some metals are perfect, and some imperfect.

units.la: Metalla perfecta sunt, quæ natura perduxit ad absolutum metallici generis terminum: Itaque cum ea contendat semper ad optimum, quod in quolibet genere fieri potest: etiam absoluta & optima vocantur, quæ perfecta: qualia sunt non tantum essentialibus principiis optimè constituta, & crasin præstantissimam in genere metallorum nacta, sed & qualitatibus, aliisq; adjunctis consummata.
units.tr: Perfect metals are those which nature has brought to the complete end of the metallic kind. Since nature always strives for the best that can be achieved in any kind, those metals are also called absolute and best which are perfect. Such are the metals that are not only constituted in the best way with respect to their essential principles and have obtained the most excellent temperament among metals, but are also brought to completion in their qualities and accompanying properties.

units.la: Est autem potissima nota perfectio-nis metallaris, fixitas perfecta : summus cum Mercurio consensus: exacta inspis-satio: quam pondus sequitur, quibus ad-stipulantur & alia, ut color, nitor, sonus, dilatatio exactissima, fusio, ignitio, &c.
units.tr: The chief mark of metallic perfection, however, is perfect fixity, the highest agreement with mercury, and exact compactness; weight follows these, and other things support them, such as colour, lustre, sound, the most exact dilatability, fusibility, ignitibility, and so on.

units.la: Corpora perfecta in metallis sunt duo: Aurum & Argentum.
units.tr: There are two perfect bodies among metals: gold and silver.

units.la: Aurum est metallum perfectum è Mer-curio maturissimo purissimoq;, vi sul-phuris præstantissimi, & unà ex ipso commistione optima tenacissimaq; fa-cta, constitutum, & citrina tinctura ex-ornatum.
units.tr: Gold is a perfect metal, constituted from very ripe and very pure mercury, by the power of the most excellent sulphur, and made into one by the best and most tenacious mixture of the two, and adorned with a lemon-yellow tincture.

units.la: Itaque nihil aliud est, quàm Mercu-rius optimè excoctus, & coagulatoq; con-stantissimè.
units.tr: Thus it is nothing other than mercury most perfectly digested and most constantly coagulated.

units.la: Unde & nata est fixitas & duratio in igne igneisq; maxima; pondus, densitas & tenacitas partium pertinacissima.
units.tr: Hence its fixity and its greatest endurance in fire and by fire, and its weight, density, and the most stubborn tenacity of its parts.

units.la: Nec ullum est, quod malleo ita dila-tari possit.
units.tr: Nor is there any substance that can be extended so much by the hammer.

units.la: In suo manifesto citrinum est, in oc-culto summam continet rubedinem: un-de & non tantùm tinctum ipsum est, sed & tincturam rubedinis confert abun-dantem, & seminarium principium sul-phuris phuris perfecti, unâ cum Mercurio absolutionis summæ.
units.tr: On the surface it is yellow, but in its hidden part it holds the highest redness; hence it not only is itself coloured, but also imparts an abundant tincture of redness, and it is the seminal principle of perfect sulphur, together with mercury of the highest completeness.

units.la: In fronte calidum, siccum moderatè; at in recessu igneam virtutem occultans.
units.tr: On the surface it is warm and moderately dry, but in its inner recesses it conceals a fiery virtue.

units.la: Itaq; & semen habet masculinum.
units.tr: For this reason it also has a masculine seed.

units.la: Eximii est splendoris, solarem imitans naturam.
units.tr: It has an outstanding brilliance, imitating the nature of the sun.

units.la: Quapropter & Chymicorum Sol est, & ob igneam virtutem in abscondito, Leo ruber; in terris item humano cordi, & leoninæ naturæ consentit.
units.tr: For this reason it is also the Sun of the chemists, and, because of its fiery virtue hidden within, a red lion; it also agrees with the human heart on earth and with the lion's nature.

units.la: In mineralibus maximè gaudet Mercurio absolutissimo, cum quo etiam intimè commiscetur plus omnibus metallis.
units.tr: Among minerals it especially delights in the most perfect mercury, with which it also mixes more intimately than with all other metals.

units.la: Tinctúram ejus æmulantur, auripigmentum, sandaraca, sulphur fixum, præcipitatus fixus Chrysammos, (ex quo auru olim factum per additamenta quædam) & Cinnabaris (in qua Picus ait auri & argenti principia inesse) rubra stibri tinctura fixa, &c.
units.tr: Its tincture is imitated by orpiment, realgar, fixed sulphur, fixed precipitate of Chrysammos (from which gold was once made by certain additions), and cinnabar (in which Pico says the principles of gold and silver are present), the red fixed tincture of antimony, and so on.

units.la: Argentum est metallum perfectum paulo infra aurum, albumq;[?] constans Mercurio prope fixo, & sulphure albo mundo, aliquantulum deficiente maturitate.
units.tr: Silver is a perfect metal, a little below gold, consisting of mercury nearly fixed and of pure white sulphur, lacking a little in maturity.

units.la: Itaq; non durat omnino in cæmen-to regali, antimonio, sulphure, cadmia, &c. solviturq; aqua fortis.
units.tr: Therefore it does not endure at all in royal cement, antimony, sulphur, cadmia, and so on, and it is dissolved by aqua fortis.

units.la: Permanet autem & absolvitur summo sui gradu in cineritio.
units.tr: However, it remains and is perfected to the highest degree of its nature in cupellation.

units.la: Dilatatur post aurum amplissimè subtilissimeq;, & in filamenta ducitur.
units.tr: After gold it is extended most widely and most finely, and it is drawn into threads.

units.la: Potestate est Lunare, Itaq; & in cœlo Lunæ ascribitur: in terra cerebro: in subterraneis argento vivo.
units.tr: In power it is lunar; therefore it is also ascribed to the moon in the heavens, to the brain on earth, and to quicksilver among subterranean things.

units.la: In artificio Philosophico tinctu-ram albam præbet, estq; mater partus Physici, in conjunctione cū Sole & Mercurio.
units.tr: In the philosophical work it yields a white tincture, and it is the mother of the physical offspring, in conjunction with the Sun and Mercury.

units.la: Minus compactum auro corpus habet.
units.tr: It has a body less compact than gold.

units.la: Itaq; & sonat, minusq; est ponderosum.
units.tr: Therefore it also rings, and is less heavy.

units.la: Tincturæ ejus æmulū quid est in cinnabari, hydrargyro, sublimato fixo, sale ammonio fixo, magnetide, sulphure albo fixo, hujusve sale, qui igne nō metuit.
units.tr: Something that imitates its tincture is found in cinnabar, quicksilver, fixed sublimate, fixed sal ammoniac, magnesia, fixed white sulphur, or its salt, which fears no fire.

units.la: Cognationem habet cum cœruleo, quæ colore etiam in occulto abscondit.
units.tr: It has a kinship with blue, which also hides its colour in secret.

units.la: Metallum imperfectum est, quod ex principiis metallicis impuris, fugacibus-que, quæ nec cœmentum nec fulmen sustinent perfectorum, constat.
units.tr: An imperfect metal is one that consists of impure and volatile metallic principles, which can endure neither the cupel nor the hammer of perfect metals.

units.la: Itaq; & ars adeo non aspirat, sed tan-tùm in perficiendis elaborat, quo modo & in hydrargyro.
units.tr: Therefore art does not aspire to it so much, but labours only in perfecting it, as it does also with quicksilver.

units.la: Imperfecta facile mutantur in speci-es cognatas inter se.
units.tr: Imperfect metals are easily changed into species that are related to one another.

units.la: Metalla imperfecta sunt duplicia: mollia & dura.
units.tr: Imperfect metals are of two kinds: soft and hard.

units.la: Mollia sunt, quæ funduntur citius, quàm igniantur.
units.tr: Soft metals are those that melt more readily than they are set on fire.

units.la: Itaq; constant hydrargyro humidio-re aquosioreq;, & minus excocto fixoq;, & sulphure adustili fusiliq; cito.
units.tr: Therefore they consist of a moister and more watery quicksilver, less digested and less fixed, and of a combustible sulphur that quickly melts.

units.la: Unde & frigidiora dicuntur, quod igneum principium sulphuris in eis sit paucum.
units.tr: Hence they are also called colder, because there is little fiery principle of sulphur in them.

units.la: Per artem indurari possunt, si sæpius extincta aquis fixatoriis, aut eis immacerata, postea ignibus lentis, donec humiditatis excessus sit deletus, torrean-tur, aut sæpius fundantur.
units.tr: They can be hardened by art, if they are often quenched in fixing waters, or steeped in them, and afterwards roasted over gentle fires until the excess of moisture is removed, or often melted.

units.la: Possunt item mollia in se mutuo verti, fierique alterum ex altero per additamenta, & lixivia mineralia, aliaque artifi-cia.
units.tr: Soft metals can also be turned into one another, and one can be made from the other by additions, mineral lyes, and other arts.

units.la: Mollia sunt duorum genêrum: Plum-bum candidum (seu stannum) & Plum-bum nigrū(quod & simpliciter plumbū.)
units.tr: Soft metals are of two kinds: white lead (or tin) and black lead (which is also simply called lead).

units.la: Plumbum candidum est metallum imperfectum, molle, album, splendens, cum livore quodam, constans Mercurio puriore, in genere imperfectorum, mollio re, fugacioreque quàm dura: stabiliore vero quàm plumbum nigrum, & magis excocto, & sulphureo albo, acri, sed minus maturo, quod in recessu tincturam citrinam & rubeam puram quodammodo gerit, manet tamen in igne pars quaedam utriusq; principii.
units.tr: White lead is an imperfect metal, soft, white, shining, with a certain bluish cast, consisting of purer quicksilver; among imperfect metals it is less soft and more volatile than the hard ones, but more stable than black lead, and more digested, and with white, sharp sulphur, but less ripe; in its inner recesses it bears in some measure a pure yellow and red tincture, yet a certain part of both principles remains in the fire.

units.la: Itaq; aliquid fixitatis habet, & quidem æqualis, quanquam sit plus de Mercurio, quàm Sulphure.
units.tr: Therefore it has some fixity, and indeed an equal amount, although there is more mercury than sulphur.

units.la: Propter mollitiem parum sonat: Et quia terrestritate quadá Mercurius comprehenditur, stridet in fusione & facilè excutitur.
units.tr: Because of its softness it gives little sound; and because mercury is held in by a certain earthiness, it crackles in melting and is easily shaken out.

units.la: Hydrargyro promptè jungitur: & ob id ad perfecta accedit propius, quemadmodum & majore puritate principiorum.
units.tr: It joins readily with quicksilver, and for that reason it comes nearer to the perfect metals, as it also does by the greater purity of its principles.

units.la: Unde & adhæret auro argentoquè pertinaciter, nec dimittit ea facilè, adeò ut etiam corrumpat, seu dissipet secum in igne fulminis aliquam eorum partem. Vertitur in plumbum nigrum pollutione & humefactione.
units.tr: Hence it also clings stubbornly to gold and silver and does not easily let them go, so much so that it even spoils them, or in the fire of the blast carries away some part of them with it. It is changed into black lead by pollution and moistening.

units.la: Ex eodem conficitur ablutione & exsiccatione conveniente, seu calcinatione ignea crebra, cum ablutione.
units.tr: The same is made by suitable washing and drying, or by frequent fiery calcination with washing.

units.la: (Alias etiam per eandem in plumbum nigrum abire potest, praesertim addito stibio.)
units.tr: (Otherwise it can also pass into black lead by the same means, especially with antimony added.)

units.la: Familiare est cum marcasitha stannea, quam bismuthum vocant.
units.tr: It is closely related to the tin-marcasite, which they call bismuth.

units.la: Calcinatione fit album Hispanicum, & vitrescit igne reverberii. Calx ejus.
units.tr: By calcination it becomes Spanish white, and it vitrifies in the reverberatory furnace. Its calx.

units.la: Reducitur inde in stannum, magno igne, & subitanea inductriaq; fusione.
units.tr: From this it is reduced back into tin by a great fire, and by a sudden induction and fusion.

units.la: Plumbum nigrum est metallum molle, imperfectum, lividius stanno, ex mercurio & sulphure leviter coagulatis, foetidis, impuris, terreis, quodammodo etiam arsenicali spiritu inquinatis, crudioribus tamen & humidioribus, quod lotione, admistione mercurii, & induratione in Plumbum album transit.
units.tr: Black lead is a soft, imperfect metal, more livid than tin, loosely coagulated from mercury and sulphur, fetid, impure, earthy, and somewhat polluted by an arsenical spirit, yet cruder and moister; it passes into white lead by washing, by the admixture of mercury, and by hardening.

units.la: Est & acre corrodens; itaq; in examine perfectorum adhibitum, imperfecta quaevis consumit, & secum in favilla scoriasve vertit.
units.tr: It is also a corrosive acid; therefore, when it is applied in the testing of perfect metals, it consumes any imperfect metals and turns them into dross or slag.

units.la: Ob mollitie & leve coagulatione principiorum funditur facilius[?] omni alio metallo.
units.tr: Because of its softness and the loose coagulation of its principles, it melts more easily than any other metal.

units.la: Nec potest calcinari facile, quia sul-phur ejus cum hydrargyro pertinaciter est conjunctum; quod non fit in stanno, ubi sulphur facilius effugit, & calcem re-linquit.
units.tr: Nor can it easily be calcined, because its sulphur is stubbornly joined to its mercury; this does not happen in tin, where the sulphur escapes more easily and leaves a calx behind.

units.la: Ob spiritus terreos acres, calcinat aurum & argentum vivum cogit.
units.tr: Because of its sharp earthy spirits, it calcines gold and forces quicksilver together.

units.la: Argento familiare est, & hydrargy-rum absumitur promte, & per artem e-tiam vertitur.
units.tr: It is familiar to silver; quicksilver is quickly consumed by it, and it is also transmuted by art.

units.la: Differt a stanno immundicie majore, humiditate, difficultate calcinationis, & copia majore sulphuris constantis.
units.tr: It differs from tin in greater filthiness, moisture, difficulty of calcination, and a greater quantity of constant sulphur.

units.la: Ejus naturae accedit Antimonii, ma-gis terrestre, foetidu, arsenicale & rapax.
units.tr: Antimony is of a similar nature, but more earthy, fetid, arsenical, and corrosive.

units.la: Metalla imperfecta dura sunt, quae ob siccum & terrestre sulphur, hydrargy-rumq; induratum igniuntur, antequam fundantur.
units.tr: Hard imperfect metals are those which, because of their dry and earthy sulphur and their hardened quicksilver, are set on fire before they melt.

units.la: Horum sulphur plus habet vitriolati succi.
units.tr: Of these, sulphur contains more of the vitriolic juice.

units.la: Itaq; magis ferreum est & crassum, potestq; utrumq; in se mutuo verti, & ex utroq; elici multum chalcanthi.
units.tr: Therefore it is more iron-like and thick, each of the two can be turned into the other, and much chalcanthum is drawn from both.

units.la: Sunt autem Duo: Æs & Ferrum: quo-rum utrumq; constat sulphure partim fixo, partim non fixo, & ob hoc etiam in igne infuscatur, & in squamas fatiscit, poros admittit, & calcinatur, effugiente parte sulphuris non fixa.
units.tr: There are two: copper and iron. Each consists of sulphur, partly fixed and partly not fixed, and for this reason each is also darkened by fire, flakes into scales, admits pores, and is calcined, as the non-fixed part of the sulphur escapes.

units.la: Æs est metallum imperfectum, durum, ex mercurio & sulphure impuro, quorum pars major fixa est, minor non fixa, copiosior tamen quàm in ferro, co-loris rubei.
units.tr: Copper is an imperfect metal, hard, made of mercury and impure sulphur, of which the greater part is fixed and the smaller part not fixed, yet more abundant than in iron. It is red in colour.

units.la: Itaque & ignitur, & funditur citius ferro, quod plus hydrargyri[?] habeat & sulphuris volatici: neq; tamen cohæret facile argento vivo, quod hujus respectu ex eo parciore constet, pluri vero terre-stri & chalcantosa materia sulphuri conjuncta.
units.tr: Therefore it ignites and melts more quickly than iron, which has more volatile mercury and sulphur. Yet it does not easily cohere with quicksilver, which, in comparison, consists of less of that, but of more earthy matter and chalcanthous material joined with sulphur.

units.la: Extenditur malleo, interimque remittit squamas, & florem ob sulphur ter-reum[?].
units.tr: It is extended by the hammer, and in the meantime gives off scales and flowers, because of its earthy sulphur.

units.la: Coloratur magnetide, & cadmia glebosa, facileq; assumit faciem utriusq; metalli perfecti.
units.tr: It is coloured by magnetite and lumpy cadmia, and easily takes on the appearance of either perfect metal.

units.la: Ex aquis acribus & fumis fatiscit in æruginem, cœruleum, flavitiem, & al-bam quandam substantiam.
units.tr: From sharp waters and fumes it crumbles into verdigris, blue, yellowness, and a certain white substance.

units.la: Ferrum est metallum imperfectum, durum, albedinis lividæ in aperto; rube-um in occulto, plurimum habens sulphuris fixi, minimum mercurii volatici, de utroq; tamen aliquam partem fixam, aliquam fugacem,sed hanc minimam.
units.tr: Iron is an imperfect metal, hard, of livid whiteness on the outside and red within. It has a great deal of fixed sulphur and very little volatile mercury; of both, some part is fixed and some fugitive, but the fugitive part is the smallest.

units.la: Itaq; & tardisime funditur, diu su-stinens ignitionem,& calcinatur prom-te, quod paucum argentum vivum,pa-rumq; sulphuris non fixi, facile abfuma-tur,& fatiscente compagem relinquat.
units.tr: Therefore it also melts very slowly, enduring ignition for a long time, and it calcines quickly, because the little quicksilver and the small amount of non-fixed sulphur are easily consumed, and it leaves its structure crumbling.

units.la: Difficilime jungitur argento vivo, ob parvam ejus quantitatem actualē; quan-quam si artificio quodam terrestris na-tura tollatur, & hydrargyrus actuetur propius; commisceatur, & pertinaciter cohæreat.
units.tr: It joins with quicksilver with the greatest difficulty, on account of its small actual quantity. Yet if the earthy nature is removed by some artifice and the mercury is made more active, they can be mixed together and cohere firmly.

units.la: Mutatur in aciem fluorum mineralium, & extinctionis adjumento, & cu-prum, auxilio chalcanthi.
units.tr: It is changed into the edge of mineral fluxes with the help of extinguishing, and copper with the help of chalcanthum.

units.la: Ignibus pluribus &refinctione in a-quis gypseis & similibus ita induratur,ut plane fundi nequeat.
units.tr: With many fires and refining in gypsum waters and similar liquids, it is hardened so that it cannot be melted at all.

units.la: Ex eo crocus conficitur, tum medi-cinae utilis, tum gradationibus metallo-rum.
units.tr: From it crocus is made, useful both for medicine and for the grading of metals.

units.la: Affinia metallis sunt Argentum vi-vum, Marcasita stannea, (bismuthum) Stibium,Sulphur, Arsenicum, Chalcan-thum, & Cinabaris.
units.tr: Akin to metals are quicksilver, marcasite of tin, bismuth, antimony, sulphur, arsenic, chalcanthum and cinnabar.

units.la: Argentum vivum est liquor mineralis, ex aqua metallica, viscida, terraque sul-phurea exacte contemperatus, spiritue-sus, frigidus, humidus, albus in manifesto, calidus, siccus, citrinus, rubens in occulto, familiarissimus metallis, quibus adhaeret intime, eaq; resolvit, & se ad eorum naturam accommodat.
units.tr: Quicksilver is a mineral liquid, exactly tempered from metallic water, viscous, and earthy sulphur. It is spirituous, cold, moist, white in appearance, hot, dry, lemon-coloured, and reddish in secret. It is most familiar to metals, to which it adheres intimately, dissolving them and adapting itself to their nature.

units.la: Quocirca etiam eorum appellatur prima materia habens in se sulphur ana-logum, cujus gratia tincturam praebet.
units.tr: Hence it is also called the first matter of metals, having in itself a sulphur analogous to theirs, by whose grace it provides the tincture.

units.la: Pondere omnia mineralia antecellit, nec quicquam in se mergi sinit statim, nisi aurum.
units.tr: In weight it surpasses all minerals, and it allows nothing to sink in it at once except gold.

units.la: Perfici potest & metallaris fieri, per sulphur metallorum.
units.tr: It can be perfected and made metallic through the sulphur of metals.

units.la: Induratur congelaturq; sublimationibus, additamentis, acribus succis, & aquis fixatoriis, &c. Volaticus cum est, totus ex igne fugit, nec potest partium ejus conjunctio solvi.
units.tr: It is hardened and congealed by sublimations, additions, sharp juices, fixing waters, and so on. When it is volatile, it flees entirely from fire, nor can the conjunction of its parts be dissolved.

units.la: Cum fixus, totus manet.
units.tr: When it is fixed, it remains entire.

units.la: Est duplex crudus seu mineralis, & corporeus.
units.tr: It is twofold: crude or mineral, and corporeal.

units.la: Ille in mineris invenitur, hic ex metallis extrahitur.
units.tr: The former is found in ores; the latter is extracted from metals.

units.la: Ex utroq; fit, qui Philosophorum nominatur.
units.tr: From both is made what is called the Philosophers' (mercury).

units.la: Bismuthum est corpus minerale, livedinis albicantis, durum, fragile, cõstans mercurio albo, terreo, sulphureq; tali & arsenico, omnibus volaticis & impuris, medium inter Plumbi genera & Antimonium.
units.tr: Bismuth is a mineral body of whitish livid colour, hard and brittle, consisting of white earthy mercury, such sulphur, and arsenic, all volatile and impure. It is midway between the kinds of lead and antimony.

units.la: Antimonium est corpus minerale, durum, terrestre, fragile, constans ex sulphure & arsenico turbido, & hydrargyro magis terreo, omnibus tamen volatilibus magis quàm bismuthum, vitiatis quadam terrea minerali vitrea.
units.tr: Antimony is a mineral body, hard, earthy and brittle, consisting of sulphur and turbid arsenic, and of mercury that is more earthy. Yet all of it is more volatile than bismuth, and it is vitiated by a certain earthy, mineral glassiness.

units.la: Itaq; halitum edit fœtidû plurimumque, qui quia est mercurialis majore ex parte, minore sulphureus & arsenicalis, niveus est, sublataq; parte spirituosiore ob sulphur in rubeā mutatur tinsturam.
units.tr: Therefore it gives off a very foul and abundant vapour, which, being for the most part mercurial and to a lesser degree sulphureous and arsenical, is snowy white; and when the more spirituous part is removed, it changes into a reddish tincture because of the sulphur.

units.la: Sulphur est succus mineralis pinguis, fœtorem acrem & pungentem emittens, habens partem subtilem, inflammatilé, partem crassam, terream, fixam, intermistam succo chalcantoso.
units.tr: Sulphur is a fat mineral juice, giving off a sharp and pungent stench. It has a subtle part, which is inflammable, and a thick, earthy, fixed part, mixed with chalcanthous juice.

units.la: Itaque ob illam inflammatur facilè, ob hanc figitur, ut nullis ignibus possit incendi.
units.tr: Therefore it is easily set alight because of the former, and fixed because of the latter, so that it cannot be burned by any fire.

units.la: Metallorum Pater dicitur, cum accedit spiritus metallicus, seminali metallo-rum rum virtute imbutus, quo fit ut coagulet hydrargyrum:
units.tr: It is called the Father of metals when the metallic spirit is added, imbued with the seminal power of metals, by which it comes about that it coagulates quicksilver.

units.la: Alias illo destitutum destruit metalla, non perficit,
units.tr: Otherwise, lacking that, it destroys metals and does not perfect them.

units.la: Sal ex eo album fixum est, & albam tinctu-ram conferre potest.
units.tr: Salt from it is white and fixed, and can confer a white tincture.

units.la: Arsenicum est succus mineralis, pin-guis, inflammatilis, vicino[?] sulphuri, viru-lentior tamen, ob salem conjunctum, constans pinguedine sulphurea, hydrar-gyro pauco, & spiritu salis albi, quorum pars volatica est, pars fixioni propior.
units.tr: Arsenic is a mineral juice, fat and inflammable, close to sulphur, yet more virulent because of the salt conjoined with it. It consists of sulphureous fatness, little quicksilver, and the spirit of white salt, of which one part is volatile and one part is nearer to fixity.

units.la: Chalcanthum est succus metallicus naturae aerosae, constans ex terra aerosa, alumine & sulphure, & ob id etiam acorem habet virosum & stipticum cum dulcedine conjunctum, resolvituráque in terram citrinam, succum aluminosum, & pinguedinem sulphuream.
units.tr: Chalcanthum is a metallic juice of coppery nature, consisting of coppery earth, alum and sulphur. For this reason it also has a poisonous and astringent taste joined with sweetness, and it dissolves into yellow earth, aluminous juice and sulphureous fatness.

units.la: Cum calcinatur rubescit, vocatur-que Colcotar.
units.tr: When it is calcined it reddens, and it is called colcothar.

units.la: Destillatur ex eo acidus liquor, & o-leum rubeum, ex quo spiritus pinguis colligitur.
units.tr: From it is distilled an acid liquor and a red oil, from which a fat spirit is collected.

units.la: Atrum colorem gignit in succis plan-tarum, unde atramentum sutorium di-ctum.
units.tr: It produces a black colour in the juices of plants, whence it is called shoemaker's black (atramentum sutorium).

units.la: Transmutat ferrum in cuprum.
units.tr: It transmutes iron into copper.

units.la: Apta fusione in aes migrat.
units.tr: With suitable fusion it passes into copper.

units.la: Unde patet terram ejus esse aream, cum mercurio & sulphure terreo.
units.tr: Whence it is clear that its earth is sandy, together with mercury and earthy sulphur.

units.la: Fit ex omnibus metallis per artem, maxime ex aere & ferro.
units.tr: It is made from all metals by art, chiefly from copper and iron.

units.la: Itaq; omnium sulphur hinc alumi-nosum seu atramentosum dicitur.
units.tr: Therefore the sulphur of all of them is called aluminous or atramentous from this.

units.la: Cinnabaris est corpus minerale, colo-ris sanguinei, constans potissimum sulphure & argento vivo mutuo comprehensis, & in duritie lapideam concretis.
units.tr: Cinnabar is a mineral body of blood-red colour, consisting chiefly of sulphur and quicksilver mutually combined, and congealed into stony hardness.

units.la: Duplex est: Nativa & artificialis.
units.tr: It is twofold: native and artificial.

units.la: Illa Minium secundarium est, praeterq; sulphur & hydrargyrum etiam arenas continet, & saxi specie invenitur in fodinis: haec ex solo sulphure & hydrargyro commistis fit per sublimationem, habetq; usum in metallica & medicinis primarium.
units.tr: The native is a secondary minium. Besides sulphur and mercury it also contains sand, and it is found in the form of rock in mines. The artificial is made from sulphur and mercury mixed alone by sublimation, and it has its chief use in metallurgy and medicine.

units.la: In metallica chymica figitur, & in tincturam mutatur; vel etiam ex fixa argentum vivum excoquitur, vel aquis gradatoriis materia est. In medicina tam foris in unguentis e fumo adhibetur ad Gallicam, &c. quam intus, sed correcta per metalla perfecta.
units.tr: In chemical metallurgy it is fixed and turned into tincture, or quicksilver is extracted from the fixed, or it is the material for gradatory waters. In medicine it is applied externally in ointments, as a fume, for the French disease, etc., and internally, but corrected by perfect metals.

units.la: Nativa est hydrargyri vena, quo ex-cocto, reliquum potest reverberio in colorem rubrum mutari, & pro cinnabari in pigmentis esse : In medicina quoque Epilepticis admovetur (sed prudenter.)
units.tr: Native cinnabar is a vein of mercury. When this is smelted, the residue can be changed by reverberation into a red colour, and it is used in pigments in place of cinnabar. In medicine it is also applied to epileptics (but prudently).

units.la: Huc refertur Bitumen, quod est cor-pus minerale, ex pinguedine radicali po-tiffimum, fuccisq; subterraneis conflatum, particeps igneæ naturæ, ante cæte-ra, quod cū flagrat, aquis infusis medio-criter, irritatur magis, aridis autem & o-leo teftinguitur citius, eftq; caloris & flammarum sub terris fomentum firmi-us, priusq; ; Et est lepticorum elenchus.
units.tr: To this is referred bitumen, which is a mineral body made chiefly from root fatness and subterranean juices. It shares the fiery nature above all others: when it burns it is irritated more by moderately infused waters, but it is extinguished more quickly by dry things and oil. It is a firmer fomentation of heat and flames under the earth, and it is a check on epilepsy.

units.la: Eftq; duplex : Hygrafphalthus, & Xe-rafphalthus.
units.tr: It is twofold: hygrasphaltus and xerasphaltus.

units.la: Hygrafphalthus est Petroleum vel Myrafphalthus.
units.tr: Hygrasphaltus is petroleum or myrasphaltus.

units.la: Petroleum est Naphtha vel Elæ-sphalthus.
units.tr: Petroleum is naphtha or elaesphaltus.

units.la: Myrafphalthꝰ est axungia bitumino-sa, & Maltha, quæ est vel meri bituminis vel lutosa.
units.tr: Myrasphaltus is bituminous axungia, and maltha, which is either pure bitumen or muddy.

units.la: Xerafphalthus est Opafphalthus vel Lithafphalthus.
units.tr: Xerasphaltus is opasphaltus or lithasphaltus.

units.la: Opafphalthus est ambra, vel pix mi-neralis.
units.tr: Opasphaltus is amber or mineral pitch.

units.la: Ambra mollis vel dura.
units.tr: Amber is soft or hard.

units.la: Mollis est vel sperma Ceti, & Hælosanthos veterum, vel ambra odorata.
units.tr: The soft is either spermaceti and the haelosanthos of the ancients, or fragrant amber.

units.la: Dura est Succinum vel Gagates.
units.tr: The hard is succinum or jet.

units.la: Succinum est Diaphanum vel Adiaphanum.
units.tr: Succinum is transparent or opaque.

units.la: Gagates est Gangitis vel Obsidian⁹.
units.tr: Jet is gangitis or obsidian.

units.la: Obsidianus est ambra vera, Ebenum sossile, & lapis Thracius.
units.tr: Obsidian is true amber, fossil ebony, and Thracian stone.

units.la: Pix mineralis est Asphalthus vel Piasphalthus.
units.tr: Mineral pitch is asphaltus or pissasphaltus.

units.la: Asphalthus est Sodomæa, vel Carthaginensis Cerea.
units.tr: Asphaltus is Sodomite or Carthaginian wax-like pitch.

units.la: Pisasphalthus seu Mumia est simplex vel sepulchralis.
units.tr: Pissasphaltus, or mummy, is simple or sepulchral.

units.la: Lithasphalthus est Geodes vel Lithodes.
units.tr: Lithasphaltus is geode or lithodes.

units.la: Geodes est terra ampelitis, vel carbo fossilis.
units.tr: Geode is ampelite earth or fossil coal.

units.la: Terra ampelitis est Communis vel Pharmacitis.
units.tr: Ampelite earth is common or pharmacite.

units.la: Carbo fossilis est Asphaltotes vel Xylodes.
units.tr: Fossil coal is asphaltotes or xylodes.

units.la: Lithodes est lapis fossilis bitumineus & marmarodis.
units.tr: Lithodes is bituminous fossil stone and marmarodes.

units.la: Marmarodis est Belemnites & Ebur fossile, vel Balanites est Dactylus,Idæus,Lyn-curius, Succinus.
units.tr: Marmarodes is belemnite and fossil ivory; or balanites is dactylus, Idaean, Lyncurius, succinus.

units.la: CAPUT XIIII. DE LAPIDIBUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 14. CONCERNING STONES.

units.la: Xplicatis metallis, sequuntur Lapides, qui sunt regulares, vel anomali.
units.tr: Having explained the metals, there follow stones, which are either regular or irregular.

units.la: Regulares sunt corpora inanimata fos-silia dura, ex sicca terrestri exhalatione, unctuositate quadam aquosa permixta, per temporis diuturnitatem vi caloris & frigoris, virtuteq; minerali coglutinata.
units.tr: Regular stones are hard, fossil, inanimate bodies, formed over a long period of time from a dry earthy exhalation mixed with a certain watery oiliness, and bound together by the force of heat and cold and by a mineral power.

units.la: Vis mineralis hic dicitur vis, quæ cælitus data est loco & materiæ ad formandum hunc vel illum lapidem: Sic ut vis mineralis dicatur vis formatrix latens in semine.
units.tr: Here the mineral power is the power given by heaven to a place and a matter to form this or that stone. Thus the mineral power is called the forming power lying hidden in the seed.

units.la: Nascuntur lapides sub terra, vel in caver-nis terræ, in locis montosis, in ripis quarundam aquarum. Terra non mollis sed solida superfi-ciei, ex qua vapor expirare non potest, multos lapides producit: Ripæ fluminum sempiterno-rum sunt solidissima, claudentes in se vapores.
units.tr: Stones arise beneath the earth, or in caverns of the earth, in mountainous places, and on the banks of certain waters. Ground that is not soft but solid on the surface, from which vapour cannot escape, produces many stones. The banks of perpetually flowing rivers are very solid, enclosing vapours within themselves.

units.la: Lapides sunt vulgares vel pretiosi.
units.tr: Stones are either common or precious.

units.la: Vulgares ex crassiore & impuriore materia concrescunt.
units.tr: Common stones coalesce from a coarser and more impure matter.

units.la: Suntq; vel porosi vel solidi.
units.tr: And they are either porous or solid.

units.la: Porosi sunt, qui ex materia non valde compacta constant, ideoq; partes habent raras, ut Tophus, Pumex.
units.tr: Porous stones are those made of matter that is not very compact, and so they have sparse parts, such as tophus and pumice.

units.la: Tophus est lapis rarior, facile friabilis, asper & haud aequus.
units.tr: Tophus is a rarer stone, easily crumbled, rough and not even.

units.la: Pumex lapis est rarus & cavernosus, seu spongiae modo fistulosus ad levigan-dum accomodatus: cujus tres sunt modi, de quibus Scal.exer. 133.
units.tr: Pumice is a light and cavernous stone, hollow like a sponge, suited to polishing. It is of three kinds, concerning which see Scaliger, Exercitationes 133.

units.la: Solidi lapides sunt, qui partes continuatas, & validius coactas habent. Et hi vel nitore carent vel nitent: Nitore carét, ut Silex, Cos, Saxum, Smiris, Pyrites.
units.tr: Solid stones are those that have continuous parts, more strongly compacted. Some of these lack lustre, others shine. Those lacking lustre include flint, whetstone, rock, emery and pyrites.

units.la: Silex est lapis solidus & durus, unde ferramenti incussu ignis elici potest. De hoc Scal. exerc. 108.
units.tr: Flint is a solid and hard stone, from which fire can be struck by a blow of iron. On this see Scaliger, Exercitationes 108.

units.la: Cos lapis est solidus, nitore carens, & granulis constans, cujus in acuendo ferro usus est. Scal. 108.
units.tr: Whetstone is a solid stone lacking lustre, made of grains, and used for sharpening iron. See Scaliger 108.

units.la: Species hujus est Coticula seu Lydi-us lapis, quo metalla affricata, sincera a nothis seu adulterinis dignoscuntur: De hoc Scal. exerc. 128. sect.1.
units.tr: A species of this is the touchstone, or Lydian stone, by rubbing metals on which, pure metals are distinguished from base or counterfeit ones. On this see Scaliger, Exercitationes 128, sect. 1.

units.la: Saxum lapis multus & durus est, ex magna quantitate materiæ fortiter concretæ constans.
units.tr: Rock is a stone that is massive and hard, consisting of a great quantity of matter strongly compacted.

units.la: Smiris lapis est durus, quo vitrum finditur. Scal. exerc.135.
units.tr: Emery is a hard stone by which glass is cut. See Scaliger, Exercitationes 135.

units.la: Pyrites vulgo Marcasita est lapis, qui chalybe percussus scintillas ignis edit.De hoc Scal. exerc, 104. sect. 21.
units.tr: Pyrites, commonly called marcasite, is a stone which, struck by steel, gives off sparks of fire. On this see Scaliger, Exercitationes 104, sect. 21.

units.la: Solidi lapides, qui nitet, sunt marmora.
units.tr: Among solid stones, those that shine are marbles.

units.la: Marmor est lapis solidus, nitidus & eximius, maculis & coloribus variis commendatus.
units.tr: Marble is a solid, shining and fine stone, commended for its spots and varied colours.

units.la: Pro colorum autem & macularum varietate, multae ejus traduntur species[?], sed praecipuae sunt, Alabastrites, Ophites, & Porphyrites.
units.tr: Because of the variety of colours and spots, many species of it are reported, but the principal ones are alabaster, ophite and porphyry.

units.la: Alabastrites est marmor perspicuum, candidum, e quo pyrides pro odoratis unguentis fiunt.
units.tr: Alabaster is a transparent, white marble, from which pyxides for fragrant ointments are made.

units.la: Ophites est marmor maculis serpen-tum simile.
units.tr: Ophite is a marble resembling the markings of serpents.

units.la: Porphyrites est marmor rubeis & quasi candidis maculis distinctum: seu potius rubeum, cum maculis internitentibus.
units.tr: Porphyry is a marble distinguished by red and as it were white spots; or rather it is red with flecked spots.

units.la: Pretiosi lapides ex subtiliore & tenui-ore materia, singulari caeli influxu con-gelascunt, & dicuntur Gemmae.
units.tr: Precious stones congeal from a finer and more subtle matter, under a singular influx of the heavens, and are called gems.

units.la: Alia tamen loca pro diversitate radiorum solarium, pretiosiores aliis producunt lapides.
units.tr: Yet some places, because of the different rays of the sun, produce gems more precious than others.

units.la: Hinc Æthiopia & India propter solis orientis & meridionalis vicinitate pretiosissimos generant lapides: ibi enim materia melius percoquitur. Vid. Scal. exerc. 99.
units.tr: Hence Ethiopia and India, on account of their nearness to the rising and southern sun, produce the most precious stones, for there the matter is better cooked. See Scaliger, Exercitationes 99.

units.la: Gemma ergo est lapis pretiosus cum materiae subtilitate & elegantia speciosus, cum viribus insignis & nobilis.
units.tr: A gem, then, is a precious stone, handsome for the fineness and elegance of its matter, remarkable and noble for its powers.

units.la: Plurimas & occulta virtute praeditas recenset Plinius lib. 37. c. 10. e quibus subsequentes notissimae sunt & nobilissimae.
units.tr: Pliny, book 37, chapter 10, enumerates very many gems endowed with hidden virtues, of which the following are the best known and most noble.

units.la: Adamas est gemma translucida, colore ferro candenti non absimilis, inenarrabilis duritiei & pretii.
units.tr: The diamond is a translucent gem, of a colour not unlike iron glowing with heat, of indescribable hardness and price.

units.la: Hic vel extra aurum vel in auro nascitur.
units.tr: It is found either outside gold or within gold.

units.la: Extra aurum nascitur Indicus avellanae nucis magnitudine, & Arabicus illo minor.
units.tr: Outside gold there are found the Indian diamond, the size of a hazelnut, and the Arabian, which is smaller than that.

units.la: In auro nascitur 1. Adamas Conchros dictus, milii grano magnitudine respondens. 2. Macedonius cucumeris semen aequans. 3. Cypricus aerei coloris. 4. Siderites, ferreo colore fulgens: quorum posteriores duo degeneres habentur.
units.tr: Within gold there are found: (1) the so-called conchros diamond, equal in size to a grain of millet; (2) the Macedonian, equal to a cucumber seed; (3) the Cyprian, of a bronze colour; (4) the siderites, shining with an iron colour. Of these, the last two are considered degenerate.

units.la: Tanta autem ejus est duritiei, ut nec mallei quidem ferrei ictibus cedat, neque ignibus atteratur, sed solo hircino sanguine frangatur, cujus ratione se nescire ipse Scal. profitetur exerc. 344. sect. 8.
units.tr: Its hardness is so great that it yields not even to blows of an iron hammer, nor is it worn down by fire, but it can be broken only by goat's blood; Scaliger himself professes ignorance of the reason for this, Exercitationes 344, sect. 8.

units.la: Sapphirus est gemma transparens, magna duritie, cæruleo & cælesti colore prædita, castitate conservans & corroborans: Castum hunc lapidem nominant, quoniam in coitu frangi creditur: Venenis etiam resistit. Scal. exerc. 33. sect.2.
units.tr: The sapphire is a transparent gem of great hardness, endowed with a blue and sky colour, preserving and strengthening chastity. They call this stone chaste, because it is believed to break when used in intercourse. It also resists poisons. Scaliger, Exercitationes 33, sect. 2.

units.la: Hyacinthus est gemma lentis magnitudine, fulgorem violaceum referens, cor confirmans, & hilaritatem excitans.
units.tr: The hyacinth is a gem the size of a lentil, reflecting a violet lustre, strengthening the heart and stirring up cheerfulness.

units.la: Deteriores habentur hyacinthi, qui propiores Chrysolitho sunt, quam qui Amethysto: Scal. exerc.,32[?]. sect. 12.
units.tr: Hyacinths that are closer to chrysolite than to amethyst are considered inferior. Scaliger, Exercitationes 32[?], sect. 12.

units.la: Amethystus eundem fere cum Hyacintho obtinet colorem nisi quod in hoc emicans fulgor purpureus, in illo languidior & dilutior fit.
units.tr: The amethyst has almost the same colour as the hyacinth, except that in the amethyst the lustre is purple and sparkling, while in the other it is fainter and paler.

units.la: Umbilico admotum vini vaporem ad se trahere & discutere, & sic a crapula vindicare, author est Aristoteles.
units.tr: Aristotle is the authority that, when placed on the navel, it draws the vapour of wine to itself and dispels it, and so protects against drunkenness.

units.la: Carbunculus seu Pyropus est Gemma, lucidissimi ignis flammâ repræsentans, venenis & toxicis inimica.
units.tr: The carbuncle, or pyropus, is a gem representing the flame of a most brilliant fire, hostile to poisons and venoms.

units.la: Huic subjicitur Chalcedonius, qui est gemma lucida & pulchra, instar stellæ refulrefulgens : cujus vis est contra tristitiam & timorem.
units.tr: Below this is placed the chalcedony, a bright and beautiful gem, shining like a star. Its power is against sadness and fear.

units.la: Rubinus est gemma rubea, per tene- bras in specie scintillæ alicujus micans : optimos autem judicant frigidissimos Scal. exerc. 118.
units.tr: The ruby is a red gem, glimmering in the dark in the appearance of some spark. Those who judge the best rubies say they are the coolest. Scaliger, Exercitationes 118.

units.la: Chrysolithus est gemma lucida, aurei coloris, varietate & nitore lucis nitens, melancholiæ adversa.
units.tr: The chrysolite is a bright gem of golden colour, shining with a variety and brightness of light, and opposed to melancholy.

units.la: Asterites est gemma dura, splendida, quæ dum convertitur, Solem aut etiam Lunam intus lucentem ostendit.
units.tr: The asterite is a hard, splendid gem which, as it is turned, shows the sun or even the moon shining within it.

units.la: Achates est gemma coloris varietate præstantissima, quæ una, quoad colores, omnibus gemmis opponitur, & venenis pestiferis adversari, prudentiam ad faciendam præstare creditur. De hoc Scal. exerc. 117.
units.tr: The agate is a gem outstanding for the variety of its colours, the only one which, in respect of colours, is set against all gems. It is believed to counter deadly poisons and to confer prudence in acting. On this see Scaliger, Exercitationes 117.

units.la: Sardius est gemma fulva, seu corneo colore rubens : ingenium acuens, homines lætos reddens, & sanguinem e naribus profluentem compescens.
units.tr: The sard is a tawny gem, or red with the colour of horn. It sharpens the wit, makes men cheerful, and checks blood flowing from the nostrils.

units.la: Jaspis est gemma viridis, maculis aut guttis sanguineis interpuncta, quæ si e directo ventriculi suspendatur, eundé confirmare dicitur.
units.tr: The jasper is a green gem, dotted with spots or drops of blood, which, if hung directly over the stomach, is said to strengthen it.

units.la: Onyx est gemma pellucida, unguis digitorum humanorum carnibus impo-siti colorem referens & mollis.
units.tr: The onyx is a translucent gem, resembling the colour of the human fingernail laid on flesh, and soft.

units.la: Turchois est gemma obscurior, coloris cœrulei, ex viridi relucentis, visum & cor recreans.
units.tr: The turquoise is a rather dark gem of blue colour, shining through with green, refreshing the sight and the heart.

units.la: Et sunt hæ gemmæ nobilisimæ: Minus nobiles sunt Criftallus, Corallium, Hæmatites, Magnes.
units.tr: These gems are the most noble. Less noble are crystal, coral, haematite and magnet.

units.la: Criftallus est lapis pellucidus, candidus, ex glacie, gelu vehementiore concretus, & ut plurimum sub terra genera-tus, ubi hybernæ nives rigent, ut in cautibus alpium. Scal. exerc.119.
units.tr: Crystal is a translucent, white stone, formed from ice, congealed by a more severe frost, and for the most part generated under the earth, where winter snows lie stiff, as in the crags of the Alps. Scaliger, Exercitationes 119.

units.la: Corallium est lapis ramosus, ex planta maris indurata aere, genitus.
units.tr: Coral is a branching stone, generated from a sea plant hardened by the air.

units.la: Eftq; album, nigrum, & rubeu, quod postremum nobilisimum est.
units.tr: And there is white, black and red coral, of which the last is the most noble.

units.la: Gagates vel succinum est lapis e liquido bitumine, e littoribus in mare deflu-ente, & rigore condensato genitus, procellisq; in littus provolutus.
units.tr: Jet or amber is a stone generated from liquid bitumen, flowing from the shores into the sea and condensed by cold, and cast up on the shore by storms.

units.la: Ejus tria præcipua genera recenfen-tur: Fulvum, quod melleo colore con-spicitur; Secundum, quod Falernum vi-num refert; Tertium candidum, quod optimum censetur.
units.tr: Its three principal kinds are enumerated: the tawny, which is seen in honey colour; the second, which resembles Falernian wine; and the third, white, which is considered the best.

units.la: Hæmatites est lapis, cujus color externus est sanguineus, intern[?]ꝰ ferrugineus, duritie tanta ut vix limam sentiat: Hic sanguinem sistere dicitur.
units.tr: Haematite is a stone whose outer colour is blood-red, and whose inner colour is rusty, of such hardness that it scarcely feels the file. It is said to stop bleeding.

units.la: Magnes seu siderites est lapis, colore ad cœruleum vergente præditus, ferrum naturali facultate attrahens. Arist,lib.7. Phys. Scal. exerc. 131.
units.tr: The magnet, or siderites, is a stone having a colour inclining to blue, which attracts iron by a natural power. Aristotle, Physics book 7; Scaliger, Exercitationes 131.

units.la: Gemmis his annumerantur lapides, qui in animantiu corporibus e peculiari glutinoso femine generantur, quod pro-gressu ætatis, nativo colore concoctum & frigore constrictum coalescit.
units.tr: Among these gems are counted the stones which are generated in the bodies of animals from a peculiar glutinous seed, which, as the animal grows, is concocted by its native heat, constricted by cold, and coalesces.

units.la: Nobiliores sunt hi, qui in terrestri animali reperiuntur.
units.tr: The more noble are those found in land animals.

units.la: Chelidonius, qui est lapillus exiguus in juvencularum Hirundinum ventriculo inventus, colore fusco, ex nigro aut subrufo permixto.
units.tr: The chelidonius is a small stone found in the stomach of young swallows, of a dusky colour, mixed from black or reddish.

units.la: Alectorius est lapis Cristallo obscuro similis, in ventriculo Capi, anno ætatis 9. & s.[?] generatus, magnitudine fabæ.
units.tr: The alectorius is a stone like dark crystal, generated in the stomach of a capon in its ninth year of life, of the size of a bean.

units.la: Aëtites est lapis cortice duro, scabro & minime levi, in Aquilæ nido inventus.
units.tr: The aetites is a stone with a hard, rough and not at all smooth shell, found in the nest of an eagle.

units.la: Borax alias Chelonites vel Bufonis est lapis in Bufonis senis[?] & magni reperto[?] capite.
units.tr: Borax, also called Chelonites or Bufonites, is a stone found in the head of an old and large toad.

units.la: Quadrus est lapis in cerebro Vulturis.
units.tr: Quadrus is a stone found in the brain of a vulture.

units.la: Quiris in nido Upupæ.
units.tr: Quiris is found in the nest of the hoopoe.

units.la: Saurites in ventre Saurae vel Lacertae.
units.tr: Saurites is found in the belly of a lizard or a gecko.

units.la: Limaceus in capite Limacis generatus.
units.tr: Limaceus is generated in the head of a slug.

units.la: In animali aquatili inveniuntur hi lapides r. Gemma Percarum in Perca piscè. 2. Carpionis, lapis in hujus faucibus reperitur. 3. Oculi cancrorum, &c.
units.tr: In aquatic animals these stones are found: (1) the Gem of the Perch, in the perch fish; (2) the Carpio stone, which is found in the throat of the carp; (3) the Eyes of crabs, etc.

units.la: Margarita est lapis e conchyliis marinis natus, corticibus rotundis constans.
units.tr: Pearl is a stone born from sea shells, consisting of round layers.

units.la: Deniq; anomalus lapis est Fulmineus, & in plantis, item homine inventus, & similis.
units.tr: Finally, the anomalus is a stone found in lightning, and also in plants and in man, and the like.

units.la: CAPUT XV. DE ANIMATI CORPORIS VITA ET MORTE.
units.tr: CAPUT XV. ON THE LIFE AND DEATH OF THE ANIMATED BODY.

units.la: Actenus exposita sunt corpora inanimata: Sequitur Animatum corpus, quod anima & vita praeditum est.
units.tr: Hitherto the inanimate bodies have been set out. Next comes the animated body, which is endowed with soul and life.

units.la: Anima est ἐντελέχεια corporis organici animati, quà animatum; adeoq; principium vitæ in corpore animato.
units.tr: The soul is the entelechy [ἐντελέχεια] of an animated organic body, as animated; and so it is the principle of life in an animated body.

units.la: Vita vero in genere est ἐντελέχεια seu actus primus viventis, quâ & prout vivens internum vitalis actionis principium.
units.tr: Life, in general, is the entelechy, or first actuality, of a living thing, by which, and insofar as it is living, it is the internal principle of vital action.

units.la: Vivens in genere est, substantia habens vitam, ut corpus vivens est corpus habens vitam.
units.tr: A living thing, in general, is a substance having life, as a living body is a body having life.

units.la: Vitalis actio seu motus est, quæ à principio illo interno, viventis substantiæ e-ditur.
units.tr: Vital action, or motion, is that which proceeds from that internal principle of a living substance.

units.la: Si placet, viri docti hæc Definitio substi-tuatur explicatior & specialior:
units.tr: If it pleases, learned men may substitute this fuller and more specific definition:

units.la: Vita est duratio corporis animati, usq; ad terminum à Deo & natura præ-scriptū, pendens ab unione animæ cum corpore organico, ad promovendam functionem cujusq; animati propriam.
units.tr: Life is the duration of an animated body, up to the limit prescribed by God and nature, depending on the union of the soul with the organic body, to promote the proper function of each animated thing.

units.la: Explicatio hujus Definitionis.
units.tr: Explanation of this Definition.

units.la: Genus vitæ proximum statuitur Du-ratio, quæ nihil aliud est hoc loco, quàm tem-pus illud, quod inter duos externos, generatio-nis & corruptionis terminos, unum, quo incipit esse, alterum quo definit esse, tanquam medium est interjectum.
units.tr: The nearest genus of life is laid down as duration, which here is nothing other than that time which lies between the two external limits of generation and corruption, as a middle, one limit being that at which a thing begins to be, the other that at which it ceases to be.

units.la: Subjectum est corpus animatum, sive sit planta, sive animal. Nihil enim vitam naturalem vivere potest, nisi sit anima infor-matum.
units.tr: The subject is an animated body, whether it be a plant or an animal. For nothing can live a natural life unless it is informed by a soul.

units.la: Causa efficiens naturalis, proxima, continens, est unio animæ cum corpore organico. Illa enim sua vi causatur vitam in corpore. Eaque posita, ponitur vita: & sublata, tollitur.
units.tr: The efficient, natural, proximate and containing cause is the union of the soul with the organic body. For it by its own power causes life in the body. When it is posited, life is posited; and when it is removed, life is removed.

units.la: Causa autem, vitæ naturalis propinqua & antecedens est, Calidum & humidum nativum, & animato corpori insitum.
units.tr: The nearer and immediately antecedent cause of natural life is the native warm and moist, implanted in the animated body.

units.la: Illud enim est, quasi vinculum & gluten, quo anima cum corpore unitur, unitaq; conservatur.
units.tr: For it is, as it were, the bond and glue by which the soul is united with the body and kept united.

units.la: Calidum nativum est calidum corpori viventi à natura insitum, quod humido radicali fovetur.
units.tr: Native heat is the heat implanted by nature in the living body, which is cherished by the radical moisture.

units.la: Humidum radicale est humor corpori vivo à natura insitus, qui calorem naturalem fovet.
units.tr: Radical moisture is the moisture implanted by nature in the living body, which cherishes the natural heat.

units.la: Vita itaq; in calido & humido consistit, quia quandiu corpus animatum vivit, tam diu calidum esse deprehenditur, qui calor viventis pabulo opus habet, quo subinde reficiatur; id ipsum autem est humidum. Deinde mors est à frigido & sicco.
units.tr: Life therefore consists in the warm and the moist, because as long as the animated body lives, it is found to be warm; and this heat needs fuel by which it is continually restored, and that fuel is moisture itself. Death, then, comes from the cold and the dry.

units.la: Non tamen omnem simpliciter frigiditatem & siccitatem excludimus, sed eas cum calido & humido ita temperatas esse dicimus, ut calidum & humidum in toto animato, quàm diu vivit, dominentur.
units.tr: Yet we do not exclude every cold and dryness absolutely, but we say that they are so tempered with the warm and the moist that the warm and the moist hold sway throughout the whole animated thing, as long as it lives.

units.la: Calidum nativum, ut conservetur, opus est refrigeratione. Hæc autem fit partim inspiratione, partim expiratione.
units.tr: For the native heat to be preserved, it needs cooling. This takes place partly by inspiration, partly by expiration.

units.la: Inspiratio fit tùm continentis proprii, tùm alimenti receptione.
units.tr: Inspiration takes place both by the reception of the surrounding element that is proper to it and by the reception of nourishment.

units.la: Continens illud est aqua vel aër.
units.tr: That surrounding element is water or air.

units.la: Alimenti receptione refrigeratur calidum, quia per alimentū reparatur humidum, quod calidum assiduè depascit.
units.tr: By the reception of nourishment the heat is cooled, because the moisture that the heat continually consumes is repaired through food.

units.la: Exspiratio est fuliginum, & halituum superfluorum vel noxiorum.
units.tr: Expiration is the throwing off of fumes and superfluous or noxious vapours.

units.la: Quicquid igitur calidum & humidum nativum vel confert, vel conservat, vel restaurat, est causa vitæ remota.
units.tr: Whatever therefore either confers, or preserves, or restores the native warm and moist, is the remote cause of life.

units.la: Finis vitæ est promotio functionis, cujusq; animati propriæ. Si enim post generationem statim interiret, animatum nunquam exequi posset sui muneris partes, cujus gratia à natura est genitum[?]. Ne autem hoc fiat, vita ei concessa est, tanquam interstitium generationem à corruptione distinguens.
units.tr: The end of life is the promotion of the proper function of each animated thing. For if it perished immediately after generation, the animated thing could never carry out the parts of its office, for the sake of which it was produced by nature. So that this does not happen, life has been granted to it, as an interval distinguishing generation from corruption.

units.la: Cæterùm vita alia est longa, alia brevis.
units.tr: Moreover, one life is long, another short.

units.la: Vita longa, est duratio corporis animati, quæ amplo temporis spacio continetur.
units.tr: A long life is the duration of an animated body that is contained within a wide span of time.

units.la: Brevis, quæ exiguo temporis circumscribitur spacio.
units.tr: A short one is that which is confined within a small span of time.

units.la: Causa efficiens naturalis tam longae quam brevis vitae est, diversa dispositio, partim calidi & humidi nativi, partim organorum corporis.
units.tr: The efficient natural cause of both long and short life is the differing disposition, partly of the native warm and moist, partly of the organs of the body.

units.la: Quò enim illa est melior & perfectior, eò vitam longiorem, quò pejor & imperfectior, eò breviorem efficit.
units.tr: For the better and more perfect this disposition is, the longer it makes life; the worse and more imperfect, the shorter.

units.la: Est autem bona calidi & humidi nativi dispositio, quando neutrum neq; in excess-su, neq; in defectu peccat, vel secundum quantitatem, vel secundum qualitatem.
units.tr: A good disposition of the native warm and moist exists when neither offends, either in excess or in deficiency, whether in quantity or in quality.

units.la: Id quod fit, quando calidum neque nimis est copiosum & forte, neq; nimis paucum & debile, sed moderatè se habet. Illud enim citò absumit & dissipat humidum, hoc verò citò refrigeratur, & corrumpitur.
units.tr: This happens when the heat is neither too abundant and strong, nor too scanty and weak, but is moderate. For the former quickly consumes and dissipates the moisture, while the latter quickly grows cold and decays.

units.la: Similiter, quando humidum neque nimis est copiosum, quod citò suffocando extinguat calidum: neq; nimis paucum, quod citò absumatur & dissipetur; neq; nimis aquosum & tenue, quod facile resolvatur & congeletur: Sed moderatè se habet, adeoq; est pingue & aereum, quod vim habet resistendi, tùm calido, tùm frigido in se agenti.
units.tr: Likewise, when the moisture is neither too abundant, since it would quickly smother and extinguish the heat; nor too scanty, since it would quickly be used up and dissipated; nor too watery and thin, since it would easily dissolve and freeze; but is moderate, and so is rich and airy, having the power to resist both the heat and the cold acting upon it.

units.la: Mala verò dispositio calidi & humidi est, quando contrario modo sese habet.
units.tr: A bad disposition of the warm and moist, however, is when they are related in the opposite way.

units.la: Ac cum varii sunt gradus ejusmodi bonitatis & malitia, partim insiti, partim adventitii, propter diversam tum seminum, ex quibus corpora animata generantur, tum locorum, in quibus vivunt, tum alimentorum, quibus nutriuntur, tum aliarum rerum extra vel intra corpus existentium, constitutionem. Hinc fit, ut etiam varii ac diversi gradus reperiantur, longitudinis & brevitatis vitae respectu animantium tum ὁμοειδῶν tum ἑτεροειδῶν[?].
units.tr: And since there are various degrees of such goodness and badness, some innate and some acquired, they arise from the differing constitution both of the seeds from which animated bodies are generated, and of the places in which they live, and of the food by which they are nourished, and of other things existing outside or inside the body. Hence it comes about that various and diverse degrees are found, with respect to the length and shortness of life, among animals both of the same kind [ὁμοειδῶν] and of different kinds [ἑτεροειδῶν].

units.la: Organa vero corporis, sunt bene disposita, quando justam habent crasin, figuram, magnitudinem, numerum, situm & continuationem partium. Tunc enim apta sunt ad functiones suas naturales bene obeundas.
units.tr: The organs of the body are well disposed when they have the proper temperament, shape, size, number, position and connection of parts. For then they are fit to discharge their natural functions well.

units.la: Male vero quando contrario modo se habent.
units.tr: They are badly disposed when they are related in the opposite way.

units.la: Porro vita naturalis distribuitur etiam secundum aetatem.
units.tr: Further, natural life is also divided according to age.

units.la: Est autem aetas periodus vitae sensibilem secum temperamenti vitalis mutationem importans.
units.tr: Age is a period of life bringing with it a perceptible change of vital temperament.

units.la: Ejus species sunt tres, secundum Aristotelem, nempe νεότης, ἀκμὴ[?] καὶ γῆρας, seu juventus, vigor, & senectus.
units.tr: There are three kinds of it, according to Aristotle, namely youth [νεότης], prime [ἀκμὴ] and old age [γῆρας], or youth, vigour and senility.

units.la: Juventus est ætas, in qua corpus animatum virium incrementum capit, propter auctionem calidi vitalis.
units.tr: Youth is the age in which the animated body gains an increase of strength, on account of the growth of the vital heat.

units.la: Vigor est ætas consistens, in qua corpus animatum plenas & integras vires est adeptū, propter vigore calidi vitalis.
units.tr: Vigour is the settled age in which the animated body has attained full and complete strength, on account of the vigour of the vital heat.

units.la: Senectus est ætas, in qua corpus animatum, virium decrementū capit, propter diminutionem calidi vitalis.
units.tr: Senility is the age in which the animated body suffers a decrease of strength, on account of the diminution of the vital heat.

units.la: Hactenus de vita: Sequitur Mors, quæ est interitus corporis viventis, factō[?] propter separationem animæ à corpore organico.
units.tr: So much concerning life. Next comes death, which is the perishing of a living body, brought about by the separation of the soul from the organic body.

units.la: Genus mortis proximum statuitur inte-ritus seu corruptio substantialis. Mori enim est interire ac corrumpi. Ergo vi conjugatorum mors est interitus & corruptio.
units.tr: The nearest genus of death is laid down as perishing, or substantial corruption. For to die is to perish and be corrupted. Therefore, by the force of the terms, death is perishing and corruption.

units.la: Subjectum mortis est corpus vivens sive planta sive animal. Nihil enim naturaliter mori potest, nisi sit substantia composita ex anima & corpore organico.
units.tr: The subject of death is a living body, whether a plant or an animal. For nothing can die naturally unless it is a substance composed of a soul and an organic body.

units.la: Causa efficiens proxima & continens est separatio animæ à corpore organico: sive anima post separationem superstes maneat, ut hominis: sive simul cum toto composito destruatur, ut plantarum & brutorum. Propinqua & antecedens est corruptio calidi & humidi nativi, quatenus secum trahit dissolutionem unionis, qua anima cum corpore organico erat copulata.
units.tr: The efficient, proximate and containing cause is the separation of the soul from the organic body; whether the soul remains surviving after the separation, as in man, or is destroyed together with the whole composite, as in plants and brutes. The nearer and antecedent cause is the corruption of the native warm and moist, insofar as it draws with it the dissolution of the union by which the soul was joined to the organic body.

units.la: Remota & primitiva est omne id, quod calidum & humidum nativum corrumpit.
units.tr: The remote and primary cause is whatever corrupts the native warm and moist.

units.la: Si naturale dicatur id, quod oritur a causis naturalibus, omnis mors est naturalis; Si violentum dicatur id, quod fit contra naturalem rei alicujus propensionem, omnis mors est violenta.
units.tr: If that is called natural which arises from natural causes, every death is natural; if that is called violent which happens contrary to the natural tendency of a thing, every death is violent.

units.la: Si vero naturale dicatur id, quod fit a causa secundum usitatum naturæ ordinem agente: violentum, quod fit a causa præter & contra usitatum naturæ ordinem agente, tum mors alia est naturalis, alia violenta.
units.tr: But if that is called natural which is brought about by a cause acting according to the usual order of nature, and that violent which is brought about by a cause acting beyond and contrary to the usual order of nature, then one death is natural and another violent.

units.la: Mors igitur naturalis est, quando calidum nativum secundum naturam & justo temporis spacio per μαρασμὸν seu marcorem spontaneum corrumpitur.
units.tr: Natural death, therefore, is when the native heat is corrupted according to nature and over a fitting span of time, through spontaneous decay [μαρασμὸν], or marasmus.

units.la: Id quod fit, quando humidum radicale, ita paulatim & successive absumitur a calido vitali, ut tandem plane deficiat.
units.tr: This happens when the radical moisture is so gradually and successively consumed by the vital heat that at last it fails altogether.

units.la: Sicut enim candela deficiente pabulo tandem marcescit & sponte interit; ita etiam calidum vitale deficiente humido radicali.
units.tr: For just as a candle, when its fuel fails, at length wastes away and goes out of its own accord, so too the vital heat does when the radical moisture fails.

units.la: At licet quotidie per humidum alimentarium reparetur id, quod est depa-stum : tamen propter admixtionem excrementorum, indies fit impurius & ineptius, ad fovendum calidum ; ideoque necesse est, ut tandem calidum marcore concidat.
units.tr: Yet although what has been consumed is restored daily by the nourishing moisture, nevertheless, because of the mixing in of excrements, it becomes day by day more impure and less fit for fostering the heat; and so it is necessary that the heat should at last sink into decay.

units.la: Mors vero violenta est, quando calidum nativū ante justum tempus vi quadam extinguitur & corrumpitur.
units.tr: Violent death, however, is when the native heat is extinguished and destroyed before its due time by some force.

units.la: Id quod fit vel per viam refrigeratio-nis; vel per viam inflammationis; vel per viam suffocationis ; vel per viam resolu-tionis & dissipationis.
units.tr: This happens either by way of refrigeration, or by way of inflammation, or by way of suffocation, or by way of resolution and dissipation.

units.la: I. Per viam refrigerationis quando calidū nativum à frigido externo & adventitio superatur, five illud fit elementum five corpus mixtum.
units.tr: I. By way of refrigeration, when the native heat is overcome by an external and adventitious cold, whether this happens to an element or to a mixed body.

units.la: Hoc modo moriuntur animantia, quæ ob nimiam frigiditatem vel aërū vel aquæ ambi-entis, vel veneni, vel pharmaci, vel potionis sumtæ enecantur.
units.tr: Animals die in this way who are killed by excessive cold of the surrounding air or water, or by poison, or by medicine, or by a drink taken.

units.la: II. Per viam inflammationis quando calidum nativum à calido externo & adventitio ita accenditur, ut plane præter natunaturalem & mortiferam dispositionem acquirat.
units.tr: II. By way of inflammation, when the native heat is so kindled by an external and adventitious heat that it acquires a quality wholly beyond its natural disposition and become deadly.

units.la: Hoc modo moriuntur animantia, quae incendiis aut febribus ardentibus, aut venenis calidis interimuntur.
units.tr: Animals die in this way who are destroyed by fires, or burning fevers, or hot poisons.

units.la: III. Per viam suffocationis quando calidum nativum conculcatur & opprimitur vel propter nimium humorem & excrementorum affluentium copiam: vel propter interceptam & prohibitam halituum calidorum eventationem & respirationem.
units.tr: III. By way of suffocation, when the native heat is trodden down and oppressed, either by excess of moisture and an abundance of flowing excrements, or by the hindering and prevention of the evaporation and breathing out of warm vapours.

units.la: Hoc modo moriuntur ebriosi, plethorici, hydropici, apoplectici, angina laborantes, strangulati, quiq; in aquis pereunt.
units.tr: In this way die drunkards, the plethoric, the dropsical, apoplectics, those suffering from quinsy, the strangled, and those who perish in waters.

units.la: IV. Per viam resolutionis & dissipationis quando calidum nativum nimis diminuitur vel propter subitam & immoderatam, cum humidi, tum spiritus vitalis absumtionem, vel propter utriusque diffusionem nimiam ac evacuationem.
units.tr: IV. By way of resolution and dissipation, when the native heat is too much diminished, either by a sudden and immoderate consumption of both the moisture and the vital spirit, or by an excessive diffusion and evacuation of either of them.

units.la: Hoc modo moriuntur, qui assiduis & immoderatis laboribus, sudoribus, vigiliis, curis, aerumnis, moeroribus corpus macerant, quiq; nimiam vel sanguinis vel seminis evacuationem patiuntur. Deniq; qui magna aliqua, subita & inopinata laetitia afficiuntur. Qui igitur mortem intempestivam & violentam sibi non vult attrahere, ille obnixè det operam, ut quantum in se est, omnia illa fugiat, quæ vim habent calidum & humidum nativum cum immi-nuendi tum corrumpendi.
units.tr: In this way die those who wear down their bodies with constant and immoderate labours, sweats, wakefulness, cares, hardships and sorrows, and those who suffer excessive loss of either blood or seed. Finally, those who are seized by some great, sudden and unexpected joy. Therefore whoever does not wish to draw upon himself an untimely and violent death, let him earnestly take pains to flee, as far as lies in him, all those things which have the power to diminish and to corrupt both the native heat and the native moisture.

units.la: CAPVT XVI. DE ANIMA VEGETANTE.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. CONCERNING THE VEGETATIVE SOUL.

units.la: Orpus autem animatum ut animatur per animam, ita & vivit per animam vegetantem & vigentem.
units.tr: The body, then, is animated because it is enlivened by the soul, and so it also lives by the vegetative and vigorous soul.

units.la: Est autem anima vegetans (quâ corpus animatum vivit: ἐντελέχεια corporis vegetabilis, quâ vegetabile, seu, actus primus naturalis organici corporis, quo illud vivit, nutrimento assumto nutritur, augetur, & simile sibi in specie gignit.
units.tr: The vegetative soul is that by which the animated body lives. It is the entelechy [ἐντελέχεια] of a vegetable body, by which it is vegetable; in other words, it is the first natural actuality of an organic body, by which that body lives: once nourishment is taken in, it is nourished, grows, and begets its like in species.

units.la: Dici potest anima vivifica qua corpus si-ta vivificatum vivit, & naturalis vitæ actiones edit.
units.tr: It may also be called the vivifying soul, by which the body, once enlivened, lives and performs the actions of natural life.

units.la: Hujus facultates sunt tres, Altrix, Auctrix, Procreatrix.
units.tr: This soul has three faculties: the nourishing, the augmenting, and the procreating.

units.la: In viventibus enim & animatis tria maxime sunt necessaria, conservatio individui, eiusdem idonea quantitas, & speciei conservatio: hinc tres illæ facultates animæ hujus. Nutrix facit, ut vivens subsistat : auctrix ut justam mensuram nanscicatur : procreatrix, ut suam speciem conservet.
units.tr: In living and animated things three things are chiefly necessary: the preservation of the individual, its fitting quantity, and the preservation of the species. Hence come those three faculties of this soul. The nourishing faculty makes the living thing subsist; the augmenting faculty makes it attain its due measure; the procreating faculty preserves its species.

units.la: ALTRIX sive NUTRIX est animæ vegetantis facultas, nutrimentum vi caloris innati in corporis animati substantiam convertens, ut reparetur id, quod absumitur.
units.tr: The NOURISHING faculty, also called the NUTRITIVE, is a faculty of the vegetative soul, which by the power of innate heat converts nourishment into the substance of the animated body, so that what is consumed may be repaired.

units.la: Hujus facultatis operatio dicitur Nutritio quæ Scaligero est alimenti transmutati unio & assimilatio. Seu: Est assumto alimento corpori assimilato naturalis indigentiæ Expletio.
units.tr: The operation of this faculty is called nutrition, which for Scaliger is the union and assimilation of the transformed food. Or: nutrition is the filling up of a natural need by food, once taken in and assimilated to the body.

units.la: Aristoteles hic doctè distinguit, inter id quod nutrit, id quod nutritur, & id quo nutritur.
units.tr: Aristotle carefully distinguishes here between that which nourishes, that which is nourished, and that by which it is nourished.

units.la: 1. Id quod nutrit est anima vegetans, quæ primum est nutritionis principium. Hæc utitur tanquam suo organo calore, qui nutritionis ita causa censetur.
units.tr: 1. That which nourishes is the vegetative soul, which is the first principle of nutrition. It uses as its organ heat, which is accordingly regarded as the cause of nutrition.

units.la: 2. Quod nutritur est compositum ex anima & corpore, seu corpus animatum & vivens.
units.tr: 2. That which is nourished is the compound of soul and body, that is, the animated and living body.

units.la: 3. Quo nutritur est Nutrimentum, quod est corpori quod nutritur contrarium, tum simile. Contrarium est, quia 1. Crudum est, multaq; eget mutatione; omnis autem mutatio fit de contrario in contrarium. 2. Patitur ab eo quod nutritur; Simile autem à Simili non patitur, inquit Aristoteles.
units.tr: 3. That by which it is nourished is nourishment, which is both contrary and similar to the body being nourished. It is contrary, because 1. it is raw, and needs much change; but all change goes from contrary to contrary. 2. It is acted upon by what it nourishes; but like is not acted upon by like, says Aristotle.

units.la: Simile est corpori nutriendo, quod jam concoctum, digestum proximumq; nutritionis est subjectum.
units.tr: It is similar to the body to be nourished, since, once digested and concocted, it is the immediate subject of nutrition.

units.la: Nutrici deinde facultati inservit minis-tra Concoctrix, cui inservit Attractrix, Retentrix, Expultrix.
units.tr: To the nourishing faculty there serves as minister the concocting faculty, to which in turn serve the attracting, the retaining, and the expelling faculties.

units.la: Concoctrix est facultas nutricis Administra, quæ alimentum receptum & aliquandiu retentum nativo calore subigit & alterat.
units.tr: The concocting faculty is the administrant of the nourishing faculty, which by its native heat works upon and alters the food received and held for a time.

units.la: Concoctio igitur Aristoteli opus caloris nativi, à quo quæcunq; concoquuntur simul ac concocta sunt, simul ac perfecta redduntur: atq; id quod potestate erat, planè essentiam formamque nanciscitur. Breviter:
units.tr: Concoction, then, according to Aristotle, is the work of native heat: as soon as things are concocted, they are at the same time made perfect, and what was in potentiality at once acquires its essence and form. In brief:

units.la: Coctio est alimentorum vi nativi caloris facta alteratio & subactio.
units.tr: Concoction is an alteration and working-over of food, brought about by the power of native heat.

units.la: Concoctioni adversatur ἀπεψία, quæ est vel imperfectio vel privatio concoctionis propter nativi caloris penuriam & frigus.
units.tr: Opposed to concoction is apepsia [ἀπεψία], which is either an imperfection or a privation of concoction, due to a lack of native heat and to cold.

units.la: Concoctionis species tres recensent Aristoteles, Elixationem, Maturationem,& Assationem.
units.tr: Aristotle lists three species of concoction: boiling, ripening, and roasting.

units.la: Elixatio est indefiniti humidi concoctio ab humido calido facta.
units.tr: Boiling is the concoction of the indefinite moist by the moist and warm.

units.la: Maturatio est alimenti ejus quod in arborum fructibus est, concoctio.
units.tr: Ripening is the concoction of the food found in the fruit of trees.

units.la: Assatio est concoctio humidi interni facta a calore sicco & extraneo.
units.tr: Roasting is the concoction of the inner moist by a dry and external heat.

units.la: Attractrix est facultas ministra, alimentum conveniens per villos rectos intra corpus nutriendum attrahens & recipiens.
units.tr: The attracting faculty is a subordinate faculty which draws in and receives suitable nourishment through the straight fibres into the body to be nourished.
