units.la: Retentrix est facultas serviens nutrici, attractum nutrimentum donec alteretur per fibras obliquas conservans.
units.tr: The retaining faculty is a faculty serving the nourishing faculty, which holds the attracted nourishment through oblique fibres until it is altered.

units.la: Expultrix est facultas ministrans nutritioni, alteratum vel secretum a partibus per villos transversos expellens.
units.tr: The expelling faculty is a faculty ministering to nutrition, which drives out through the transverse fibres what has been altered or separated from the parts.

units.la: Auctrix facultas est animae Vegetantis vis, qua corpus animatum ex assimilato alimento nutritu in omnes dimensiones extenditur, & justam magnitudinem consequitur, ad edendas proprias & convenientes actiones.
units.tr: The augmenting faculty is the power of the vegetative soul by which the animated body, nourished by assimilated food, is extended in all dimensions and attains its due size, so as to perform its own proper and fitting actions.

units.la: NB. 1. Ut altricis facultatis est finis, partium consumtarum instauratio: Sic auctricis finis est acquisitio justa magnitudinis.
units.tr: NB. 1. As the end of the nourishing faculty is the restoration of the parts that have been consumed, so the end of the augmenting faculty is the attainment of due size.

units.la: 2. Vt nutritionis forma est in ipsa assimila-tione: ita auctricis in motu extensionis. 3. Vt in nutritione fit non localis motus: sic in augmentatione fit mutatio secundū locum. 4. Nutrix facultas durat omni tempore vitæ: auctrix habet definitum spacium.
units.tr: 2. As the form of nutrition lies in assimilation itself, so that of augmentation lies in the motion of extension. 3. As in nutrition there is no local motion, so in augmentation there is change of place. 4. The nourishing faculty lasts for the whole of life; the augmenting faculty has a fixed span.

units.la: Cessat auctrix suo tempore, nec enim infinitum appetit.
units.tr: The augmenting faculty ceases at its appointed time, for it does not aim at the infinite.

units.la: Facultatem non semper opus est esse in actu secundo & operari: Ipsi enim nos non semper intelligimus actu, non semper mutamus locum.
units.tr: The faculty does not always need to be in second actuality and operating: for we do not always understand in actuality, and we do not always change place.

units.la: Finis etiam in incremento justo impletus est: Natura enim cum suum opus ad justam magnitudinem perduxit, inutiliter deinde & nullo usu augeret.
units.tr: The end of growth is also reached at due size: for nature, when it has brought its work to the proper size, would then grow it uselessly and to no purpose.

units.la: Procreatrix facultas restat, quæ est vis animæ vegetantis ex semine (sive proprie dicto, sive analogo:) novam substantiam efformans ei similem, quæ nutritur, ad perpetuam specierum conservationē.
units.tr: There remains the procreating faculty, which is the power of the vegetative soul, operating through seed (whether properly so called or by analogy), forming a new substance like the nourished body, for the perpetual preservation of the species.

units.la: Hæc igitur ex genitali semine corpus animatum aliud sui simile procreat & generat.
units.tr: This faculty, then, from the genital seed, produces and generates another animated body like itself.

units.la: NB. Generatio in genere a Physicis dicitur cum corpus physicum formam novam induit exuta vetere. Ea distinguitur in univocam & æquivocam. Univoca dicitur cum gene-
units.tr: NB. Generation in general is called by the natural philosophers the process by which a physical body takes on a new form, having put off the old. It is divided into univocal and equivocal. It is called univocal when the generator and the generated are of the same species, as when man generates man, or ox generates ox, from seed.

units.la: a Species hic est res formata. rans & generatum sunt ejusdem speciei, ut cum homo generat hominem, bos bovem, ex femine. Æquivoca est cum gignens & genitum sunt diversæ speciei, ut cum à Sole generatur mus per putrefactionem; cum ex carnibus humanis generantur vermes: cum ex putrefacto vino generantur parvæ muscæ.
units.tr: a Here "species" means a formed thing. Generation is equivocal when the begetter and the begotten are of different species, as when a mouse is generated by the sun through putrefaction, when worms are generated from human flesh, or when small flies are generated from spoiled wine.

units.la: Generatricis facultatis administrat sunt Alteratrix & Formatrix.
units.tr: The administrants of the generative faculty are the alterative and the formative.

units.la: Alteratrix seu immutatrix, est quæ semen, subjectam scilicet generationis materiam in qualitatibus mutat & alterat. Nisi enim semen patiatur & alteretur neq; herbam neq; animal generare poterit.
units.tr: The alterative, or changing faculty, is that which alters and changes the seed, that is, the matter subject to generation, in its qualities. For unless the seed is acted upon and altered, it will be unable to generate either a plant or an animal.

units.la: Formatrix seu plastica vis est quæ corpus ipsum animatum distinctius efformat, ut separatam formam acquirat. Omnia viventia, quibus nihil deest, possunt generare.
units.tr: The formative, or plastic, power is that which shapes the animated body itself more distinctly, so that it acquires a separate form. All living things that lack nothing can generate.

units.la: CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: DE PLANTIS SEU STIRPIBUS, earumq; partibus.
units.tr: ON PLANTS OR STALKS, AND THEIR PARTS.

units.la: Hæc de anima Vegetante: Porro corpus animatum vivens est Planta, vel Animal.
units.tr: So much concerning the vegetative soul. Next, a living animated body is either a plant or an animal.

units.la: Plantarum doctrina dicitur Phytologia, (φυτὸν ἐστὶ ἐ terra editum;) Phytologia est doctrina e terra nascentium.
units.tr: The doctrine of plants is called phytology (a plant is what has come out of the earth [φυτὸν ἐστὶ ἐκ γῆς]); phytology is the doctrine of things growing out of the earth.

units.la: Planta est corpus animatum vivens, vigente seu vegetante anima tantum praeditum, quâ e terra nascitur, viget, viret, alitur & augetur.
units.tr: A plant is a living animated body, endowed only with a vegetative or growing soul, by which it springs up from the earth, grows green, flourishes, is nourished and increases.

units.la: Excipiuntur ζωοφυτὰ seu plantanimalia, quæ insuper sensu quopiam, ac motu se contrahendi dilatandiq; prædita esse videntur.
units.tr: Excepted are the zoophytes [ζωοφυτὰ], or plant-animals, which seem moreover to be endowed with a certain sense and with the power of contracting and dilating themselves by motion.

units.la: Hæc enim svaviter attacta & affecta se dilatant, compuncta se contrahunt: figurâ plantæ referunt omnia quæ vel saxis, vel arenâ, vel fimo adhærent: Uti sunt Holothurii, stellæ marinæ, marinus pulmo, urtica, spongia.
units.tr: For these, when gently touched and affected, dilate themselves, and when pricked they contract. They resemble plants in form, all of them clinging to rocks, sand or dung: such are the sea-cucumbers, the starfish, the sea-lung, the nettle-animal, the sponge.

units.la: Planta tùm sunt partes, tùm affectiones.
units.tr: The parts of a plant are both parts and affections.

units.la: Partes planta sunt partes corporis plantæ compositi & organici, quod ani-ma vegetans informat & vivificat.
units.tr: The parts of a plant are the parts of the composite and organic body of the plant, which the vegetative soul forms and enlivens.

units.la: Hæ partes sunt principales vel minus principales.
units.tr: These parts are either principal or less principal.

units.la: Principales hic dicimus, quibus ani-ma vegetans nutritione præcipuè per-ficit, earumq; vitam conservat.
units.tr: Principal parts we call those by which the vegetative soul chiefly carries out nutrition, and by which it preserves their life.

units.la: Suntque Similares aut dissimila-res.
units.tr: And they are either similar or dissimilar.

units.la: Similares quæ unam & eandem omnino habent substantiam: & quia propriis vocabulis pleræq; carent, analogia quadam ex animalium partibus appellationem mutuantur.
units.tr: Similar parts are those which have one and the same substance throughout; and since most of them lack proper names, they borrow their appellations by some analogy from the parts of animals.

units.la: Hæ sunt vel Liquidæ vel Solidæ.
units.tr: These are either liquid or solid.

units.la: Liquidæ sunt succi & lacrymæ.
units.tr: The liquid parts are sap and tears.

units.la: Succus est pars liquida, in ipsis stirpium substantiis diffusa, quæ quasi sanguis earum conservat vitam.
units.tr: Sap is the liquid part diffused through the very substance of plants, which, like their blood, preserves their life.

units.la: Lacryma sunt humores, qui ex plantis sua sponte exeuntes, vel Solis calore eductì, vel copia expressi, vel ab ipsis plantis aliqua occasione dehiscentibus expulsi.
units.tr: Tears are the humours which flow out of plants of their own accord, or are drawn out by the heat of the sun, or are squeezed out by force, or are expelled by the plants themselves on some occasion when they burst open.

units.la: Suntque vel Aquea ut quæ in gummi concrescunt: vel Picea quæ in resinam coeunt.
units.tr: They are either watery, like those that harden into gum, or resinous, like those that unite into resin.

units.la: Solidæ sunt Caro, Fibræ.
units.tr: The solid parts are flesh and fibres.

units.la: Caro est crassior stirpis substantia, constans ex humore concreto, musculis animalium respondens.
units.tr: Flesh is the thicker substance of the stalk, consisting of concreted humour, and corresponding to the muscles of animals.

units.la: Fibræ sunt partes crassiores continuæ, fissiles, quæ eodem modo in plantam universam feruntur, quo venæ & nervi in animalibus, quorum exemplo hæ quoq; in plantis, aliæ venæ, aliæ nervi appelappellantur: venae quidem majores, & succulentiores fibrae: nervi autem tenuiores & ficciores.
units.tr: Fibres are continuous, thicker, cleavable parts which run through the whole plant in the same way as veins and nerves do in animals; by analogy with these, in plants too some are called veins and others nerves: the veins are the larger and juicier fibres, the nerves the finer and drier ones.

units.la: Dissimilares sunt, quae ex similaribus illis constant.
units.tr: Dissimilar parts are those which consist of those similar parts.

units.la: Et hae sunt, aut Perennes aut Anniversariae.
units.tr: And these are either perennial or annual.

units.la: Perennes sive longo tempore durantes sunt Radix, Caulis sive caudex, Matrix, Ramus.
units.tr: Perennial, or lasting for a long time, are the root, the stalk or trunk, the matrix, and the branch.

units.la: Radix est ima pars plantae, quae quasi vi in terra defixa, congruens alimentum attrahit & partibus omnibus suppeditat.
units.tr: The root is the lowest part of the plant, which, fixed in the earth as if by force, draws suitable nourishment and supplies it to all the parts.

units.la: CAUDEX vel caulis vel etiam truncus, item stipes, est pars plantae, quae à radice proximè supra terram assurgit, in quam tanquam in venam cavam alimentum ex radice primum ascendit, & plenius concoctum ad reliquas partes defertur.
units.tr: The STALK, or caudex, or also trunk, likewise the stem, is the part of the plant which rises immediately above the ground from the root, into which, as into a vena cava, nourishment first ascends from the root, and is then conveyed, more fully concocted, to the other parts.

units.la: Matrix seu medulla sive κορδία[?] est pars plantae interna, in medio stirpis latitans, constans ex carne & humore.
units.tr: The matrix, or marrow, or [κορδία] is the inner part of the plant, lying hidden in the middle of the stalk, consisting of flesh and humour.

units.la: Rami sunt partes plantae, quae tanquam brachia à caule vel caudice in multitudinem diffunduntur.
units.tr: The branches are the parts of the plant which spread out in numbers from the stalk or trunk, like arms.

units.la: Anniversariae h. e.[?] annuatim renascentes partes sunt Surculi, Flores, Fructus.
units.tr: Annual, that is, parts renewed each year, are the shoots, the flowers and the fruits.

units.la: Surculus est pars, quæ ex Ramis simplex annuatim oritur: ex surculis autem flores & fructus pendent.
units.tr: A shoot is a part which grows each year, simple, from the branches; and from the shoots hang the flowers and fruits.

units.la: Partes minus principales sunt Cortex & Folia.
units.tr: The less principal parts are the bark and the leaves.

units.la: CORTEX est veluti tunica quædam, ex fibris contenta, qua plantæ obducun-tur: Hæc ubi tenuior fuerit, cutis; ubi crassior cortex dicitur.
units.tr: The BARK is a kind of covering, made up of fibres, with which plants are clothed; where it is thinner it is called skin, where thicker it is called bark.

units.la: Folia quasi excrementa sunt planta-rum, & constant humore & fibris.
units.tr: Leaves are, as it were, the excrements of plants, and consist of humour and fibres.

units.la: Caput XVIII. DE VARIIS PLANTARUM AFFECTIONIBUS.
units.tr: Chapter 18. ON THE VARIOUS AFFECTIONS OF PLANTS.

units.la: Affectio plantarum seu stirpium est primi generis aut secundi.
units.tr: The affections of plants or herbs are of the first kind or of the second kind.

units.la: Primi generis est tum Ortus & propagatio, tū Transmutatio, tūm corruptio seu Mors.
units.tr: The first kind comprises origin and propagation, transmutation, and corruption or death.

units.la: Ortus & propagatio plantarum est Naturalis aut Artificialis.
units.tr: The origin and propagation of plants is either natural or artificial.

units.la: Naturalis qua sponte & natura sua nascuntur ex semine aut manifesto, aut nobis obscuro.
units.tr: Natural origin is when plants spring up of their own accord and by their own nature from seed, either from a seed that is visible to us or from one hidden from us.

units.la: Ex manifesto nascuntur feminæ quædam, quæ unam tantum sui ortus & generationis habent rationem: quædam vero pluribus modis propagantur.
units.tr: From a visible seed, some plants arise which have only one manner of origin and generation, while others are propagated in several ways.

units.la: Quæ uno modo pronascuntur, è fo-lo nascuntur feminæ & quidem hoc modo: Semen in terram humidam incidens emollitur, & calore tum naturali tum cœlesti fovetur & intumescens propter humore illi a terra influente rumpitur: Eaque parte, qua jam ruptum est, germen enascitur, molle quidem & tenue principio, sed tamen postea firmius ac crassius redditur: Cujus pars una æ-reæ naturæ particeps ascendit sursum: altera vero quia terrestris & crassa in terris residens coalescit.
units.tr: Those that come up in one way spring from a seed alone, and in this manner: the seed, falling into moist earth, is softened and warmed by both natural and heavenly heat. Swelling because of the moisture flowing into it from the earth, it bursts, and from the part already burst a sprout emerges, soft and slender at first but afterwards made firmer and thicker. One part of it, sharing in the airy nature, rises upward; the other, being earthly and thick, stays in the ground and takes root.

units.la: Ortum deinde plantæ fovet humor calore decoctus & ab interna ipsorū natura attract[?]: Et quæ succo plus affluunt, earum quoq; incrementum est & majus & celerius: Quæ tamen in incremento varietas potius ex forma dependet.
units.tr: Next, the moisture, warmed and digested by heat and drawn in by the plant's own inner nature, nourishes the young plant. Those plants that receive more sap also grow larger and faster. Yet the variety in growth depends rather on the form.

units.la: Tempus autem ortus non omnibus plantis est unum & idem, sed varium, quædam citius, quædam tardius pronascuntur.
units.tr: The time of origin, however, is not the same for all plants; it varies, some sprouting sooner, some later.

units.la: Ratio diuersitatis est vis formæ, vis vel imbecillitas insiti caloris, feminum mollities aut durities, raritas aut densitas.
units.tr: The reason for the difference is the power of the form, the strength or weakness of the innate heat, and the softness or hardness, rarity or density, of the seeds.

units.la: Sine semine manifesto quasdam oriri plantas auctor est Theophrast⁹: Earumque causam esse docet certam quandam terræ & aquæ putrescentis permissione, quæ deinde calore tum solis, tum proprio in ista materia coservato, apta reddatur generationi spontanearum plantarum. Adde quod aër terraq; sui proprietate ortus, qui sponte fit, plantarum sunt causæ; siquidem pro earum vario in substantia & qualitatibus statu, varias mutationes ac generationes rerum fieri certum est.
units.tr: Theophrastus is the authority that some plants arise without a visible seed. He teaches that the cause of these is a certain permitted putrefaction of earth and water, which, once made fit by the heat of the sun and by the heat kept in that matter itself, becomes apt for the generation of spontaneous plants. Add to this that air and earth, by their own properties, are causes of the origin which comes about spontaneously, since it is certain that various changes and generations of things occur according to the varying state of their substance and qualities.

units.la: Planta nonnunquam ex duro prodit lapide: Aër siquidem lapidi inclusus nititur ascendere, sed cum non inveniat exitum reflectitur, & ex sui agitatione calefit, & humorem, qui est in lapide reliquum, trahit sursum, exitq; vapor cum humore illo, & ex illo vapore & humore, è lapide educto generatur planta, concurrente vi caloris solaris.
units.tr: Sometimes a plant comes forth from hard stone. For air enclosed in a stone strives to rise, but, finding no way out, it is turned back and is heated by its own agitation, and it draws upward the moisture remaining in the stone. The vapour goes out with that moisture, and from that vapour and moisture drawn out of the stone a plant is generated, with the power of the sun's heat cooperating.

units.la: Artificialis plantarum ortus fit arte industria hominum. Et quidem vel e Radice, vel Stolone sive surculo.
units.tr: Artificial origin of plants is brought about by human skill and industry, either from a root, or from a stolon or shoot.

units.la: Radice, scilicet in terra depressa: hæ facile alimentum e terra attrahere & vivere possunt.
units.tr: From a root, namely one laid in the ground: such roots can easily draw nourishment from the earth and live.

units.la: Stolone sive surculo vel terræ infixo, vel plantæ trunco.
units.tr: From a stolon or shoot, either fixed in the earth or grafted onto the trunk of a plant.

units.la: Terra infixo: ut Rosa, Salix, Vitis, &c.
units.tr: Fixed in the earth, as with the rose, willow, vine, etc.

units.la: Planta trunco, videlicet intrusione surculi, inter lignum & corticem, & di-citur proprie Insitio, Græcè ἐμφύτευσις[?].
units.tr: Grafted onto a trunk, namely by inserting a shoot between the wood and the bark. This is properly called insition (grafting), in Greek [ἐμφύτευσις].

units.la: Quamvis quædam plantæ omnibus his modis propagentur.
units.tr: Although some plants are propagated in all these ways,

units.la: Atq; hi sunt propagationis modi artificiales frequentiores: præter quos illé quoq; est longè rarior, quo folium terræ infossum germinat in novam prolem.
units.tr: these are the more common artificial modes of propagation. Besides them there is also a much rarer one, in which a leaf buried in the earth sprouts into a new offspring.

units.la: Ea pars Rami, quæ terræ infoditur, in se conservat caloris, humoris atq; adeò animæ vim, & attractio humore intumescit, & spiritum concipit: detenta verò vis animæ & caloris ope adjuta, partes humoris grauissimas deorsum distribuit, unde radices efformantur, & leuissimas sursum, unde alitur superficies.
units.tr: That part of the branch which is buried in the earth preserves within itself the power of heat, moisture, and indeed of life. Swelling with drawn-in moisture, it takes in a spirit; and the power of life and heat, held back and aided by its action, distributes the heavier parts of the moisture downward, whence roots are formed, and the lightest parts upward, whence the surface is nourished.

units.la: Eadem fere est ratio in insitione: sicut enim stirpes ex terra tanquam utero; ita infi[?]tæ[?] ex eâ, cui inferuntur, planta nutrimentum, vi animæ & calcris, quem ex sua allatum planta conservant, attrahunt nutrimentum, ejusq; vi & continua actione, earum partium fit generatio, quæ desunt. Nutri-mentum autem, quod insitum trahit, longè est elaboratius tum quod in matre jam antea concoctum erat, tum quod in novo hospitio exactius conficitur. Hinc fit ut plantæ sylvestres, si sint insitæ mansuescant, quia sinceriori nutriuntur alimento.
units.tr: The reasoning is almost the same in grafting. For just as stocks are drawn from the earth as from a womb, so the grafted shoots, by the power of life and heat which they keep from their own source, draw nourishment from that into which they are inserted, and by its power and continual action the parts that are lacking are generated. The nourishment which the graft draws in is far more refined than that which was already digested in the mother plant, and more exactly prepared than what is completed in its new host. Hence wild plants, if grafted, become tame, because they are nourished by a purer food.

units.la: Hæc de Ortu plantarum: Sequitur Transmutatio quædam qua ipsæ transmutantur, & quidem: I. Seminum transmutatione, ut triticum in quibusdam terris seminatum degenerat, & secundo vel tertio anno fit siligo; vicissim siligo mutatur in triticum. II. Fit amputatione seu præcisione, ut præcisis sylvis quercinis & faginis repullulant Myricæ. III. Insitione in corpus plantæ ut in truncum seu stipitem. Per hunc modum fieri possunt uvæ, maturescentes cum cerasis, pyris aut malis: Si enim vitis plantata fuerit juxta cerasum vel pyrum, hac perforata & vitæ per foramen tracta, ita ut concrescant vitis & arbor, fiantque earum lingua continua & tum vitis ex parte radicis praescindatur, ut non nutriatur nisi per radicem & stipitem cerasi vel pyri, uvae cum fructibus cerasi vel pyri maturescunt. Elini femi-ne caepis insito, herbam nasci scribit, Sca-liger, quae dicitur, Draco.
units.tr: So much for the origin of plants. There follows a certain transmutation by which plants themselves are changed, namely: I. By transmutation of seeds, as wheat sown in certain lands degenerates, and in the second or third year becomes rye; conversely, rye changes into wheat. II. It comes about by cutting back or pruning, as when oak and beech woods are cut down, the tamarisk sprouts again. III. By grafting into the body of a plant, as into a trunk or stock. In this way grapes can be made to ripen together with cherries, pears, or apples: if a vine is planted beside a cherry or pear tree, and it is pierced, and its shoot is drawn through the hole, so that the vine and the tree grow together and their tongues become continuous, and then the vine is cut off at its root so that it is nourished only through the root and trunk of the cherry or pear, the grapes ripen together with the fruit of the cherry or pear. Scaliger writes that when the seed of the elm is grafted onto an onion, there grows a herb called "dragon".

units.la: IV. Motu locali, ut si decerpas furculum unius plantae, & cum terrae infigas.
units.tr: IV. By local motion, as when you pluck a twig from one plant and fix it into the earth.

units.la: Superest plantae mors, quae est ejus ex defectu caloris & humoris nativi ariditas vel corruptio.
units.tr: There remains the death of a plant, which is its drying up or corruption, arising from a lack of innate heat and moisture.

units.la: Corruptio haec plantae est totalis vel partialis.
units.tr: This corruption of a plant is either total or partial.

units.la: Totalis qua tota planta corrupta moritur. Estq; naturalis, vel praeternaturalis.
units.tr: Total corruption is when the whole plant is corrupted and dies. It is either natural or unnatural.

units.la: Naturalis fit quando plantae ficciores redduntur ob calorem internum progressu temporis humorem absumente.
units.tr: Natural corruption happens when plants are made drier over time, as the internal heat consumes the moisture.

units.la: Aliae autem citius aliae serius ita corrumpuntur: prout illarum vita aut diuturnior, aut brevior est.
units.tr: Some plants are corrupted sooner, others later, according as their life is longer or shorter.

units.la: Causa hujus rei est praecipua forma, cui accedit tum lentor & copia insiti humoris, quo innatus nutritur calor, formae instrumentum: tum totius stirpis firmitas & soliditas.
units.tr: The chief cause of this is the form, to which are added the tenacity and quantity of the innate moisture, by which the inborn heat, the instrument of the form, is nourished; and also the firmness and solidity of the whole stock.

units.la: Diuturniores enim sunt illæ plantæ. 1. Quibus humiditas innata multa, lentaq; incest. 2. Quibus solida etiam est substantia. 3. Quæ radices longas & crassas & altius in terram defixas habent. 4. Quæ sunt steriles. 5. Quæ in siccio nascuntur loco. 6. Denique quibus amputatio justo adhibetur tempore: siquidem cohibito in radice humore, ipsarum quoq; vita producitur & serius moriuntur.
units.tr: Those plants are longer-lived which: 1. have much innate moisture that is thick and sticky. 2. have a solid substance. 3. have long and thick roots driven deep into the earth. 4. are barren. 5. grow in a dry place. 6. finally, those which are pruned at the proper time; for when the moisture is held back in the root, their life too is prolonged and they die later.

units.la: Contrario modo affectæ plantæ breviores sunt vitæ & citius corruptione naturali pereunt.
units.tr: Plants affected in the opposite way have shorter lives and perish sooner by natural corruption.

units.la: Præternaturalis seu violenta corruptio contingit aut ὑπὸ σβέσιν[?], aut ὑπὸ μαράνσιν[?].
units.tr: Unnatural or violent corruption comes about either by [ὑπὸ σβέσιν] extinction or by [ὑπὸ μαράνσιν] withering.

units.la: Corruptio ὑπὸ σβέσιν[?] fit quando nimio frigore stirps aut planta perit.
units.tr: Corruption by extinction [ὑπὸ σβέσιν] happens when a stock or plant perishes from excessive cold.

units.la: Frigus enim in profundum subiens, tepi-dum vaporem seu calorem a radicibus influentem arcet, longiusq; prosecutum enecat. Non fit hæc, nisi summa sit frigoris immanitas, tum enim ipsius radices invadit.
units.tr: For cold, penetrating deep, keeps off the tepid vapour or heat flowing from the roots, and, pursuing it further, kills it. This happens only when the severity of the cold is extreme, for then it attacks the roots themselves.

units.la: Corruptio ὑπὸ μαράνσιν[?] fit æstu, qui plantas veluti torret, & humidum, caloris scilicet subjectum & pabulum exhaurit, attenuando illud & resolvendo: Et ita cum humido expirat, etiam calor ab aestu evocatus.
units.tr: Corruption by withering [ὑπὸ μαράνσιν] happens through heat, which as it were scorches the plants and drains the moisture, which is the seat and nourishment of heat, by thinning and dissolving it. And so, with the moisture, the heat too, drawn out by the heat of summer, expires.

units.la: Duo autem tempora sunt quibus Plantae his caeli injuriis potissimum sunt expositae. I. Quando germinaturiunt, quia tunc sunt laxiores. II. Post fructificationem: tum enim omni succo exhausta & debilitatae sunt.
units.tr: There are two times when plants are especially exposed to these injuries of the sky. I. When they are about to sprout, because then they are looser. II. After fruiting, for then they are exhausted and weakened, having been drained of all their sap.

units.la: Partialis corruptio est, quae partem aliquam plantae infestat. Et dicitur Sideratio qua alicujus partis calor nativus vel a frigore, vel aestu, vel etiam vulnere extinguitur, quam sequitur Mortificatio.
units.tr: Partial corruption is that which afflicts some part of a plant. It is called sideration, when the innate heat of some part is extinguished by cold, heat, or even a wound, and it is followed by mortification.

units.la: Atque hactenus primi generis affectiones plantarum fuerunt: Secundi generis sequuntur, quae in primis ex natali suo, varietate in germinatione, foecunditate, substantiae proprietate, denique qualitatibus definiuntur.
units.tr: So far have been the affections of the first kind in plants. The affections of the second kind follow, which are defined above all by their native place, variety in germination, fruitfulness, the properties of their substance, and finally their qualities.

units.la: I. Ratione ergo soli plantae aut terrestres sunt, aut aquatiles.
units.tr: By reason, therefore, plants are either terrestrial or aquatic.

units.la: Terrestres quarum locus natalis est terra. Et sunt vel Urbanae & mites vel Agrestes.
units.tr: Terrestrial plants have the earth as their natural place. They are either urban and gentle, or wild.

units.la: Urbana seu Domestica in hortis nascuntur.
units.tr: Urban, or domestic, plants grow in gardens.

units.la: Agrestes vel in montibus, vel in valli-bus bus, vel in planis nascuntur & melius habent.
units.tr: Wild plants grow either on mountains, in valleys, or on plains, and thrive better there.

units.la: Aquatiles sunt, quarum in aquis, ut vel in mari, vel in minoribus aquis, & vel in montibus, vel in mollioribus rivis, aut in stagnanti aqua, est ortus.
units.tr: Aquatic plants are those whose origin is in water: either in the sea, in smaller waters, or on mountains, in gentler streams, or in standing water.

units.la: Deinde plantæ aliquæ delectantur loco calido, aliæ loco frigido; quædam aprico aliæ umbrosiore loco; quædam saxis, pauca etiam arena gaudent, inquit Scaliger.
units.tr: Further, some plants delight in a warm place, others in a cold one; some in a sunny place, others in a shadier one; some in rocks, and a few also in sand, says Scaliger.

units.la: Ratio hujus varietatis potest hæc reddi, quod cum rerum sublunarium conservator dicatur locus, ideò diversæ stirpes ad alimentum conveniens attrahendum & ad vitam conservandam diverso loco gaudent.
units.tr: The reason for this variety may be given as follows: since a place is said to be the preserver of earthly things, different kinds of plants, to draw in suitable nourishment and preserve their life, delight in different places.

units.la: II. In germinatione porrò spectatur tùm tempus germina proferendi, tùm celeritas tarditasq;.
units.tr: II. In germination we consider both the time of putting forth shoots and their speed or slowness.

units.la: Tempus est spacium, quo justa humoris copia hyeme collecta, ipseque etiam innatus calor, vi externi caloris excitatur, atque plantarum cutis, corporisque universi patefacti jam sunt meatus, forasque succus educitur, & incipit germinatio.
units.tr: The time is the interval during which a proper quantity of moisture, gathered in winter, and the innate heat itself are roused by the force of external heat, and the skin of the plant and the passages of its whole body are now opened, the sap is drawn outward, and germination begins.

units.la: Aliæ autem aliis naturâ celerius aut serius expullulant, nimirùm, quo major aut minor est vis caloris innati humorisque, atq; plantæ corporis raritas. Cul-tæ tamen stirpes plerumq; incultis seriùs germina proferunt. Causæ tres afferri possunt. 1. Ob insiti caloris revocationem ad intimas partes, ob vulnera, quæ putando inferuntur. 2. Vel etiam ob ejusdē caloris, ob denudationem radicis, torporem, humoris q; incrassationem: 3. Obq; plantæ densitatem vi nocturnæ frigiditatis, radici, ac per radicem universæ stirpi inductam.
units.tr: Some plants sprout earlier by nature, others later, according as the force of their innate heat and moisture is greater or less, and according to the rarity of the plant's body. Cultivated plants nonetheless usually put forth shoots later than wild ones. Three causes may be given: (1) because the innate heat is drawn back to the inner parts, on account of the wounds inflicted by pruning; (2) or also because of the torpor of that same heat and the thickening of the moisture, owing to the stripping of the root; (3) and because of the density of the plant, induced by the force of night-time cold, into the root and through the root into the whole plant.

units.la: Atq; generant non prima statim ætate (sicuti neq; animantia, quam diu tenera sunt, fœtus ferunt) I. Quia alimentum omne hoc tempore in incrementum absumitur: II. Et nutrimentum est humidius: III. Vis etiam imbecillior, quæ id concoquere & in fructum condensare nequit.
units.tr: And plants do not bear fruit in the first period of their life, just as animals do not bear offspring while they are still young: (1) because all their nourishment is spent on growth at this time; (2) and the nutriment is more watery; (3) and the force is also too weak to digest it and condense it into fruit.

units.la: Neq; generant omnes, aliæ enim fœcundæ sunt, aliæ infœcundæ.
units.tr: Nor do all plants bear fruit: some are fruitful, others unfruitful.

units.la: Fœcunditatis causam omnē, in solo [?]calore nonnulli referunt: Cum autem calor sine materia, hoc est, copioso alimento nihil effingere possit, succosæ & calidæ stirpes tantum erunt fœcundæ; reli-quæ steriles. Fœ-
units.tr: Some attribute every cause of fertility to the heat of the soil. But since heat without matter, that is, abundant nourishment, can produce nothing, only juicy and warm plants will be fertile; the rest sterile. Fer-

units.la: Foecundarum quaedam fructificant semel tantum tota vita: aliae saepius.
units.tr: Of the fertile plants, some bear fruit only once in their whole life, others more often.

units.la: Et quae saepius, illarum quaedam semel tantum in anno, quaedam bis, aliae etiam ter flores & fructus ferunt; Cujus rei causa proxima nulla alia erit, quàm forma proxima singularum specierum.
units.tr: And of those that bear fruit more often, some flower and fruit only once a year, some twice, others even three times. The proximate cause of this will be none other than the proximate form of each species.

units.la: Foecundarum quaedam fertiles sunt continenter, idq; propter abundantiam caloris & humoris pinguis, ut ficus: quaedam alternis tantum annis fructuum sunt feraces, quod in malis pyrisq; observatur.
units.tr: Of the fertile plants, some bear fruit continuously, and this because of an abundance of heat and rich moisture, as with the fig; others bear fruit only in alternate years, as is observed in apples and pears.

units.la: Profusissimae enim hae arbores sunt, tantumq; alimenti anno uno in fructuum generatione absumunt, ut ad inopiam redactas, steriles sequenti esse anno necesse sit.
units.tr: For these trees are very prodigal, and they use up so much nourishment in producing fruit in one year that, reduced to poverty, they must be barren the following year.

units.la: Substantiae porro stirpium proprietas in variis, iisq; privatis, quos edunt & exercent, spectatur effectibus.
units.tr: Further, the property of the substance of plants is observed in the various and peculiar effects which they produce and exercise.

units.la: Et exercent plantae has vires, in res vel animatas vel inanimatas.
units.tr: Plants exercise these powers on things either animate or inanimate.

units.la: In res animatas, nimirum vel stirpes alias, vel animalia.
units.tr: On animate things, namely on other plants or on animals.

units.la: In stirpes exercent vel amicitias, vel inimicitias. Sic enim Olea Quercum aversatur: Brassica viti & rutæ est odiosa: filici Arundo: Contrà autem Ruta fico ita amica deprehenditur, ut altera alterius vicinitate magis magisq; proficiat.
units.tr: On plants they exercise either friendships or enmities. Thus the olive shuns the oak; cabbage is hateful to the vine and to rue; the reed to fern. On the other hand, rue is found so friendly to the fig that each thrives more and more by the nearness of the other.

units.la: Harum rerum inquisitio admodùm est obscura: Ideò alii in causas obscuras, alii in manifestas horum effectuum ori-ginem referunt.
units.tr: The investigation of these matters is very obscure. Therefore some refer their causes to hidden things, others to the manifest origin of these effects.

units.la: Illud autem verisimile est, præter ob-scuram vim formæ quam inimicitiæ il-læ in primis sequuntur, etiam manife-stam subesse rationem; & hæc potissi-mum consistit in alimenti subtractione, aut etiam corruptione. Ob id enim ubi fuit Quercus, non vivit Olea, quasi ali-mentum siccitate quercus sit corrupti, & factum aridius, quàm pro oleæ natura sit ex usu. Ita brassica sub vite non prosi-cit. 1. Quoniam vitis radices alimen-tum copiosius exhauriunt; 2. Vitisque umbra Solis illustrationem impedit.
units.tr: It is likely, however, that besides the obscure power of the form, which chiefly produces those enmities, there also lies a manifest reason, and this consists chiefly in the withdrawal, or even the corruption, of nourishment. For this reason, where the oak has been, the olive does not live, as if the oak had corrupted the nourishment by its dryness, and the soil had become drier than is suitable for the nature of the olive. Thus cabbage does not thrive under the vine: (1) because the vine's roots draw off the nourishment more abundantly; (2) and the vine's shade hinders the sun's light.

units.la: Sic verò etiam amicitiæ illius, quam ruta cum ficu habet, nutrimentum videtur esse causa, siquidem è ficu arbore na-tura calida, calidum nutrimentum, rutæ naturæ opportunum, suggeritur.
units.tr: In the same way, the friendship which rue has with the fig seems to be caused by nourishment, since from the fig tree, which is warm by nature, warm nourishment is supplied, suited to the nature of rue.

units.la: Cum animalibus intercedunt plantis amicitiæ atq; inimicitiæ, vel cum solo homine, vel reliquis etiam animalibus.
units.tr: Friendships and enmities between plants and animals arise, either with man alone or also with the other animals.

units.la: Hominum generi & vitæ, aliæ stir-pes sunt amicæ, aliæ adversæ: aliæ verò media quadam ratione ancipites.
units.tr: Some plants are friendly to the human race and to life, others hostile, and others again are doubtful, in a certain middle way.

units.la: Amicæ vel familiares & salutares reficiunt & tuentur, vel corpus universum, vel determinatas partes.
units.tr: Friendly, or familiar and wholesome, plants refresh and preserve either the whole body or particular parts.

units.la: Quæ corpus universum ejusq; vitam conser-vant vim habent alendi: cujus causa est principiorum consensus, siquidem omnia nutriuntur similibus.
units.tr: Those which preserve the whole body and its life have the power of nourishing. The cause of this is the agreement of their principles, since all things are nourished by like things.

units.la: Num verò a forma hic sit consensus, an potius a materia, dubitatio est intricata: mate-ria quidem habilitas admodum est necessaria, sed formæ quoq; consensus accedat oportet.
units.tr: Whether this agreement comes from the form or rather from the matter is an intricate question: indeed, the suitability of matter is very necessary, but agreement of form must also be present.

units.la: Et alunt hæ plantæ vel integræ, vel earum tantum partes.
units.tr: These plants nourish either whole, or only their parts.

units.la: Integræ plantæ ut, Olera, Lactuca, Bras-sica, Nasturtium, Rapunculus.
units.tr: Whole plants, such as herbs, lettuce, cabbage, watercress, rampion.

units.la: Partes plantarum, ut, radices; nimi-rum, Rapæ, Pastinacæ, Raphani: Fructus, scilicet Melones, Cucumeres: Semina & fruges, quo referuntur legumina, Fabæ, Pisa: & Frumeta, Avena, Triticum, Zea.
units.tr: Parts of plants, such as roots, namely turnips, parsnips, radishes; fruits, namely melons and cucumbers; seeds and grains, to which belong pulses, beans, peas; and grains, oats, wheat, maize.

units.la: Quæ partem corporis certam tuentur sunt variæ: Sic enim Pœonia caput, Crocus cor; Menta ventriculum: Eupatorium jecur; Cappares splenem. Hermodactylus articulos: cujus rei causa est similitudo & consensus illius stirpis cum certæ partis forma.
units.tr: Those which protect a certain part of the body are various. Thus peony protects the head, saffron the heart, mint the stomach, eupatory the liver, capers the spleen, and hermodactyl the joints. The cause of this is the likeness and agreement of that plant with the form of a certain part.

units.la: Perniciosæ sive exitiales plantæ vel toti corpori inimicæ, illud corrumpunt, & evertunt vitam: vel parti tantum, ut capiti Hyosciamus; Mezereon jecori; Ervus renibus & vesicæ; Aloë hæmorrhoidibus. Cujus corruptionis causa est formæ controversia.
units.tr: Pernicious, or deadly, plants are either hostile to the whole body, corrupt it and overthrow its life, or only to a part: thus henbane to the head; mezereon to the liver; vetch to the kidneys and bladder; aloe to the haemorrhoids. The cause of this corruption is a dispute about form.

units.la: Eadem etiam planta uni homini salutaris est, alteri noxam aut mortem adfert, propter peculiarem individui constitutionem.
units.tr: The same plant may be wholesome to one man, and bring harm or death to another, on account of the peculiar constitution of the individual.

units.la: Plantæ, quæ sunt naturæ ancipitis corporibus nostris partim sunt amicæ partim inimicæ.
units.tr: Plants which are of doubtful nature are partly friendly and partly hostile to our bodies.

units.la: Inimicæ quidem, quod parvo sapore odoreve infectæ sunt: Amicæ vero & salutares quia inutiles corporis succos educendo nobis benefaciunt, ut Colocyntis & reliquæ purgantes plantæ.
units.tr: They are hostile indeed because they are tainted with little taste or smell; they are friendly and wholesome because, by drawing out the useless juices of the body, they do us good, as colocynth and the other purgative plants do.

units.la: Quatenus ergo ut medicamenta purgado agunt eo nomine generatim, dum humanum corpus superant, non autem superantur, vim inferunt, & sunt inimica : eadem autem cum humoribus, quos trahunt, amica sunt, cum eos similitudine quadam trahere censeantur.
units.tr: Insofar, then, as they act as purgative medicines in that respect, they are generally regarded as enemies, because they overcome the human body but are not overcome by it, and they do harm. Yet they are friends to the same humours which they draw off, since they are thought to draw them by a certain likeness.

units.la: Cum reliquis porro animalibus amicitiarum & inimicitiarum vires plantis quoque intercedunt: Serpenti enim est amicus Fæniculus, inimica Ruta, Fraxinus: Scorpioni infestum Aconitum, cujus ille vicinia torpescit, amicum vero est album Veratrum, quo admoto revi-viscit, & Ocymum, in quo & ex quo nasci observatur: sic & Oenothoram Cratævæ, & Lysimachiam, fera animalia, indomitosq; tauros, illorum collo suspensas, antiquitas cicurare observavit: quæ omnia tacitum quendam formarū consensum necessario exprimunt.
units.tr: Friendships and enmities with the other animals also hold between plants: fennel is a friend to the serpent, rue and ash are hostile to it; aconite is hostile to the scorpion, whose neighbourhood numbs it, while white hellebore is its friend, and when it is applied to the scorpion it revives, and basil, in which and from which it is observed to be born. So too antiquity observed that oenothera and lysimachia, which are hanged on the necks of wild animals and untamed bulls, tame them: all of which necessarily express a certain hidden agreement of forms.

units.la: In res inanimatas varios effectus plantæ pariunt: sic namq; Visci & Æthiopidis vi & contactu claustra omnia recludi scriptitant: Spina Theophrasti aquam congelat, Hybisci radix & Portulacæ ac mercurialis succus, nostri temporis experimento, ignis vim eludunt, quæ omnia si quid tale præstant, nō alia quàm formae proprie potentia praestare, omnino ratione persuademur.
units.tr: Plants produce various effects on inanimate things. Thus they write that mistletoe and the Ethiopian plant unlock all bolts by their force and touch; Theophrastus' thorn freezes water; the root of hibiscus, and the juice of purslane and mercury, by the experience of our own time, defeat the power of fire. All of these, if they do anything of the kind, we are fully persuaded by reason that they do only through the power of the form proper to each.

units.la: Deniq; pro coalitu & contemperatione qualitatum elementarium quatuor in plantis constituuntur gradus, nimirū ut quaedam sint calidae vel frigidae, humidae vel siccae, primo vel secundo vel tertio vel quarto gradu.
units.tr: Finally, from the combination and tempering of the four elemental qualities, four degrees are established in plants: some are hot or cold, moist or dry, in the first, second, third or fourth degree.

units.la: Et hi gradus respectivè sumti, vel remissiores, vel intensiores sunt. Remissior enim est primus gradus, reliqui intensiores, ita ut quartus sit summus, omninoq; mediocritatem excedat.
units.tr: And these degrees, taken relatively, are either milder or more intense. For the first degree is milder, the others more intense, so that the fourth is the highest and altogether exceeds the mean.

units.la: CAPUT XIX. DE DENDROGRAPHIA, ET BOTANOLOGIA generatim.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. CONCERNING DENDROGRAPHY AND BOTANOLOGY IN GENERAL.

units.la: Porrò Phytologiae partes duae sunt: Dendrographia & Botanologia.
units.tr: Moreover, the parts of Phytology are two: Dendrographia and Botanologia.

units.la: Dendrographia est pars Phytologiae, explicans naturā majorū plantarū.
units.tr: Dendrographia is the part of Phytology that explains the nature of the larger plants.

units.la: Majores plantae sunt Arbor & Frutex: Arbor tamen frutice major.
units.tr: The larger plants are the tree and the shrub, though the tree is larger than the shrub.

units.la: ARBOR est planta major, quae à radice per caudicem simplicem ramosam & surculosam assurgit.
units.tr: A TREE is a larger plant that rises from the root through a single trunk, branched and sprouting.

units.la: Seu : est planta lignosa dissolutu contumax, crassitudine & altitudine major; cui caudex pro superficie est perennis & natura simplex.
units.tr: Or: it is a woody plant, stubborn against dissolution, greater in girth and height, whose trunk is perennial on the outside and simple in nature.

units.la: Arbor gaudet aut solo potissimum calidiore, aut alio alius regionis.
units.tr: A tree delights either mainly in a warmer soil, or in the soil of another region.

units.la: Solo gaudent calidiore tantum, Thus, Myrrha, Macer, Arbor piperis, Palma, Balsamum, Malus punica, Malus citrina, Cedrus, &c.
units.tr: Trees that delight in a warmer soil only are frankincense, myrrh, mace, the pepper tree, the palm, balsam, the pomegranate, the citron, the cedar, etc.

units.la: Alio etiam alius regionis solo gaudent & nascuntur arbores, quæ sunt rursum aut Fructiferæ aut steriles.
units.tr: Trees also grow and are found in the soil of another region, and these are again either fruit-bearing or barren.

units.la: 1. Fructiferæ sunt variæ, & quidè primum aut sunt Pomiferæ, aut Bacciferæ.
units.tr: 1. Fruit-bearing trees are of various kinds, and first they are either pome-bearing or berry-bearing.

units.la: Pomiferæ, quæ poma ferunt, sunt Ficꝰ, Olea, Malus, ejusq; species variæ, Pyrꝰ, arbor Prunorum, Mespilꝰ, Cerasus, &c.
units.tr: Pome-bearing trees, which bear apples, are the fig, the olive, the apple and its various kinds, the pear, the plum tree, the medlar, the cherry, etc.

units.la: Bacciferæ quarum fructus sunt Baccæ minores & rotundiores, ut sunt Laurus, Iuniperus, Morus, &c.
units.tr: Berry-bearing trees, whose fruits are smaller and rounder berries, are the laurel, the juniper, the mulberry, etc.

units.la: 2. Deinde Frugiferæ arbores sunt aut Nuciferæ, ut Amygdalus, Juglans, Castanea, Fagus: aut Glandiferæ, ut Quercꝰ, Suber: aut Strobiliferæ, ut Pinus, Picea, Larix.
units.tr: 2. Then the grain-bearing trees are either nut-bearing, such as the almond, walnut, chestnut and beech; or acorn-bearing, such as the oak and cork; or cone-bearing, such as the pine, spruce and larch.

units.la: Steriles arbores sunt Ulmus, Alnus, Tilia, Buxus, Betula, Salices, Populus & aliæ ejusmodi.
units.tr: Barren trees are the elm, alder, lime, box, birch, willows, poplar and others of this kind.

units.la: Frutex est planta seu stirps major (arbore tamen minor) quæ caudice multi-plici humiliq; è radice exurgit.
units.tr: A shrub is a plant or stock larger than herbs but smaller than a tree, which rises from the root with a multiple, low trunk.

units.la: Suffrutex & tempore & natura prior est quàm frutex. Suffrutex enim est simplex. Fit autem pullulatione stolonum frutex. Non tamen ex omni suffrutice fit frutex frequentia supervenientium stolonum. Quidam suffruti-cem herbis subjiciunt, & definiunt herbam vel arborescentem vel fruticescentem pluribus li-gnosisq; surculis, ex radice simplici vel multi-plici caudice prodeuntibus, minutis foliis, cætera herbæ similem.
units.tr: The undershrub is prior to the shrub both in time and in nature. For the undershrub is simple. A shrub, however, comes about through the sprouting of runners. Yet not every undershrub becomes a shrub through the frequent arrival of runners. Some subordinate the undershrub to herbs, and define it as an herb that becomes either tree-like or shrub-like, with several woody shoots springing from a simple or multiple-trunked root, with small leaves, and otherwise similar to an herb.

units.la: Frutices sunt nobiliores vel ignobi-liores.
units.tr: Shrubs are either nobler or less noble.

units.la: Nobiliores sunt Cinamomum, Cassia fistula, &c.
units.tr: The nobler ones are cinnamon, the senna pod, etc.

units.la: Ignobiliores sunt Corylus, Sambucus, Oxyacantha, Ribes, Rosa, Rubus, Pote-rion, Colatea.
units.tr: The less noble ones are hazel, elder, hawthorn, currant, rose, bramble, burnet, and bladder senna.

units.la: Botanologia est pars phytologiæ expli-cans naturam minorum plantarum.
units.tr: Botanologia is the part of phytology that explains the nature of the smaller plants.

units.la: Minores plantæ sunt Herbæ.
units.tr: The smaller plants are herbs.

units.la: Herba est planta minor sine caudice & radice proveniens foliata, plerumque tenui caule.
units.tr: An herb is a smaller plant, arising without a trunk or root-stock, leafy, usually with a slender stalk.

units.la: Seu : est stirps minor cujus superficies ex caule sed non perenni verum annuo & ligni experte constat: Sub hac comprehendimus fruges & olera.
units.tr: Or: it is a smaller stock whose body consists of a stalk that is not perennial but annual, and without wood. Under this heading we include grains and vegetables.

units.la: Herba deinde aut sunt alimentariæ, aut minus alimentariæ.
units.tr: Herbs are then either alimentary or less alimentary.

units.la: Alimentariæ sunt, quarum potissimus usus est in alimentis hominum.
units.tr: Alimentary herbs are those whose chief use is in human food.

units.la: Alimentariæ herbæ sunt triplices, 1. Fru-mentaceæ, ut Triticum, Hordeum, Spelta, Siligo, Avena. 2. Leguminosæ cujusmodi sunt, Oryza, Milium, Lentes, Pisa, Fa-bæ, &c. 3. Oleraceæ, ut sunt Brassica, Spi-nacea, Lactuca, Beta, Portulaca, Cepa, Porrum, Petroselinum & aliæ.
units.tr: Alimentary herbs are of three kinds: 1. cereals, such as wheat, barley, spelt, rye, oats. 2. pulses, of which sorts are rice, millet, lentils, peas, beans, etc. 3. vegetables, such as cabbage, spinach, lettuce, beet, purslane, onion, leek, parsley and others.

units.la: Alimentum autem præbent vel integræ plantæ, vel plantarum partes vel fœtus, ut 1. Semina quæ sunt aut Cerealia, ut triticum, hordeum, avena, zea, far, secale, milium: aut Legumina, ut faba, pisa, phaseoli, lentes, oryza, cicer. 2. Folia, ut lactuca, brassica, beta, spinacea, portulaca, malva, intybus. 3. Flores Buglossi, Borraginis, Genistæ, Sambuci. 4. Fructus non modo quarundam arborum, sed & herbarum, ut Curcubitæ, Melones, Pepones, Cucumeres, Fragæ, &c. 5. Radices, ut Rapæ, Napi, Raphani, Pastinacæ, Petroselini.
units.tr: They provide food either as whole plants, or as parts of plants, or as fruits, such as 1. seeds, which are either cereal, such as wheat, barley, oats, maize, spelt, rye and millet; or pulses, such as the bean, pea, kidney bean, lentil, rice and chickpea. 2. Leaves, such as lettuce, cabbage, beet, spinach, purslane, mallow and chicory. 3. Flowers of bugloss, borage, broom and elder. 4. Fruits not only of certain trees but also of herbs, such as gourds, melons, pumpkins, cucumbers, strawberries, etc. 5. Roots, such as turnips, rape, radishes, parsnips and parsley root.

units.la: Minus alimentariæ herbæ sunt[?] vel Coronariæ vel Medicamentosæ. Coronariæ, quæ præter alios usus maximè in corollis expetuntur, ad ornatum propter colorem & odorem: quales sunt: Violæ eijsque species, Herba trinitatis, Bellis, flos Caryophyllorum, Majorana, Rosmarinus, Nardus, Narcissus, Lychnis, Coronaria & aliæ.
units.tr: Less alimentary herbs are either garland herbs or medicinal herbs. Garland herbs are sought above all for wreaths, apart from their other uses, for ornament because of their colour and scent. Such are violets and their kinds, heartsease, daisy, the clove pink, marjoram, rosemary, spikenard, narcissus, lychnis, coronaria and others.

units.la: Medicamentosæ sunt, quarum potior & crebrior usus est in morborum remediis. Suntq; vel Simplices ut Mercurialis saporosa, vel Aromaticæ quæ præter odoris fragrantiam & saporis acrimoniam in tenuem pulverem cotritæ odoris suavitate magis magisq; nares gustumque afficiunt, ut sunt Crocus, Zinziber, Zeduaria, Galanga, Calamus aromaticus, Acorus & aliæ similes.
units.tr: Medicinal herbs are those whose chief and more frequent use is in remedies for diseases. They are either simple, such as the savoury mercury, or aromatic, which, besides the fragrance of their smell and the sharpness of their taste, when ground into a fine powder affect the nose and the palate more and more with the sweetness of their odour. Such are saffron, ginger, zedoary, galangal, sweet flag, acorus and other similar ones.

units.la: CAPUT XX. SPECIALIUS EXPLICANS STIRPIUM SEU PLANTARUM
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. THE STIRPES OR PLANTS, EXPLAINED MORE PARTICULARLY

units.la: Vires ac facultates.
units.tr: Powers and faculties.

units.la: P[?]Lantarum differentias planius manifestant Vires ac facultates carundem.
units.tr: The powers and faculties of plants make the differences between them clearer.

units.la: Facultas autem illa est à Forma quippe ipsas distinguit species.
units.tr: That faculty, indeed, comes from the form, which is what distinguishes the species themselves.

units.la: Ipsa vero utitur qualitatibus ceu instrumentis (ut supra.)
units.tr: The faculty itself uses the qualities as its instruments (as above).

units.la: Qualitatum illarum, pro intensionis & remissionis modo distincti quidam GRADUS sunt.
units.tr: Of these qualities there are certain grades, distinguished by the degree of their intensity and remission.

units.la: Hinc nonnullae in gradu primo, aliae in secundo, tertio, quarto dicuntur calidae, humidae, frigidae, siccae.+
units.tr: Hence some plants are said to be hot, moist, cold or dry in the first degree, others in the second, third or fourth.

units.la: Facultates porro hae consistunt vel in tota planta, vel in partibus ejus.
units.tr: These faculties reside either in the whole plant or in its parts.

units.la: I. RADIX plantae vel alterat, vel purgat.
units.tr: I. The ROOT of a plant either alters or purges.

units.la: Alterat qualitate vel manifesta, vel occulta.
units.tr: It alters by a quality that is either manifest or occult.

units.la: Manifesta conservat vel corrumpit.+
units.tr: The manifest qualities either preserve or corrupt.

units.la: Quae cōservat aut prima aut secunda est.+
units.tr: The preserving quality is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Prima qualitate alterantes radices calidae sunt, frigidae, humidae aut siccae.
units.tr: Roots that alter by a primary quality are hot, cold, moist or dry.

units.la: Idque in primo, secundo, tertio aut quarto gradu: Uti fere in reliquis etiam partibus.
units.tr: This holds in the first, second, third or fourth degree; and much the same is true of the other parts as well.

units.la: Radices primo gradu calidae sunt, Altheae, Acanthi, Buglossae, Glycyrrhi-zae,&c. Secundo: Apii, Capparorum, Peuce-dani, Pimpinellæ, Rapæ, Scyllæ, Zedu-ariæ, Rhodiæ, Cavæ radicis <bl>Holwurtzel[?]</bl>.
units.tr: Roots hot in the first degree: Marsh mallow (Althaea), Acanthus, Bugloss, Liquorice, etc. Second degree: Celery, Caper, Masterwort, Burnet saxifrage, Turnip, Squill, Zedoary, Rhodian root, the hollow root (Holwurtzel).

units.la: Tertio: Acori, Ari, Dictamni, Asari, Doronici, Fœniculi, Galangæ, Helenii, Petroselini, Raphani, Angelicæ, &c.
units.tr: Third degree: Sweet flag, Arum, Dittany, Asarabacca, Doronicum, Fennel, Galangal, Elecampane, Parsley, Radish, Angelica, etc.

units.la: Quarto: Allii, Cepæ, Costi, Porri, Pirethri, &c.
units.tr: Fourth degree: Garlic, Onion, Costus, Leek, Pellitory, etc.

units.la: FRIGIDÆ primo gradu, ut Malvæ, &c.
units.tr: COLD roots in the first degree, such as Mallow, etc.

units.la: Secundo, ut Cichorii, &c. Tertio, Mandragoræ, &c.
units.tr: Second degree, such as Chicory, etc. Third degree, Mandrake, etc.

units.la: Humidæ primo gradu & principio secundi, ut: Buglossæ, Glycyrrhizæ, Malvæ, Rapæ, Satyrii, &c.
units.tr: Moist roots in the first degree and the beginning of the second, such as Bugloss, Liquorice, Mallow, Turnip, Satyrion, etc.

units.la: Siccæ primo gradu, Althææ, Ari, Bryoniæ, Fæniculi, Cenanthæ, Tamariscis, &c.
units.tr: Dry roots in the first degree: Marsh mallow, Arum, Bryony, Fennel, Cnanthe, Tamarisk, etc.

units.la: Secundo, Capparorum, Cichorii, Raphani, &c.
units.tr: Second degree: Caper, Chicory, Radish, etc.

units.la: Tertio, Acori, Apii, Asari, Doronici, Petroselini, Pentaphylli, &c.
units.tr: Third degree: Sweet flag, Celery, Asarabacca, Doronicum, Parsley, Cinquefoil, etc.

units.la: Radices secunda qualitate alterantes. 1. Aut sunt Astringentes, ut Cyperi, Bistortæ, Gentianæ, Pentaphylli, Rhapontici, &c.
units.tr: Roots that alter by a secondary quality: (1) some are astringent, such as Galingale, Bistort, Gentian, Cinquefoil, Rhapontic, etc.

units.la: 2. Discutientes, ut Aristolochiæ, Asphodeli, Bryoniæ, Capparorum.
units.tr: (2) Discutient, such as Birthwort, Asphodel, Bryony, Caper.

units.la: 3. Abstergentes, Aristolochiæ, Ari, Asparagi, Asphodeli, Bulbi, Chelidonii.
units.tr: (3) Abstersive (cleansing), such as Birthwort, Arum, Asparagus, Asphodel, Bulb, Celandine.

units.la: 4. Aperientes, ut Allii, Cepæ, Curcumæ, Rhapontici &c.
units.tr: (4) Opening, such as Garlic, Onion, Turmeric, Rhapontic, etc.

units.la: 5. Extenuantes, ut Iridis, Illyricæ, &c.
units.tr: (5) Attenuating, such as Iris, Orris, etc.

units.la: 6. Adurentes, ut Allii, Pyrethri, &c.
units.tr: (6) Caustic, such as Garlic, Pellitory, etc.

units.la: 7. Emollientes, ut Malvæ, Bismalvæ, &c.
units.tr: (7) Softening, such as Mallow, Marsh mallow, etc.

units.la: 8. Suppurantes, ut Altheæ, Bryoniæ, Liliorum alborum.
units.tr: (8) Suppurating, such as Marsh mallow, Bryony, white lily.

units.la: 9. Glutinantes, ut Aristolochiæ, Dracunculi, Gentianæ, Sigilli Salomonis, Symphyti.
units.tr: (9) Gluing together, such as Birthwort, Dragonwort, Gentian, Solomon's seal, Comfrey.

units.la: 10. Flatus discutientes, Apii, Acori, Allii, Costi, Dauci, Enulæ, Fœniculi, Galangæ, Petroselini, Peucedani, Zedoariæ, Spicæ Celticæ & Nardi.
units.tr: (10) Dispersing wind: Celery, Sweet flag, Garlic, Costus, Carrot, Elecampane, Fennel, Galangal, Parsley, Hog's fennel, Zedoary, Celtic spike and Spikenard.

units.la: 11. Semen generantes, ut, Acori, Bulbi, Eryngii, Satyrii, Pastinacæ.
units.tr: (11) Generating seed: Sweet flag, Bulb, Eryngo, Satyrion, Parsnip.

units.la: 12. Menses moventes; Asari, Ari, Acori, Aristolochiæ, Asphodeli, Allii, Bryoniæ, Centaurii majoris, Cyperi, Costi, Capparorum, Calami aromatici, Dauci, Dictamni, Filipendulæ, Fœniculi, Graminis, Helenii, Lilii, Petroselini, Poeoniae, Raphani, Valerianae, &c.
units.tr: (12) Moving the menses: Asarabacca, Arum, Sweet flag, Birthwort, Asphodel, Garlic, Bryony, greater Centaury, Galingale, Costus, Caper, Sweet cane, Carrot, Dittany, Dropwort, Fennel, Couch grass, Elecampane, Parsley, Peony, Radish, Valerian, etc.

units.la: 13. Menses sistentes; Tormentillae, Symphyti.
units.tr: (13) Stopping the menses: Tormentil, Comfrey.

units.la: 14. Sudore provocantes: Chinae, Salsae paulinae.
units.tr: (14) Provoking sweat: China root, Salsa paulina.

units.la: 15. Venenis resistentes: Angelicae, Apii, Allii, Aristolochiae longae, Bryoniae, Cyperi, Costi, Foeniculi, Gentianae, Carlinae, Doronici, &c.
units.tr: (15) Resisting poisons: Angelica, Celery, Garlic, long Birthwort, Bryony, Galingale, Costus, Fennel, Gentian, Carline thistle, Doronicum, etc.

units.la: 16. Ambusta sanantes; Asphodeli, Bulbi, Hyacinthi, Liliorum alborum.
units.tr: (16) Healing burns: Asphodel, Bulb, Hyacinth, white lily.

units.la: 17. Dolorem mitigantes; ut, Acori, Dauci, Eryngii, Ireos, Mandragorae, Ononis.
units.tr: (17) Relieving pain: such as Sweet flag, Carrot, Eryngo, Iris, Mandrake, Restharrow.

units.la: Occulta qualitate alterat: radix Bryoniae, Paeoniae, &c.
units.tr: Altering by an occult quality: root of Bryony, Peony, etc.

units.la: Corrumpendo vero alterant Venena,ut: Mandragorae, Fungi, Ephemerum, Veratrum album.
units.tr: Roots that alter by corrupting, as poisons: Mandrake, Fungus, Ephemerum, white Hellebore.

units.la: Purgantes radices sequuntur quae vel Bilem vel Pituitam expurgant.
units.tr: The purging roots follow, which expel either bile or phlegm.

units.la: BILEM Flavam, vel Atram.
units.tr: BILE, either yellow or black.

units.la: Flavam; Rhabarbarum, Rhaponticum, Filicis.
units.tr: Yellow bile: Rhubarb, Rhapontic, Fern.

units.la: Atram; Elleborus niger, Polypodiu.
units.tr: Black bile: black Hellebore, Polypody.

units.la: Pituitam : Agarici, Cucumeris fylvestris, Esulae majoris & minoris, Ebu-li, Hermodactylus, Sambuci, Turpe-tum.
units.tr: Phlegm: Agaric, wild Cucumber, greater and lesser Spurge, Dwarf elder, Hermodactyl, Elder, Turpeth.

units.la: II. Folia sunt Temperata vel Intem-perata.
units.tr: II. Leaves are either temperate or intemperate.

units.la: Temperata, Adianthum, Asparagus, Atractylis, &c.
units.tr: Temperate: Maidenhair, Asparagus, Atractylis, etc.

units.la: Intemperata vel sunt Calida, Frigida, Humida aut Sicca.
units.tr: Intemperate leaves are either hot, cold, moist or dry.

units.la: Folia Primo gradu Calida sunt: Absinthium, Althea, Borrago, Buglossa, Beta, Brasica, Chamomilla, Cuscutha, Eupatorium, Melilotus, Malabatrum, Linaria, Spicanardi, Scolopendrium, Symphytum, &c.
units.tr: Leaves hot in the first degree: Wormwood, Marsh mallow, Borage, Bugloss, Beet, Cabbage, Chamomile, Dodder, Eupatory, Melilot, Malabathrum, Toadflax, Spikenard, Hart's tongue, Comfrey, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Anethum, Angelica, Apium, Artemisia, Betonica, Chamæpytis, Hypericum, Hedera, Lupulus, Melissa, Marrubium, Myrrhis, Ocymum, Pimpinella, Peucedanum, Rosmarinus, Salvia, Scabiosa, Scordiu, Stœchas, Parthenium.
units.tr: Second degree: Dill, Angelica, Celery, Mugwort, Betony, Germander, St John's wort, Ivy, Hop, Balm, Horehound, Sweet cicely, Basil, Burnet saxifrage, Masterwort, Rosemary, Sage, Scabious, Scordium, Stoechas, Feverfew.

units.la: Tertio: Abrotanum, Anethum aridum, Asarum, Agnus castus, A-momum, Ammi, Baccharis, Dictam-num, Charyophyllata, Chamædrys, Carthamus, Centaurium, Chelidonium, Calamintha, Conyza, Fæniculū, Iuniperus, Helenium, Hyssopum, Laurꝰ, Majorana, Mentha, Menthastrum, Nigella, Oenanthe, Origanum, Periclymenum, Petroselinum, Ptarmica, Pulegiū, Ruta, Sabina, Serpillum, Sisymbrium, Thymus, Satureia, Trifolium, Verbena-ca, Urtica.
units.tr: Third degree: Southernwood, dry Dill, Asarabacca, Chaste tree, Amomum, Ammi, Baccharis, Dittany, Clove gillyflower, Germander, Safflower, Centaury, Celandine, Calamint, Fleabane, Fennel, Juniper, Elecampane, Hyssop, Laurel, Marjoram, Mint, Calamint, Nigella, Water dropwort, Oregano, Honeysuckle, Parsley, Pennyroyal, Pulegium, Rue, Savin, Wild thyme, Sisymbrium, Thyme, Savory, Clover, Vervain, Nettle.

units.la: Quarto: Allium, Lepidium, Nasturtium, Porrum, Struthium, Thapsia, &c.
units.tr: Fourth degree: Garlic, Pepperwort, Watercress, Leek, Struthium, Thapsia, etc.

units.la: Folia gradu primo frigida sunt: Atri-plex, Fumaria, Lapathum, Malva, Myr-tus, Parietaria, &c.
units.tr: Leaves cold in the first degree: Orache, Fumitory, Dock, Mallow, Myrtle, Pellitory, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Blitum, Condrilla, Lactu-ca, Endivia, Cichorea, Hyacinthꝰ, Oxa-lis seu Acetosa, Plantago, Polygonum, Psyllium, Rhus obsoniorum, Sola-num.
units.tr: Second degree: Blite, Chondrilla, Lettuce, Endive, Chicory, Hyacinth, Wood sorrel or Sorrel, Plantain, Knotgrass, Psyllium, Sumac, Nightshade.

units.la: Tertio: Portulaca, Mandragora, Sempervivum, Hyoscyamus, &c.
units.tr: Third degree: Purslane, Mandrake, Houseleek, Henbane, etc.

units.la: Quarto: Cicuta, Papaver, &c.
units.tr: Fourth degree: Hemlock, Poppy, etc.

units.la: Folia gradu primo humida; Buglossum, Intybum, Malva, Helxine, &c.
units.tr: Leaves moist in the first degree: Bugloss, Chicory, Mallow, Helxine, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Atriplex, Lactuca, Blitum, Portulaca, Viola, Nenuphar, seu flos Nymphææ[?], &c.
units.tr: Second degree: Orache, Lettuce, Blite, Purslane, Violet, water lily (Nenuphar), etc.

units.la: Folia primo gradu sicca: Beta, Brassica, Chamomilla, Foeniculum, Hyacinthus, Malabathrum, Myrtus, Verbascum, &c.
units.tr: Leaves dry in the first degree: Beet, Cabbage, Chamomile, Fennel, Hyacinth, Malabathrum, Myrtle, Mullein, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Artemisia, Anethum viride, Brassica marina seu Soldanella, Bursa pastoris, Cuscutha, Equisetum, Gnigidium, Intybum, Plantago, Mentha, Menthastrum, Spicanardi, Rosmarinus, Verbenaca, &c.
units.tr: Second degree: Mugwort, dill leaves, sea cabbage or Soldanella, shepherd's purse, Dodder, Horsetail, Gingidium, Chicory, Plantain, Mint, Calamint, Spikenard, Rosemary, vervain, etc.

units.la: Tertio: Abrotanum ustum, Anethum ustum, Apium, Asarum, Ammi, Absinthiü, Calamintha, Chamaedrys, Filix, Hyssopum, Majorana, Marrubiü, Millefolium, Origanum, Peucedanum, Petrofelinü, Pentaphyllum, Polium, Ptarmica, Rhus obsoniorum, Ruta, Sabina, Salix, Sisymbrium, &c.
units.tr: Third degree: burnt Southernwood, burnt Dill, Celery, Asarabacca, Ammi, Wormwood, Calamint, Germander, Fern, Hyssop, Marjoram, Horehound, Milfoil, Oregano, Masterwort, Parsley, Cinquefoil, Polium, Water dropwort, Sumac, Rue, Savin, Willow, Sisymbrium, etc.

units.la: Quarto: Allium, Nasturtium, Ruta sylvestris, Synapi, &c.
units.tr: Fourth degree: Garlic, Watercress, wild Rue, Mustard, etc.

units.la: Et hæc fuerunt folia alterantia qualitate prima; Sequuntur quæ alterant qualitate secunda.
units.tr: These were the leaves that alter by the first quality. There follow those that alter by the second quality.

units.la: Ea sunt astringentia; ut, Absinthium, Amomum, Agnus castus, Bursa pastoris, Brassica cocta, Cypressus, Equisetum, Ebulus, Hypocisthis, Hedera, Helxine, Hieracium, Intybum, Lauri folia, Lyfimachia, Melilotum, Myrtus, Mentha, Oxalis, Polygonum, Pentaphyllum, Pfillium, Plantago, Portulaca, Folia quercus, Ruta, Rhus obsoniorum, Sempervivum, Salix, Verbascum, Vitex, Vitis, Asperula odorata, &c.
units.tr: These are astringent, such as: Wormwood, Amomum, Chaste tree, shepherd's purse, boiled cabbage, Cypress, Horsetail, Dwarf elder, Hypocistis, Ivy, Helxine, Hawkweed, Chicory, bay leaves, Loosestrife, Melilot, Myrtle, Mint, Wood sorrel, Knotgrass, Cinquefoil, Plantain, Purslane, Oak leaves, Rue, Sumac, Houseleek, Willow, Mullein, Chaste tree, Vine, sweet woodruff, etc. Psyllium, etc.

units.la: Aperientia: Allium, Cepa, Cyclaminus, Dulcamara, &c.
units.tr: Opening: Garlic, Onion, Cyclamen, Bittersweet, etc.

units.la: Emollientia; Atriplex, Althea, Cupressus, Laurus, Malva, Psyllium, &c.
units.tr: Softening: Orache, Marsh mallow, Cypress, Laurel, Mallow, Psyllium, etc.

units.la: Indurantia: Portulaca, Lenticula palustris, Sempervivum, Solanum, &c.
units.tr: Hardening: Purslane, marsh lentil, Houseleek, Nightshade, etc.

units.la: Extenuantia: Artemisia, Chamæmelum, Hyssopus, Juniperus, Pulegium, Stœchas, &c.
units.tr: Attenuating: Mugwort, Chamomile, Hyssop, Juniper, Pennyroyal, Stoechas, etc.

units.la: Discutientia: Abrotanum, Althea, Anethum, Adianthum, Atriplex, Brassica, Chamæmelum, folia Lilii, Malva, Mentha, Melilotum, Origanum, Ruta, Stœchas, Sampsuchus.
units.tr: Dispersing: Southernwood, Marsh mallow, Dill, Maidenhair, Orache, Cabbage, Chamomile, leaves of lily, Mallow, Mint, Melilot, Oregano, Rue, Stoechas, Sampsuchus.

units.la: Extrahentia: Anagallis, Aristolochia, Cyclaminus, Dictamnus, Porrum, Thapsia, &c.
units.tr: Drawing out: Pimpernel, Birthwort, Cyclamen, Dittany, Leek, Thapsia, etc.

units.la: Suppurantia: Amomum, Althea, Smyrnium.
units.tr: Suppurating: Amomum, Marsh mallow, Smyrnium.

units.la: Abstergentia: Anagallis, Abrotanum, Asparagus, Asplenum, Atriplex, Absinthium, Beta, Chamæpytis, Cuscutha, Lichen, Marrubium, Parietaria, Salix.
units.tr: Cleansing: Pimpernel, Southernwood, Asparagus, Spleenwort, Orache, Wormwood, Beet, Germander, Cuscuta, Lichen, Horehound, Pellitory, Willow.

units.la: Glutinantia & Cicatricem inducentia: Althea, Anagallis, Centaurium, Chamæpitys, Chamædrys, Equisetum, Eupatorium, Ebulus, Fragaria, Isatis, Myrtus, Plantago, Quinquefolium, Symphytum majus, Sanicula, Tormentilla, Verbenaca, Herniaria, Nicotiana, &c.
units.tr: Gluing together and inducing a scar: Marsh mallow, Pimpernel, Centaury, Germander, Germander, Horsetail, Agrimony, Dwarf elder, Strawberry, Woad, Myrtle, Plantain, Cinquefoil, Comfrey, greater comfrey, Sanicle, Tormentil, Vervain, Rupturewort, Tobacco, etc.

units.la: Flatus discutientia: Absinthium, Allium, Anethum, Apiu, Chamæmelu, Epithymum, Fœniculum, Juniperus, Majorana, Origanum, Petrofelinum, Ruta, Squinantum, Spicanardi, Smyrnium, Sescli, &c.
units.tr: Dispersing wind: Wormwood, Garlic, Dill, Celery, Chamomile, Dodder, Fennel, Juniper, Marjoram, Oregano, Parsley, Rue, Squinanth, Spikenard, Smyrnium, Seseli, etc.

units.la: Semen generat: Horminum, Eruca, &c.
units.tr: Generating seed: Horminum, Rocket, etc.

units.la: Menses movent: Asarum, Abrotanum, Allium, Adianthum, Amomum, Absinthium, Artemisia, Alisma, Ammi, Brassica sativa, Betonica, Centaurium, Chamæmelum, Calamintha, Chamædrys, Cuscuta, Cyclaminus, Dictamnus, Daucus, Gingidium, Fœnicu-lum lum, Hipericum, Heliochrysos, Lapa-thum, Majorana, Marrubium, Melis-sa, Nasturtium, Origanum, Ocymum, Pulegium, Polium, Petrofelinum, Oreo-felinum, Raphanus, Ruta, Rosmari-nus, Smyrnium, Salvia, Sabina, Seseli, Serpillum, Trifolium odoratum, Vitex, Urtica.
units.tr: Moving the menses: Asarabacca, Southernwood, Garlic, Maidenhair, Amomum, Wormwood, Mugwort, Alisma, Ammi, cultivated cabbage, Betony, Centaury, Chamomile, Calamint, Germander, Dodder, Cyclamen, Dittany, Carrot, Gingidium, Fennel, St John's wort, Heliochrysos, Sumac, Marjoram, Horehound, Balm, Nasturtium, Oregano, Basil, Pennyroyal, Polium, Parsley, Mountain parsley, Radish, Rue, Rosemary, Smyrnium, Sage, Savin, Seseli, Wild thyme, sweet clover, Vitex, Nettle.

units.la: Menses sistunt : Bursa pastoris, Fragaria, Hyoscyamus, Limonium, Lysimachia, Myrtus, Nymphaæ[?], Plantago, Ru-bus, Sempervivum, Symphytum, Solanum,&c.
units.tr: Stopping the menses: Shepherd's purse, Strawberry, Henbane, Sea lavender, Loosestrife, Myrtle, water lily, Plantain, Bramble, Houseleek, Comfrey, Nightshade, etc.

units.la: Venenis resistunt : Abrotanum, Ab-sinthium, Allium, Adianthum, Apium, Brassica, Betonica, Carduus benedictus, Chamaedrys, Cyclaminus, Calamintha, Eupatorium, Eryfimum, Fæniculum, Iuniperus, Lybisticum, Carlina, Marru-bium, Origanum, Pulegium, Polium, Ruta, Scordium, &c.
units.tr: Resisting poisons: Southernwood, Wormwood, Garlic, Maidenhair, Celery, Cabbage, Betony, blessed thistle, Germander, Cyclamen, Calamint, Eupatory, Eryngium, Fennel, Juniper, Lybisticum, Carline thistle, Horehound, Oregano, Pennyroyal, Polium, Rue, Scordium, etc.

units.la: Strumas discutiunt : Adianthum, A-parine, Althea, Lupinus, Lapathum, Melissa, Galiopsis, Nasturtium, Penta-phyllum, Scordium, &c.
units.tr: Dispersing scrofulous swellings: Maidenhair, Aparine, Marsh mallow, Lupin, Dock, Balm, Galeopsis, Watercress, Cinquefoil, Scordium, etc.

units.la: Dolorem mitigant : Anethum, Ab-sinthium, Asclepias, Atriplex, Chamaemelum, Calamintha, Centaurium majus, Chamaepitys, Hyoscyamus, Lybifti-cum, Lupulus, Peucedanum, Petroselinum, Rosmarinus, Ruta, Sisymbrium, Serpillum & Sampsuchus,&c.
units.tr: Relieving pain: Dill, Wormwood, Asclepias, Orache, Chamomile, Calamint, greater Centaury, Chamaepitys, Henbane, Lybisticum, Hop, Masterwort, Parsley, Rosemary, Rue, Sisymbrium, Wild thyme and Sampsuchus, etc.

units.la: Adhuc fuerunt folia manifesta qualitate alterantia. Sequuntur quae occulta: ut, Personata, Brassica, Hedera, Hyoscyamus, Ebulus, Trifolium, Aconitum, Pentaphyllum, &c.
units.tr: Thus far were the leaves that alter by a manifest quality. There follow those that do so by an occult quality, such as: Honeysuckle, Cabbage, Ivy, Henbane, Dwarf elder, Clover, Aconite, Cinquefoil, etc.

units.la: Quae vero corrumpendo alterant, sunt: Aconitum, Cicuta, Hyoscyamus, Papaver corniculatum, Sardonia herba, Taxus, Thapsia, Toxicum, Pharicum[?], &c.
units.tr: Those that alter by corrupting are: Aconitum, Cicuta, Hyoscyamus, Papaver corniculatum, Sardonia herba, Taxus, Thapsia, Toxicum, Pharicum[?], etc.

units.la: Hactenus folia alterantia; Sequuntur purgantia.
units.tr: So far the leaves that alter. Next come the purging ones.

units.la: Purgant autē vel Bilem, vel Pituitam, vel Aquam.
units.tr: Purgatives purge either bile, phlegm, or water.

units.la: Bilem Flavam, vel Atram.
units.tr: Bile is either yellow or black.

units.la: Flavam; Absinthium, Centaurium, Lupulus salictarius[?], Persici folia, &c.
units.tr: Yellow bile: Absinthium, Centaurium, Lupulus salictarius[?], peach leaves, etc.

units.la: Atram; Sena, Fumaria, Cuscuta, Epithymus.
units.tr: Black bile: Sena, Fumaria, Cuscuta, Epithymus.

units.la: Pituitam; Gratiola, Peplion, Daphnoides, etc.
units.tr: Phlegm: Gratiola, Peplion, Daphnoides, etc.

units.la: Aquam; Cyclaminus, Ebulus, Sambucus, Chamaelea, Tithymali omnes, &c.
units.tr: Water: Cyclaminus, Ebulus, Sambucus, Chamaelea, all the Tithymali, etc. ## So far concerning leaves.

units.la: Hucusque de Foliis.
Sequuntur Flores :
units.tr: Next, flowers.

units.la: Sunt autem Calidi, Frigidi, Humidi vel Sicci.
units.tr: They are either hot, cold, moist or dry.

units.la: Primo gradu calefaciunt : Borragi-nis, Buglossæ, Betonicæ, Buphtalmi, Me-liloti, Chamomillæ, Stœchadis.
units.tr: In the first degree they warm: Borraginis, Buglossa, Betonica, Buphthalmum, Melilotus, Chamomilla, Stoechas.

units.la: Secundo : Amomi, Croci, Charyophyllorum, Ericæ, Melissæ, Spicænardi, Lupulorum, Junci odorati, Rosmarini, Lavendulæ, &c.
units.tr: In the second: Amomum, Crocus, Caryophylli, Erica, Melissa, Spica nardi, hops, scented rush, Rosmarinus, Lavandula, etc.

units.la: Tertio : Agni casti, Epithymi, Leucori, Oenanthe, Periclymeni, &c.
units.tr: In the third: Agnus castus, Epithymum, Leucorium, Oenanthe, Periclymenum, etc.

units.la: Frigidi primo gradu ; Malvæ, Rosa-rum, Violarum, &c.
units.tr: Cold in the first degree: Malva, roses, violets, etc.

units.la: Secundo : Anemone, Hyacinthi, In-tybi, Nymphaæ, &c.
units.tr: In the second: Anemone, Hyacinthus, Intybus, Nymphaea, etc.

units.la: Tertio : Balaustiæ. Quarto : Hyo-scyami, &c.
units.tr: In the third: Balaustia. In the fourth: Hyoscyamus, etc.

units.la: Humidi primo Gradu : Buglossæ, Malvæ, Cicorii, &c.
units.tr: Moist in the first degree: Buglossa, Malva, Cichorium, etc.

units.la: Secundo ; Nymphææ, Violarum, &c.
units.tr: In the second: Nymphaea, violets, etc.

units.la: Sicci in primo Gradu : Buphthalmi, Chamomillæ, Hyacinthi, Meliloti, Ro-farum, &c.
units.tr: Dry in the first degree: Buphthalmum, Chamomilla, Hyacinthus, Melilotus, roses, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Anemone, Amomi, Croci, Charyophyllorum, Ericæ, Junci odorati, Lavendulæ, Lupuli, Pæoniæ, Rorismarini, Spicænardi, &c.
units.tr: In the second: Anemone, Amomum, Crocus, Caryophylli, Erica, scented rush, Lavandula, hops, Paeonia, Rosmarinus, Spica nardi, etc.

units.la: Tertio · Balaustiæ, Epithymi, Jasmini, Chamæpitheos, Periclymeni, &c.
units.tr: In the third: Balaustia, Epithymum, jasmine, Chamaepitys, Periclymenum, etc.

units.la: Hucusque de Floribus alterantibus prima qualitate: Sequuntur, quæ alte-rant Secunda.
units.tr: Thus far the flowers that alter by the first quality. Next are those that alter by the second.

units.la: Suntque vel adstringentes, ut Balau-stiæ, Croci, Cichorii, Meliloti, Rosarum, Verbasci, Viticis, &c.
units.tr: These are either astringent, such as Balaustia, Crocus, Cichorium, Melilotus, roses, Verbascum, Vitex, etc.

units.la: Discutientes: ut Anethi, Chamomil-læ, Malvę, Meliloti, Stœchados, &c.
units.tr: Discutient, such as dill, Chamomilla, Malva, Melilotus, Stoechas, etc.

units.la: Abstergentes: ut Tiliæ, Fabarū, &c.
units.tr: Abstergent, such as lime blossom, beans, etc.

units.la: Extenuantes: ut Chamomillæ viri-dis, Illyricæ, Stœchados, &c.
units.tr: Thinning, such as green Chamomilla, Illyrian, Stoechas, etc.

units.la: Emolliunt: Croci, Liliorū, Malvæ, &c.
units.tr: Emollient: saffron, lilies, Malva, etc.

units.la: Suppurant: Croci, Liliorū alborū, &c.
units.tr: Suppurating: saffron, white lilies, etc.

units.la: Glutinant & cicatricem inducunt, Balaustiæ, Centarii, &c.
units.tr: Gluing together and inducing a scar: Balaustia, Centaurium, etc.

units.la: Menses movent; Betonicæ, Centau-rii, Chamomillæ, Junci odorati, Leucorii, Melissæ, Pæoniæ, Rosmarini, Salviæ, Viticis, &c.
units.tr: Moving the menses: Betonica, Centaurium, Chamomilla, scented rush, Leucorium, Melissa, Paeonia, Rosmarinus, Salvia, Vitex, etc.

units.la: Menses sistunt: Balaustæ, Hyoscyami, Nymphæ.
units.tr: Stopping the menses: Balaustia, Hyoscyamus, Nymphaea.

units.la: Flatus discutiunt; Anethi, Chamomillæ, Junci odorati, Spicanardi, &c.
units.tr: Dispersing wind: dill, Chamomilla, scented rush, Spica nardi, etc.

units.la: Ambustis medentur, Liliorum albo-rum, Malvæ, Verbasci, &c.
units.tr: Healing burns: white lilies, Malva, Verbascum, etc.

units.la: Venenis resistunt: Betonicæ, Citri, &c.
units.tr: Resisting poisons: Betonica, Citrus, etc.

units.la: Dolorem mitigant: Anethi, Chamomillæ, Centaurii, Hyoscyami, Meliloti, Rosmarini.
units.tr: Relieving pain: dill, Chamomilla, Centaurium, Hyoscyamus, Melilotus, Rosmarinus.

units.la: Adhuc fuerunt flores alterantes: Sequuntur purgantes, & quidem:
units.tr: Thus far the altering flowers. Next are the purging ones, namely:

units.la: Bilem vel Pituitam,
units.tr: Those purging bile or phlegm:
