units.la: Bilem, ut flores Persicorum, Cerasorum, Prunorum sylvestrium, Violarum, Rosarum, &c.
units.tr: Bile: such as the flowers of peaches, cherries, wild plums, violets, roses, etc.

units.la: Pituitam & Serum, ut Carthami, Genistæ, Sambuci, &c.
units.tr: Phlegm and serum: such as Carthamus, Genista, Sambucus, etc.

units.la: Hucusq; de Floribus, Sequuntur Fructus & Semina.
units.tr: So far on flowers. Next come fruits and seeds.

units.la: Suntq; Temperati vel Intemperati.
units.tr: They are either temperate or intemperate.

units.la: Temperati fructus sunt: Ficus, Nux, Pinea, Palmulæ, Sebesten, Uvæ passæ, etc.
units.tr: Temperate fruits are: fig, walnut, pine nut, date palms, sebesten, raisins, etc.

units.la: Intemperati sunt Calidi, Frigidi, Humidi, vel Sicci.
units.tr: Intemperate fruits are hot, cold, moist or dry.

units.la: Calidi, & quidem primo gradu sunt:
units.tr: Hot, in the first degree:

units.la: Amygdalæ dulces, Jujubæ, Nux cupresi, Nux viridis, Uva matura.
units.tr: Sweet almonds, jujubes, cypress nut, green walnut, ripe grape.

units.la: Secundo: Been, Capparis, nux Moschata, Nuces siccę, Pistacia, &c.
units.tr: In the second: Ben, capers, nutmeg, dry nuts, pistachio, etc.

units.la: Tertio ; Baccæ Juniperi, Charyophylli, Carpobalsamum, Anacandium, &c.
units.tr: In the third: juniper berries, cloves, carpobalsamum, anacardium, etc.

units.la: Quarto: Piger longum, album, nigrum.
units.tr: In the fourth: long pepper, white pepper, black pepper.

units.la: Frigidi gradu primo sunt: Citri caro, Cotonea, Pyra, Pruna, &c.
units.tr: Cold in the first degree: citron pulp, quince, pear, plum, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Cucurbita, Cucumis, Gallia, Mala aurea, Citria, Granata, Limones, Pepones, Melones, Persica, &c.
units.tr: In the second: gourd, cucumber, Gallia, golden apples, citrons, pomegranates, lemons, pepons, melons, peaches, etc.

units.la: Tertio: Mala insana:
units.tr: In the third: mad apples:

units.la: Quarto: Stramonia, &c.
units.tr: In the fourth: thorn apple, etc.

units.la: Humidi in primo gradu sunt: Caro Citri, Jujubæ, &c.
units.tr: Moist in the first degree: citron pulp, jujubes, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Cucurbitæ, Melones, Pepones, Persica, pruna Damascena, Uva matura, &c.
units.tr: In the second: gourds, melons, pepons, peaches, Damascene plums, ripe grapes, etc.

units.la: Sicci in primo: baccæ Juniperi, &c.
units.tr: Dry in the first degree: juniper berries, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Been, Capparis, Cotonea, nux Cupresi, nux Moschata, Pyra, Pistacia, &c.
units.tr: In the second: Ben, capers, quince, cypress nut, nutmeg, pears, pistachio, etc.

units.la: Tertio: Charyophylli, Carpobalsamum, Gallæ, &c.
units.tr: In the third: cloves, carpobalsamum, galls, etc.

units.la: Hactenus fuerunt Fructus alteran-tes qualitate prima; Sequuntur,quæ alterant qualitate Secunda.
units.tr: Thus far the fruits that alter by the first quality. Next are those that alter by the second.

units.la: Illi aut astringunt; ut baccæ Myrti, Berberis, Castanea, Cornus, Cotonea, Galla, Glans, Mespila, Mala punica, nux Moschata, Olivæ, Omphacium, Palmulæ, Pyra, Persica, &c.
units.tr: These either astringe, such as myrtle berries, barberry, chestnut, dogwood, quince, galls, acorns, medlar, pomegranates, nutmeg, olives, unripe olives, palm dates, pears, peaches, etc.

units.la: Aut discutiunt: ut Capparis, Piper, &c.
units.tr: Or they discuss, such as capers, pepper, etc.

units.la: Aut extenuant; ut Amygdalæ dulces, baccæ Juniperi, &c.
units.tr: Or they thin, such as sweet almonds, juniper berries, etc.

units.la: Aut glutinant; ut Glans, Palmula, &c.
units.tr: Or they glue, such as acorns, palm dates, etc.

units.la: Aut Flatus discutiunt: ut baccæ Lauri, Juniperi, nux Moschata, Piper, &c.
units.tr: Or they disperse wind, such as laurel berries, juniper berries, nutmeg, pepper, etc.

units.la: Aut Semen generant: Ficus, nux Pinea, nux Indica, &c.
units.tr: Or they generate seed: figs, pine nuts, Indian nuts, etc.

units.la: Aut Urinam cient: Halicacabus, &c.
units.tr: Or they provoke urine: Halicacabus, etc.

units.la: Aut Menses movent: baccæ Hederæ, Cappares, Nuclei Persicorum, Piper.
units.tr: Or they move the menses: ivy berries, capers, peach kernels, pepper.

units.la: Aut Menses sistunt: Berberis, Uva passa cum Nucleis.
units.tr: Or they stop the menses: barberry, raisins with their stones.

units.la: Aut Venenis resistunt: baccæ Juniperi, Juglans, mala Citria, Piper. Aut Dolorem mitigant: Baccæ Juniperi, Hederæ, Ficus, Iuglans, Piper.
units.tr: Or they resist poisons: juniper berries, walnuts, citrons, pepper. Or they relieve pain: juniper berries, ivy, figs, walnuts, pepper.

units.la: Adhuc fructus alterantes; Sequun-tur purgantes.
units.tr: Thus far the fruits that alter. Next are the purging ones.

units.la: Purgant verò Bilem, aut Pituitam.
units.tr: They purge either bile or phlegm.

units.la: Bilem Flavam vel Atram.
units.tr: Yellow or black bile.

units.la: Flavam: Cassia fistula, Myrobalani citrini, Pruna, Sebesten, Tamarindi, Uvæ passæ, &c.
units.tr: Yellow: cassia fistula, citrine myrobalans, plums, sebesten, tamarinds, raisins, etc.

units.la: Atram; Myrobalani indi, &c.
units.tr: Black: Indian myrobalans, etc.

units.la: Pituitam exturbant; Colocynthis, Cucumis asininus, Myrobalani, Chebuli, Bellerici, Emblici, &c.
units.tr: They expel phlegm: colocynth, wild cucumber, myrobalans, chebulic, belleric, emblic myrobalans, etc.

units.la: Hactenus de Fructibus: Sequuntur Semina.
units.tr: So far on fruits. Next come seeds.

units.la: Semina.
units.tr: Seeds.

units.la: Semen est ea pars plantæ, ex qua in terrâ projecta similis producitur planta.
units.tr: A seed is that part of a plant from which, when cast into the earth, a similar plant is produced.

units.la: Primo gradu calida sunt Semina: Coriandrum, Fœnum græcum, Linum, Lithospermum, Lupini, Oryza, &c.
units.tr: Hot in the first degree are seeds such as coriander, fenugreek, flax, gromwell, lupins, rice, etc.

units.la: Secundo; Anethi, Apii, Ervum, Erucæ, Ocymi, Urticæ, &c.
units.tr: In the second degree: dill, parsley, vetch, rocket, basil, nettle, etc.

units.la: Tertio; Ammi, Anisi, Anethi, Amomi, Carei, Cardamomum, Fœniculi, Cyminí, Dauci, Nigellæ, Napi, Petroselini, Seseleos, Stachydis, Agriæ, Viticis, &c.
units.tr: In the third degree: bishop's weed, anise, dill, amomum, caraway, cardamom, fennel, cumin, carrot, nigella, turnip, parsley, seseli, woundwort, agrimony, chaste tree, etc.

units.la: Quarto; Nasturtii, Sinapi, &c.
units.tr: In the fourth degree: watercress, mustard, etc.

units.la: Primo gradu frigida sunt: Hordeum, Milium.
units.tr: Cold in the first degree are barley and millet.

units.la: Secundo: Acetosæ, Cichorii, Solani, &c.
units.tr: In the second degree: sorrel, chicory, nightshade, etc.

units.la: Tertio: Cicutæ, Hyoscyami, Papaveris, &c.
units.tr: In the third degree: hemlock, henbane, poppy, etc.

units.la: Sicca in primo gradu: Faba, Fœnum græcum, Fœniculi, Hordeum, &c.
units.tr: Dry in the first degree: bean, fenugreek, fennel, barley, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Ervum, Lens, Oryza, Papaveris, Solani, &c.
units.tr: In the second degree: vetch, lentil, rice, poppy, nightshade, etc.

units.la: Tertio: Anethi, Apii, Ammi, Anisum, Careum, Cyminum, Coriandrum, Granum tinctorium, Nigella, Milium, Petroselinum, &c.
units.tr: In the third degree: dill, parsley, bishop's weed, anise, caraway, cumin, coriander, dyer's grain, nigella, millet, parsley, etc.

units.la: Hæc sunt semina alterantia qualitate prima; Sequuntur quæ secunda.
units.tr: These are the seeds that alter by the first quality; there follow those that alter by the second.

units.la: Hæc vel astringunt; ut Antheæ seu antorae, Berberorum, Bursæ pastoris, Granum tinctorium, Milium, Portulacæ, &c.
units.tr: These either astringe, as anthera or antora, barberry, shepherd's purse, dyer's grain, millet, purslane, etc.

units.la: Discutiunt: Anethi, Dauci, Fœnum græcum, Nigellæ, Sesami, &c.
units.tr: They disperse: dill, carrot, fenugreek, nigella, sesame, etc.

units.la: Abstergunt: Faba, Ervum, Hordeum, Lupini, Urticæ, &c.
units.tr: They cleanse: bean, vetch, barley, lupins, nettle, etc.

units.la: Emolliunt Fœnum græcum, Malvæ, Nigellæ, &c.
units.tr: They soften: fenugreek, mallow, nigella, etc.

units.la: Indurant: Portulacæ, &c.
units.tr: They harden: purslane, etc.

units.la: Suppurant; Fœnum græcum, Hordeum, Lilium, Lolium, &c.
units.tr: They promote suppuration: fenugreek, barley, lily, darnel, etc.

units.la: Glutinant; Ervum, Lolium, Lupinus.
units.tr: They glue together: vetch, darnel, lupins.

units.la: Flatus discutiunt; Anisi, Anethi, Apii, Carei, Cymini, Dauci, Fœniculi, Nigellæ, Petroselini, Sefeleos, Santonici, &c.
units.tr: They disperse wind: anise, dill, parsley, caraway, cumin, carrot, fennel, nigella, parsley, seseli, santonica, etc.

units.la: Semen generant; Cicer, Faba, Erucæ, Lini, Fraxini, &c.
units.tr: They generate seed: chickpea, bean, rocket, flax, ash, etc.

units.la: Menses movent; Amomi, Asparagi, Anisi, Ammi, Cicer, Dauci, Apii, Fœniculi, Petroselini, Sefeleos, Levisticî, &c.
units.tr: They move the menses: amomum, asparagus, anise, bishop's weed, chickpea, carrot, parsley, fennel, parsley, seseli, lovage, etc.

units.la: Calculum frangunt: Malvæ, Milii Solis, &c.
units.tr: They break up stones: mallow, sun-millet, etc.

units.la: Menses sistunt; Antorae, Cymini, Pæoniæ, Lappæ, &c.
units.tr: They stop the menses: anthora, cumin, peony, burdock, etc.

units.la: Venenis resistunt; Ammi, Anisi, Apii, Cardamomum, Citrii mali, Fœniculi, Raparum.
units.tr: They resist poisons: bishop's weed, anise, parsley, cardamom, citron, fennel, radish.

units.la: Dolorem mitigant; Anethi, Amomi, Cardamomum, Cymini, Dauci, Ervum, Fœnugræci, Lini, Hyoscyami, Milium, Panicum, Petroselini, &c.
units.tr: They relieve pain: dill, amomum, cardamom, cumin, carrot, vetch, fenugreek, flax, henbane, millet, panic grass, parsley, etc.

units.la: Vel denique strumas discutiunt: ut Althææ, Coriandri, Hordeum, Lentes, Lupini, Lolium, Lithospermum, &c. Corrumpendo vero alterant ; Coriandrum, Psyllium, &c.
units.tr: Lastly, they disperse swellings, as marshmallow, coriander, barley, lentils, lupins, darnel, gromwell, etc. But by corrupting they alter: coriander, fleawort, etc.

units.la: Hactenus semina alterantia: Sequu-tur purgantia.
units.tr: So much for seeds that alter; there follow those that purge.

units.la: Purgant autem Bilem vel Pituitam.
units.tr: They purge either bile or phlegm.

units.la: Bilem: ut Psillii, Thymelaeae seu coc-cognidii, Thlaspi, &c.
units.tr: Bile: as fleawort, spurge laurel (or mezereon), thlaspi, etc.

units.la: Pituitam, Carthami seu Cnici, Geni-stae, Latyris seu cataputicae[?], Ricini, &c.
units.tr: Phlegm: safflower or cnicus, broom, latyris or cataputia, castor bean, etc.

units.la: Adhuc de feminibus: Sequuntur li-gna, &c.
units.tr: So much on seeds; there follow woods, etc.

units.la: Ligna sunt partes plantarum tanquam ossa in animalibus durissimae ac firmissimae.
units.tr: Woods are the parts of plants, very hard and firm, like the bones in animals.

units.la: Horum quaedam alterant manifesta, quaedam occulta qualitate.
units.tr: Some of these alter by a manifest quality, some by a hidden quality.

units.la: Manifesta alterantia, Calida sunt vel Frigida.
units.tr: Those that alter manifestly are either hot or cold.

units.la: Calida: Lignum aloes, Aspalatus[?], Buxus, Guaiacum, Indicum, Ebenum, Juniperinum, Narcaphthum, Viscum quercinum, Xylo casia sassafras, Lignum aromaticum, Lignum ad renū affectiones, &c.
units.tr: Hot: aloeswood, aspalathus, box, guaiacum, Indian wood, ebony, juniper wood, narcaphthum, oak mistletoe, xylocassia, sassafras, aromatic wood, wood for kidney complaints, etc.

units.la: Frigida: Cypressi, Loti arboris, Santalum album, rubrum & citrinum, Tamaricis, &c.
units.tr: Cold: cypress, lotus tree, white, red and yellow sandalwood, tamarisk, etc.

units.la: Occulta qualitate alterant; Lignum laricis, Lignum ficus, Viscum querci-num,&c.
units.tr: They alter by a hidden quality: larch wood, fig wood, oak mistletoe, etc.

units.la: Tantū de lignis,sequuntur Cortices.
units.tr: So much for woods; there follow barks.

units.la: Hi sunt in triplici differentia: vel enim sunt Arborū & Fruticum, vel Fructuum; vel Radicum.
units.tr: These are of a threefold kind: they are either of trees and shrubs, or of fruits, or of roots.

units.la: Arborum & fruticum quidam sunt alterantes, quidam purgantes.
units.tr: Of trees and shrubs, some alter, some purge.

units.la: Alterantes qualitate prima vel secunda.
units.tr: Those that alter do so by the first or second quality.

units.la: Prima qualitate alterantes, sunt vel calidi in primo gradu, ut: Macer, cortex Guajaci, Tamaricis: Vel in secundo; ut Cinnamomum, Thuris · Vel in tertio, ut: Mac.
units.tr: Those that alter by the first quality are either hot in the first degree, as mace, guaiacum bark, tamarisk; or in the second, as cinnamon, frankincense; or in the third, as Mac.

units.la: Secunda qualitate alterantes vel aperiunt; ut Thymiama; vel dolorem leniunt; ut Fraxini.
units.tr: Those that alter by the second quality either open, as thymiama; or relieve pain, as ash.

units.la: Purgat cortex Sambuci medius.
units.tr: The middle bark of the elder purges.

units.la: χόλιον[?].
units.tr: Cholion [χόλιον].

units.la: Abraditur cultello, siccatur & servatur per annum; trahit aquam, & Hydropicos juvat.
units.tr: It is scraped off with a knife, dried and kept for a year; it draws water and helps dropsical people.

units.la: THEOREMA.
units.tr: THEOREM.

units.la: Fructuum cortices vel sunt calidi; ut mali Citrii, mali Aurantii, vel frigidi; ut, Glandium cuticulæ, seu cupulæ, &c. Vel adstringentes: ut Granatorum, Juglandium viridium, &c.
units.tr: Bark of fruits is either hot, as the bark of citron and of orange, or cold, as the skin or cup of acorns, etc. Or astringent, as that of pomegranates and of green walnuts, etc.

units.la: Radicum cortices vel calidi sunt in secundo, ut Capparis, vel frigidi in tertio gradu, ut Mandragorae, &c.
units.tr: Bark of roots is either hot in the second degree, as caper, or cold in the third degree, as mandrake, etc.

units.la: Purgantes vero vel purgant Bilem & Pituitam, vel Aquam.
units.tr: Purging barks either purge bile and phlegm, or water.

units.la: Bilem & Pituitam: cortex Esulae, Cucumeris sylvestris. Aquam; Sambuci, Ebuli, &c.
units.tr: Bile and phlegm: the bark of spurge and of wild cucumber. Water: of elder, dwarf elder, etc.

units.la: Hęc de corticibus: Sequuntur Succi.
units.tr: So much for barks; there follow juices.

units.la: Succus proprie dicitur, qui contusione & conquassatione exprimitur, vel ex Herbis, Fructibus, aut Seminibus, &c.
units.tr: Juice is properly what is pressed out by bruising and crushing, from herbs, fruits or seeds, etc.

units.la: Herbarum succi vel manifeste alterant vel occulte.
units.tr: The juices of herbs either alter manifestly or obscurely.

units.la: Manifeste, vel Temperate, vel Intemperate.
units.tr: Manifestly, they are either temperate or intemperate.

units.la: Temperate ut; succus Betae, Buglossae, &c.
units.tr: Temperate, as the juice of beet, of bugloss, etc.

units.la: Intemperate vel calore, vel frigore.
units.tr: Intemperate, either by heat or by cold.

units.la: Succi primo gradu calidi sunt, Absinthii, Brassicæ, &c.
units.tr: Juices hot in the first degree are wormwood, cabbage, etc.

units.la: Secundo; Apii, Calaminthae, Lupuli, Mentae, Rutae, Scordii, &c.
units.tr: In the second: parsley, calamint, hops, mint, rue, water germander, etc.

units.la: Tertio: Chelidonii, &c. Quarto : Efulæ, Latiridis, qui etiam corrumpendo alterant.
units.tr: In the third: celandine, etc. In the fourth: spurge, and sun-spurge, which also alter by corrupting.

units.la: Frigidi in primo gradu sunt: Fuma-riæ, Intybi, Rosarum, Violarum, &c.
units.tr: Cold in the first degree are fumitory, endive, roses, violets, etc.

units.la: Secundo; Acetosæ, Cotyledonis, La-ctucæ, Plantaginis, Solani.
units.tr: In the second: sorrel, navelwort, lettuce, plantain, nightshade.

units.la: Tertio ; Cucurbitæ, Portulacæ, Sem-pervivi, &c.
units.tr: In the third: gourd, purslane, houseleek, etc.

units.la: Quarto ; Papaveris.
units.tr: In the fourth: poppy.

units.la: Occultè alterant ; succus Polygoni, humor in folliculis ulmi.
units.tr: Obscurely they alter: the juice of knotgrass, the moisture in the pods of elm.

units.la: Fructuum succi alii sunt calidi ; ut malorum dulcium: Alii frigidi; ut Coto-neorum, malorum Punicorum, Berbe-rorum, Ribes.
units.tr: Juices of fruits: some are hot, as of sweet apples; others cold, as of quinces, pomegranates, barberries, and currants.

units.la: Seminum succi similiter alii calidi sunt ut : cremor seminis Lini, fænugræ-ci, &c. Alii frigidi, ut: cremor Psyllii, cremor seminum Cucurbitæ, Cucumeris, Melonum, Endiviæ, Portulacæ.
units.tr: Likewise juices of seeds: some are hot, as the cream of flax seed, of fenugreek, etc. Others cold, as the cream of fleawort, the cream of gourd seed, of cucumber, of melons, of endive, of purslane.

units.la: Tantum de Succis ; Sequntur liquo-res.
units.tr: So much on juices; there follow liquors.

units.la: Liquor est, qui incisa vel scarificata Plantæ alicujus parte exstillat sive ema-nat.
units.tr: A liquor is that which exudes or flows from a wounded or scarified part of some plant.

units.la: Suntq; vel Liquidi vel Concreti.
units.tr: Liquors are either liquid or solid.

units.la: Liquidi, Non pingues vel
units.tr: Liquid: not oily or

units.la: Pingues calidi : Oleum Olivarum, Amygdalarum dulcium & amararum, Balaninum, Nucum, Avellanarū, è baccis Lauri, Lini, Sesaminum, &c.
units.tr: Oily and hot: olive oil, oil of sweet and bitter almonds, of acorns, of nuts, of hazelnuts, from laurel berries, of flax, of sesame, etc.

units.la: Pingues frigidi · Oleum papaveris, Hyoscyami.
units.tr: Oily and cold: oil of poppy, of henbane.

units.la: Non pingues calidi: Sapa, id est, Mustum igni decoctum, Vinum.
units.tr: Not oily and hot: sapa, that is, must boiled over the fire, wine.

units.la: Non pingues frigidi ; Agresta seu Omphacium, Acetum, &c.
units.tr: Not oily and cold: unripe grape juice or verjuice, vinegar, etc.

units.la: Concreti alterant vel purgant.
units.tr: Solid liquors either alter or purge.

units.la: Alterant Calore vel Frigore.
units.tr: They alter by heat or by cold.

units.la: Calore, Moderatè vel Immoderatè.
units.tr: By heat, moderately or immoderately.

units.la: Moderatè calefaciunt; Amylum, succus Glycyrrhizæ, Licium.
units.tr: Moderately warming: starch, juice of liquorice, licium.

units.la: Immoderatè ; Saccharum, Primo; Laudanum, Secundo, &c. Assa dulcis & Assa fœtida, tertio Gradu.
units.tr: Immoderately: sugar, in the first degree; laudanum, in the second, etc. Sweet asafoetida and asafoetida, in the third degree.

units.la: Frigefaciunt; Agacia, sanguis Draconis, in primo; Hypocystis, tertio; Meconium, Opium, in quarto.
units.tr: They cool: acacia, dragon's blood, in the first; hypocist, in the third; meconium, opium, in the fourth.

units.la: Liquores purgantes respiciunt Bi-lem, ut Manna, Scammonium, Diagridium, &c. vel Pituitam, ut: Elaterium, Opoponax, &c.
units.tr: Purging liquors are aimed at bile, as manna, scammony, diagrydium, etc., or at phlegm, as elaterium, opopanax, etc.

units.la: Hucusque de liquoribus: Sequuntur, Gummi & Resinæ.
units.tr: So far on liquors; there follow gums and resins.

units.la: Gummi est Lacryma aquosa ; Refi-na vero Oleosa & flagrabilis.
units.tr: Gum is a watery tear; resin, however, is oily and flammable.

units.la: Naturæ sunt calidæ vel frigidæ,
units.tr: By nature they are hot or cold.

units.la: Calidæ, Temperatæ vel Intemperatæ, Temperatæ, ut : Cancamum seu Lac-ca, gummi Elemi, Tragacanthum, &c.
units.tr: Hot, temperate or intemperate. Temperate, as lac (or cancamum), gum elemi, tragacanth, etc.

units.la: Intemperatæ, & quidem calidæ in primo Gradu ; Bdellium, gummi Hedera, Secundo ; Maftyx, Myrrha, Galbanum, Thus, Pix, Resina, Styrax. Tertio ; Ammoniacum, Cedri liquor, Quarto ; Benzoi, Euforbium.
units.tr: Intemperate, and indeed hot: bdellium and ivy gum in the first degree; in the second, mastic, myrrh, galbanum, frankincense, pitch, resin, styrax. In the third, ammoniac, cedar liquor; in the fourth, benzoin, euphorbium.

units.la: Frigidæ sunt : Camphora, gummi Arabicum, &c. De Camphora tamen dubitari potest, aliquis enim gradus caloris in ea esse videtur.
units.tr: Cold: camphor, gum arabic, etc. Yet concerning camphor there may be doubt, for some degree of heat seems to be in it.

units.la: Inter Gummi nonnulla etiam fecunda qualitate alterant, ut ; gummi Amygdalarū, Tragacanthum, Manna thuris, Sandaracha, Sarcocolla, Et hæc quidé adstringunt. Molliunt : Colophonia, Styrax, &c. Calculos pellit : gummi Cerasorum. Menses ciet Styrax.
units.tr: Among gums, some also alter by the second quality, as gum of almond, tragacanth, manna of frankincense, sandarach, sarcocolla; and these indeed astringe. They soften: colophony, styrax, etc. They expel stones: gum of cherries. Styrax moves the menses.

units.la: Inter purgantia & quidem Pituitam sunt : Sagapenum sive Serapinum, Sarcocolla, Opoponax, &c.
units.tr: Among purging ones, indeed those for phlegm are: sagapenum or serapinum, sarcocolla, opopanax, etc.

units.la: De Gummi & Refinu
units.tr: Concerning gum and resin.

units.la: Tantum de Gummi & Resinis.
units.tr: So much on gums and resins.

units.la: P O S T R E M O Radicú, Foliorum, Florum, Fructuum & Seminum quaedam mirando quodam Sympathias mysterio respiciunt certa loca & membra in corpore humano calefaciendo, refrigerando, &c.
units.tr: LASTLY, some of the roots, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds, by a certain wondrous mystery of sympathy, act upon certain places and members of the human body by warming, cooling, etc.

units.la: CAPUT XXI. DE SENSU ANIMALIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI. ON THE SENSATION OF ANIMALS.

units.la: ADhuc fuit Planta: Succedit Ani-mal quod est corpus animatum non modò vegetante, sed insuper etiam sentiente anima; adeoq; non tantum vita naturali, sed etiam sensu & motu præditum.
units.tr: So far we have had the plant. The animal follows: a body animated not only by a vegetative soul but also by a sentient soul, and therefore endowed not merely with natural life but also with sense and motion.

units.la: Hujus doctrina dicitur Zoogra-phia, quæ explicat generalem animalis doctrinam.
units.tr: The doctrine of this is called zoography, which sets out the general doctrine of the animal.

units.la: ANIMALIS duæ sunt partes: Ani-ma sentiens, & Corpus animatum.
units.tr: The animal has two parts: the sentient soul and the animated body.

units.la: ANIMA SENTIENS est ἐντελέχεια[?] corporis animati sentientis, quâ sentiens; seu per quam corpus animatum sentit, hoc est, cognoscit sensibilia. Potest dici anima sensifica cujus vi corpus animatum sentit, seq; movet. Unde ab anima sentiente promanat Vis seu facultas sentiens & Motus.
units.tr: The sentient soul is the entelechy [ἐντελέχεια] of a sentient animated body, insofar as it is sentient; that is, the soul by which the animated body perceives, that is, knows sensible things. It may be called the sensitive soul, by whose power the animated body senses and moves itself. Hence from the sentient soul flow the power or faculty of sensing, and motion.

units.la: Actio itaque animalis qua animal, est Sensus & Motus; Quibus actionibus a-ctu vigentibus in animali, ipsum Vigilare dicitur.
units.tr: The action of the animal, as animal, is sensation and motion. When these actions are active in the animal, it is said to be awake.

units.la: Vigilia itaque est facultatum animalium, id est sensuum & motuū in animali vigor & actus.
units.tr: Wakefulness, then, is the vigour and activity of the animal faculties, that is, of the senses and motions, in the animal.

units.la: Sentientis anima facultas duplex est: Apprehendens & Movens.
units.tr: The faculty of the sentient soul is twofold: apprehending and moving.

units.la: Apprehendens quae sensuum beneficio, objecta percipit, dijudicat, retinet.
units.tr: The apprehending faculty is that which, by the aid of the senses, perceives, judges and retains objects.

units.la: Sensus est hic facultas, qua animal aptum est ad cognoscendum sensilia, ab anima sentiente per Emanationem producta. Breviter: est facultas sensilia percipiens.
units.tr: Sense here is the faculty by which the animal is fitted to know sensible things, produced by the sentient soul through emanation. In brief: it is the faculty of perceiving sensible things.

units.la: Sensus actio dicitur Sensio aliis Sensatio, quae est objecti sensilis, quatenus est sensile, cognitio, in animali excitata per species in sensorio recepti apprehensione & dijudicatione.
units.tr: The act of sense is called sensing, by others sensation. It is the knowledge of a sensible object, insofar as it is sensible, excited in the animal through the apprehension and judgement of the species received in the sensory organ.

units.la: Brevius: est sensilis perceptio.
units.tr: More briefly: it is the perception of the sensible.

units.la: Sensio enim est motus, qui est actio aut passio. At sensio non passio, quia sentire non est pati, sed agere; Ergo est actio.
units.tr: For sensing is a motion, and a motion is an action or a passion. But sensing is not a passion, because to sense is not to suffer but to act; therefore it is an action.

units.la: At non quaelibet actio, sed certa. Cum igitur sentire sit cognoscere; Sensio quoque est cognitio. Sic cognitio est Genus, Sensio & Intellectio Species ejus.
units.tr: But it is not just any action, but a definite one. Since to sense is to know, sensing is also a kind of knowing. So knowing is the genus, and sensing and understanding are its species.

units.la: SENSUUM tum generalia Theoremata, tum specialia observabimus. Generalia explicabunt 1. Sensuum requisita sita; 2. Necessitatem cum certitudine eorum.
units.tr: We shall observe both the general theorems of the senses and the special ones. The general theorems will explain (1) the requisites of sensation, and (2) its necessity and certainty.

units.la: Requisita Senfionis sunt quatuor præcipua.
units.tr: There are four principal requisites of sensation.

units.la: 1. Primum requisitum est τὸ ἀισθητὸν, hoc est, objectum sensile, sub quo comprehenditur omne id, quod sensu apprehendi potest, qualecunq; etiam fuerit.
units.tr: 1. The first requisite is τὸ αἰσθητόν [to aisthēton], that is, the sensible object, under which is included everything that can be apprehended by sense, of whatever kind it may be.

units.la: Hujus officium est agere in sensorium, idq; alterare, vel per propriam, vel per alienam speciem seu imaginem.
units.tr: The office of this object is to act upon the sensory organ and alter it, either through its own species or through an alien species or image.

units.la: Unde sensile duplex dicitur: Unum per se sensile, unum per accidens.
units.tr: Hence the sensible is said to be twofold: one thing sensible in itself, another sensible by accident.

units.la: Sensile per se est, quod per propriam speciem à se productam, & ad sensorium transmissam sentiri aptum est.
units.tr: That is sensible in itself which is fitted to be sensed through its own species, produced by itself and transmitted to the sensory organ.

units.la: Et rursus vel est proprium, vel commune.
units.tr: And again this is either proper or common.

units.la: Proprium est, quod uno duntaxat sensu apprehendi potest, cujusmodi est omne id, quod tantum vel visibile, vel audibile, vel olfactile, vel gustabile, vel tactile.
units.tr: The proper sensible is that which can be apprehended by one sense only, such as everything that is only visible, or audible, or odorous, or tasteable, or tangible.

units.la: Commune est, quod pluribus sensibus indeterminatè percipi potest, cujusmodi sunt motus, quies, numerus, figura, magnitudo, & quæ cum his conjuncta sunt, distantia, situs, identitas, diversitas, tas, itemq; subjecta, in quibus hæc accidentia inhærent.
units.tr: The common sensible is that which can be perceived indeterminately by several senses, such as motion, rest, number, figure, magnitude, and what is joined with these: distance, position, identity, difference, and the rest, as well as the subjects in which these accidents inhere.

units.la: Atque hoc commune sensile, ita artissime cum proprio sensili est conjunctum, ut sine eo nunquam sentiri queat; licet proprium semper πεῶτως: commune δευτέρως cognoscatur.
units.tr: This common sensible is so closely joined with the proper sensible that it can never be sensed without it; yet the proper is always known primarily [πρώτως], the common secondarily [δευτέρως].

units.la: Utrumque vero vel est immediatum, vel mediatum.
units.tr: Each of these is either immediate or mediate.

units.la: Immediatum est, quod sine interventu alterius per se sensilis est perceptibile, cujusmodi sunt accidentia corporum per se sensilia: verbi gratia, lux, color, sapor, odor, calor, frigus, humiditas, siccitas, & quæ ex his oriuntur.
units.tr: The immediate is that which is perceptible without the intervention of anything else that is sensible in itself, such as the accidents of bodies that are sensible in themselves: for example, light, colour, taste, odour, heat, cold, moisture, dryness, and whatever arises from these.

units.la: Mediatum est, quod per interventum alterius per se sensilis est perceptibile, cujusmodi est omnis substantia corporea & physica, quâ talis.
units.tr: The mediate is that which is perceptible through the intervention of something else that is sensible in itself, such as every corporeal and physical substance, as such.

units.la: Sensile per accidens est, quod non per propriam speciem seu imaginem à se productam & ad sensorium transmissam, sentiri potest, sed per alienam: cujusmodi est omnis substantia incorporea, adeoque omnis res spiritalis, divina & cœlestis, itemq; privationes Entium & id genus alia.
units.tr: The sensible by accident is that which can be sensed not through its own species or image produced by itself and transmitted to the sensory organ, but through an alien one. Such is every incorporeal substance, and therefore every spiritual, divine and heavenly thing, as well as privations of beings and other things of that kind.

units.la: Tantum de primo requisito : Sequi-tur alterum, quod dicitur τὸ αἰσθητήριον [?] h.e.
units.tr: So much for the first requisite. There follows the second, which is called τὸ αἰσθητήριον [to aisthētērion], that is,

units.la: Sensorium.
units.tr: The sensory organ.

units.la: Illud nihil aliud est quàm organum corporis à natura ad sensum perficiendum ordinatum.
units.tr: This is nothing other than the organ of the body, ordained by nature to bring about sense.

units.la: Ejus officium est recipere species seu imagines ab objecto sensibili ad se transmissas, & sic per illas alterari.
units.tr: Its office is to receive the species or images transmitted to it from the sensible object, and so be altered by them.

units.la: Et est vel commune, vel proprium.
units.tr: It is either common or proper.

units.la: Commune sensorium est, quod omnibus aut saltem multis sensibus ex æquo inservit, cujusmodi sunt spiritus animalis & vitalis, cor, cerebrum & similia.
units.tr: The common sensory is that which serves all the senses, or at least many of them, alike; such are the animal and vital spirits, the heart, the brain and similar things.

units.la: Proprium sensorium est, quod uni duntaxat sensui primario inservit; cujusmodi sunt oculi respectu visus, aures respectu auditus, &c.
units.tr: The proper sensory is that which serves only one primary sense; such are the eyes with respect to sight, the ears with respect to hearing, and so on.

units.la: Tertium requisitum est : τὸ μεταξύ [?] h.e.
units.tr: The third requisite is τὸ μεταξύ [to metaxy], that is, the medium.

units.la: Medium.
units.tr: The medium.

units.la: Illud est intervallum inter objectum sensile & sensorium interjectum.
units.tr: This is the interval between the sensible object and the sense organ placed between them.

units.la: Ejus officium est, speciem ab objecto sensili sibi impressam ad sensorium vel proprium vel commune transmittere.
units.tr: Its office is to transmit the likeness impressed upon it by the sensible object to the sensory, whether the proper or the common sense.

units.la: Quartum requisitum est τὸ αἰσθανόμενον [?], h. e. Sentiens quod non est, vel anima sensi-tiva, tiva, vel corpus animalis, vel pars corporis: verbi gratia; cerebrū, nervi, ut vulgaris habet Physicorum opinio; sed ipsum totum animal.
units.tr: The fourth requisite is the perceiving [?] thing, that is, the sentient, which is not either the sensitive soul, or the body of the animal, or a part of the body (for example the brain or the nerves, as the common opinion of the natural philosophers holds), but the whole animal itself.

units.la: Ejus officium est apprehendere & dijudicare simulacrum objecti sensilis in sensorio receptum: & sic illo mediante ipsum objectum sensile cognoscere.
units.tr: Its office is to apprehend and judge the image of the sensible object received in the sensory, and so by means of it to know the sensible object itself.

units.la: Atq; hinc patet, primum quomodo sensio fiat, nimirum non per actionem sensorii in objectum sensile: sed contra per actionem objecti sensilis in sensorium.
units.tr: And from this it is clear, first, how sensation comes about: namely, not by the action of the sensory upon the sensible object, but on the contrary by the action of the sensible object upon the sensory.

units.la: Deinde, quae sint causae naturales efficientes sensionis per se sibi invicé subordinatae, nempe. 1. Anima sensitiva. 2. Facultas sentiendi. 3. Oblatio objecti sensilis. 4. Productio speciei sensilis facta ab objecto. 5. Delatio speciei sensilis per medium ad sensorium. 6. Apprehensio & dijudicatio speciei sensilis in sensorio receptae. Ex quibus omnibus causis sola ultima est proxima & immediata: Reliquae omnes sunt remotae: quia licet hae omnes actu ponantur, tamen sensio fieri non potest, nisi ultima actu sit posita.
units.tr: Next, what are the natural efficient causes of sensation, subordinated to one another per se: namely, (1) the sensitive soul; (2) the faculty of sensing; (3) the presentation of the sensible object; (4) the production of the sensible likeness made by the object; (5) the conveyance of the sensible likeness through the medium to the sensory; (6) the apprehension and judgement of the sensible likeness received in the sensory. Of all these causes only the last is proximate and immediate; all the rest are remote, because although all of them are actually posited, sensation cannot take place unless the last is actually posited.

units.la: NECESSITAS sensus inde perspicitur, quod animal sine eo neq; bene vive-re, neq; omnino vivere potest.
units.tr: The necessity of sense is seen from this, that without it an animal can neither live well nor live at all.

units.la: Est enim sensus singulare vitæ præsi-dium, quo si destituatur animal, fieri non potest, ut cognoscat & dijudicet bonum & malum sensitivum: multo minus ut bonum appetat & persequatur; malum aversetur & fugiat.
units.tr: For sense is the unique safeguard of life, and without it an animal cannot know and judge what is sensibly good and evil, much less seek out the good and pursue it, or shun and flee the evil.

units.la: Præterea sensus homini peculiariter est necessarium adminiculum ad comparandâ intelligentiam & notitiam rerum tàm cœlestium, quàm terrestrium; tàm naturalium quàm supernaturaliũ, adeoq; ad cæteras functiones obeundas, quæ sunt hominis propriæ.
units.tr: Moreover, sense is a peculiarly necessary aid to man for acquiring understanding and knowledge of things both heavenly and earthly, both natural and supernatural, and so for performing the other functions which are proper to man.

units.la: Impossibile enim hominem quic-quam intelligere sine ope phantasma-tum seu simulacrorum sensilium; illa au-tem naturaliter non nisi per sensum ac-quiri possunt.
units.tr: For it is impossible for man to understand anything without the help of phantasms, that is, sensible images; and these can naturally be acquired only through sense.

units.la: CERTITUDO sensuum ex sequenti-bus conditionibus intelligi potest.
units.tr: The CERTAINTY of the senses can be understood from the following conditions.

units.la: Prima conditio spectat ad ipsum obje-ctum sensile & vult, 1. Ut justa sit distantia inter sensile & sensorium. Si enim unum ab altero fit nimis remotum, contigit animal in sentiendo aberrare. Unde procul dissita, aut plane non, aut minora apparent, quàm revera sunt: 2. Ut sensile justam habeat magnitudinem. Si enim nimis sit minutum & parvum, sentiri non potest. 3. Ut sit-tum justum habeat, modoque convenienteque sensorio objiciatur. Hinc animal non videt objectum præsens, nisi secundum rectam lineam oculis occurrat. 4. Ut justo tempore commoretur ante sensorium. Si enim subito & quasi in momento prætervolat sensorium, rectè sensu dijudicari non potest. 5. Ut mediocriter seu non nimis vehementer sensorium afficiat. Hinc solem oculis intentis directè non possumus intueri. 6. Ut sensile per se suam speciem ad sensorium transmittat. Hinc stellas interdum non videmus, quia à majore Solis lumine radii earum obscurantur, ut ad oculos nostros pervenire non possint.
units.tr: The first condition concerns the sensible object itself, and requires: (1) that the distance between the sensible and the sensory be just. For if one is made too far from the other, the animal may go wrong in sensing; hence things at a great distance appear either not at all or smaller than they really are. (2) That the sensible have a due magnitude. For if it is too small and slight, it cannot be sensed. (3) That it have a due position and be presented to the sensory in a suitable manner; hence an animal does not see a present object unless it meets the eyes along a straight line. (4) That it linger before the sensory for the proper time. For if it flies past the sensory suddenly and as if in a moment, it cannot be rightly judged by sense. (5) That it affect the sensory moderately, or not too violently; hence we cannot look directly at the sun with fixed eyes. (6) That the sensible, of its own nature, transmit its likeness to the sensory. Hence we sometimes do not see the stars, because their rays are obscured by the greater light of the sun, so that they cannot reach our eyes.

units.la: Altera conditio concernit sensorium, & vult, ut illud sit rectè, & secundum naturam dispositum, h. e. sanum, vigens, integrum, illæsum & quietum, Si enim fit vitiatum & præter naturam dispositum, contigit animal in senti-endo hallucinari. Hinc febricitantes, quorum lingua humore bilioso est imbuta, judi-cant ea esse amara, quæ per se sunt dulcia. Hinc ebrius omnia videntur circumagi aut duplicari, propter commotionem & turbationem spiritum animalium in oculis excitatam, à copia ha-lituum ex ventriculo ad caput ascendentium. Hinc senes in videndo aberrant, quia humores oculorum in iis crassescunt, tunicæ exiccatæ corrugantur, & spiritus imminuuntur, ut ita oculi fiant opaci & inepti ad visum.
units.tr: The second condition concerns the sensory, and requires that it be rightly disposed and according to nature, that is, sound, vigorous, whole, unharmed and at rest. For if it is corrupted and disposed contrary to nature, the animal may go astray in sensing. Hence feverish people, whose tongue is steeped in bilious humour, judge those things to be bitter which are sweet in themselves. Hence the drunk man sees everything seem to spin or to double, on account of the commotion and disturbance of the animal spirits in the eyes, excited by the abundance of vapours rising from the stomach to the head. Hence old men err in seeing, because the humours of their eyes thicken, the coats dry out and wrinkle, and the spirits diminish, so that their eyes become dim and unfit for sight.

units.la: Tertia conditio pertinet ad medium, quod inter sensile & sensorium est inter-jectum, & vult ut illud sit conveniens, re-ctèq; & secundum naturam affectum. Si enim aliena qualitate vel dispositione il-legitima sit imbutum, evenit animal in sentiendo aberrare. Hinc per vitrum aut perspicillum rubrum omnia objecta sensilia videntur rubra.
units.tr: The third condition pertains to the medium which is interposed between the sensible and the sensory, and requires that it be suitable, rightly and according to nature disposed. For if it is imbued with a foreign quality or an unlawful disposition, the animal comes to err in sensing. Hence through red glass or red spectacles all sensible objects appear red.

units.la: Quarta conditio infertur ad animal sentiens & vult, ut illud non sit inten-tum aliis rebus; sed his tantum quæ sensui objiciuntur. Si enim contrarium fiat, objecta sensilia rectè sentiri non possunt. Hinc fit ut homo aliis cogitationibus deditus, sæpe apertis oculis etiam notissimos prætereuntes non videat.
units.tr: The fourth condition applies to the sensing animal, and requires that it not be intent on other things, but only on those that are presented to the senses. For if the contrary happens, sensible objects cannot be rightly sensed. Hence it comes about that a man given over to other thoughts often does not see even the most familiar people passing by, though his eyes are open.

units.la: Quando igitur hæ conditiones omnes adsunt, sensus judicium semper verum est & certum : quando vero aliqua earum adsit, contingit, idem esse falsum & incertum.
units.tr: When therefore all these conditions are present, the judgement of sense is always true and certain; but when any of them is lacking, it happens that the same judgement is false and uncertain.

units.la: CAPUT XXII. DE SENSIBUS EXTERIORIBUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 22. ON THE EXTERNAL SENSES.

units.la: Actenus fuerunt Generalia sensuum theoremata : Specialia singulas sensuum species considerant.
units.tr: So far we have set out the general theorems about the senses; the particular ones consider each kind of sense separately.

units.la: Sensus animalis aut Exteriores sunt, aut Interiores.
units.tr: The animal senses are either external or internal.

units.la: Exteriores sunt, qui externarum rerum & quidem præsentium species corporeis organis percipiunt.
units.tr: The external senses are those which perceive, by bodily organs, the forms of external things, and of things that are present.

units.la: Hi externis instrumentis vires suas exercent, exteriusq; hærent. Horum objectum est rei duntaxat præsentis species.
units.tr: These exercise their powers through external instruments and cling to the outside. Their object is only the form of a thing that is present.

units.la: Sensus exteriores sunt quinque: quorum alii sensilia admota sentiunt, alii remota.
units.tr: There are five external senses, some of which perceive objects that are close at hand, and others objects at a distance.

units.la: Platoni sensus exterior alius est crassius, alius lius purus, alius medius pro varietate Elemen-torum; nempe: Tactus & gustus sunt crassi: Ille terreus, hic aqueus; & hi habent medium internum seu conjunctum. Visus & auditus puri sunt: Ille igneus, hic aereus; Et hi habent medium externum & separatum. Odoratus medius est, nulliq; Elemento tribuitur, sed substantia media, scilicet halitui. Alii docti ita distinguunt: Sensus exteriores vel totius corporis sunt communes; ut Tactus: vel certarum partium proprii, ut reliqui.
units.tr: According to Plato, the external senses differ: some are coarse, some pure, and some intermediate, according to the variety of the elements. Namely, touch and taste are coarse: the one earthy, the other watery; and these have an internal or conjoined medium. Sight and hearing are pure: the one fiery, the other airy; and these have an external and separate medium. Smell is intermediate, and is not assigned to any element, but to a middle substance, namely vapour. Other learned writers distinguish them thus: the external senses are either common to the whole body, like touch, or proper to certain parts, like the rest.

units.la: Admota sensilia sentiunt Tactus & Gustus.
units.tr: Touch and taste perceive objects that are applied to them.

units.la: Tactus est sensus exterior, omnes corporum qualitates tactiles apprehen-dens.
units.tr: Touch is the external sense which apprehends all the tactile qualities of bodies.

units.la: Obiectum tactus uno nomine dicitur ἁπτόν[?], Tactile, ut sunt qualitates primae & secundae.
units.tr: The object of touch is called by one name haptón [ἁπτόν], the tangible, as are the primary and secondary qualities.

units.la: Hæ quomodo percipiuntur, per species an vero materialiter? respondet, Archan. Mercenarius: Tactus recipit spiritaliter, quia sensus est: Et tamen mediante transmutatione reali percipit.
units.tr: How are these perceived, through species or materially? Archangelus Mercenarius answers: touch receives spiritually, because it is a sense; and yet it perceives by means of a real transmutation.

units.la: Organum tactus est nervea Pellicula, per totum corpus instar retis expansi, ut nulla pars sit sine tactu, & quo subtilior nervus, eo exquisitior tactus.
units.tr: The organ of touch is the nervous membrane, spread through the whole body like an extended net, so that no part is without touch; and the finer the nerve, the more exquisite the touch.

units.la: Medium tactus internum dicitur non-nullis caro, aliis cutis.
units.tr: Some call the internal medium of touch the flesh, others the skin.

units.la: Fiet itaq; tactus, ut Fernelius ait: Si tractabiles qualitates aut cutis, aut carnis, aut etiam nullius corporis interventu proximè ad tangendum nervum accedunt. Calor enim vel pungens stylus, si in nudum apertumq; nervum incidat, eximiè & acriter sentitur, quanquam nulla accedat caro.
units.tr: So, as Fernel says, touch comes about if tangible qualities approach the nerve directly, either through the skin or the flesh, or even without the intervention of any body. For heat or a sharp stylus, if it strikes a bare and exposed nerve, is felt keenly and sharply, even though no flesh intervenes.

units.la: Gustus est sensus exterior sensiliagustabilia percipiens.
units.tr: Taste is the external sense which perceives tasteable objects that are applied to it.

units.la: Gustabilia vocantur sapores.Objectum igitur gustus est νευσὶν seu sapor.
units.tr: Tasteable things are called flavours. The object of taste is therefore the flavour [χυμόν] or savour.

units.la: Organum gustatus internum est nervus gustatorius:
units.tr: The internal organ of taste is the gustatory nerve.

units.la: Externum est lingua, cui additur palatum, cui etiā gustandi vis acuta inest.
units.tr: The external organ is the tongue, to which the palate is added, which also has a keen power of tasting.

units.la: Medium gustus internum est Musculosa caro linguae, ut & caro palati: Externum quod illi inservit, est humor salivalis seu saliva. Nimis sicca lingua vix ullos percipit sapores.
units.tr: The internal medium of taste is the muscular flesh of the tongue, and also the flesh of the palate. The external medium which serves it is the salivary humour, or saliva. A tongue that is too dry perceives scarcely any flavours.

units.la: Sensus exteriores remota objecta percipientes sunt Nobiliores vel Ignobiliores.
units.tr: The external senses which perceive distant objects are either more noble or less noble.

units.la: Nobiliores sunt Visus & Auditus·
units.tr: The more noble are sight and hearing.

units.la: Visus est sensus nobilior objectum visibile percipiens,
units.tr: Sight is the more noble sense, which perceives a visible object.

units.la: Nobilior est 1. Ratione objecti, percipit enim totum corpus. 2. Maxime etiam confert ad rei cognitionem. 3. Ratione velocissima conceptionis, & mirifica organi structura, Objectum igitur visus dicitur ὁρατὸν [?] i.e. visibile, quod radiandi vim in se habet. Radiare est radiis continuatis successive per medium speciem sui diffundere.
units.tr: It is more noble: first, by reason of its object, for it perceives the whole body; second, it contributes most of all to the knowledge of a thing; third, by reason of the very rapid conception and the wonderful structure of its organ. The object of sight is therefore called horatón [ὁρατόν], that is, visible, which has in itself the power of radiating. To radiate is to diffuse one's own species, successively, through a medium by continuous rays.

units.la: Radius est Opticis, linea sensilis, qua species figurae visibilis diffunditur.
units.tr: For the optical writers, a ray is a sensible line along which the species of a visible shape is diffused.

units.la: Radiandi autem in se vim habent Colores, luminosa seu lucentia corpora, & illa quae noctu tantum videntur, interdiu autem propter luminis majoris praesentiam non lucent.
units.tr: Colours, luminous or shining bodies, and those things which are seen only at night, but on account of the greater presence of light do not shine by day, have in themselves the power of radiating.

units.la: Medium visionis est corpus pellucidum, impune radiis pervium.
units.tr: The medium of vision is a transparent body, through which rays pass without hindrance.

units.la: Ea enim est perspicui corporis proprietas, ut natura sua salva, radios species q; visibilium recipiat, immutabiles q; corporibus oppositis reddat.
units.tr: For this is the property of a transparent body: that, its nature remaining intact, it receives the rays and the species of visible things, and renders them unaltered to the bodies opposite.

units.la: Medium illud fit actu perspicuum à lumine, cum alias per se non nisi potentia sit perspicuum. Actu perspicuum Medium est, quo proprius cujusq; rei color perspicitur, & sine lumine nullus omnino color videri potest.
units.tr: That medium is made actually transparent by light, whereas otherwise it is transparent only potentially. A medium is actually transparent when the proper colour of each thing is seen through it, and without light no colour at all can be seen.

units.la: Perspicua & radiis pervia sunt aër & aqua, item quædam composita, ut vitrum, tenue cornu, Crystallus.
units.tr: Air and water are transparent and pervious to rays, and so are certain compound things, such as glass, thin horn, and crystal.

units.la: Organum visus exterius est Oculus, seu pupilla binorum oculorum, qui sunt tanquam speculatores in suprema corporis arce collocati rotundi, ut capiendæ quantitati sufficerent, & celerius visu apprehendere valeant multa.
units.tr: The external organ of sight is the eye, or the pupil of the two eyes, which are placed in the highest citadel of the body like watchtowers, round, so that they suffice for grasping the quantity of things and can apprehend many things more quickly by sight.

units.la: Interius est Nervus opticus & Spiritus animalis.
units.tr: The internal organ is the optic nerve and the animal spirit.

units.la: Fit autem visio non emittendo, sed specie visibili extrinsecus in oculum receptâ, & inde beneficio Spiritus animalis per nervos opticos in pupillam oculi deducti, ad cerebrum, ubi sensus communis est, delata.
units.tr: Sight, however, comes about not by emitting anything, but by the visible species being received from outside into the eye, and thence, by the agency of the animal spirit, being conveyed along the optic nerves to the pupil of the eye, and so to the brain, where the common sense is.

units.la: Cujus receptionis modus talis est: Primùm à corporibus aspectabilibus manant species quædam in circumfusum aërem, luce solis vel ignis illustratum, ipsumque afficiunt & in eo semper hærent: & tam longè sese, nisi ab interveniente quodam corpore opaco impedi-antur,
units.tr: The manner of this reception is as follows. First, certain species flow from visible bodies into the surrounding air, illuminated by the light of the sun or of fire, and they affect it and always remain in it; and they spread out as far as they are not hindered by some intervening opaque body,

units.la: antur, diffundunt, donec propter nimiam distantiam attenuentur: Unde fit, ut res nimis procul sita non conspiciatur. Postea se subito in oculos, ut destinatam à natura sedem, minimo temporis momento inferunt, ita ut quocunq; locorum oculos verteris, semper praesto sint, quod videlicet loge jam ante à corporibus in aërem quasi avolarint.
units.tr: and they spread out until they are weakened by excessive distance. Hence it happens that a thing situated too far away is not seen. Afterwards they suddenly rush into the eyes, as into the seat appointed by nature, in the least moment of time, so that wherever you turn your eyes they are always at hand; because, of course, they have already flown off into the air, far from the bodies.

units.la: Species autem illæ visibiles spargun- tur rectâ linea à corporibus figura pyramidis, cujus basis est in corpore aspectabili; Mucro verò seu conus est in ipso oculo.
units.tr: Moreover, those visible species are spread out in a straight line from the bodies, in the figure of a pyramid, whose base is on the visible body, and whose apex or cone is in the eye itself.

units.la: Nam quæ rectà oculis sunt oppositâ, fortius species suas fundunt in aliorum oculos: & hæ faciunt visionem rectam, quæ certa etiam dicitur. Quæ verò ad latera vel post tergum sunt collocata, debiliùs fundunt species suas ad oculos aliorum.
units.tr: For those things which are placed directly opposite the eyes diffuse their species more strongly into the eyes of others; and these produce direct vision, which is also called certain. But those which are placed at the sides or behind diffuse their species more weakly to the eyes of others.

units.la: Hæ faciunt visionem obliquam, quæ dicitur etiam incerta.
units.tr: These produce oblique vision, which is also called uncertain.

units.la: Visio enim Certior est aut Incertior.
units.tr: For vision is either more certain or less certain.

units.la: Certior est, cum linea recta speciem objecti per medium simplex, hoc est, unum & idem ad oculum defert, sine obstaculo. Incertior est, cùm linea obliqua speciem rei objecta ad oculum defert.
units.tr: It is more certain when a straight line conveys the species of the object through a simple medium to the eye, that is, one and the same medium, without obstacle. It is less certain when an oblique line conveys the species of the thing to the eye.

units.la: Porrò hæ species visibiles efficiunt pyramidem, quæ est vel Major vel Minor.
units.tr: Furthermore, these visible species form a pyramid, which is either greater or smaller.

units.la: Major, si videns corpori aspectabili est propior, Minor contrà. Unde fit, ut corpora vel maxima ex nimis longo intervallo multò minora quàm sunt, conspiciantur, & minuta corpora omninò non[?].
units.tr: It is greater if the seeing person is nearer to the visible body; smaller on the contrary. Hence it happens that very large bodies seen from too great a distance look much smaller than they are, and minute bodies are not seen at all.

units.la: Auditus est sensus nobilior objectum audibile percipiens. Objectum audibile, Græcis ἀκουστόν[?], est Sonus.
units.tr: Hearing is the more noble sense, which perceives an audible object. The audible object, in Greek akoustón [ἀκουστόν], is sound.

units.la: Organum auditus Externum sunt aures habentes cavitatem, multos flexus & anfractus.
units.tr: The external organ of hearing is the ears, which have a cavity, with many windings and turnings.

units.la: Internum organum sunt nervi auditorii, qui in cavitate tribus ossiculis, malleo, incude, & stapede conjunguntur.
units.tr: The internal organ is the auditory nerves, which in the cavity are joined by three little bones: the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup.

units.la: Medium auditus species audibiles organo auditorio deferens aptissimum est aër, minus aptum est aqua.
units.tr: The medium which conveys audible species to the auditory organ is most suitable of all air; water is less suitable.

units.la: AER ille est Externus vel Internus.
units.tr: That air is either external or internal.

units.la: Externus est, in quo species excitatæ per gyros feriunt aures. Internus qui est in foramine ossis du-rifsimi seu petrosi, ut gyros illos accipiat & feriat panniculos & ossicula.
units.tr: External air is that in which the species, excited, strike the ears through its circular motions. Internal air is that which is in the cavity of the hardest or petrous bone, so that it may receive those circular motions and strike the membranes and the little bones.

units.la: Modus auditionis hic est: Species ex laceratione aëris per gyros ad ossicula tria cochleatim fertur, fitq; ibi quædam repercussio ad ciendum sonitum, qui sentitur. Facta repercussione, cedente membrana, hæc ossicula invicem mo-ventur atque confricantur. Gyri vero illi alterando aërem successivè deferun-tur ad aures. Sonus etiam in aure effor-matus per nervum ἀκουστικὸν[?] defertur ad cerebrum.
units.tr: The manner of hearing is this: the species, from the agitation of the air, are carried in spiral motion to the three little bones, and there a certain reverberation arises to produce the sound which is perceived. When the reverberation has occurred, the membrane giving way, these little bones move and rub against one another. Those spiral motions, by altering the air successively, are conveyed to the ears. The sound formed in the ear is also carried by the auditory nerve to the brain.

units.la: IGNOBILIOR restat sensus nempe OLFACTVS, quo objectum olfactile si-ve odorabile percipitur.
units.tr: There remains the LESS NOBLE sense, namely SMELL, by which an olfactory or odorous object is perceived.

units.la: Illud autem objectum est odor, sive suaveolens, sive graveolens.
units.tr: That object is odour, whether sweet-smelling or foul-smelling.

units.la: Organum seu sensorium odoratus principale & internum sunt nonnullis nervei du-ctus, qui dicuntur processus mammil-lares.
units.tr: The principal and internal organ or sensory of smell is, for some, the nervous ducts which are called the mammillary processes.

units.la: Minus principale seu externum est Na-sus extra faciem prominens, Exhalatio-nes odoriferas excipiens, & ad suum sen-sorium per nares celeriter deferens.
units.tr: The less principal or external organ is the nose, projecting beyond the face, which receives odoriferous exhalations and quickly conveys them through the nostrils to its sensory.

units.la: Medium olfactus est aër & aqua. In aë-re olfaciunt animalia sanguine prædita, tum exanguia in aëre degentia, tum aquatilia pulmonem habentia. Hoc fit inspirando aërem per pulmones.
units.tr: The medium of smell is air and water. Animals endowed with blood smell in air, and so do bloodless animals that live in air, and water animals that have lungs. This happens by breathing in air through the lungs.

units.la: Infecta quæ non respirant absque attrac-tione aëris odorantur.
units.tr: Things that do not breathe are perceived by smell without the drawing in of air.

units.la: In aqua aquatilia & pulmone caren-tia olfaciunt.
units.tr: Water animals which lack lungs smell in water.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII. DE SENSIBUS INTERIORIBUS; ITEM DE Somno.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. ON THE INTERIOR SENSES; ALSO ON SLEEP.

units.la: ADhuc de Exterioribus sensibus; Sequùtur Interiores, qui species rerum sensilium ab Exterioribus allatas in cerebro percipiunt.
units.tr: Still on the external senses; now follow the interior senses, which perceive in the brain the forms of sensible things brought in by the external senses.

units.la: Hi sensilia intra cerebrum recipiendo percipiunt. Hi intra cranium in cerebro sua munia exsequuntur, nec organum extra se positum habent.
units.tr: These perceive by receiving sensible things within the brain. They perform their functions within the cranium, in the brain, and do not have an organ placed outside themselves.

units.la: Objecta horum sunt sensilia non modò præsentia, sed etiam absentia, verùm quæ antea in sensibus plerumq; fuerant.
units.tr: The objects of these are sensible things not only when present but also when absent, though they were mostly once in the senses.

units.la: Interiores sensus sunt duplices: Cogno-scentes, & conservantes.
units.tr: The interior senses are twofold: knowing and preserving.

units.la: Cognoscentes seu concipientes tùm discernunt, tùm plenius æstimant.
units.tr: The knowing or conceiving senses both discern and estimate more fully.

units.la: DISCERNIT SENSUS COMMUNIS, qui est sensus internus omnium externorum sensuum species per nervos apprehendens & à se invicem discernens ac dignoscens.
units.tr: THE COMMON SENSE discerns, which is the internal sense that apprehends through the nerves the forms of all the external senses, and distinguishes and recognises them from one another.

units.la: Communis dicitur, quia communis omnium sensilium est judex, quæ sì in cerebrum per foramina & vias à natura datas confluunt, sensus hic communis tanquam æstimator & arbiter illorum ibi sedet. Ab hoc judicium de dulci & amaro, de nigro & albo, &c. Ut quinq; lineæ ad centrum: ita quinque sensus se habent ad sensum commune: & hujus organo læso sensus quoq; omnis læditur. Sensu communi bruta acrius occupata, multa non sentiunt: homines verò & hujus & intellectus vehementiori potentia abducti, multa, quæ sub sensus cadunt, nō capiunt.
units.tr: It is called common because it is the judge common to all sensible things. When these flow together into the brain through the foramina and passages given by nature, this common sense sits there as their estimator and arbiter. By it comes the judgement about sweet and bitter, black and white, and so on. As five lines run to a centre, so the five senses stand related to the common sense; and when its organ is injured, every sense is injured too. Animals, busied more keenly, do not perceive many things through the common sense; men, however, drawn away by the more vehement power of both this sense and the intellect, do not grasp many things that fall under the senses.

units.la: Sensus communis si non operatur, sed cessat, fit SOMNVS, logicè vigiliarum privatio, physicè naturalis cessatio sensionis primæ.
units.tr: If the common sense does not operate but ceases, sleep occurs: logically, a privation of waking; physically, a natural cessation of the first sensation.

units.la: Unde Averroes: Somnus est ligamentum & quies sensuum.
units.tr: Hence Averroes: "Sleep is a bond and rest of the senses."

units.la: Causa somni est revocás,& obstruens.
units.tr: The cause of sleep is that which recalls and that which obstructs.

units.la: Revocans, quæ spiritus vitales è corde & animales è cerebro dispensat ope & operâ virtutum distribuentium & attrahentium.
units.tr: That which recalls is what distributes the vital spirits from the heart and the animal spirits from the brain, by the aid and work of the powers that distribute and attract.

units.la: Obstruens est vapor ille,qui à partibus exhalans ibi suaviter liquescit & passim fluens obstruit sensuum meatus.
units.tr: That which obstructs is that vapour which, exhaling from the parts, there gently liquefies and, flowing everywhere, blocks the passages of the senses.

units.la: In somno accidere potest Somnium, quod est visum,quod in somno intus apparet.
units.tr: During sleep there may occur a dream, which is a vision appearing inwardly in sleep.

units.la: Hujus causa sunt hyperphysicæ, vel physicæ.
units.tr: Its causes are either hyperphysical or physical.

units.la: Hyperphysica sunt Deus & Angeli, tùm boni, tùm mali : Unde somnia divina, & diabolica.
units.tr: The hyperphysical causes are God and angels, both good and evil; hence there are divine and diabolical dreams.

units.la: Physica sunt spiritus & vapores,qui primò & per se illas species in cerebro contentas excitant & diversimodè agitant.
units.tr: The physical causes are spirits and vapours, which first and of themselves rouse those forms contained in the brain and stir them in various ways.

units.la: Plenius Æstimat Phantasia quæ species à sensu communi perceptas, vel àle formatas diutius retinet, disper sas colligit,& diligentius examinat.
units.tr: The fancy (phantasia), which retains for a longer time the forms perceived or formed by the common sense, gathers them scattered and examines them more diligently.

units.la: Hujus species sensiles phantasmata appellantur.
units.tr: Its sensible forms are called phantasms.

units.la: Objecta sunt sensilia à communi sensu comunicata,tùm etiam alia quędâ hujus sensus ope formata. Videmus enim bruta etiâ somniare,quod utiq; à phantasia est. A phantasia, omnes animalium cogitationes proficiscuntur, unde huc facultas & æstimatrix & cogitatrix pertinet.
units.tr: Its objects are sensible things communicated by the common sense, and also certain other things formed by the operation of this sense. For we see that even brutes dream, which certainly comes from the fancy. From the fancy all the thoughts of animals proceed, and to it belong the faculty that estimates and the faculty that thinks.

units.la: Conservans internus sensus est MEMORIA, quæ est sensus interior, species sensiles discretas, examinatasq; conservans, revocantiq; reddens.
units.tr: The internal sense that preserves is the MEMORY, which is the interior sense, preserving sensible forms that have been discerned and examined, and rendering them back when recalled.

units.la: Obiecta memoriæ sunt species rerum præteritarum & prius cognitarum. Præ-sentia enim tantùm sensui communi, præterita tantùm memoriæ, absentia verò & præsentia phantasiæ insunt.
units.tr: The objects of memory are the forms of past things and things previously known. For present things belong only to the common sense, past things only to memory, while absent and present things alike belong to the fancy.

units.la: Memoria verò alia est Sensitiva, alia Intellectiva. Illa brutis cum hominibus communis est: hæc, solis hominibus con-cessa, dicitur Recordatio. Quæcunque animalia habent temporis vel sensum quendam, (ut bruta) vel intellectum, (ut homines.) Ea etiam habent memoriam.
units.tr: Memory, however, is one thing in its sensitive form and another in its intellectual form. The former is common to brutes and men; the latter, granted to men alone, is called recollection. Whatever animals have some sense of time (as brutes do) or intellect (as men do), those also have memory.

units.la: Non verò omnia bruta habent illum: Et licet bruta perfectiora non habeant cognitam naturam temporis & distinctam ejus notionem: tamen exilem, confusam, rudem, adumbratamq; quandam cognitionem seu sensionem temporis per sensum communem, cum qua facultas memoriæ conjuncta est, iis largiri debere nos putamus·
units.tr: Yet not all brutes have it. And although the more perfect brutes do not have a known nature of time or a distinct notion of it, we think that they must be granted some slight, confused, rough and shadowy cognition or sensing of time through the common sense, with which the faculty of memory is joined.

units.la: Modus memoriæ nostræ hic esse videtur: Sensilia in sentiente anima & organo ejusdem præcipuo, ut cerebro, veluti pi-cturam quandam inprimunt, seu vestigia quædam relinquunt, perinde ut sigillum in ceram vestigium sui inprimit, quæ deinde amoto & absente sigillo tamen remanet, ejusmodi picturæ, seu affectionis, quæ animo & cerebro contigit, habitus memoria dicitur: id est, quam diu simulacrum illud, quod impressum est, manserit, tam diu meminimus, cum verò habitus simulacri, seu pictura ejus non extat, id est, aut imprimi non potest vestigium, aut cum deletum fuerit, non meminimus.
units.tr: The manner of our memory seems to be this: sensible things impress upon the sentient soul and its principal organ, the brain, as it were a certain picture, or leave certain traces, just as a seal impresses its trace on wax, which then remains when the seal is removed and absent. Such a picture or affection, which has happened to the mind and brain, is called a habit of memory. That is, as long as that likeness which has been impressed remains, so long do we remember; but when the habit of the likeness, or its picture, is not there—that is, either the trace cannot be impressed, or when it has been effaced—we do not remember.

units.la: Hic modus confirmari potest exemplo & experientia: Qui vehementi terrore cōcutiun-tur, qui amore insaniunt, qui ingenti ira exardescunt, non bene tum meminerunt, quia toto commoventur corpore & spiritibus, neq; bona aut valida potest fieri expressio rei, cujus meminisse debent, veluti si quis signum annuli velit in fluminis superficiem imprimere, frustra laborabit, nam propter continuum motum aqua non recipit ejusmodi impressionem, sicuti nec aqua etiam quiescens recipit, quia statim amota re imprimente relabitur aqua, & obliterat vestigia impressionis, inde proverbium natum de oblivione rei alicujus;
units.tr: This manner can be confirmed by example and experience. Those who are shaken by violent terror, who go mad with love, who blaze up with great anger, do not remember well at that time, because they are stirred through the whole body and spirits, and no good or firm expression of the thing they ought to remember can be made. It is as if someone wished to imprint the sign of a ring upon the surface of a river: he will labour in vain, for on account of the constant motion the water does not receive such an impression; nor does even still water receive it, because as soon as the imprinting thing is removed the water flows back and blots out the traces of the impression. Hence the proverb arose about the forgetting of something.

units.la: In vento & rapida scribere oportet aqua, id est, non meminisse. Ita quoq; tametsi impressio imaginis rei alicujus facta fuerit in sic affectis humoribus, tamen motiones illæ vehementes obliterant, & quasi eluunt atq; delent habitum imaginis.
units.tr: "One must write in wind and rapid water," that is, not remember. So too, although an impression of the image of some thing has been made in humours so affected, those vehement motions nonetheless obliterate it and, as it were, wash away and destroy the habit of the image.

units.la: Quare consentaneum est, fieri memoriam per impressionem notarum ortam à rebus, quæ sensibus prius perceptæ sunt, quæ dum habentur & revera manent, earum dicitur memoria.
units.tr: Wherefore it is consistent that memory comes about through the impression of marks arising from things that were previously perceived by the senses; while these are held and really remain, memory of them is said to exist.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV. DE MOTU ANIMALIUM ET AFFECTIBUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV. ON THE MOTION OF ANIMALS AND THE AFFECTIONS.

units.la: Ic fuit apprehendens facultas animæ sentientis: Motrix est ejusdem animæ facultas, quæ motus animales in corpore ciet.
units.tr: Having dealt with the apprehending faculty of the sentient soul, we turn to the motive faculty of the same soul, which stirs the animal motions in the body.

units.la: Estq; duplex: ζωϊκὴ, καὶ Αἰσθητικὴ.
units.tr: This is twofold: the vital [ζωϊκὴ] and the sensitive [αἰσθητικὴ].

units.la: ζωτικὴ est, quæ vitæ principium, sequens vitalem virtutem in animali defendit:
units.tr: The vital [ζωτικὴ] faculty is the one that, following the vital power in the animal, maintains the principle of life.

units.la: Hæc igitur consistit in Spirituum & caloris nativi conservatione; Conservantur autem illa tum Spiratione, tum Pulsu.
units.tr: This therefore consists in the preservation of the spirits and of the native heat. These are preserved both by breathing and by the pulse.

units.la: Spiratio, est aëris inspirati motio. Estq; Insensilis, aut Sensilis.
units.tr: Breathing is the motion of inhaled air. It is either insensible or sensible.

units.la: Insensilis dicitur Respiratio, quæ fit in toto corpore per insensiles poros.
units.tr: Insensible breathing is that which takes place through the whole body by way of imperceptible pores.

units.la: Sensilis dicitur Respiratio, qua aër per pulmones cordi inspiratur, & postmodum expiratur ad vitæ conservationem.
units.tr: Sensible breathing is that by which air is drawn through the lungs into the heart and afterwards breathed out, for the preservation of life.

units.la: Pulsus est motus cordis & arteriarum, constans διαστολὴ καὶ συστολή, consequens actionem animæ circa generationem spirituum vitalium occupatæ, ut calor eventiletur & fuligines expellantur.
units.tr: The pulse is the motion of the heart and arteries, consisting of dilation and contraction [διαστολὴ καὶ συστολή], following the activity of the soul that is busy generating the vital spirits, so that the heat may be fanned and the soot expelled.

units.la: Αἰσθητικὴ facultas ex sentiendi principio orta, cognitione sensuum insequitur.
units.tr: The sensitive [αἰσθητικὴ] faculty, arising from the principle of sensation, follows upon the knowledge of the senses.

units.la: Estq; Appetens, vel Locomovens.
units.tr: It is either appetitive or locomotive.

units.la: Appetens, unde APPETITUS est vis animæ sentientis, quâ sui conservandi causâ inclinatur & fertur animal in suum bonum, vel aversatur sibi malum, prout ipsi sensus judicaverint.
units.tr: The appetitive faculty, from which appetite comes, is the power of the sentient soul by which the animal, for the sake of its own preservation, is inclined and carried towards what is good for it, or turns away from what is harmful, as its senses have judged.

units.la: Ut enim duplex est cognitio, una per sensum, altera per intellectum: ita appetitus animalis qui sequitur animæ cognitionem est sensitivus & rationalis. Hic de illo. Sensitivus est, qui comitatur cognitionem sensitivam. Inclinatur n. animal partim ad ea quæ sibi conveniunt, ex forma naturali: & sic habet appetitum naturalem: partim ad ea quæ cognoscit per formas aliunde acceptas, & sic habet proprie appetitum sensitivum.
units.tr: Just as knowledge is twofold, one through the sense and the other through the intellect, so the animal appetite that follows the knowledge of the soul is sensitive and rational. Let this be said of the one. The sensitive appetite is that which accompanies sensitive knowledge. For the animal is inclined partly to those things that suit it, from its natural form, and so it has natural appetite; and partly to those things it knows through forms received from elsewhere, and so it has properly sensitive appetite.

units.la: Estq; hic appetitus Concupiscens vel Irascens.
units.tr: This appetite is either concupiscible or irascible.

units.la: Concupiscens datus est ad boni prosecutionem.
units.tr: The concupiscible appetite is given for the pursuit of good.

units.la: Irascens ad resistendum impedientibus prosequutionem & conservationem boni.
units.tr: The irascible appetite is given for resisting whatever hinders the pursuit and preservation of good.

units.la: Hanc insequuntur affectus, perpes-siones & motus animæ.
units.tr: These are followed by the affections, passions and motions of the soul.

units.la: AFFECTUS sunt motus cordis à cognitione objecti excitati, ut illud vel prosequatur vel fugiat animal ad vitandam molestiam & jucunditate perfruendum.
units.tr: AFFECTIONS are motions of the heart, excited by the knowledge of an object, by which the animal either pursues or flees that object, in order to avoid discomfort and enjoy pleasure.

units.la: Affectus vero habent objectum vel Approbatum, vel Improbatum.
units.tr: Affections have an object that is either approved or disapproved.

units.la: Approbatum objectum est, quod bonum & gratum approbatum est. Hoc ciet cordi[?] leni & amico spirituum & caloris motu, nisi modum violaverit commotio.
units.tr: An approved object is that which is judged good and pleasant. It stirs the heart gently and kindly, with a motion of the spirits and heat, unless the agitation exceeds due measure.

units.la: Affectus approbati objecti vel tantum præsenti, vel tantum absente bono per-movetur, vel etiam utroq;.
units.tr: The affection toward an approved object is stirred either by a good that is only present, or only absent, or by both.

units.la: Præsente bono citus[?] affectus est lætitia seu gaudium.
units.tr: The affection toward a present good is quickly joy or gladness.

units.la: Lætitia est affectus, quo animus in bono præsenti acquiescens, illud corde, spiritibus vibrato & dilatato ad fruendum, amplectitur.
units.tr: Joy is an affection by which the mind, resting in a present good, embraces it with the heart, the spirits being set vibrating and dilated for enjoyment.

units.la: Lætitiæ motu spiritus feruntur extrà, cum similia maximè appetant unionē, unde spiritus ad lætitiæ auctorem exire quasi conatur.
units.tr: By the motion of joy the spirits are carried outward, since like things most desire union; hence the spirits seem to rush out toward the author of the joy.

units.la: Hunc internum affectum extrinsecus in corpore sequitur & arguit Hilaritas, qui est affectus vultus à lætitia procedens.
units.tr: This inner affection is followed and revealed outwardly in the body by cheerfulness, which is the expression of the face arising from joy.

units.la: Affectus absentis boni est Spes, qua animus futurum & absens bonum aperto quasi & hiante corde sperat.
units.tr: The affection toward an absent good is hope, by which the mind hopes for a future and absent good, as it were with the heart open and gaping.

units.la: Spei motu spiritus fibris cor diffundunt, ut objectum expectatum & desideratum intra sinus quasi suos recipiat.
units.tr: By the motion of hope the spirits spread through the fibres of the heart, so that it may receive, as it were within its own bosom, the expected and desired object.

units.la: Affectus objecti approbati, cùm præsentis, tùm absentis boni est Amor.
units.tr: The affection toward an approved object, both present and absent good, is love.

units.la: AMOR est affectus, quo animus, corde calore spiritū & sanguinis villis suis magis expanso, rem amatam sibi adunit. Hic unionis affectus cum præsentem tum absentem amatam rem nobis unit, unionemq; tuetur.
units.tr: LOVE is an affection by which the mind, with the heart expanded by the heat of the spirits and the fibres of the blood, joins the beloved thing to itself. This affection of union, whether the beloved is present or absent, unites it to us and preserves the union.

units.la: Improbatum objectum commovens est, quod malum & ingratum est æstimatum. Hoc ciet cor motu insuavi & aspero.
units.tr: An object that stirs us as disapproved is one judged evil and unpleasant. It moves the heart with a rough and unpleasant motion.

units.la: Affectus improbati objecti est simplex, vel mistus.
units.tr: The affection toward a disapproved object is either simple or mixed.

units.la: Simplex malo & ingrato objecto cie-tur vel præsente vel absente.
units.tr: The simple affection is stirred by an evil and unpleasant object, either present or absent.

units.la: Simplex præsentis mali affectus est vel nostri, vel alieni.
units.tr: The simple affection toward a present evil is either for oneself or for another.

units.la: Nostri præsentis mali affectus est Tristi-tia.
units.tr: The affection toward one's own present evil is sadness.

units.la: Tristitia est affectus quo animus ob sibi præsens malum retractis ad principia sua spiritibus cor constringit & comprimit.
