units.tr: Sadness is an affection by which the mind, because of an evil present to it, draws its spirits back to their origins and constricts and compresses the heart.

units.la: Tristitia si diuturna sit Mæror dicitur.
units.tr: If sadness is lasting, it is called grief.

units.la: Alieni præsentis mali affectus dicitur Misericordia.
units.tr: The affection toward another's present evil is called pity.

units.la: Misericordia est, quo animus torpen-tibus & compresis spiritibus constri-ctionis motu cor ob alius tantum miseriam corripit.
units.tr: Pity is that by which the mind, with the spirits numbed and compressed, seizes the heart with a motion of constriction on account of another's misery alone.

units.la: Simplex absentis & futuri mali affectus est Metus.
units.tr: The simple affection toward an absent and future evil is fear.

units.la: Metus est, quo animus demissum cor constringit futuri mali expectatione.
units.tr: Fear is that by which the mind, in expectation of a future evil, constricts the downcast heart.

units.la: Metus si magnus est Pavor dicitur, cum animus verberatur quasi imminentis mali opinione.
units.tr: If fear is great it is called dread, when the mind is struck, as it were, by the belief that evil is at hand.

units.la: Summum metus fastigium dicitur Con-sternatio, qua ex perculsione concidit animus, & spe & consiliis abjectis.
units.tr: The highest peak of fear is called consternation, by which the mind collapses from being struck down, with hope and counsel cast aside.

units.la: Internum metus effectu sequitur corporis affectio, Tremor, Horror, & Trepidatio.
units.tr: The bodily effects that follow the inner effect of fear are trembling, horror and trepidation.

units.la: Tremor est corporis motus ex contra-riis motibus.
units.tr: Trembling is a motion of the body arising from contrary motions.

units.la: Horror est corporis spiritu introrsum fugiente cutemq; destituente, asperitas.
units.tr: Horror is a roughness of the body, the spirit fleeing inward and leaving the skin.

units.la: Trepidatio est impulsio & inordina-tus spirituum motus, adeo ut consistere non possimus.
units.tr: Trepidation is an agitation and disordered motion of the spirits, so that we cannot stand still.

units.la: Mistus affectus est Ira & Odium, Zelus & ἐπιχαιρεκακία[?].
units.tr: A mixed affection is anger and hatred, zeal and epichairekakia [ἐπιχαιρεκακία].

units.la: Ira est affectus ex tristitia & ulciscen-di cupiditate mixtus.
units.tr: Anger is an affection mixed of sadness and the desire for revenge.

units.la: Tristitia hic objectum ingratum re-pellit: cupiditas objecti illius illati est ulciscendi avida.
units.tr: In this case, sadness repels the unpleasant object; the desire for that object, once inflicted, is eager for revenge.

units.la: Hic itaq; duplex est cordis motus: Pri-mus est astrictio cordisq; compressio, orta ex præsenti malo, quâ cor à se illud depellit: & hac ratione est affectus depulsionis, ut vult Scaliger.
units.tr: Thus there is a twofold motion of the heart. The first is the tightening and compression of the heart, arising from the present evil, by which the heart thrusts that evil away from itself; and in this respect it is an affection of repulsion, as Scaliger maintains.

units.la: Alter est dilatatio: avidè enim expetit i-psum malum in ipsum auctorem rejicere.
units.tr: The second is dilation, for the heart eagerly desires to throw the evil itself back upon its author.

units.la: Hinc sanguis è præcordiis foràs erumpit quasi telum, quo cor mali auctorem petat.
units.tr: Hence the blood bursts forth from the inner parts like a weapon, by which the heart attacks the author of the evil.

units.la: Odium est affectus corde coactu suo quasi refugiente objectú ingratum cum offensione longa.
units.tr: Hatred is an affection in which the heart, by its own act, as it were, shrinks from an unpleasant object with lasting offence.

units.la: Zelus est affectus, ex ira & amore mixtus, cum scilicet irascimur ei à quo lædi-tur id quod amamus.
units.tr: Zeal is an affection mixed of anger and love, when we are angry with the one by whom what we love is injured.

units.la: Ἐπιχαιρεκακία est affectus, ex odio & gaudio mixtus, cum odio impulsi alienis gaudemus malis.
units.tr: Epichairekakia [ἐπιχαιρεκακία] is an affection mixed of hatred and joy, when, driven by hatred, we rejoice in the misfortunes of others.

units.la: Loco movens restat, quâ totum corpus de loco in locum transfertur & progreditur, cujus ordo talis est: 1. Objectum movet sensum. 2. A sensu oritur notitia. 3. Notitiam sequitur appetitio & rei desideratio. 4. Cogniti appetitio vibrat ac ferit cerebrum ac spiritus animales. 5. Cerebrum motos spiritus animales ejaculatur in nervos. 6. Spiritus animales transeunt per nervos ad musculum partis movendæ. 7. Musculus ille ictus & vibratus animali spiritu contrahit & movet sese sua carne versus caput, seu initium musculi. 8. Musculus contractus attrahit ad se chordas, 9. Chorda attracta trahit & ciet membrum, cui est insitum.
units.tr: Local motion remains, by which the whole body is transferred and advances from place to place. Its order is as follows: (1) the object moves the sense; (2) knowledge arises from the sense; (3) appetite and the desire for the thing follow the knowledge; (4) the appetite of the thing known strikes and sets vibrating the brain and the animal spirits; (5) the brain throws the moved animal spirits into the nerves; (6) the animal spirits pass through the nerves to the muscle of the part to be moved; (7) that muscle, struck and vibrated by the animal spirit, contracts and moves itself with its flesh towards the head, or the origin of the muscle; (8) the contracted muscle draws the cords to itself; (9) the drawn cord pulls and moves the limb to which it is attached.

units.la: CAPUT XXV. DE ANIMALIUM CORPORE.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV. ON THE BODY OF ANIMALS.

units.la: Adhuc generaliter exposita est Anima sentiens: Corpus animalis se-quitur, quod ab anima sentien-te animatur, ut sentiat seq; moveat:
units.tr: Having thus generally set out the sentient soul, we follow with the body of the animal, which is animated by the sentient soul so that it may sense and move.

units.la: Corpus animalis distinguitur membris, quæ sunt animæ sentientis distincta organa, ipsi operanti usum sui exhibentia.
units.tr: The body of the animal is distinguished into members, which are the distinct organs of the sentient soul, presenting their use to the soul that operates through them.

units.la: Membra illa sunt principalia, vel minus principalia.
units.tr: These members are either principal or less principal.

units.la: Principalia sunt Caput & Truncus. Omnia enim animalia habent Caput & Cor, vel aliquid eis analogon.
units.tr: The principal members are the head and the trunk. For all animals have a head and a heart, or something analogous to them.

units.la: Caput, est membrum animalis prin-cipale continens principia & organa sensus & motus.
units.tr: The head is the principal member of the animal, containing the principles and organs of sense and motion.

units.la: Truncus, est reliqua pars corporis, capiti subjecta, comprehendens reliquarum facultatum præcipuè vitalium &na-turalium organa.
units.tr: The trunk is the remaining part of the body, subject to the head, comprising chiefly the organs of the remaining faculties, especially the vital and natural ones.

units.la: Trunci partes sunt Mediæ vel Extremæ.
units.tr: The parts of the trunk are the middle and the extreme.

units.la: Mediæ sunt in perfectioribus præcipuè Thorax & Venter.
units.tr: The middle parts, in the more perfect animals, are chiefly the chest and the belly.

units.la: Thorax est superior pars trunci, continens præcipuè fontem caloris, micationis & respirationis organa.
units.tr: The chest is the upper part of the trunk, containing chiefly the source of heat, the pulse, and the organs of breathing.

units.la: Venter est inferior pars trunci, complectens nutritionis & generationis membra.
units.tr: The belly is the lower part of the trunk, embracing the organs of nutrition and generation.

units.la: Extremæ partes sunt quasi rami & radices in trunco arboris, in homine, Manus & pedes ; In aliis nonnullis, alæ aut branchiæ, in quibus nulli pedes.
units.tr: The extreme parts are, as it were, the branches and roots on the trunk of a tree: in man, the hands and feet; in some other animals, wings or gills, in which there are no feet.

units.la: Verùm quia bestialium corporum ingens est varietas, ut ea breviter comprehendi nequeat, ideo reliqua corporis animalis membra in exemplari perfectioris corporis, scilicet humani, paulò fusius explicabimus, & infrà dispiciemus minus principalia membra.
units.tr: But since the variety of animal bodies is so great that it cannot be briefly comprehended, we shall therefore explain the remaining members of the animal body more fully in the model of the more perfect body, namely the human, and below we shall examine the less principal members.

units.la: Corpus porrò animalis est Masculeum vel Fœmineum.
units.tr: Furthermore, the animal body is either male or female.

units.la: Masculeum corpus est, quod membris genitalibus fœminam imprægnantibus & progenerantibus præditum.
units.tr: The male body is that which is endowed with genital members that impregnate and beget the female.

units.la: Fœmineum corpus quod membris ge-nitalibus concipientibus & parientibus præditum. Illud plerunq; calidius, hoc frigidius censetur.
units.tr: The female body is that which is endowed with genital members that conceive and bring forth. The former is commonly judged warmer, the latter colder.

units.la: NB. Quædam tamen animalia carent se-xu. In quibusdam promiscuus est uterq; sexus. Coitus animalium aut est ejusdem generis, aut diversorum etiam. Unde Scaliger: Uno sub ge-nere lupus, canis, vulpes, hyæna, tigris: Concipiunt enim ex aliena æque atq; è sua quisq; specie. Scribunt quidam de mutatione sexus, fœminas esse factas masculos. Idq; quidam putant naturæ non esse ἀδύνατον quia puer à puella non diffe-rat natura, sed genitalium membrorum for-matione.
units.tr: NB. Some animals, however, lack sex. In some both sexes are found together. The mating of animals is either within the same kind or even between different kinds. Hence Scaliger: under one genus are the wolf, dog, fox, hyena, tiger; for each conceives from another's species just as from its own. Some write of a change of sex, of females having been made males. Some think this is not impossible in nature, since a boy differs from a girl in nature only in the formation of the genital members.

units.la: Axiomata.
units.tr: Axioms.

units.la: I. Masculi & fœminæ mutua est ad con-gressum propensio: Genitalis enim calor eos stimulat.
units.tr: I. Males and females have a mutual inclination towards union, for genital heat stirs them.

units.la: 2. In animantibus sexu præditis, cum fœmina sufficit ad nutritionem prolis, masculus ubi fœmellam implevit, pluribus se conjungere solet fœminis. At in quibus sola fœmina non par est ferendo oneri sobolis, unus masculus uni fœminæ copulatur.
units.tr: 2. In animals endowed with sex, where the female suffices for nourishing the offspring, the male, once he has filled a female, is accustomed to join himself to several females. But in those where the female alone is not equal to bearing the burden of the offspring, one male is joined to one female.

units.la: 3. Ex adulterina diversorum animalium coitione multæ novæ species enascuntur.
units.tr: 3. From the adulterous mating of different animals many new species arise.

units.la: 4. Non nisi ex masculo & fœmella ducunt ortus suos animalia perfectiora.
units.tr: 4. More perfect animals arise only from a male and a female.

units.la: 5. Fœmina voce plerumq; est acutiore propter speciem tenuiorem, quàm mas.
units.tr: 5. The female's voice is usually higher than the male's, on account of her thinner species.

units.la: 6. Mares ferè calidiores & potentiores sunt fœminis.
units.tr: 6. Males are generally warmer and stronger than females.

units.la: CAPUT XXVI. DE THERIOGRAPHIA, SEU BRUTORUM DISTINCTIONE.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI. ON THERIOGRAPHY, OR THE DISTINCTION OF BRUTES.

units.la: Oographiæ species duæ sunt: Theriographia & Antropologia. Est enim duplex Animal; Brutum, aut Rationis particeps.
units.tr: There are two kinds of zoography: theriography and anthropology. For an animal is either a brute or a creature that partakes of reason.

units.la: Theriographia est pars ζωογραφίας, quæ explicat naturam animalium brutorum seu bestiarum.
units.tr: Theriography is a part of zoography, which explains the nature of brute animals or beasts.

units.la: Brutum seu Bestia est animal ratione carens, sensu tantum & motu præditum.
units.tr: A brute or beast is an animal that lacks reason and is endowed only with sense and motion.

units.la: Est autem hic sensus, quo prædita sunt animalia, manifestus vel occultus. Manifesto sensu prædita sunt omnia animalia bruta, præter Zoophyta de quibus supra. Brutum est perfectius vel imperfectius.
units.tr: The sense with which animals are endowed is either manifest or hidden. All brute animals are endowed with manifest sense, except the zoophytes, of which above. A brute is either more perfect or less perfect.

units.la: Perfectius est, quod habet corpus integrum, quod caesura caret.
units.tr: More perfect is that which has a whole body, without any cut or division.

units.la: Perfectius est Heterobium vel Amphibium.
units.tr: More perfect is the heterobium or amphibium.

units.la: Heterobium(id est, una tantum in sede vivens, seu ut vox ipsa innuit, in altera seu alterutra tantum, puta aut in aqua tantum, aut in terra tantum:) est brutum perfectius, quod in uno tantum vivit Elemento, (scilicet terra aut aqua.)
units.tr: A heterobium (that is, one living in only one habitat, or, as the word itself suggests, in only one of two, for example only in water or only on land) is a more perfect brute which lives in only one element (namely earth or water).

units.la: Estq; terrestre, vel aquatile.
units.tr: It is either terrestrial or aquatic.

units.la: Terrestre est quod aërem inspiratione haurit, & extra aquam in terra degit, vel saltem ex eadem victum petit.
units.tr: Terrestrial is that which draws in air by breathing and lives on land outside water, or at least seeks its food from it.

units.la: Estque Gressile, vel Volatile.
units.tr: It is either walking or flying.

units.la: Gressile quod utitur gressu in terra.
units.tr: Walking is that which moves on foot on the land.

units.la: Estq; Quadrupes vel Reptile.
units.tr: It is either a quadruped or a reptile.

units.la: Quadrupes gressile est, quod quaternis pedibus incedens iisdem prope, quibus homo partibus constat, nisi quod pro brachiis pedes habeat priores.
units.tr: A walking quadruped is one which, going on four feet, is made up of nearly the same parts as man, except that it has forefeet in place of arms.

units.la: Harum bestiarum, ut & hominis temperamentu, constitutio est diversa. Nam in canibus bilis, in porcis phlegma, in aliis alia excellunt
units.tr: The constitution of these beasts, as of the human temperament, is varied. For in dogs bile, in pigs phlegm, and in others other humours predominate

units.la: Brutorum distinctiones. lunt humores, unde eorum temperamentum maximè pendet.
units.tr: Distinctions of brutes. humours, on which their temperament depends most.

units.la: Quadrupes est Oviparum, vel Vivi-parum.
units.tr: A quadruped is either oviparous or viviparous.

units.la: Oviparum est, quod ova parit, ex qui-bus deinde foris animal excluditur.
units.tr: Oviparous is that which lays eggs, from which the animal is then hatched outside.

units.la: Viviparum vivum animal & perse-ctum parit. Hoc habet pulmonè amplù & sanguine refertum: ideoq; respirat.
units.tr: Viviparous brings forth a living and fully formed animal. This has a large lung full of blood, and therefore it breathes.

units.la: Fœtus etiam eodem propemodum modo in uteris maternis, quo in mulieri-bus concipitur, alitur & in lucem editur.
units.tr: The foetus is also nourished and brought to light in the mother's womb in nearly the same way as it is conceived in women.

units.la: Viviparum vel paucos fœtus edere so-let, ut quod habet pedem solidum, item bisulcum, quod plerumq; est cornutum: aut multos, ut multifidum, quod in plu-res partes dissectos pedes habet.
units.tr: Viviparous animals usually bear either few young, such as those with a solid hoof or a cloven hoof, which is mostly horned; or many, like the multifid, which has feet divided into several parts.

units.la: Hinc nascuntur hæ distinctiones. 1. Gressi-le brutum aut cornutum est, aut non. Cornu-tum aut habet cornua ramosiora, ut Cervus: aut bina habet, ut Taurus, aut unum, ut Monoceros. 2. Gressile quoddam habet ungulam pedum bifidam, ut Bos; quoddam non divisam, ut Cuniculus; quoddam est solipedum, planam quod habet ungulam; quoddam denique in quinq; digitos divisum pedem, ut Feles. 3. Quoddam vestitur corio nudo, quoddam pilis, quoddam villis, quoddam setis, quoddam lana. 4. Quoddam est ruminans. Rumen est guttur seu interior cavitas, per quam cibum ad tempus ruminans demittit, & postea ad os revocat. Ruminare est cibum jam mansum, & in unum stomachi sinum jam delapsum per guttur revocare & iterum mandere, transmittere ad alterum sinum stomachi melius attritum & praeparatum. Ruminantibus, quod careant superiore ordine dentium, dedit natura ventriculos plures uno, quorum alius ab alio cibum accipit. 5. Terrestre animal est mansuetum vel sylvestre. Mansuetum quod vel greges vel armenta constituit & ruminat; vel quod est jumentum & solipedum. Sylvestre seu ferum est cornutum vel non cornutum, idque majoris, mediae vel minoris magnitudinis.
units.tr: From this arise these distinctions. (1) A walking brute is either horned or not. A horned one has either branching horns, like the stag; or two, like the bull; or one, like the unicorn. (2) Some walking animal has a cloven hoof, like the ox; some has an undivided hoof, like the rabbit; some is solipede, having a flat hoof; and finally some has a foot divided into five digits, like the cat. (3) Some is covered with bare skin, some with hair, some with fur, some with bristles, and some with wool. (4) Some is ruminant. The rumen is the throat or inner cavity through which a ruminant sends down its food for a time and afterwards brings it back to the mouth. To ruminate is to bring back through the throat food already chewed and already slipped into one compartment of the stomach, and to chew it again, passing it to another compartment of the stomach better ground and prepared. Because ruminants lack the upper row of teeth, nature gave them several stomachs rather than one, each taking food from the other. (5) A terrestrial animal is either tame or wild. Tame is that which either forms flocks or herds and ruminates, or which is a beast of burden and solipede. Wild or feral is either horned or not horned, and of greater, middling or lesser size.

units.la: REPTILE est, quod humi repit. Alii dicunt, quod corporis contractioni & extensioni innititur, ad se promovendum. Parte quidem interiore se extendit, reliquum corpus post se trahit. At angustius hi definiunt.
units.tr: A REPTILE is that which crawls on the ground. Some say it relies on contracting and extending its body to move itself forward: it stretches its front part and drags the rest of its body behind. But these define it too narrowly.

units.la: REPTILE est Serpens, vel Vermis.
units.tr: A REPTILE is a serpent or a worm.

units.la: Serpens est reptile sanguineum, minutiore corporis nisu, non apertis passibus repens. Hic pectori innitens totum corpus uno nisu trahit, quanquam etiam orbibus seu spiris se convolvat. GeGenerantur autem serpentes vel ex femine seu prolifico humore in matrice fœmellæ, vel ex putri materia. Coeunt autem non solùm attritu, sed etiam mutuo complexu.
units.tr: A serpent is a blooded reptile, creeping with a slighter effort of the body, without open steps. Resting on its breast, it draws its whole body along in one effort, though it also coils itself in loops or spirals. Serpents are generated either from seed or prolific moisture in the female's womb, or from putrid matter. They mate not only by rubbing but also by mutual embrace.

units.la: Axiomata.
units.tr: Axioms.

units.la: 1. Nullum animal tam celeriter linguam movet atq; serpens.
units.tr: 1. No animal moves its tongue as quickly as a serpent.

units.la: 2. Præcipuè vescitur pulvere terræ. Comedit etiam venenosas carnes & herbas.
units.tr: 2. It feeds chiefly on dust from the earth. It also eats poisonous flesh and herbs.

units.la: 3. Potest vivere diu absq; cibo.
units.tr: 3. It can live a long time without food.

units.la: 4. Ruta odorem fugit. Vini & lactis odorem sequitur.
units.tr: 4. It flees the smell of rue. It follows the smell of wine and milk.

units.la: 5. Jejuni hominis saliva serpentibus venenum.
units.tr: 5. The saliva of a fasting man is poison to serpents.

units.la: 6. Creditur timere hominem nudum, nec contingere nisi vestitum.
units.tr: 6. It is believed to fear a naked man, and to touch only one who is clothed.

units.la: 7. Astutum & sagax est brutum. 1. Quia totius corporis venenum in collo colligit, ut statim in promtu habeat, quo se defendere possit. 2. Descendens in aquam, venenum in tuto loco reponit, unde ab aquis recedens resumit. 3. Pellem quotannis exuit, per angustum foramen transiens.
units.tr: 7. The brute is crafty and shrewd. (1) Because it gathers all its venom in the neck, so that it has it ready at hand to defend itself. (2) Going down into water, it stores its venom in a safe place, and takes it up again when it leaves the waters. (3) It sheds its skin every year, passing through a narrow hole.

units.la: Serpens aut noxius seu venenosus, aut innoxius venenum non habens.
units.tr: A serpent is either harmful or venomous, or harmless, having no venom.

units.la: Noxiorum quidam habent vehementer acutum venenum, ut Basiliscus & Aspis. Horum morsus dicuntur muti & surdi, quia vix sentiuntur. Quidam habet quasi medium venenum, intra 7. horas necans, ut Vipera. Quidam obtusi habent, cujus morsus sanari[?] potest.
units.tr: Some of the harmful have very sharp venom, like the basilisk and the asp. Their bites are said to be mute and deaf, because they are hardly felt. Some have a middling venom, killing within seven hours, like the viper. Some have blunt venom, and their bite can be healed.

units.la: NOTA,
units.tr: NOTE,

units.la: 1. Senes sunt deteriores junioribus. 2. Incolentes loca montana deteriores sunt habitantibus ad loca aquarum. 3. Venenum repletorum minoris est nocumenti, quàm jejunorum. 4. Masculi pauciores habent dentes, plus autem veneni: Fœmina verò deteriores sunt ratione plurium dentium in morsu. 5. Irati & provocati deteriores sunt. 6. Tempore calido & sicco venenum est deterius, quàm tempore frigido & humido.
units.tr: 1. Old people are worse than young ones. 2. Those living in mountainous places are worse than those living near waters. 3. The venom of the full is less harmful than that of the fasting. 4. Males have fewer teeth but more venom; females, however, are worse because of the greater number of teeth in the bite. 5. Those who are angry or provoked are worse. 6. In hot and dry weather the venom is worse than in cold and damp weather.

units.la: II. Rursum quorundam venenum est frigidum, quorundam calidum.
units.tr: II. Again, the venom of some is cold, and of others hot.

units.la: III. Quidam serpentes morsu, quidam ictu, nonnulli visu, afflatu, olfactu suo nocent.
units.tr: III. Some serpents harm by their bite, some by their strike, some by their sight, breath, or smell.

units.la: IV. Quidam corpore majores, quidam exigui. Alii habet squamas, alii non. Quidam nigri, quidam maculosi. Quidam semper serpunt flexuosè, quidà recta[?] sine reflexu. Quidam tardi, quidam veloces. Quidam in terra, quidam in aquis latent.
units.tr: IV. Some are larger in body, some small. Some have scales, others do not. Some are black, some spotted. Some always crawl in winding fashion, others straight without bending back. Some are slow, some swift. Some lie hidden on land, some in water.

units.la: VERMIS est reptile, quod corpusculi sui partes indirectè gradatimque porrigendo contractas, contrahendo porrectas motum expedit.
units.tr: A WORM is a reptile which moves by stretching out the parts of its little body that were drawn together, and by drawing together the parts that were stretched out, advancing indirectly and by degrees.

units.la: Vermes generantur in carnibus, in intestinis, in cute, inter pellem & carnem, in capillis, in lardo, in frondibus & oleribus, in radicibus, in lignis, in vestibus, in sordibus aridi solis, in chartis & paleis, in vino acescente, in nive, in quacunq; fere re terrena ex humorum corruptione.
units.tr: Worms are generated in flesh, in the intestines, in the skin, between the hide and the flesh, in hair, in lard, in leaves and vegetables, in roots, in wood, in clothes, in the dirt of the dry sun, in paper and straw, in sour wine, in snow, and in almost any earthly thing from the corruption of humours.

units.la: Volatile brutum est, quod utitur volatu maximè in aëre, diciturq; AVIS quæ alis per aëra se movet.
units.tr: A flying animal is one that uses flight chiefly in the air, and it is called a BIRD, which moves through the air on wings.

units.la: Est autem Avis aëreæ naturæ, bipes, multifidos pedes habens; corpus ejus ex iisdem humoribus quatuor, & horum legitima commixtione, partibus item similaribus & dissimilaribus constat. Caret tamen renibus & vesica: Unde urinam non emittit.
units.tr: A bird is of an airy nature, two-footed, and has many-cleft feet; its body consists of the same four humours, and of their lawful mixture, and likewise of similar and dissimilar parts. Yet it lacks kidneys and bladder, so it does not pass urine.

units.la: Generatio avis fit ex ovo, atq; imprimis ex albugine. Vitello enim enutritur, donec excludatur. Vegetantur autem & vitam concipiunt ova, à calore fœminarum incubantium.
units.tr: The generation of a bird takes place from an egg, and especially from the white. For the chick is nourished by the yolk until it is hatched. Eggs are quickened and receive life from the warmth of the hens that sit on them.

units.la: Excipit Scaliger paucas aves ἄπόδες[?] & quadrupedes. Omnes fere aves longorum pedum & crurium longum habent collum, & volant extenso collo.
units.tr: Scaliger excepts a few birds which are footless, and quadrupeds. Almost all birds with long feet and shins have a long neck, and they fly with the neck stretched out.

units.la: Omnes aves sunt pennatæ & aligeræ: habent rostra, quibus dentium loco quodammodo utuntur. Excipit Scaliger avem peregrinam quæ habeat intus rostrum denticulatum.
units.tr: All birds are feathered and winged; they have beaks, which they use in some way in place of teeth. Scaliger excepts a foreign bird which has a toothed beak inside.

units.la: Præcipuæ avium distinctiones hæ inveniuntur.
units.tr: The principal distinctions of birds are these.

units.la: 1. Quædam aves habent crura, quædam non. Crura habentes sunt ἀπόδες[?], vel καμψόπόδες[?], vel ἀπόδες[?].
units.tr: 1. Some birds have legs, some do not. Those having legs are footed, or bent-footed, or ...

units.la: Quædam sunt bifidis pedibus; quædam multifidis. Quibusdam sunt ungues recti; quibusdam unci. Quædam habent rostrum corneum; quædam osseum & carneum. Quædam rostrum aduncum; aliæ rectum, &c.
units.tr: Some have two-cleft feet, some many-cleft. Some have straight claws, some hooked. Some have a horny beak, some a bony and fleshy one. Some have a hooked beak, others a straight one, and so on.

units.la: II. Quædam sunt minus vocales, quædam canoræ, quædam mutæ. Quædã hominum conversatione & domiciliis delectantur; quædã in desertis locis secretam agunt vitã. Quædã gregatim volât; quædã sunt solivagæ. Quædã manent in suis regionibus ; quaedam alias quaerunt & suo tempore revertuntur. Quaedam sunt diurnae ; quaedam nocturnae.
units.tr: II. Some are less vocal, some are melodious, some are mute. Some delight in the company and dwellings of men; some live a secluded life in deserted places. Some fly in flocks; some wander alone. Some remain in their own regions; some seek others and return at their own time. Some are diurnal; some nocturnal.

units.la: III. Quaedam aves sunt carnivorae, quaedam piscivorae, quaedam frugivorae, quaedam herbivorae, quaedam vermivorae. Quaedam aliis atque aliis vescuntur cibis.
units.tr: III. Some birds are carnivorous, some fish-eating, some fruit-eating, some herb-eating, some worm-eating. Some feed on various foods, one after another.

units.la: IV. Quaedam semel pariunt, quaedam aliquoties.
units.tr: IV. Some lay eggs once, some several times.

units.la: V. Quaedam sunt aptae esui, quaedam non.
units.tr: V. Some are fit for eating, some are not.

units.la: VI. Quaedam in terra, quaedam in arboribus quiescunt.
units.tr: VI. Some rest on the ground, some in trees.

units.la: VII. Avis alia est plane aerea, quae in montibus & siccis locis versatur: alia aquatica, quae in mari, stagnis, paludibus, lacustribus locis & fluviis maxime volat & degit.
units.tr: VII. One bird is wholly aerial, which dwells on mountains and dry places; another is aquatic, which flies and lives chiefly on the sea, in pools, marshes, lake-places and rivers.

units.la: Aquatile brutum est, quod in aqua degit, ejusque naturam & temperamentum obtinet, & dicitur Pisces.
units.tr: An aquatic animal is one that lives in water and has the nature and constitution of water, and it is called fish.

units.la: Pisces est brutum aquae & frigidae substantiae, corpore oblongo, cute squammata, in aqua degens.
units.tr: A fish is an animal of watery and cold substance, with an elongated body and scaly skin, living in water.

units.la: Propagatio piscium plerunque fit per seminalem propagationem, sed cum hoc discridiscrimine, ut quidam ova generent, & aquis fovenda committant, quidam vero pariant vivos fœtus.
units.tr: The propagation of fish usually takes place by seed, but with this difference: some produce eggs and commit them to the waters to be cherished, while others bring forth live young.

units.la: Cor inest plerisque piscibus, sed inversum, à quo in branchias meatus quidam porriguntur, per quos humorem quem ore acceperunt, reddunt. Dentes fere omnes sunt serrati, & in lingua quoque nonnullis sunt dentes. Linguam plerique duram habent & valde adhærescentem: Oculos sine palpebris. Pulmone carent & aspera arteria, ideoque nec e-duint vocem, nec respirant.
units.tr: Most fish have a heart, but inverted, from which certain passages extend into the gills, through which they release the water they took in by the mouth. Nearly all fish have serrated teeth, and some have teeth on the tongue as well. Most have a hard tongue that clings very closely. Their eyes have no eyelids. They lack lungs and a windpipe, and so they neither emit a voice nor breathe.

units.la: Distinctio hæc potest esse: Aquatilia aut sunt sanguinea, aut exanguia.
units.tr: This division may be made: aquatic animals are either blooded or bloodless.

units.la: Sanguinea sunt, i. Marina, quæ mare nunquam egrediuntur.
units.tr: Blooded ones are marine, that is, those which never leave the sea.

units.la: Marini pisces sunt pelagii, aut littorales.
units.tr: Marine fish are either pelagic or littoral.

units.la: Pelagii, qui in profundo maris summi procul à littoribus versantur.
units.tr: Pelagic ones are those which live in the deep of the open sea, far from the shores.

units.la: Suntque Cetacei, vel non Cetacei.
units.tr: And they are either cetaceans or not cetaceans.

units.la: Cetacei sunt grandes, & perfectum animal ex femina non ex ovo gignunt, ut Balæna, Delphin, &c.
units.tr: Cetaceans are large, and they bring forth a perfect animal from a womb, not from an egg, such as the whale, the dolphin, etc.

units.la: Non cetacei sunt crassi seu corpulenti, aut lati. Crassi sunt lati, squamosi, vel rotundi, rubescentes.
units.tr: Non-cetaceans are thick or corpulent, or broad. Thick ones are broad, scaly, or round, and reddish.

units.la: Lati sunt spinosi, ut: Rhombi, Passeres: aut Cartilaginei, iiq; aut sunt plani, aut longi.
units.tr: Broad ones are spiny, such as the turbot and the sparrow; or cartilaginous, and these are either flat or long.

units.la: Littorales, qui ad littora & terræ propinquas partes sedes captant & in mare summum raro recurrunt, &c.
units.tr: Littoral fish are those that take up their seats by the shores and near the land, and seldom return to the open sea, etc.

units.la: 2. Sanguinei, sunt lacustres qui in lacubus degunt.
units.tr: 2. Blooded fish are lacustrine, which live in lakes.

units.la: 3. Fluviales, qui flumina, rivulosq; incolunt.
units.tr: 3. River fish, which inhabit rivers and streams.

units.la: 4. Palustres qui loca cœnosa ac sordida seu paludes amant.
units.tr: 4. Marsh fish, which love muddy and filthy places or marshes.

units.la: Exanguia aquatilia sunt 1. Mollia ut Sepia, Loligines. 2. Crustacea, id est, crustis intecta, ut Locusta, Squilla. 3. Testacea Muschelen. 4. Insecta, ut Scolopendra marina, Hirudo.
units.tr: Bloodless aquatic animals are: 1. Soft-bodied, such as the cuttlefish and squids; 2. Crustacea, that is, covered with shells, such as the lobster and the squill; 3. Shelled, the mussels; 4. Insects, such as the sea-centipede and the leech.

units.la: Amphibia bruta sunt, quæ & in aquis & supra terram degunt, quorum item quædam quadrupeda, quædam reptilia, quædam volucria sunt. Vide Gesnerum.
units.tr: Amphibious animals are those which live both in water and on land; some of these are quadrupeds, some reptiles, some winged. See Gesner.

units.la: Imperfectiora restant bruta, quæ integrum corpus non habent, sed cæsura quadam sunt incisa, & dicuntur INSECTA.
units.tr: There remain the less perfect animals, which do not have a whole body but are cut into by a certain incision, and they are called INSECTS.

units.la: Imperfectiora dicuntur, quia sunt exanguia, Epar quippe non habent. Ideò facilis est eorum ortus & interitus.
units.tr: They are called less perfect because they are bloodless; they do not have a liver. For this reason their coming into being and their perishing is easy.

units.la: -Infecta autem quædam nascuntur. 1. Ex sola putredine & sordibus, ut Tineæ, Culices, Pulices, Cimices, Erucæ. 2. Ex semine & coitu animaliū sui generis ut Cicindela item Cicadæ & Locustæ, quæ ova pariunt. Nā etsi in quibusdam sexº distingui nequit, in quibusdam tamen potest : ut Muscarum una init, altera initur.
units.tr: Some insects are born: 1. From putrefaction and filth alone, such as moths, gnats, fleas, bedbugs, and caterpillars; 2. From seed and the mating of animals of their own kind, such as the tiger-beetle, likewise cicadas and locusts, which lay eggs. For although in some the sexes cannot be distinguished, in others they can: as one kind of fly mates, and another is mated with.

units.la: II. Quædam infecta sunt pennata, quædam pennarum expertia.
units.tr: II. Some insects are winged, some without wings.

units.la: Pennata quædam binis, ut Muscæ, Papiliones. quædam quaternis constant pennis, ut Apes, Vespæ, Fuci, Cicadæ, &c.
units.tr: Some winged ones have two wings, such as flies and butterflies; some consist of four wings, such as bees, wasps, drones, cicadas, etc.

units.la: Expertia pennarum sunt, quæ humi se continent, ut Formicæ, Arandi, Locustæ, Pulices, Bruchus, Aurelia, Eruca. Locustæ tamen habent alarum quædam rudi-menta.
units.tr: Those without wings are the ones that keep close to the ground, such as ants, woodlice, locusts, fleas, the bruchus, the aurelia, and the caterpillar. Locusts, however, have some rudiments of wings.

units.la: III. Infecta alia vivunt rore & humore ut Apes, Cicadæ; alia venatu, ut Aranei; Alia herbis, ut Locusta; alia fructibus, ut Bombyces, Erucæ, Bruchi, Formicæ; alia deniq; quovis cibo, ut Musca. Et hæc de Brutis.
units.tr: III. Some insects live on dew and moisture, such as bees and cicadas; some by hunting, such as spiders; some on herbs, such as the locust; some on fruits, such as silkworms, caterpillars, bruchi, and ants; and finally some on any food, such as the fly. And these are the things about animals.

units.la: CAPUT XXVII. DE PSYCHOLOGIA HUMANA, SEU ANIMA Hominis rationali.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII. ON HUMAN PSYCHOLOGY, OR THE RATIONAL SOUL OF MAN

units.la: ANthropologia est pars Zoographiæ, hominis naturam explicans.
units.tr: Anthropology is the part of zoography that explains the nature of man.

units.la: Hominis natura est essentia spiritualis & corporeæ naturæ in unum ὑφιστάμενον [?] u-nitæ particeps.
units.tr: The nature of man is the essence that partakes of both spiritual and corporeal nature, united into one subsisting [ὑφιστάμενον] thing.

units.la: Adeoque Homo est animal rationale.
units.tr: Hence man is a rational animal.

units.la: Hominis partes sunt duæ: Anima logi-ca seu Spiritus humanus, & Corpus humanum.
units.tr: The parts of man are two: the rational soul, or human spirit, and the human body.

units.la: Proinde Antropologiæ partes duæ sunt, Psychologia, & Somatotomia.
units.tr: Accordingly, the parts of anthropology are two: psychology and somatotomy.

units.la: PSYCHOLOGIA est prior pars Anthropologiæ, quæ docet naturam animæ seu spiritus humani per ejusdem fa-cultates.
units.tr: PSYCHOLOGY is the first part of anthropology, which teaches the nature of the soul or human spirit through its faculties.

units.la: Est autem Anima rationalis pars hominis essentialis, nimirum Spiritus humano corpori animando destinatus, eiq; in unam hypostasin unitꝰ [?], suis facultatibus actiones in illo vel per illud ciens.
units.tr: The rational soul is an essential part of man, namely a spirit destined to animate the human body and united with it in one hypostasis, bringing about its actions in and through the body by means of its faculties.

units.la: Facultas animæ rationalis est vis in ani-ma agendi seu actiones edendi. Hæc in anima est naturaliter & originaliter, ab anima ceu fonte & principio manans, seq; per actiones humanas exerens.
units.tr: A faculty of the rational soul is the power in the soul to act, or to produce actions. It is in the soul naturally and originally, flowing from the soul as from a source and principle, and it manifests itself through human actions.

units.la: Facultas animæ rationalis propria est, vel communis.
units.tr: A faculty of the rational soul is either proper or common.

units.la: Propria discriminat hominé à bruto.
units.tr: A proper faculty distinguishes man from the brute.

units.la: Estq; Primaria, aut Secundaria.
units.tr: And it is either primary or secondary.

units.la: PRIMARIA animæ logicæ facultas est superior & nobilior, & quidem immaterialis, non ita alligata corporeis organis, ut Ratio & Voluntas.
units.tr: The primary faculty of the rational soul is superior and nobler, and indeed immaterial, not bound so closely to bodily organs, as reason and will are.

units.la: RATIO est animæ humanæ vis suprema, qua homo intelligit: dicituq; Intellectus.
units.tr: REASON is the highest power of the human soul, by which man understands; it is called the intellect.

units.la: INTELLECTUS est vis animæ rationalis, quæ res quasvis percipere ac de iis disserere potest.
units.tr: INTELLECT is the power of the rational soul which can perceive any things whatever and reason about them.

units.la: Scaliger inquit: Mens sua natura infinita est & aspernatur certorum finium præscriptionem.
units.tr: Scaliger says: The mind is by its nature infinite and disdains being confined within fixed limits.

units.la: Intellectus tùm actio est, tùm distin-ctio & adjunctum.
units.tr: The intellect is both an act and a distinction and an attribute.

units.la: Actio intellectus dicitur INTEL-LECTIO, quæ actio est, quatenus refertur ad mentem, quæ sua vi intelligit.
units.tr: The act of the intellect is called INTELLECTION, which is an action insofar as it is referred to the mind, which understands by its own power.

units.la: Passio vero dicitur respectu Speciei intelligibilis, quae ab ea recipitur. Receptio autem vulgo dicitur Passio.
units.tr: Passion, however, is spoken of with respect to the intelligible species that is received by it. Moreover, the reception is commonly called passion.

units.la: Intellectio est Recta, vel Reflexa.
units.tr: Intellection is either direct or reflexive.

units.la: RECTA est perceptio rerum per species intelligibiles.
units.tr: DIRECT intellection is the perception of things through intelligible species.

units.la: Hic itaque consideranda. 1. Species intelligibiles. 2. Res quarum species recipiuntur. 3. Ordo intellectionis.
units.tr: Here, therefore, three things are to be considered: 1. intelligible species; 2. the things whose species are received; 3. the order of intellection.

units.la: 1. Species intelligibilis est accidens spirituale, quod a phantasia intellectui transmissum rem materialem repraesentat.
units.tr: 1. An intelligible species is a spiritual accident which, transmitted from the phantasy to the intellect, represents a material thing.

units.la: 2. Res autem illae quae per species recipiuntur vel singulares sunt, vel universales. Itaq; intellectus tam singularia, quam universalia intelligit.
units.tr: 2. The things whose species are received are either singular or universal. Therefore the intellect understands singulars as well as universals.

units.la: 3. Ordo intellectionis directe intelligitur ex his requisitis. 1. Requiritur id, quod educit speciem e materia, ut lux ad visionem. 2. Species quae educitur. 3. Ipsa impressio speciei in intellectum. 4. Intellectus. His positis, res ipsa quoque, unde species sive notio evocatur, statuenda est, dicente Scaligero.
units.tr: 3. The order of direct intellection is understood from these requisites: 1. that which draws the species out of matter, as light does for vision; 2. the species that is drawn out; 3. the very impression of the species on the intellect; 4. the intellect. With these posited, the thing itself from which the species or notion is evoked must also be granted, as Scaliger says.

units.la: REFLEXA est intellectio sui & suarum actionum. Ergo intellectus noster non intelligit se per speciem, sed per reflexionem.
units.tr: REFLEXIVE intellection is the understanding of itself and its own acts. Therefore our intellect does not understand itself through a species, but through reflection.

units.la: Jam de distinctione: Etsi essentia intellectus est unus: tamen propter diversum modum intelligendi, & objecta diversa dicitur multiplex.
units.tr: Now concerning distinction: although the essence of the intellect is one, it is nonetheless called manifold on account of its different mode of understanding and its different objects.

units.la: Præcipuæ distinctiones sunt tres :
units.tr: The principal distinctions are three:

units.la: 1. Intellectus, quatenus species rerum intelligibilium efformat, atq; efficit, agens est: quatenus non in alio aliquo sed in seipso hanc speciem effectam recipit, patiens est. Ergo est agens vel patiens.
units.tr: 1. The intellect, insofar as it forms and brings about species of intelligible things, is an agent; insofar as it receives this species, once made, not in something else but in itself, it is a patient. Therefore it is either agent or patient.

units.la: 2. Intellectus simplex est vel compositus.
units.tr: 2. The intellect is either simple or composite.

units.la: SIMPLEX quando notiones rerum simplices tantum apprehendit & cognoscit.
units.tr: SIMPLE when it apprehends and knows only simple notions of things.

units.la: COMPOSITUS est notionum conjunctarum, quando res simplices animo componit & judicat.
units.tr: COMPOSITE is of conjoined notions, when the mind combines simple things and judges them.

units.la: Hæc vis mentis composita est Noëtica, vel Dianoëtica.
units.tr: This composite power of the mind is either noetic or dianoetic.

units.la: Noëtica est, cum sine discursu mens notiones duas disponit componendo vel dividendo. Dicitur alias operatio secunda intellectus naturalis, ordinis ratione. Necessario enim simplicium apprehensio præcedit compositas.
units.tr: Noetic is when the mind, without discursive reasoning, arranges two notions by combining or dividing them. It is otherwise called the second operation of the natural intellect, by reason of order. For the apprehension of simples necessarily precedes that of composites.

units.la: In his ita intellectus inest aut Veritas aut Falsitas.
units.tr: In these, truth or falsity is present in the intellect.

units.la: VERITAS est adæquatio notionum, quæ sunt in intellectu cum rebus.
units.tr: TRUTH is the correspondence of the notions that are in the intellect with things.

units.la: FALSITAS est in notionibus, quæ sunt in mente ideò, quod eæ rebus non sint adæquatæ.
units.tr: FALSITY is in the notions that are in the mind, because they do not correspond to things.

units.la: Dianoëtica est, cum mens unum ex alio deducendo & ab uno ad aliud transeundo plura noëmata disponit.
units.tr: Dianoetic is when the mind, by deducing one thing from another and passing from one to another, arranges several noemata.

units.la: Discurrit autem mens ratiocinando, & ordinando.
units.tr: The mind moves discursively by reasoning and ordering.

units.la: Ratiocinatio est mentis discursus, ex trium noematum discursu necessariam consequentiam inferens. Hac judicatur consequentia & inconsequentia.
units.tr: Reasoning is the discourse of the mind, inferring a necessary consequence from the discourse of three noemata. By it consequence and inconsequence are judged.

units.la: Ordinatio est discursus mentis, quo mens compositas è noematis sententias discurrens, eas sibi cognatas pro naturæ suæ luce & claritate collocat, & in ordinem redigit. Hac judicatur Ordo & Confusio.
units.tr: Ordering is the discourse of the mind by which the mind, running through the composite judgments of noemata, places those that are akin to one another according to the light and clarity of their nature, and brings them into order. By it order and confusion are judged.

units.la: III. Intellectus est Contemplativus, vel Practicus.
units.tr: III. The intellect is either contemplative or practical.

units.la: Intellectus contemplativus tantùm intelligit & ratiocinatur propter cognitionem, ut res vere cognoscat.
units.tr: The contemplative intellect only understands and reasons for the sake of knowledge, that it may know things truly.

units.la: Intellectus actiuus intelligit & ratiocinatur natur propter opus, ut agat & efficiat id quod bonum esse intelligit.
units.tr: The active intellect understands and reasons for the sake of work, that it may act and bring about what it understands to be good.

units.la: Intellectus practici est syllogismus pra-cticus, in quo propositio est universalis, ostendens, quid rectum sit, & quod sit judicium Dei: Assumtionem & conclusionem Conscientia, id est, intellectus applicans antegressam notitiam ad singulare πρακτὸν[?]. Ea movetur animus ad prosecutionem boni & detestationem mali.
units.tr: The practical intellect is a practical syllogism, in which the major premise is universal, showing what is right and what is the judgment of God; the minor premise and the conclusion belong to conscience, that is, the intellect applying prior knowledge to the particular practical thing [πρακτόν]. By this the mind is moved to pursue the good and to detest the evil.

units.la: Adjunctum intellectus est Notitia & Habitus.
units.tr: The attributes of the intellect are notion and habit.

units.la: Notitiæ sunt communes notiones animis hominum insitæ, quibus omnium artium principia continentur.
units.tr: Notions are common concepts implanted in the minds of men, in which the principles of all the arts are contained.

units.la: Habitus, qui intellectui adjungitur est Innatus, vel Acquisitus.
units.tr: The habit which is joined to the intellect is either innate or acquired.

units.la: Ad Innatum refertur Dictamen rationis, quæ dicitur semper hortari ad optima.
units.tr: To the innate belongs the dictate of reason, which is said always to urge toward what is best.

units.la: Ex hoc dictamine rationis exsistit Conscientia, de qua alibi.
units.tr: From this dictate of reason arises conscience, of which elsewhere.

units.la: Habitus acquisitus est Certus, vel Incertus.
units.tr: An acquired habit is either certain or uncertain.

units.la: Certus est primo propter necessitatem rei, quæ scitur ab animo scientis: unde SCIENTIA. Vel certus secunda-rio, rio, unde in singularibus Experientia; Ex experientia Inductio.
units.tr: A certain habit is primarily on account of the necessity of the thing known by the mind of the knower, whence SCIENCE. Or it is certain secondarily, whence in singulars there is experience; from experience, induction.

units.la: Incertus dicitur Opinio, quæ est assensus(Scaligero)nō necessario necessari»[?].
units.tr: An uncertain habit is called opinion, which is assent (according to Scaliger) not necessarily given to what is necessary.

units.la: CAPUT XXVIII. DE VOLUNTATE.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII. CONCERNING THE WILL.

units.la: VOLUNTAS est animæ rationalis altera primaria facultas, per quam id quod intelligimus sive cognoscimus, eligendum aut fugiendum judicamus.
units.tr: The will is the second primary faculty of the rational soul, by which we judge that what we understand or know is to be chosen or avoided.

units.la: Eligimus autem ea quæ tanquam bonum approbamus, unde voluntas boni cujusdam opinione ducta, quod bonum & utile videtur, eligit.
units.tr: We choose those things which we approve as good. Hence the will, led by an opinion of some good, chooses what seems good and useful.

units.la: Fugimus ea quæ tanquam malum improbamus, unde voluntas mali quadam specie mota, quod malum & inutile videtur, rejicit.
units.tr: We avoid those things which we disapprove as evil. Hence the will, moved by some appearance of evil, rejects what seems bad and harmful.

units.la: Voluntatis itaq; obiectum est vel bonum, quod prosequitur: vel malum, quod aversatur.
units.tr: The object of the will is therefore either the good, which it pursues, or the evil, which it shuns.

units.la: Bonum est vel revera bonum, vel φαινόμενον, id est, apparens bonum.
units.tr: The good is either really good, or φαινόμενον [phainomenon], that is, an apparent good.

units.la: Voluntati quæ alias dicitur naturalis appetitus, adjacet, tum Libertas, tum naturalis Inclinatio.
units.tr: Two things attach to the will, which is also called the natural appetite: liberty and natural inclination.

units.la: Libertas qua libere vult, quicquid vult. Cogi enim non potest.
units.tr: Liberty, by which it wills freely whatever it wills. For it cannot be compelled.

units.la: Inclinatio naturalis est, quae oritur ex temperamento hominis, & saepius voluntatem flectit vel rapit.
units.tr: Natural inclination arises from the temperament of a person, and often bends or carries the will along.

units.la: Voluntatis actiones sunt Velle, Nolle, Suspendere actionem vel assensum.
units.tr: The actions of the will are to will, to be unwilling, and to suspend action or assent.

units.la: Actiones hae voluntatis sunt Elicitae, vel Imperatae.
units.tr: These actions of the will are either elicited or commanded.

units.la: Elicitae sunt, quas voluntas elicit per se, non per alias potentias, suntque duplices; Primariae & Secundariae.
units.tr: Elicited actions are those which the will brings forth of itself, not through other powers. They are of two kinds: primary and secondary.

units.la: Primariae: cum voluntas serio eligit, hoc est, expetit, aut auersatur aliquid: ut cum Princeps ex animo vult statum Reipub. tranquillum esse. Cum Joseph serio aversatur adulterium.
units.tr: Primary: when the will earnestly chooses, that is, desires or shrinks from something, as when a prince sincerely wishes the state to be peaceful, or when Joseph earnestly abhors adultery.

units.la: Secundariae: cum quis fingit & simulat aliquod propositum in voluntate sua, id aliquando fide non bona & δίκης[?] causa agi dicitur.
units.tr: Secondary: when someone feigns and pretends a purpose in his will. This is sometimes said to be done in bad faith and for the sake of a lawsuit [δίκης].

units.la: Imperatae actiones sunt, quae jubet voluntas fieri per alias potentias, quae obedire possunt. Sic speculamur quando volumus, & voluptas imperat pedibus, ut corpus alio transmoveat; oculis, ut aperiant palpebras ad ὑπακοήν. Obedire possunt potentia locomovens, & appetitus sensitivus.
units.tr: Commanded actions are those which the will orders to be done through other powers that can obey. So we move when we will, and the will commands the feet to carry the body elsewhere, and the eyes to open the eyelids in obedience [ὑπακοή]. The powers that can obey are the locomotive power and the sensitive appetite.

units.la: In locomotrice voluntas habet imperium δεσποτικὸν[?], id est, herile, ut cogere eam possit pro arbitrio.
units.tr: Over the locomotive power the will has a despotic [δεσποτικόν] rule, that is, a lordly rule, so that it can compel it at its pleasure.

units.la: In appetente cum sensu conjuncta seu sensum comitante, etsi ea non possit nō appetere bonum sensu ostensum; lucta tamen deprehenditur.
units.tr: Over the appetite joined to sense, or accompanying it, the will cannot fail to desire a good that is shown to the senses; yet a struggle is nonetheless detected.

units.la: In ea interdum excutitur gubernatio voluntatis, &c.
units.tr: In this case the government of the will is sometimes thrown off, and so on.

units.la: Fertur equis auriga, nec audit currus habenas:
units.tr: The charioteer is carried off by his horses, and the chariot does not heed the reins.

units.la: Interdum admittitur, sed blande ad obtemperantiam invitando, & civiliter sine vi persuadendo: quae gubernatio πολι-τικὴ[?] dicitur.
units.tr: Sometimes the will is admitted, but it is won over gently, inviting obedience and persuading without force, in a civil manner. This governance is called political [πολιτικὴ].

units.la: Ex his intellige: appetitus sensitivum & intellectivum saepe esse contrarios, ut videre est in Incontinente. In eo plus valet ille quàm hic, quippe qui repugnet.
units.tr: From these things understand that the sensitive and the intellective appetites are often opposed, as may be seen in the incontinent man. In him the former prevails over the latter, since it resists.

units.la: In continente fit contra: Hic intellectivus dominatur per rationem sensitivo appetitui, ejusq; actiones impedit.
units.tr: In the continent man it happens the other way: here the intellective part rules the sensitive appetite through reason, and checks its actions.

units.la: In vegetatricem seu naturalem potentiam nihil prorsus juris & imperii habet voluntas; quia illa agit omnino naturaliter non ex arbitrio, aut hujus μετοχῆ[?] seu participatione. Nulla hic coactio, nulla persuasio. Quomodo accipiendum illud: Venter caret auribus.
units.tr: The will has absolutely no right or authority over the vegetative or natural power, because that power acts wholly by nature and not by choice, or by any participation [μετοχή] in it. Here there is no compulsion and no persuasion. Consider how that saying should be understood: The belly has no ears.

units.la: Actionibus voluntatis Elicitis & propriis nō potest vis inferri. Est enim contra rationem & naturam voluntatis, ut sit coacta. Fieri quidem potest, ut Lucretia violenter trahatur ad nefas, sed ut hoc fiat ex libero arbitrio, fieri non potest: quia implicaret contradictionem, neq; esset violenta tractio.
units.tr: Force cannot be applied to the elicited and proper actions of the will. For it is contrary to the reason and nature of the will that it should be compelled. It is indeed possible that Lucretia be dragged violently into wickedness, but that this happen by free choice is impossible, because it would imply a contradiction, and the dragging would not be violent.

units.la: Actionibus imperatis potest vis inferri, cum scilicet organa locomotricis, cui voluntas mandat, causa aliqua exteriore violenta impediuntur, ne fiat imperii voluntatis executio; ut cū quis vinctis pedibus non potest fugere. Hic nihilominus manet libera voluntas in appetendo, imo fit intensa; quod Desiderium dicitur.
units.tr: Force can be applied to commanded actions, namely when the organs of locomotion, which the will directs, are hindered by some external violent cause, so that the will's command cannot be carried out, as when someone with bound feet cannot flee. Here the will nonetheless remains free in its desiring; indeed it becomes more intense, and this is called longing.

units.la: Porro voluntas est plena seu integra, vel remissa seu fracta. Illius actiones sunt simpliciter voluntariae (non dico spontaneae: quia & bestiae quaedam sponte agunt:) Hujus vero mixtae vel mediae.
units.tr: Furthermore, the will is either whole and complete, or relaxed and broken. Its actions are either simply voluntary (I do not say spontaneous, since some beasts also act spontaneously), or mixed and intermediate.

units.la: Simpliciter voluntariae: cum voluntas plane libera est. Mixtæ seu mediæ sunt, in quibus voluntarium & invitum concurrunt.
units.tr: Simply voluntary actions are those in which the will is wholly free. Mixed or intermediate actions are those in which the voluntary and the unwilling come together.

units.la: Voluntarium quidem, quod in homine sit principiū volendi: Invitum vero quo homo vi majore, ut necessitate loci aut temporis, veluti constrictus sit.
units.tr: The voluntary is that which has its origin in the person's own willing; the unwilling is that to which a person is bound by a greater force, such as the necessity of place or time.

units.la: Hæ non fiunt sine lucta voluntatis magna, & in iis voluntas quasi cogi solet; ut cum in periculosa tempestate metu naufragii navigantes projiciunt merces in mare.
units.tr: These actions do not occur without a great struggle of the will, and in them the will is usually, as it were, compelled, as when sailors, in a dangerous storm and in fear of shipwreck, throw their cargo into the sea.

units.la: In arduis & gravibus voluntatis actionibus, hæc cerni potest gradatio.
units.tr: In difficult and weighty actions of the will, the following gradation can be discerned.

units.la: 1. Gradus: In mente γνώσις cognitio seu notitia rei, quam volumus suscipere.
units.tr: First stage: in the mind, γνῶσις [gnōsis], that is, knowledge or awareness of the thing we are willing to undertake.

units.la: 2. Voluntas βούλησις[?], quæ excitatur à cognitione. 3. βούλευσις[?], consultatio & deliberatio, quæ necessaria est, ne voluntas decipiatur falsa à specie boni. 4. γνώμη id est, sententia & decretum, quod ex deliberatione proficiscitur. Estq; velut conclusio consultationis. 5. Προαίρεσις id est, electio rei deliberatæ & conclusæ: Ut autem γνώμη rationis est seu judicii: ita προαίρεσις voluntatis. 6. Ipsa πρᾶξις[?] seu actio, omnium præcedentium finis, cui solet inservire θυμὸς vis animosa, ὁρμὴ & locomotrix facultas. 7. πρᾶξιν[?] tandem sequitur præmium, pœna, lætitia, pœnitudo, felicitas, infelicitas.
units.tr: Second, the will, βούλησις [boulēsis], which is aroused by knowledge. Third, βούλευσις [bouleusis], consultation and deliberation, which is necessary so that the will is not deceived by a false appearance of good. Fourth, γνώμη [gnōmē], that is, judgement and decision, which proceeds from deliberation and is like the conclusion of the consultation. Fifth, προαίρεσις [proairesis], that is, the choice of the deliberated and concluded matter: just as γνώμη belongs to reason or judgement, so προαίρεσις belongs to the will. Sixth, πρᾶξις [praxis] itself, or the action, the end of all that precedes, which is served by θυμός [thymos], the spirited force, and ὁρμή [hormē], the locomotive faculty. Seventh, after πρᾶξις there finally follows the reward or punishment: joy, regret, happiness, unhappiness.

units.la: CAPUT XXIX. DE FACULTATE LOQUENDI ET RIDENDI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX. CONCERNING THE FACULTY OF SPEAKING AND LAUGHING.

units.la: Secundaria facultas animæ rationalis superest, quæ primariam insequitur; Estque materialis, multis corporeis organis alligata & utens: Potentia scilicet loquendi, unde homo dicitur animal loquens; & potentia ridendi, unde homo dicitur animal γελα-στικόν[?], quod ridere potest.
units.tr: A secondary faculty of the rational soul remains, which follows the primary one; it is material, bound to and making use of many bodily organs: namely, the power of speech, whence man is called a speaking animal, and the power of laughter, whence man is called an animal capable of laughing (γελαστικόν), that is, able to laugh.

units.la: Potentia loquendi seu Sermocinatrix vis, qua sermo seu oratio efformatur.
units.tr: The power of speaking, or the faculty that forms speech, by which discourse or oration is shaped.

units.la: Sermo a ratione fluit, estque rationis Minister & Effectus, seu animi interpres, qui sensa mentis imperatu voluntatis foris voce profert, & significanter enunciat.
units.tr: Speech flows from reason; it is the minister and effect of reason, or the interpreter of the mind, which, at the command of the will, utters outwardly with the voice the thoughts of the mind and declares them meaningfully.

units.la: Hæc constat vocum efformatione, & formatarum vocum articulata distin-ctione.
units.tr: This consists in the forming of voices and in the articulated distinction of the formed voices.

units.la: Vocum humanarum efformatio est, qua voces, rerum significandarum symbola, destinatis ad id instrumentis efformantur.
units.tr: The formation of human voices is that by which voices, the symbols of the things to be signified, are shaped by the instruments made for this purpose.

units.la: Hic primum agens est aër spiratione attractus.
units.tr: The first agent here is the air, drawn in by breathing.

units.la: 2. Pulmo, qui thorace compressus aërem expellit.
units.tr: (2) The lung, which, compressed by the chest, expels the air.

units.la: 3. Trachea vehens aërem, & in ea præcipuè rimula.
units.tr: (3) The windpipe, conveying the air, and especially in it the little slit (the glottis).

units.la: Fit autem allusio ad trachęam, quæ cum sit annulis distincta, fit vocis modulatio. In cæteris verò editur in Unisono. Fit item propulsio aëris per rimulam ubi vox fit acuta vel gravis pro diversitate expulsionis.
units.tr: Now there is an adjustment toward the windpipe, which, being divided by rings, produces modulation of the voice; in the others, it is produced in unison. Likewise there is a propulsion of air through the slit, where the voice becomes high or low according to the variation of the expulsion.

units.la: Deniq; fit in ore dispositio, (lingua enim motu suo aërem variè disponit intra oris cavitatem) ac ibi fiunt consonantes, ex quibus deinde syllabæ, distinctiones, orationes.
units.tr: Finally, there is an arrangement in the mouth (for the tongue, by its motion, variously disposes the air within the cavity of the mouth), and there the consonants are formed, from which then come syllables, distinctions, and sentences.

units.la: Articulata igitur vocum distinctio est, qua voces efformatæ ad animi sensa juxta mentis conceptum & voluntatis imperium distinctè coaptantur.
units.tr: The articulated distinction of voices is therefore that by which the formed voices are distinctly fitted to the thoughts of the mind, in accordance with the concept of the intellect and the command of the will.

units.la: Ridendi facultas est, quâ cietur risus, quâq; ipsi ad ridendum apti sumus.
units.tr: The faculty of laughing is that by which laughter is stirred up, and by which we are fitted to laugh.

units.la: Risus est motus ab anima ratio-nali cum sentiente conjuncta ortus, ideo-que que homini proprius, objecto risibili per organa certa corporis motus ac manifestatus.
units.tr: Laughter is a motion arising from the rational soul joined with the sentient soul, and therefore proper to man, produced and made manifest through certain organs of the body by a laughable object.

units.la: Risibile est quod movet risum.
units.tr: That which moves laughter is laughable.

units.la: Primum corporale principium & organum risus alii putarunt esse Lienem: Alii Diaphragma, quod est musculus latus, sensu & spiritu affatim abundans: Alii vero ipsum Cor. Cum enim homines profusius rident, laetantur & gestiunt, dicunt se ex corde ridere, &c. Hinc autem defectus & syncope fiunt iis, qui plus aequo rident, evacuato scilicet nimium ex corde spiritu. Alii deniq; Cerebrum faciunt primum principium, sed ita ut potissimum in corde vigeat, quod sensus ejus partis sit vegetior, & conjunctus parti animosae ac vitali, cum multo calore & spiritu.
units.tr: Some have thought the first bodily principle and organ of laughter to be the spleen; others the diaphragm, which is a broad muscle, abundantly full of sense and spirit; others indeed the heart itself. For when men laugh very freely, rejoice and exult, they say that they laugh from the heart, and so on. Hence faintings and swoonings come upon those who laugh more than is proper, the spirit being emptied too much from the heart. Others finally make the brain the first principle, but in such a way that it flourishes chiefly in the heart, since the sense of that part is more vigorous and is joined to the animal and vital part, with much heat and spirit.

units.la: Generatio Risus Aristoteli est, quaedam velox emissio spiritus, similis sternutationi, cum propter laetitiam redundet, corde nimirum & praecordiis una gestientibus. Laetitia enim gestiens concalefactio quaedam est, idque vel minuta agitatione spiritus in se ipso facta: vel totius primi sensitivi una cum spiritu & calore proprio, suspensa praesertim respiratione, ut subinde utraque ratione ac[?]cesio fiat ad calorem, conclusio spiritus, & propensio ad motum. Ex eo deinceps calore solvitur humor in vaporem, qui cum redundet excernitur affatim. Itaque videtur Aristoteles æstimare, hanc spiritus ubertatem fieri propter vim caloris ob intrinsecam voluptatem hilaremq; affectum concepti: Cum vero spiritum hunc conentur emittere, non esse aliam viam præter motu spirationis, ideoque septum statim contrahitur, & pulmones succussantur, recipientes eandem rationis speciem à diaphragmate. Hinc fit retractio musculorum, qui movent buccas, &c.
units.tr: For Aristotle, the generation of laughter is a certain swift emission of spirit, similar to sneezing, when it overflows on account of joy, the heart and the precordia rejoicing together. For joyful exultation is a certain warming, and this either by a slight agitation of the spirit within itself, or of the whole primary sensitive part together with the spirit and its own heat, the breathing being especially held in suspension, so that in either way there is subsequently a kindling of heat, a constriction of the spirit, and an inclination to motion. From that heat the moisture is then dissolved into vapour, which, when it overflows, is discharged abundantly. Thus Aristotle seems to judge that this abundance of spirit arises from the force of heat, on account of the intrinsic pleasure and cheerful affection conceived; but when they try to send this spirit out, there is no other way except by a motion of breathing, and therefore the diaphragm at once contracts and the lungs are shaken, receiving the same kind of impulse from the diaphragm. Hence comes the drawing back of the muscles which move the cheeks, and so on.

units.la: Sequuntur facultates communes homini cum brutis, quarum excellentior & eminentior ratio est in hominis viribus. Harum alia est Vitalis & vegetans, eaque Princeps & Ministra. Illa procreatrix & conservatrix vitæ: Procreatrix, Generatrix, & Progeneratrix. Conservatrix, Nutrix, ac Auctrix. Ministra Attractrix, Retentrix, Alteratrix, Expultrix. Alia vero est animalis, eaque est Apprehensiva per sensus, vel Motiva, de quibus alibi generalius: huc verò[?] speciatim hominis animae applicari solent.
units.tr: There follow the faculties common to man with the brutes, of which the more excellent and eminent reason lies in the powers of man. Of these, one is vital and vegetative, and this is the chief and the minister. That one is the procreator and conservator of life: procreative, generative, and progenerative; conservative, nutritive, and augmentative. As minister: attractive, retentive, alterative, and expulsive. The other is animal, and it is apprehensive through the senses, or motive, concerning which more generally elsewhere; but these are usually applied specifically to the soul of man.

units.la: Caput XXX. DE SPIRITU, CALORE ET HUMIDO INNATO.
units.tr: Chapter 30. ON THE SPIRIT, HEAT AND INNATE MOISTURE.

units.la: [?]actenus prior pars Anthropologiae scilicet Psychologia: Sequitur SOMATOTOMIA, humani corporis naturam & fabricam membratim explicans.
units.tr: So far we have treated the first part of Anthropology, namely Psychology. Next comes SOMATOTOMY, which explains the nature and structure of the human body, member by member.

units.la: CORPUS HUMANUM, est pars hominis essentialis, corporeum nempe, ac erectum, animae humanae ipsum animantis domicilium & organum, variis membris sui usum ad edendas actiones animae praebentibus constans.
units.tr: The HUMAN BODY is the essential part of the human being, namely the corporeal and upright part, the dwelling place and instrument of the human soul, consisting of various members that provide it with the means of carrying out the soul's actions.

units.la: Distinguitur igitur corpus humanum Membris & distinctis animae organis.
units.tr: The human body is therefore distinguished into members and distinct organs of the soul.

units.la: Organum autem & membrum humani corporis est Primarium aut Secundarium.
units.tr: An organ and member of the human body is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Primarium animae organum, quo anima immediatè & primariò ad functiones suas expediendas utitur in corpore.
units.tr: The primary organ of the soul is that which the soul uses directly and primarily in the body to carry out its functions.

units.la: Dici etiam potest universale, quia universaliter in universo corpore animae functionibus suam navat operam.
units.tr: It can also be called universal, because it works universally throughout the whole body for the soul's functions.

units.la: Tale organum est spiritus corporis: Spiritus dicitur, quia subtili & aerea tenuitate, qua etiam Visus aciem effugit, quodammodo ad spirituum naturam accedit: Est autem corporeus; quia e materia corporea & quidem non nisi in corpore fit.
units.tr: Such an organ is the spirit of the body. It is called spirit because, by its subtle and airy thinness, which escapes even the sight, it in some way approaches the nature of spirits. It is, however, corporeal, because it is made of corporeal matter and indeed only exists in a body.

units.la: Spiritus autem hic corporis est substantia pertenuis subtilitatis, aerea ac vaporosa, e sanguinis vapore & aeris permistione genita, universale facultatis vitalis & animalis organum, unionisq; animae & corporis vinculum.
units.tr: This spirit of the body is a substance of very fine subtlety, airy and vaporous, produced from the vapour of the blood mixed with air, the universal organ of the vital and animal faculty, and the bond of union between soul and body.

units.la: Hic spiritus in toto corpore substantia idem; Evariis functionibus & variarum partium subjectarum, in quibus nonnihil temperari videtur, natura, diversa nomina ac ingenia sortitur.
units.tr: This spirit is the same substance throughout the whole body, but it takes on different names and qualities according to its various functions and the nature of the different parts in which it is found and in which it is somewhat tempered.

units.la: In omnium membrorum corporeorum universitate ex primis naturae principiis (femine & sanguine) in singulis membris relictus & continuatus, dicisolet Insitus & Complantatus.
units.tr: When it is left and continued in each of the members, from the first principles of nature (seed and blood) throughout the whole body of the members, it is called innate and implanted.

units.la: Qui vero continuo quotidie, propter continuam dissipationem in corpore generatus membris affluit & accedit, insitum & primigenium reparans, confervans, & augens; Influens spiritus nuncupatur.
units.tr: But the spirit which is generated continually every day, because of the constant dissipation in the body, flows to and reaches the members, restoring, preserving and increasing the innate and original spirit. It is called the influent spirit.

units.la: Influentis hujus materia adhuc in Epate rudior, nimirum sanguinis ibi elaborati vapor tenuis & calidus; quibusdam Naturalis Spiritus dicitur.
units.tr: The matter of this influent spirit is still cruder in the liver, namely the thin and warm vapour of the blood worked up there. Some call it the natural spirit.

units.la: In corde vero copia illa halituu[?] sub-tilium & flammulae instar accensorum e sanguine magis extenuato &probe concocto, cum admixto & contemperato aere per inspirationem aucto, virtute sinistri thalami elaborata & inde per arterias in totum corpus diffusa, recte Vitalis dicitur Spiritus.
units.tr: In the heart, however, that abundance of subtle breaths, kindled like little flames, is produced from blood that is more attenuated and well concocted, with air drawn in by inspiration mixed and tempered in, through the power of the left ventricle; from there it is diffused through the arteries into the whole body, and it is rightly called the vital spirit.

units.la: Ex corde vero per cervicis arterias sursum ad cerebrum latus in plexum re-tiformem: vel, ut alii, in ventriculos cerebri, ibiq; vel motu cerebri (secundum quosdam) vel vi proprietateq; spiritus cerebro ingeniti (secundum alios) cum aere per nares attracto contemperatus mixtione, dici solet Animalis.
units.tr: From the heart, through the arteries of the neck, it rises to the brain, into the reticular plexus, or, as others say, into the ventricles of the brain. There, tempered with air drawn in through the nostrils, it is called the animal spirit, either by the motion of the brain (according to some) or by the power and property of the spirit implanted in the brain (according to others).

units.la: Vitalis etiam hic per arterias in testes infertas in genituram deportatus, vi testiculorum cum humore albo permixtus, & semen fæcundans, Spermaticus seu Seminalis dici posset.
units.tr: The vital spirit, too, is carried through the arteries inserted into the testicles to the seed, where by the power of the testicles it is mixed with the white fluid and makes the semen fruitful; it could be called spermatic or seminal.

units.la: Spiritus hic universus subjectum & vehiculum est caloris innati.
units.tr: This whole spirit is the subject and vehicle of innate heat.

units.la: Calor autem hic Spiritui inhærens est, qui Corpori humano per subjectum Spiritum salutariter inest.
units.tr: This heat, which inheres in the spirit, is what dwells in the human body healthfully through the spirit as its subject.

units.la: Est autem hic calor vel insitus, vel influens.
units.tr: This heat is either innate or influent.

units.la: Insitus est, qui toti corpori singulisque ejus partibus ab ipso ortu inest. Eum fixum etiam & primigenium vocant.
units.tr: Innate heat is that which is present in the whole body and in each of its parts from birth. They also call it fixed and original.

units.la: Influens est, qui e corde (caloris & spiritus quasi officina) insiti illius conservandi gratia in ceteras partes per arterias, tanquam canales, diffunditur.
units.tr: Influent heat is that which flows out from the heart (as it were the workshop of heat and spirit) through the arteries, as through channels, into the other parts, for the sake of preserving that innate heat.

units.la: Caloris hujus innati nativum pabulum, quo fruitur, est humidū nativum, ac humor benignus.
units.tr: The natural food of this innate heat, on which it feeds, is the natural moisture and the benign humour.

units.la: Humidum nativum est vel Insitum, vel Adventitium.
units.tr: Natural moisture is either innate or adventitious.

units.la: Insitum, à semine & sanguine menstruo ortum, corpori ab ipsa conformatione inest. Solet dici radicale & primigenium.
units.tr: Innate moisture, arising from seed and menstrual blood, is present in the body from its very formation. It is usually called radical and original.

units.la: Adventitium insiti reparandi gratia ab alimentorum utiliore parte proficiscitur.
units.tr: Adventitious moisture comes from the more useful part of the food, for the sake of restoring the innate moisture.

units.la: Radicale humidum ab infantia maximum est, minus ætate consistente, minimum in senectute: in causa est caloris innati absumtio; quæ quò longius progreditur, eò plus humidi depascitur.
units.tr: Radical moisture is greatest in infancy, less in mature age, and least in old age. The cause is the consumption of innate heat; the further this proceeds, the more of the radical moisture is devoured.

units.la: Ut autem ab ipsa nativitate humidum radicale ad obitum usque decrescit; ita contra adventitium initio crescit, deinde consistit, postea unà cum radicali paulatim deficit.
units.tr: Just as radical moisture decreases from birth until death, so on the contrary adventitious moisture at first increases, then stays at a certain level, and afterwards gradually fails along with the radical moisture.

units.la: CAPVT XXXI. DE PARTIBUS ET CONIVNCTIONE OSSIVM.
units.tr: CAPUT XXXI. ON THE PARTS AND JOINING OF THE BONES.

units.la: Secundarium membrum est organum, quo anima mediatè & secundarió ad distinctas actiones utitur. Estq; sustentans vel sustentatum.
units.tr: The secondary member is an organ by which the soul, mediately and secondarily, uses for its distinct actions. It is either supporting or supported.

units.la: Sustentans est membrum reliquas corporis partes suo robore sustinens vel muniens.
units.tr: A supporting member is one that sustains or protects the other parts of the body by its strength.

units.la: Sustentatio hæc est cum fulcimenti & stabilimenti, tum munimenti & firmamenti.
units.tr: This support consists both of propping and stabilising, and of defending and strengthening.

units.la: Proinde anima hoc membro utitur ad corpus, ejus reliqua membra tam munienda & firmanda, ut tuta & firma sint, quam stabilienda & fulcienda, ut sic sustentata consistant.
units.tr: Accordingly, the soul uses this member for the body, so that its other members may be both protected and strengthened, to be safe and firm, and both steadied and propped, so that thus supported they may stand.

units.la: Membrum sustentans est primi generis, vel secundi.
units.tr: A supporting member is of the first kind or of the second.

units.la: Primi generis sustinens membrum est Os[?].
units.tr: A member that supports, of the first kind, is the bone.

units.la: Os est membrum sustinens durissimum & siccissimum. In ossibus spectantur Partes, & Conjunctio.
units.tr: The bone is the member that supports, being very hard and very dry. In bones two things are considered: their parts and their joining.

units.la: Pars Ossis adnata ossi ἀπόφυσις[?] ac appendix dicitur.
units.tr: A part of a bone that grows onto the bone is called the apophysis [ἀπόφυσις] or appendix.
