units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVI. CONCERNING HUMAN SEED AND MENSTRUAL BLOOD, the principles of generation.

units.la: Actenus de involventibus membris: sequuntur involuta, quæ ab involventibus contegu ntur. funtq; organa animæ facultatibus præ-cipuum fui usum præbentia.
units.tr: So far concerning the enveloping parts; there follow the enveloped parts, which are covered by the enveloping ones, and which furnish the principal use of the faculties of the soul.

units.la: Involuta igitur sunt organa vel vitalia, vel animalia.
units.tr: The enveloped parts, therefore, are either vital or animal.

units.la: Vitalia membra sunt organa per quæ humanæ vitæ actiones eduntur.
units.tr: Vital parts are the organs through which the actions of human life are carried out.

units.la: Inserviunt itaq; exercendis animæ vegetantis facultatibus.
units.tr: Accordingly they serve to exercise the faculties of the vegetative soul.

units.la: Vitalia membra sunt organa famulantia facultati vel procreatrici, vel conservatrici.
units.tr: Vital parts are organs serving either the procreative or the conservative faculty.

units.la: Procreatricis facultatis membra vitalia sunt organa, hominis generationi & propagationi inservientia.
units.tr: The vital parts of the procreative faculty are the organs serving the generation and propagation of man.

units.la: Generationis materia est SEMEN & Sanguis menstruus.
units.tr: The matter of generation is seed and menstrual blood.

units.la: SEMEN HUMANUM est humor albicans é sanguine purissimo, præcipuè vero portione alimenti ejus, quod assimilatur membris spermaticis commix-tus, & perfectius elaboratus, humanæ generationis princeps principium.
units.tr: HUMAN SEED is a whitish humour from the purest blood, especially from the finer portion of its nourishment, which is assimilated to the seminal parts, mixed with them and more perfectly worked up; it is the chief first principle of human generation.

units.la: SÉMEN porro est masculum, vel fœmineum.
units.tr: Seed, moreover, is either male or female.

units.la: Masculum est marium semen, albius, calore magis excoctum, potentius & ef-ficacius.
units.tr: Male seed is that of males, whiter, more thoroughly cooked by heat, more powerful and more effective.

units.la: Fœmineum est fœminarum femena-[?]quofius, minus quidé ob humidam fri-giditatem excoctum & impotentius.
units.tr: Female seed is that of females, less cooked indeed, because of its moist coldness, and weaker.

units.la: Utriusq; feminis pars quaedam spiritu-osa, quaedam vero corpulenta.
units.tr: Each kind of seed has a part that is spirituous and a part that is corporeal.

units.la: Spirituosa pars feminis est spiritus com-plantatus multus, in vasis spermaticis probius elaboratus, per lentum & visci-dum feminis corpus diffusus, in quo praecipue vis activa & facultas generationis viva residet.
units.tr: The spirituous part of the seed is a copious, finely compounded spirit, worked up more thoroughly in the seminal vessels, diffused through the slow and viscous body of the seed, in which the active power and the living faculty of generation chiefly reside.

units.la: Corpulenta est pars feminis crassior, materiam & principium seminale pas-sivum generatrici facultati exhibens, & se formationi subjiciens.
units.tr: The corporeal part is the thicker portion of the seed, which supplies the material and passive seminal principle to the generative faculty and submits itself to formation.

units.la: Estque interna, vel superficiaria.
units.tr: It is either internal or superficial.

units.la: Interna pars corpulenta membris foetus spermaticis materiam largitur.
units.tr: The internal corporeal part supplies material to the seminal parts of the foetus.

units.la: Superficiaria vero ex se producit foetus involucra.
units.tr: The superficial part, on the other hand, produces from itself the coverings of the foetus.

units.la: Involucra foetus alia totum foetum, alia partem ejus involvunt.
units.tr: The coverings of the foetus enclose, some the whole foetus, others a part of it.

units.la: Totum involvunt Amnios & Allanto-eides[?].
units.tr: Those enclosing the whole are the amnion and the allantoides.

units.la: Amnios est involucrum foetus, imme-diate universum foetum involvens, sudorem à fœtu emanantem, in quo innatat, continens.
units.tr: The amnion is the covering of the foetus, immediately enclosing the whole foetus and containing the sweat emanating from the foetus, in which it floats.

units.la: Allantoides intermedium est involucrum, totum fœtum ambiens mediatè, inter quod & amnion reservatur urina infantis.
units.tr: The allantoides is an intermediate covering, surrounding the whole foetus mediately, between which and the amnion the urine of the infant is kept.

units.la: Partem fœtus involvens dicitur Secun-dina; quæ est involucrum insigniter cras-sum & nigricans, extimum, orbicularis placentæ modo, fœtum complectens.
units.tr: The covering enclosing a part of the foetus is called the secundina, which is a notably thick and blackish covering, outermost, shaped like a round cake, enfolding the foetus.

units.la: Hæc de femine principali principio generationis; Hujus partis activæ & potentiori tanquam opifici Sanguis menstruus in generatione substernitur, qui primum semini appositus materiam exhibet formandis partibus sanguineis; deinde vero detentus fœtum formatum auget & nutrit.
units.tr: So much concerning the seed, the principal first principle of generation. To this active and more powerful part, as to the craftsman, menstrual blood is placed beneath in generation; it first, applied to the seed, supplies material for forming the blood-related parts; then, retained, it increases and nourishes the foetus once formed.

units.la: Est autem Sanguis menstruus in mulie-ribus ob frigidius, humidius & imbecil-lius temperamentum, copiosius & non satis excoctus & confectus sanguis, tam diu vasis suis retentus, donec natura vel eo quasi onusta statis temporibus in ejus expulsionem incumbit, vel eum, si ad generationem & nutritionem fœtus opus est, adsciscit.
units.tr: Menstrual blood, moreover, in women, owing to their colder, moister and weaker constitution, is blood that is more abundant and not sufficiently cooked and perfected; it is retained in its vessels for so long until nature, as though burdened by it, at set times sets about expelling it, or takes it up, if it is needed for the generation and nourishment of the foetus.

units.la: CAPUT XXXVII: DE COMMUNIBUS [?]&E-nerationis membris.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII: ON THE PARTS COMMON TO GENERATION

units.la: Materia generationis sic fuit in semi-ne, & sanguine menstruo: Membra generationis sunt vel communia, vel propria.
units.tr: The matter of generation is in the seed and in the menstrual blood. The members of generation are either common or proper.

units.la: Communia sunt utriusq; sexus.
units.tr: The common members belong to both sexes.

units.la: Suntq; vel praeparantia, vel conser-vantia semen.
units.tr: They are either those that prepare the seed or those that preserve it.

units.la: Praeparantia sunt, quae semini materiam ex sanguinis seu ultimi alimenti portione & spiritu praeparant & elabo-rant.
units.tr: The preparing members are those which prepare and work up the matter of the seed from a portion of the blood, or of the final nourishment, together with spirit.

units.la: Sunt autem vel longa, vel rotunda seu oblonga.
units.tr: They are either long or round, or oblong.

units.la: Longa sunt canales longi, partim a vena Cava, partim ab Aorta ad testes descendentes, paululum supra eos con-juncti & implicati.
units.tr: The long members are long channels, descending to the testicles partly from the vena cava and partly from the aorta, joined and intertwined a little above them.

units.la: Suntque cùm venæ, tùm arteriæ se-minales.
units.tr: And these are both the seminal veins and the seminal arteries.

units.la: Venæ seminales sanguinem praeparant seu portionem ultimi alimenti semini cognatam excipiunt & deferunt. Sunt-que duae: Dextra à vena cavâ sub emul-gente gente pullulat ; Sinistra ab ipsa emulgente deducitur.
units.tr: The seminal veins prepare the blood, or receive and carry the portion of final nourishment akin to the seed. There are two: the right arises from the vena cava below the emulgent vein; the left is drawn from the emulgent vein itself.

units.la: Arteriæ feminales spiritum & calorem, quo sanguinis portio seminalis perfunditur, animatur, & fœcunda redditur, præparant ac deferunt.
units.tr: The seminal arteries prepare and convey the spirit and heat by which the seminal portion of the blood is infused, quickened and made fruitful.

units.la: Hæc vasa primùm aliquantulùm distant; postmodùm ita per Anastomosin implicantur, ut vena arteriam, & arteria venam ingrediatur.
units.tr: These vessels at first lie somewhat apart; afterwards they are so intertwined by anastomosis that the vein enters the artery and the artery the vein.

units.la: Rotunda seu oblonga vasa sunt Testes.
units.tr: The round or oblong vessels are the testicles.

units.la: Sunt autem Testes vasa cavernosa, laxa, femini conficiendo (vel à vasis spermaticis serosum excrementum suscipiendo, secundum alios:) destinata.
units.tr: The testicles are cavernous, loose vessels, destined for the making of the seed (or, according to others, for receiving the watery excrement from the spermatic vessels).

units.la: Testes sunt cum marium, tum fœminarum.
units.tr: There are testicles both in males and in females.

units.la: Testes marium sub ventre foràs abducti penduli prominent, majores & validiores.
units.tr: The testicles of males hang outside, drawn down beneath the belly, larger and stronger.

units.la: Testes fœminarum sunt intus inclusi ad uteri cornua, minores, frigidiores & molliores.
units.tr: The testicles of females are enclosed within, beside the horns of the womb, smaller, colder and softer.

units.la: Sunt autem in utroq; sexu ordinarie gemini, dexter & sinister : videturque dexter sinistro varicosior, fortior & calidior.
units.tr: In each sex there are ordinarily two, a right and a left; the right seems more varicose, stronger and warmer than the left.

units.la: Tunica ac involucrum quo masculi testes involuntur, dicitur Scrotum.
units.tr: The membrane and covering in which the male testicles are wrapped is called the scrotum.

units.la: Vasa conservantia semen sunt, quae semen virtute vasorum praeparantium elaboratum retinent, & in tempus ejaculationis conservant.
units.tr: The members that preserve the seed are those which, by the power of the preparing vessels, keep the worked-up seed and hold it until the time of ejaculation.

units.la: Dicuntur in maribus PARASTATÆ; qui sunt canales glandulosi, utrinq; à testibus ad virgam ascendentes.
units.tr: In males these are called the parastatae: glandular channels rising on each side from the testicles to the penis.

units.la: CAPUT XXXVIII: DE PROPRIIS MARIS ET Fœminæ genitalibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII: ON THE PROPER GENITALS OF THE MALE AND FEMALE.

units.la: Adhuc fuerunt communia utriq; sexui membra. Unicuiq; propria generationis vasa sunt membra genitalia, quae alteri duntaxat sexui proprie conveniunt.
units.tr: The parts still common to both sexes have been treated. The genital organs, the proper vessels of generation for each sex, are those members which belong properly to one sex alone.

units.la: Suntq; vel maris, vel fœminæ.
units.tr: These are either of the male or of the female.

units.la: Proprium maris genitale est VIRGA sive PENIS, nempe pudendum virile nervosum & arteriosum, prælongum in medio continens canalem, ejaculando feminis & reddendæ urinæ inservientem.
units.tr: The proper genital of the male is the PENIS or VIRGA, namely the sinewy and arterial male member, very long, containing in its middle a channel that serves for ejaculating seed into the female and for passing urine.

units.la: In regione enim ossis sacri utrinque ex ramis venæ & arteriæ magnæ oriuntur propagines plurimæ, quarum arteriales excedunt venosas: his nervi ex osse sacro prosilientes copulantur, & simul ad anteriora progredientes, degenerant in quasdam corpora spongiformia. & ubi ad latera corporis glandulosi & cervicis vesicæ aliquantisper progressa fuerint, gradatim ampliora redduntur, simulq; conjuncta membrum virile efformant, quod toti medio ossis pubis inhærendo, tandem extra corpus aperte propendet.
units.tr: For in the region of the sacrum, on each side, many offshoots arise from the branches of the great vein and artery; of these the arterial exceed the venous. Nerves springing from the sacrum join them, and proceeding together forward, they turn into certain spongy bodies. When they have advanced to the sides of the glandular body and the neck of the bladder, they gradually become larger and, joined together, form the male member, which, adhering along the whole middle of the pubic bone, finally hangs openly outside the body.

units.la: In pene considerantur, præter musculos motus, etiam organa, tunicæ, glans, præputium & fræœnum.
units.tr: In the penis are considered, besides the muscles that move it, also the parts: the coats, the glans, the foreskin and the frenulum.

units.la: Tunicæ sunt nervosæ, membranosæ, densæ & robustæ, obducentes spongiformem penis substantiam, ne spiritus influens per porositates spongiformes exhalet.
units.tr: The coats are sinewy, membranous, dense and strong, covering the spongy substance of the penis, so that the spirit flowing in does not escape through its spongy pores.

units.la: Glans est extrema pars penis glandulosa seu carnosa, excedens ambitu reliquum penis corpus, ut pro ratione magnitudinis suæ, veluti cucurbitulæ fundus, magis spiritibus inflatus incalesce-ret.
units.tr: The glans is the glandular or fleshy extremity of the penis, exceeding in girth the rest of the body of the penis, so that, in proportion to its size, like the base of a cupping-glass, it may grow hot when more inflated with spirits.

units.la: Præputium est pellis integens glandem, quæ in actu venereo arctiore motu & attritu glandem plurimum calefacit.
units.tr: The foreskin is the skin covering the glans, which, in the venereal act, by a closer movement and friction, greatly warms the glans.

units.la: Frænum est membrana quædam in extremo glandis sub ipso ultimo orificio præputium ibi alligans, cujus interventu non potest ita retrocedere, ut in aliis partibus.
units.tr: The frenulum is a certain membrane at the end of the glans, under the very last opening, binding the foreskin there; by its intervention it cannot retract in the way it does in other parts.

units.la: Proprium mulierum genitale est UTERUS, qui est membrum generationis fœmine-um, membraneum, densum, piro majusculo excavato in fundo simile, in coxarum capacitate inter vesicá & rectum intestinum collocatum, materiæ generationis suscipiendæ, & fœtui formando gestandoq; destinatum.
units.tr: The proper genital of women is the UTERUS, which is the female organ of generation, membranous and dense, somewhat like a pear of moderate size hollowed out at the base, placed in the cavity of the hips between the bladder and the rectum, destined for receiving the matter of generation and for forming and carrying the foetus.

units.la: Matricis seu uteri partes sunt collum, seu Cervix, & Hystera seu fundus.
units.tr: The parts of the womb, or uterus, are the neck, or cervix, and the hystera, or fundus.

units.la: Cervix uteri est pars ejus longiuscula, multis rugosis cuticulis implicata, aditum ad fundum præbens, forasq; in partes obscœnas desinens.
units.tr: The cervix of the uterus is its somewhat longer part, wrapped in many wrinkled membranes, offering access to the fundus, and ending outwardly in the private parts.

units.la: Cervici adhæret Nympha, & ut quidam volunt Hymen.
units.tr: To the cervix is attached the nympha and, as some wish, the hymen.

units.la: Nympha (Latini colliculos & alas vocant) est caruncula orificio cervicis, virilis pudendi præputio similis, adnata.
units.tr: The nympha (the Latins call them little hillocks and wings) is a small fleshy outgrowth, grown on at the opening of the cervix, similar to the foreskin of the male private parts.

units.la: Hymen est (ut ajunt) membrana venulis perspersa, cervicis mediù in virginibus transversum dirimens, à cujus ruptione in primo congressu magnam sanguinis profusionem manare volunt.
units.tr: The hymen is (as they say) a membrane sprinkled with small veins, stretched across the middle of the cervix in virgins, from whose rupture at the first intercourse they claim a great flow of blood issues.

units.la: Hystera seu fundus uteri est pars ejus supra cervicè, membranosum receptaculum, & humanæ formationis officina, involvendo fœtui accommodata.
units.tr: The hystera, or fundus of the uterus, is the part of it above the cervix, a membranous receptacle and workshop of human formation, fitted to enclose the foetus.

units.la: Superficies fundi uterini est cum Exterior, tum Interior.
units.tr: The surface of the fundus of the uterus has both an exterior and an interior.

units.la: Exterior est vitulinæ fronti, cornua jam producenti, non absimilis, duos obtusos angulos instar cornuum, in qua vasa semen deferentia inseruntur, prose-rens.
units.tr: The exterior is not unlike the forehead of a calf that is now beginning to produce horns, projecting two blunt angles like horns, into which the vessels that carry the seed are inserted.

units.la: Interior est aspera, plurimis porositatibus conspicuis prædita, & quidem sinus simplex, non multis cellulis direm-tus.
units.tr: The interior is rough, provided with very many visible pores, and indeed a single cavity, not divided by many little cells.

units.la: Fundi uteri os seu orificium est rimula semper connivens, nisi naturali instinctu vel semen admittat, vel fœtui mensibusq; iter præbeat. Hic, egrediente fœtu, sedes acutissimi est doloris, mulierum in partu.
units.tr: The mouth or orifice of the fundus of the uterus is a little slit that always remains closed, unless by natural impulse it admits either seed or gives passage to the foetus and the menses. Here, when the foetus comes out, is the seat of the most acute pain of women in labour.

units.la: CAPUT XXXIX. DE FIBRIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 39. CONCERNING THE FIBRES.

units.la: Actenus fuerunt membra procreatricis facultatis; succedunt conservatricis vitalis organa.
units.tr: So far we have dealt with the members of the procreative faculty; next come the organs of the conserving vital faculty.

units.la: CONSERVATRICIS VITALIS organa sunt vitae procreatae confervandae & tuendae destinata instrumenta.
units.tr: The organs of the conserving vital faculty are the instruments destined for preserving and protecting the life once begotten.

units.la: Suntq; communia, vel peculiaria.
units.tr: They are either common or peculiar.

units.la: Communia sunt, quae communiter non solùm conservatrici, sed generatri-ci etiam facultati inserviunt.
units.tr: Common organs are those that serve in common not only the conserving faculty but also the generative faculty.

units.la: Ea autem sunt fibrae, seu villi.
units.tr: These are the fibres, or villi.

units.la: FIBRÆ sunt exilia quasi filamenta, praecipuè sui usum exhibentia facultati-bus ministris seu naturalibus. Seu: Villi sunt partes tenaciores, solidae, filisque si-miles motui destinatae naturali & voluntario.
units.tr: Fibres are slender, thread-like filaments, which chiefly provide their use to the subordinate or natural faculties. Or: villi are tenacious, solid parts, similar to threads, destined for natural and voluntary motion.

units.la: Motricis etiam organa Musculi fibras ad motum arbitrarium, ut illa ad natu-ralem omnino obtinent. Imò cordis e-tiam sunt fibrae.
units.tr: Muscles too are the organs of the motive faculty, as fibres are entirely for the natural one; indeed the fibres of the heart are also of this kind.

units.la: Fibra seu villi sunt Recti, vel Curvi.
units.tr: Fibres, or villi, are either straight or curved.

units.la: Recti sunt, qui recta protensi, inser-viunt attractrici facultati.
units.tr: Straight fibres are those stretched out in a straight line, which serve the attractive faculty.

units.la: Curvi sunt transversi, vel obliqui.
units.tr: Curved fibres are transverse or oblique.

units.la: Transversi sunt, qui transversum du-cti expulsrici navant operam. Obliqui sunt, qui ductu obliquo protensi retentrici virtuti ministrant.
units.tr: Transverse fibres are those drawn across, which perform the work of the expulsive faculty. Oblique fibres are those stretched in an oblique direction, which serve the retentive power.

units.la: CAPUT XL. DE VENTRICVLO.
units.tr: CHAPTER XL. CONCERNING THE STOMACH.

units.la: Peculiaria[?] membra conservatricis vitalis sunt, quae soli conservatrici vitali facultati peculiarem sui usum & ministerium exhibent.
units.tr: The peculiar members of the conserving vital faculty are those which render their own special use and service to that faculty alone.

units.la: Suntq; organa vel concoctionis nutrimenti, vel expulsionis excrementi.
units.tr: They are organs either of the concoction of nourishment or of the expulsion of excrement.

units.la: Membra concoctionis sunt, quae alterando, elaborando, & concoquendo alimento inserviunt.
units.tr: Members of concoction are those which serve to alter, work up and concoct food.

units.la: Concoctionis membrum est vel mediatae, vel immediatae concoctionis.
units.tr: A member of concoction is either of mediate or of immediate concoction.

units.la: Utrumq; est principale, vel minus principale seu administrum.
units.tr: Each of these is either principal or less principal, that is, subordinate.

units.la: Mediata concoctionis membrum est χυλώ-σεως, vel αἱματώσεως.
units.tr: A member of mediate concoction is of chylosis [χυλώσεως] or of haematosis [αἱματώσεως].

units.la: Membrum chylofeos est quasi culina pri-ma, in qua nutrimenta sumta prima alteratione in chylum elaborata, & versa excoquuntur.
units.tr: The member of chylosis is, as it were, the first kitchen, in which foods taken in are worked by a first alteration into chyle and, having been turned, are cooked through.

units.la: CHYLUS est succus candidus, seu cremor ptisanæ ac pulti similis ex alimento virtute ventriculi concoctus.
units.tr: CHYLE is a white juice, or a gruel like barley water and porridge, concocted from food by the power of the stomach.

units.la: Membrum chyloseos est principale, vel administrum.
units.tr: The member of chylosis is either principal or subordinate.

units.la: Principale est VENTRICVLVS, qui nimirum est membrum princeps primæ concoctionis, magnæ cavitatis, membranosum, sphæricum, oblongum, multis omnis generis fibris intertextum, cibum masticatum & comprehensum propria caloris sui facultate conficiens, ac in chylum transmutans.
units.tr: The principal one is the STOMACH, which is indeed the chief member of first concoction: it is of great capacity, membranous, spherical, oblong, interwoven with many fibres of every kind, and by its own power of heat it works up the chewed and swallowed food and changes it into chyle.

units.la: Ventriculi sunt cum tunicæ, ex-qui-bus constat, tum orificia.
units.tr: The stomach consists of coats and of orifices.

units.la: Tunicæ seu membranæ sunt propriæ, vel communes.
units.tr: The coats or membranes are either proper or common.

units.la: Propriæ sunt fibrosæ tunicæ, quæ in-tertextas habent fibras.
units.tr: The proper coats are fibrous coats, having fibres interwoven.

units.la: Propriarum tunicarum alia est Interior, alia Exterior.
units.tr: Of the proper coats, one is interior and the other exterior.

units.la: Interior, est durior, asperior scru-gosior[?]; fibras habens obliquas cibum retinentes, donec fit in chylum immutatum.
units.tr: The interior is harder, rougher and more rugged; it has oblique fibres that retain the food until it is changed into chyle.

units.la: Exterior est minus dura & aspera, habens villos transversos, concoctum cibum expellentes.
units.tr: The exterior is less hard and rough, having transverse villi that expel the concocted food.

units.la: Communis tunica est sine fibris, à periritoneo nata, stomachi quasi commune inuolucrum.
units.tr: The common coat has no fibres and arises from the peritoneum; it is, as it were, a common covering of the stomach.

units.la: Orificia ventriculi sunt, quæ cibo coquendo aditum, costoue exitum præbent.
units.tr: The orifices of the stomach are those which give food an entrance for concoction and an exit.

units.la: Hæc orificia sunt rugosa & crassiora, fibrisq; orbicularibus prædita, quæ natura iubente dilatari arctariuè possunt, adeoque permittunt cibos ingredi & egredi.
units.tr: These orifices are wrinkled and thicker, and endowed with orbicular fibres which, at nature's command, can be dilated or contracted, and so allow food to enter and leave.

units.la: Suntq; duo; superius, & inferius.
units.tr: There are two: the upper and the lower.

units.la: Superius continuum est Oesophago amplius, quo cibus ore masticatus & ventriculo concoquendus recipitur.
units.tr: The upper, continuous with the gullet, is wider than it; through it the food, chewed in the mouth, is received to be concocted in the stomach.

units.la: Inferius, nempe Pyloros, arctius est angusto collo obductum, & leviter quasi sursum reflexum, per quod chylus concoctus ad intestina delabitur.
units.tr: The lower, namely the pylorus, is narrower, covered like a narrow neck and slightly bent back upward; through it the concocted chyle slides down into the intestines.

units.la: Figura ventriculi oblonga est, instar lyripipii, cum ratione capacitatis, tum ratione orificiorum.
units.tr: The shape of the stomach is oblong, like a bagpipe, both in its capacity and in its orifices.

units.la: Locum in ventre medium occupat, fere inter Lienem & Epar, sub diaphragmate.
units.tr: It occupies the middle of the belly, roughly between the spleen and the liver, beneath the diaphragm.

units.la: CAPUT XLI. DE OESOPHAGO, ET INTESTINIS GRACILIORIBUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLI. CONCERNING THE GULLET AND THE SMALLER INTESTINES.

units.la: ADministra χυλώσεως membra iunt[?], quæ confectioni & elaboratio-ni chyli ministerium exhibent.
units.tr: The subordinate members of chylosis are those which furnish service for the making and working up of chyle.

units.la: Suntq; organa vel ingestionis, vel e-gestionis.
units.tr: They are organs either of ingestion or of egestion.

units.la: Organa ingestionis sunt, quæ cibum in ventriculos superiùs ingerunt.
units.tr: Organs of ingestion are those which convey food upward into the stomach.

units.la: Suntq; rursus alia masticationis, alia deglutionis.
units.tr: Again, some are for mastication and others for deglutition.

units.la: Ingeritur autem cibus ad masticationem per Os, cui subserviunt musculi Maxillares, quorum alii os referant, alii obserant.
units.tr: Food is taken in for mastication through the mouth, and the masseter muscles serve it: some of them open the mouth, others close it.

units.la: Masticatio fit dentibus, aliis incidens-tibus, & frangentibus, aliis conterenti-bus & levigantibus.
units.tr: Mastication is performed by the teeth: some cut and break, others grind and smooth.

units.la: 1. Masticationi subserviunt: Gingiva, scilicet caro dentes circumvallans, eorumque calorem fovens, imò in senibus edentulis qualescunq; dentium vices su-stinens.
units.tr: 1. The following serve mastication: the gums, namely the flesh surrounding the teeth and keeping their warmth, and in old, toothless people even taking the place of the teeth in some way.

units.la: 2. Secundò, Musculus quartus maxillaris, qui circumagendo maxillam inferiorem, masticationem promovet.
units.tr: 2. Second, the fourth maxillary muscle, which by turning the lower jaw promotes mastication.

units.la: 3. Tertiò, Lingua masticationis opus quasi regit, dapes, dum in ore moluntur, ele-vans & deorsum tendentes sustinens.
units.tr: 3. Third, the tongue, which as it were directs the work of mastication, lifting the food as it is worked in the mouth and holding it while it tends downward.

units.la: Quarto, Tunica palati duritie munita, inter quam & linguam cibi volutati magis attenuantur.
units.tr: Fourth, the membrane of the palate, fortified by its hardness, between which and the tongue the rolled morsels are made finer.

units.la: Deglutionis membrum est Gula seu Oesophagus, qui est membraneus, nerveus & exanguis canalis, à faucibus ad ventriculum usque continuè porrectus, via nimirum deglutionis, per quam cibus ex ore masticatus in ventriculū descendit.
units.tr: The member of deglutition is the throat or gullet, a membranous, sinewy and bloodless canal, extending continuously from the fauces to the stomach; it is the path of swallowing, by which food chewed in the mouth goes down into the stomach.

units.la: Ut commodior esset deglutio, substantia gulæ modò extendi, modò concidere potest, in principio quidem densior, quàm in ventre.
units.tr: So that swallowing may be easier, the substance of the gullet can be extended or contracted; it is indeed denser at the beginning than in the belly.

units.la: Deglutioni ferunt suppetias primùm fibræ tunicæ exterioris latæ seu transversæ, quæ expellunt in ventrem.
units.tr: For swallowing, first, the broad or transverse fibres of the outer coat lend aid, pushing the food into the belly.

units.la: Secundò, quatuor Musculi Faucium, & duo, qui è pectore sursum ducuntur ad gulam, ad alimentum deducendum de-orsum.
units.tr: Second, the four muscles of the fauces, and the two that are drawn up from the chest to the gullet, bring the food down.

units.la: Tertiò, Motus Epiglottidis, quæ tempore ingestionis ascendit, & gulæ tunc descendenti locum præbet, simulque aspe-ram arteriam obturat, ne à cibo deviante molestetur.
units.tr: Third, the movement of the epiglottis, which rises at the time of ingestion and gives way to the descending gullet, and at the same time closes the windpipe, so that it is not troubled by food going the wrong way.

units.la: Organa egestionis sunt vasa chylumex ventriculo delapsum excipientia, & distribuentia.
units.tr: Organs of egestion are the vessels that receive and distribute the chyle which has slipped down from the stomach.

units.la: Ea autem sunt intestina, quae sunt vasa oblonga, spermatica, & concava, multis gyris & anfractibus sinuosa, chyli distributioni & excrementorum ejus lentorum excretioni inservientia.
units.tr: These are the intestines, which are oblong, spermatic and hollow vessels, winding in many coils and turns, serving the distribution of chyle and the excretion of its slower excrements.

units.la: Intestina aut sunt gracilia, aut crassa.
units.tr: Intestines are either slender or thick.

units.la: Gracilia sunt substantiae tenuioris superiora intestina, quae praeter excretionem etiam distribuendo chylo serviunt.
units.tr: The slender intestines are the upper ones, of finer substance; besides excretion, they also serve in distributing chyle.

units.la: Ad haec plurimae venae ex mesenterio proveniunt, quae hiantibus orificiis suis, atque in intimam intestinorum cavitatem penetrantibus, quicquid in chylo benignum & succulentum est, allicunt.
units.tr: To these many veins come from the mesentery; their gaping openings penetrate into the innermost cavity of the intestines and draw in whatever in the chyle is good and juicy.

units.la: Gracilia intestina sunt Duodenum, Jejunum, & Ileos.
units.tr: The slender intestines are the duodenum, the jejunum and the ileum.

units.la: Duodenum est intestinum gracile, cum inferiori ventriculi orificio continuatum, duodecim digitorum longitudinem transversum adaequans.
units.tr: The duodenum is a slender intestine, continuous with the lower orifice of the stomach, and as long as twelve finger-breadths laid across.

units.la: Jejunum est duodeno proximum, ibi incipiens, ubi duodenum in gyros primum circumvolvitur, elatiorem ventris partem juxta umbilicum occupans.
units.tr: The jejunum lies next to the duodenum, beginning where the duodenum first turns into coils, and occupies the higher part of the belly near the navel.

units.la: Ileos est intestinum a jejuno incipiens, & in dextro rene terminatum plurimis anfractibus & gyris juxta umbilicū implicitum, & omnium longissimum*
units.tr: The ileum is an intestine beginning at the jejunum and ending at the right kidney, entangled in very many turns and coils near the navel, and the longest of all.

units.la: CAPUT XLII. DE CHYMO, SANGVINE, ET PITUITA.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLII. CONCERNING CHYME, BLOOD, AND PHLEGM.

units.la: ADhuc de membris chylosceos: sequuntur haematosceos membra.
units.tr: Further on the parts of the chylosis; there follow the parts of the haematosis.

units.la: Membra Haematosceos sunt quasi culina altera, in qua Chylus elaboratus secunda alteratione in Chymum convertitur & excoquitur.
units.tr: The parts of the haematosis are, as it were, a second kitchen, in which the chyle, worked over by a second alteration, is turned into chyme and cooked through.

units.la: Chymus est succus rubens, ex chylo in epaticis praecipuè venis vi caloris proprii genitus, quatuor in se continens humores.
units.tr: Chyme is a reddish juice, generated from the chyle chiefly in the veins of the liver by the force of its own heat, containing within itself four humours.

units.la: Humores isti sunt partes chymo permixtae.
units.tr: These humours are the parts mixed together in the chyme.

units.la: Suntq; duorum generum: Prius continet Sanguinem & Pituitam: Posterius utramq; Bilem.
units.tr: They are of two kinds: the first contains blood and phlegm; the second contains both kinds of bile.

units.la: Sanguis est humor primi generis, substantiae mediocris (nec nimis tenuis, nec admodum crassae) sapore dulcis, colore ex rubedine purpurascens, plenus fibris, propter quas facile coit, & coagulatur extra vasa sua effusus, confectus calore temperato ex partibus chyli temperatioribus, pinguidioribus & aereis, praecipua nutrimenti portio.
units.tr: Blood is a humour of the first kind, of moderate substance (neither too thin nor very thick), sweet in taste, purplish in colour from a ruddy hue, full of fibres, on account of which it readily clots and coagulates when poured out outside its vessels; it is made by the heat of the body from the milder, fattier and airier parts of the chyle, and is the chief portion of nourishment.

units.la: PITUITA est humor primi generis, substantiae lentae & viscidae, colore subalbus, sapore insipidus fere, ex chylia-quosfis & crudis partibus, quae elaborari satis nequiverunt, excoctus, ulteriore tamen coctione sanguinis dulcedinem acquirens; dicitur & Phlegma.
units.tr: Phlegm is a humour of the first kind, of a sluggish and viscid substance, whitish in colour, almost tasteless, produced from the watery and crude parts of the chyle which could not be worked up sufficiently; yet, by further cooking, it acquires the sweetness of blood; it is also called phlegm.

units.la: Haec est vel alimentaria, vel excre-mentitia.
units.tr: This is either nutritive or excrementitious.

units.la: Alimentaria quae cedit partibus quibusdam corporis in alimentum, praecipue in sanguinis defectu conversa in sanguinem.
units.tr: The nutritive phlegm is that which passes as nourishment to certain parts of the body, and, especially when there is a lack of blood, is turned into blood.

units.la: Excrementitia quae ut inutilis ejicitur, quaeq; est ratione substantiae, vel aquea, vel mucea, vel gypsea.
units.tr: The excrementitious phlegm is that which is cast out as useless, and which, according to the nature of its substance, is either watery, or mucous, or chalky.

units.la: CAPUT XLIII. DE BILE FLAVA ET ATRA; ITEM DE VESICULA Fellis & Liene.
units.tr: CHAPTER 43. OF YELLOW AND BLACK BILE; ALSO OF THE GALL-BLADDER AND THE SPLEEN.

units.la: Secundi generis humores sunt Bilis, cum Flava, tum Atra.
units.tr: The humours of the second kind are bile, both yellow and black.

units.la: CAPUT XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIII.

units.la: Flava bilis seu cholera est humor secundi generis, substantiâ tenuis, δυνάμει calidus & siccus, sapore amarus, colore flavus, ex tenuioribus & calidioribus ehyli[?] partibus enatus, qui secretus in fellis vesicam recedit, & exemtus venis, non coagulatur.
units.tr: Yellow bile, or choler, is a humour of the second kind, thin in substance, hot and dry in potency [δυνάμει], bitter in taste and yellow in colour. It arises from the thinner and hotter parts of the chyle and, once separated, withdraws into the gall bladder; when drawn out of the veins, it does not coagulate.

units.la: Hæc bilis est vel alimentaria, vel non alimentaria. Alimentaria est massæ sanguineæ pars tenuissima, per venas distributa, alens particulas suæ naturæ affines, & sanguini per venas perlabenti transvectionis promtitudinem afferens.
units.tr: This bile is either nutritive or non-nutritive. The nutritive bile is the thinnest part of the mass of blood, distributed through the veins, nourishing particles akin to its own nature, and giving readiness of transport to the blood as it flows through the veins.

units.la: Non alimentaria à sanguine secernitur, & in vesiculâ fellis amandatur, proprio deinde ductu in intestina labens.
units.tr: The non-nutritive bile is secreted from the blood and sent to the gall bladder, and then, by its own duct, flows into the intestines.

units.la: Vesicula fellis est oblongum & membraneum receptaculum flavæ bilis à sanguine separatæ, sub jecoris parte dextrâ & concavâ situm.
units.tr: The gall bladder is an oblong, membranous receptacle for yellow bile separated from the blood, situated beneath the right and concave part of the liver.

units.la: Meatus habet hæc duos: alterum ab Epate, per quem bilis influit in vesiculam: alterum, qui à vesicula porrigitur, in initium intestini Jejuni insertus.
units.tr: It has two passages: one from the liver, through which the bile flows into the gall bladder; the other, which extends from the gall bladder and is inserted at the beginning of the jejunum.

units.la: Hujus in intestinis usus est, ad excrementorum dejectionem intestina stimulare (unde & flavo apparent colore) deinde lentam & adhærescentem illis pituitam detergere & exturbare.
units.tr: Its use in the intestines is to stimulate the intestines to expel the excrements (whence they also appear yellow in colour), and then to wipe away and drive out the sluggish phlegm that clings to them.

units.la: Atra bilis seu Melancholia est secundi generis humor, substantia crassus gravisque, colore nigricans, sapore acidus, è chyli partibus crasisis ac terreis calore non eliquatis, confectus, qui secretus in lienem allectus secedit.
units.tr: Black bile, or melancholy, is a humour of the second kind, thick and heavy in substance, blackish in colour and sour in taste. It is made from the thick and earthy parts of the chyle, which the heat has not liquefied, and once secreted it is drawn into the spleen and settles there.

units.la: Hujus portio alia dicitur cum san-guine in venis existens alendo corpori idonea: alia vero, quam lien sanguinem expurgans per truncum venæ portæ pro-licit, & in se recondit.
units.tr: One part of it, they say, exists in the veins with the blood and is suitable for nourishing the body; the other part, which the spleen, cleansing the blood, drives out through the trunk of the portal vein and stores within itself.

units.la: Lien igitur seu Splen est spongiosum laxumque in sinistro hypochondrio sub mendosis costis, succi Melancholici, à sanguine discreti, receptaculum.
units.tr: The spleen, or Splen, is therefore a spongy and loose receptacle in the left hypochondrium, beneath the false ribs, for the melancholic juice separated from the blood.

units.la: Meatus per quem in lienem influit succus hic secretus, ducitur à vena portæ: Deinde à liene ad sinistram ventricu-li sedem, versus orificium superius meatus contingit, ut per ipsum succus Melancholicus sua natura acidus ad ventriculum regurgitet & post ingressum Chyli ad epar rursus ibi famis appetitum promoveat.
units.tr: The passage by which this secreted juice flows into the spleen is led from the portal vein. Then from the spleen it reaches the left seat of the stomach and touches the upper opening of the passage, so that through it the melancholic juice, acid by nature, regurgitates into the stomach and, after the chyle has entered, again promotes there the appetite of hunger, which turns back toward the liver.

units.la: Caput XLIV. DE EPATE.
units.tr: Chapter 44. Of the Liver.

units.la: Æc de chymi humoribus : Membrum Hæmatôseos est princeps, vel administrum.
units.tr: These things concerning the humours of the chyme. The member of haematosis is either the chief or the servant.

units.la: Princeps est Epar.
units.tr: The chief is the liver.

units.la: Epar igitur est princeps Hæmatôseos membrum, instar concreti sanguinis rubescens, plurimis perspersum venis chyli advectam massam in rubicundam seu chymi sanguineam massam convertentibus, eumq; in quatuor humores distinguentibus.
units.tr: The liver, then, is the chief member of haematosis, reddish like coagulated blood, sprinkled throughout with many veins, which convert the mass of chyle brought to it into a reddish, chyme-like mass of blood, and distinguish it into the four humours.

units.la: Epatis substantia duabus constat partibus, carnosa & venosa.
units.tr: The substance of the liver consists of two parts, the fleshy and the venous.

units.la: Carnosa pars epatis dicitur PARENCHYMA, quod est caro concretum & congelatum sanguinem referens.
units.tr: The fleshy part of the liver is called the PARENCHYMA, which is flesh, a concretion that resembles congealed blood.

units.la: Venosa est multitudo venarum, per totum parenchymatis corpus disseminata.
units.tr: The venous part is a multitude of veins, scattered throughout the whole body of the parenchyma.

units.la: Figura epatis qua ventriculum spectat, cava est, qua diaphragma, gibba est.
units.tr: The figure of the liver is hollow on the side facing the stomach, and convex on the side facing the diaphragm.

units.la: Situs epatis est in dextro latere, in sublimi sub diaphragmate.
units.tr: The situation of the liver is on the right side, high up beneath the diaphragm.

units.la: CAPUT XLV. DE VENIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLV. CONCERNING THE VEINS.

units.la: Dministrum hæmatoseos membrum est Vena.
units.tr: The veins are the servant member of the blood-making.

units.la: Vena est organum album, tenue, intus excavatum, una constans tunica, ex triplici contextum fibrarum genere, corporis nutrimentum vehens ac fundens.
units.tr: A vein is a white, thin organ, hollow within, consisting of a single coat, woven from a threefold kind of fibres, carrying and pouring out the nourishment of the body.

units.la: Alia vena est importans chylum in jecur, alia sanguinem ex jecore exportans, & distribuens.
units.tr: One vein brings chyle into the liver, another carries blood out of the liver and distributes it.

units.la: Vena importans chylum in epar est cum Mesaraica, cum Vena portæ.
units.tr: The vein bringing chyle to the liver is the mesaraic vein together with the portal vein.

units.la: Mesaraicæ venæ sunt quàm plurimæ, quæ mesenterii centrum subeuntes instar radicum arboris, chylum ex intestinis suctu hauriunt, præparant, & ad venam portæ transmittunt.
units.tr: The mesaraic veins are very many; running to the centre of the mesentery like the roots of a tree, they draw up chyle from the intestines by suction, prepare it, and pass it on to the portal vein.

units.la: Mesaræum seu Mesenterium est vinculum membranæ durēq; substātiæ, complectens venas mesaraicas, intestina in medio in orbem inter sese convinciens, & ad dorsum alligans.
units.tr: The mesaraeum, or mesentery, is a bond of membrane and firm substance, enclosing the mesaraic veins, binding the intestines together in a circle in the middle, and fastening them to the back.

units.la: Vena portæ est vena amplà in cavo jecoris ex mesaraicis in unum confluenti-bus bus coflata, per quam veluti portam advectus chyl» ex intestinis Epati illabitur.
units.tr: The portal vein is a wide vein formed in the hollow of the liver from the mesaraic veins flowing together into one; through it the chyle, carried as if through a gate from the intestines, flows into the liver.

units.la: Vena exportans sanguinem ex Epate quę scilicet excipit sanguinem & deinceps in membra per ramos & partes distribuit & diffundit, dicitur Vena cava.
units.tr: The vein carrying blood out of the liver, which of course receives the blood and then distributes and diffuses it into the limbs through its branches and parts, is called the vena cava.

units.la: Vena cava est Venarum maxima & quasi truncus, sanguinem confectum & beneficio vesiculæ fellis & lienis duplici humore expurgatum, ductu suo per multiplices propagines in universum corpus distribuens.
units.tr: The vena cava is the greatest of the veins and, as it were, the trunk, distributing by its course, through its manifold offshoots, the blood that has been made and cleansed by the benefit of the gall bladder and the spleen with their two humours, into the whole body.

units.la: Vena cavæ propagines serie quadam cum supra jecur ascendunt, tum infra ipsum descendunt, partibus comeatum advehentes, quæ omnes non possunt distributionum vinculo colligari.
units.tr: The offshoots of the vena cava ascend above the liver in a certain order, and then descend below it, bringing passage to the parts; all of these cannot be bound together by the tie of distribution.

units.la: CAPUT XLVI. DE MEMBRIS CONCOCTIONIS TERTIÆ.
units.tr: CHAPTER 46. ON THE MEMBERS OF THE THIRD CONCOCTION.

units.la: ADhuc fuerunt organa concoctionis mediatæ: Organa concoctionis immediatè nutritioni inservientes sunt venæ Capillares seu extremitates venularum in singulis alendis membris, in quibus purior sanguinis portio, antecedente antecedente concoctione mediata exquisi-tè elaborata, perfectè absolvitur, & ex venulis illis elabens, per singularum partium substantiam effunditur, eidemque agglutinata assimilatur.
units.tr: There are still the organs of the mediate concoction. The organs immediately serving nutrition are the capillary veins, or the extremities of the little veins in each of the parts to be nourished. In these, the purer portion of the blood, having first been thoroughly worked over by the preceding mediate concoction, is perfectly completed; and, flowing out of those little veins, it is poured into the substance of each individual part and is assimilated by being joined to it.

units.la: Hujus concoctionis organa produ-cunt & conficiùt ex sanguine humorem alimentarium, qui roris speciem refe-rens natura,partibus,quibus opponitur, assimilatur.
units.tr: These organs produce and prepare from the blood the nourishing humour, which nature, resembling dew in appearance, assimilates to the parts it is set against.

units.la: Ministra organa sunt rami, du&us, & propagines antecedentium venarum, quæ sua virtute sanguine é cava vena ac-ceptum, ulterius elaborant, & tertiæ concoctioni præparant, itaq; elaborate præparatum advehunt alendis partibus.
units.tr: The serving organs are the branches, ducts, and offshoots of the veins mentioned above, which by their own power take up the blood from the hollow vein, work it further, prepare it for the third concoction, and so carry the prepared blood to the parts to be nourished.

units.la: CAPUT XLVII. DE MEMBRIS EXPULSIONI EXCREMENTORUM inservientibus.
units.tr: Chapter 47. On the Members Serving the Expulsion of Excrements

units.la: Actenus membra concoctionis fuere: Succedunt expulsionis, quæ excrementorum ejectioni inser-viunt.
units.tr: Hitherto we have dealt with the members of concoction. Next come those of expulsion, which serve the ejection of excrements.

units.la: Excrementa sunt alimentorum partes crascrassiores, ad nutritionem inutiles, quæ postea discretæ excernuntur.
units.tr: Excrements are the grosser parts of the aliments, useless for nutrition, which are afterwards separated and voided.

units.la: Suntq; vel crassa & lenta; vel tenuia & fluida.
units.tr: They are either thick and viscous, or thin and fluid.

units.la: Crassa & lenta sunt potissimùm primæ concoctionis excrementa, quæ per alvum excernuntur.
units.tr: Thick and viscous excrements are chiefly those of the first concoction, which are voided through the bowel.

units.la: Excrementa crassa & lenta expellentia membra sunt intestina crassiora, quæ sunt inferiora, densioris tunicæ, solius excretionis organa.
units.tr: The members expelling thick and viscous excrements are the larger intestines, which lie lower, have a denser coat, and serve excretion alone.

units.la: Suntq; Cæcum, Colon & Rectum.
units.tr: These are the caecum, the colon and the rectum.

units.la: Cæcum est intestinum crassum, breve, habens ingressum, sed non egressum. Di-ci solet Monoculum & Saccus; Estque veluti secundus ventriculus, in quo chylus immoratur.
units.tr: The caecum is a short, thick intestine, having an inlet but no outlet. It is commonly called the monoculus and the sack; it is like a second stomach, in which the chyle lingers.

units.la: Cæco est valvula quædam apposita, excrementorum regres-sum impediens.
units.tr: A small valve is placed at the caecum, preventing the backward flow of excrements.

units.la: Colon est intestinum crassum, con-stans multis & magnis anfractibus, à cæ-co in dex-tro ileo exortum, hinc ad dex-trum renem deorsum flexum, cui annectitur, deinde verò convolutum, sursum reflexum, & abdomen sub ventriculo transversim latum. Hoc veluti receptaculū pituitæ est, in eoq; colici dolores generantur.
units.tr: The colon is a thick intestine, made up of many large windings, arising from the caecum in the right ileum; from there it bends downward to the right kidney, to which it is attached, then turns back on itself, is reflected upward, and runs across the abdomen beneath the stomach. This serves as a kind of receptacle for phlegm, and in it colic pains are produced.

units.la: Rectum est intestinum crassum, spinæ recta incumbens, seu à summo osse sacro ad extremum usq; coccygen delatum, atq; ita recto ductu in podicem desinés.
units.tr: The rectum is a thick intestine lying straight upon the spine, or extending from the upper sacral bone to the very end of the coccyx, and so, in a straight course, ending at the anus.

units.la: In hoc sunt venæ Hæmorrhoidales, ductæ à vena portæ, & in hoc directæ, per quas sanguis expurgatur Melancholi-cus.
units.tr: In it are the haemorrhoidal veins, drawn from the portal vein and running straight into it, through which the melancholic blood is purged.

units.la: Excrementa porrò tenuia & fluida sunt vel secundæ, vel tertiæ concoctionis.
units.tr: Excrements that are thin and fluid, moreover, are either of the second or of the third concoction.

units.la: Secundæ concoctionis excrementum est præcipuè serosus humor, qui dicitur Urina.
units.tr: The excrement of the second concoction is chiefly the serous humour called urine.

units.la: Urina est excrementum serosum, è sanguine emulctum, in renes secretum, & in vesicam plenius expurgatum.
units.tr: Urine is a serous excrement, drawn off from the blood, secreted in the kidneys, and more fully purged in the bladder.

units.la: Urinæ excernendæ membra sunt duorum generum: Primum continet venas emulgentes & renes.
units.tr: The members for excreting urine are of two kinds. The first contains the emulgent veins and the kidneys.

units.la: Venæ emulgentes, sunt vasa è vena cavâ descendentia, quæ quicquid in sanguine est serosum & aqueum emulgent, & in renes devehunt.
units.tr: The emulgent veins are vessels descending from the vena cava, which draw off whatever in the blood is serous and watery and convey it to the kidneys.

units.la: Renes, sunt membra excretioni urinæ inservientia, substantiæ solidæ & compactæ, spinam versus gibba, cava quà viscéviscera spectant, coloris subrubri, per quorum corpus arteriæ & venæ emulgentes insertæ disperguntur, quæq; attractum sanguinem serosum magis excoquunt & discernunt, merumq; aqueum ad vesicam per ureteres.
units.tr: The kidneys are members serving the excretion of urine, solid and compact in substance, curved toward the spine, hollow on the side facing the viscera, of a reddish colour; through their body the emulgent arteries and veins are inserted and spread out, and they further concoct and separate the serous blood drawn in, and send the pure watery matter down to the bladder by the ureters.

units.la: Suntq; in utroq; latere singuli, quorum dexter elatiorem, sinister depressiorem obtinet situm.
units.tr: There is one on each side; the right one occupies a higher position, the left a lower.

units.la: Secundi generis membra excernentia urinam sunt Ureteres, & Vesica.
units.tr: The members of the second kind, excreting urine, are the ureters and the bladder.

units.la: Ureteres sunt canales concavi, albi, crassiqué, arteriarum instar, nervei admodum, à renibus ad vesicam usque progredientes, quibus urina à renibus in vesicam usq; defluit.
units.tr: The ureters are hollow, white and rather thick canals, much like arteries and very sinewy, running from the kidneys down to the bladder, by which the urine flows from the kidneys into the bladder.

units.la: Urinarii hi ductus ubi pertinguntur sub vesica collum versus, habent ostiola, quæ membranis clauduntur, quæ labente è renibus urina aperiuntur, non secus atq; in folle corium illud, quod est in posteriore parte, cum aërem attrahimus, postea clauduntur, ne quid in ureteres & renes refluat.
units.tr: Where these urinary ducts are bent under the bladder toward the neck, they have small openings closed by membranes, which open as the urine slides down from the kidneys, just as that skin in the back part of a bellows, when we draw in air, and afterwards close, so that nothing flows back into the ureters and kidneys.

units.la: Vesica est membrum excipiendæ urinæ destinatum, concavum, nervosum, tribus fibrarum generibus donatum, in imo ventre situm, ita ut sursum sit fundus; deorsum vero in quod urina influit, ut postea excernatur.
units.tr: The bladder is a member designed to receive the urine, hollow, sinewy, endowed with three kinds of fibres, situated in the lowest part of the belly, so that its base is upward, while downward is the opening into which the urine flows, to be afterwards excreted.

units.la: definit in viris in penem, in foeminis in collum matricis.
units.tr: It ends in men in the penis, in women in the neck of the womb.

units.la: Hujus item sunt duae tunicae, altera propria, altera adscititia. Propria est, qua peculiariter constat, quaq; extenditur & contrahitur: Adscititia a peritonaeo mutuo sumitur, qua tegitur.
units.tr: It has likewise two coats: one proper to it, the other borrowed. The proper coat is that which is peculiar to it, and by which it is extended and contracted; the borrowed one is taken from the peritoneum, by which it is covered.

units.la: In orificio ejus duo sunt musculi, os constringentes, ne scilicet urina incautis nobis effluat. Vesica mulierum sublimior est, quam virorum.
units.tr: At its outlet there are two muscles, constricting the opening, so that the urine may not run out unawares upon us. The bladder of women is higher than that of men.

units.la: sunt vel universi corporis, quae perporos & spiramenta cutis calore resoluta expirant vel effluunt, ut fuliginess & sudor: vel certarum corporis partium, ut cerebri per majorem oculorum angulum, ut lachrymae; per aures, ut sordes aurium; per nares, ut mucus, &c.
units.tr: Some are of the whole body, which breathe out or flow out through the pores and openings of the skin when loosened by heat, such as soot and sweat; others of certain parts of the body: such as from the brain through the greater corner of the eyes, as tears; through the ears, as ear-wax; through the nostrils, as mucus, etc.

units.la: Caput XLVIII. De Cerebro et Cerebello
units.tr: Chapter 48. On the Brain and Cerebellum

units.la: HActenus exposita sunt membra vitalia vegetatrici facultati famulantia; Succedunt membra animalia, per quæ eduntur actiones animales propriæ.
units.tr: Thus far the vital parts serving the vegetative faculty have been set out. There follow the animal parts, through which the proper animal actions are performed.

units.la: Suntq; Communia, vel Propria.
units.tr: They are either common or proper.

units.la: Communia sunt, quæ sensitrici & motrici facultati communiter fere inserviunt.
units.tr: Common parts are those which serve, more or less in common, both the sensitive and the motor faculty.

units.la: Commune animale membrum est primarium, vel secundarium.
units.tr: A common animal part is either primary or secondary.

units.la: Primarium est, ad quod prima sensus & motus origo refertur, estq; Cerebrum; quod scilicet est sensuum exteriorum ἡγεμονικὸν αἰσθητήριον[?], sed internorum proprium & immediatum organum.
units.tr: The primary one is that to which the first origin of sensation and motion is referred, and this is the brain; which is, as it were, the leading sensory organ of the external senses, but the proper and immediate organ of the internal ones.

units.la: CEREBRUM est membrum animale sensus & motus primarium, molle, albumque, in cranio duplici meninge benè septum & obvallatum.
units.tr: The BRAIN is the primary animal part of sensation and motion, soft and white, well enclosed and fortified in the skull by a double membrane.

units.la: Cerebrum oritur è subtilissima parte seminis, & plena spirituum, quæ in formatione fœtus in summam quasi arcem exaeftaat, eftq; in multos plexus & sinus instar intestinorum convolutum.
units.tr: The brain arises from the most subtle part of the seed, full of spirits, which in the formation of the foetus swells up, as it were, into a highest citadel, and is folded into many plexuses and sinuses like the intestines.

units.la: Cerebrum distingui videtur ventricu-lis, quae sunt cerebri cavitates spirituum animalium plenissimæ; (Varolius addit excrementorum cerebri receptacula.)
units.tr: The brain seems to be distinguished by its ventricles, which are the cavities of the brain, most full of animal spirits; (Varolius adds receptacles for the excrements of the brain.)

units.la: Ventriculi autem cerebri sunt anterio-res vel posteriores.
units.tr: The ventricles of the brain, however, are either anterior or posterior.

units.la: Anteriores sunt in parte cerebri ante-riore, oblongi, anfractuosi, lunam falcatam referentes.
units.tr: The anterior ones lie in the front part of the brain; they are oblong and winding, resembling a sickle-shaped moon.

units.la: Estq; dexter in parte dextra, & fini-ster in parte capitis sinistra.
units.tr: And there is a right one in the right part, and a left one in the left part of the head.

units.la: Inter utrumq; anteriorem interja-cet medius cerebri ventriculus, longi-usculus, & recta ab anteriori ad posteriorem tendens cerebri partem.
units.tr: Between the two anterior ventricles lies the middle ventricle of the brain, somewhat elongated, and running straight from the front part of the brain to the back.

units.la: Posterior ventriculus est ultimus sinus inter Medullae spinalis initium & cerebel-lum.
units.tr: The posterior ventricle is the last sinus, lying between the beginning of the spinal marrow and the cerebellum.

units.la: Cerebro cognata pars est Cerebellum, in eodem cranio contentum, nempe minoris liquiditatis seu molliciei & albedinis, in posteriori calvarię sede collo-catum, minus cerebro, & ab eo per duram matrem direm-tum.
units.tr: The part related to the brain is the Cerebellum, contained in the same skull, namely of lesser fluidity or softness and whiteness, placed in the back part of the cranium, and separated from the brain by the dura mater.

units.la: Caput XLIX: DE MEDVLLA SPINALI, ET NERVIS.
units.tr: Chapter 49: CONCERNING THE SPINAL MARROW AND THE NERVES.

units.la: HActenus de cerebro, & cerebello; quod è cranio in mobiles vertebras & sacrum os deductum, & involucris membraneis in longum obductum, dicitur Medulla spinalis.
units.tr: Thus far concerning the brain and the cerebellum. The marrow that is drawn from the skull through the movable vertebrae and the sacrum, and is extended lengthwise enclosed in membranous coverings, is called the spinal marrow.

units.la: Secundarium organum sensus & motus est, per quod à primario organo sensus & motus in universum corpus defertur.
units.tr: The secondary organ of sense and motion is that through which sense and motion are conveyed from the primary organ of sense and motion to the whole body.

units.la: Secundarium hoc organû est Nervus, qui est tale organum substantiæ spermaticæ mollis, albæ, fibris quasi multis perspersę, exquisitissimi sensus, teres & exangue, à cerebro & spinali medulla per universum corpus instar filamentorû diffusum.
units.tr: This secondary organ is the nerve: an organ of soft, white, seminal substance, as it were sprinkled with many fibres, of the most exquisite sensitivity, cylindrical and bloodless, diffused through the whole body like threads, from the brain and the spinal marrow.

units.la: Nervorum alii exurgunt & dimanant à cerebro, alii à spinali medulla; (Varolio etiam à Cerebello.)
units.tr: Some nerves arise and spring from the brain, others from the spinal marrow (Varolius also says from the cerebellum).

units.la: A cerebro procedentes nervi tûm sensum, tûm motum diffundunt à cerebro in corporis partes, & organa sensuum.
units.tr: The nerves proceeding from the brain spread both sense and motion from the brain into the parts of the body and the organs of the senses.

units.la: Horum paria dicuntur septem.
units.tr: These are said to be seven pairs.

units.la: Primû par in oculos inseritur: hi duo nervi mox ab ortu coëunt, atq; è calvariâ duducendi mox iterum dirimuntur, & quilibet ad oculum e regione situm tendit.
units.tr: The first pair is inserted into the eyes; these two nerves come together immediately from their origin, and, having been led out of the skull, are soon separated again, and each runs to the eye lying opposite it.

units.la: Secundum par prope istorum ortum ex cerebri basis lateribus initium sumit, per oculi foramen ad oculi musculos in plures ramos divisum disseminatur, & ad ipsam frontem motus causa progreditur.
units.tr: The second pair takes its beginning near their origin from the sides of the base of the brain, passes through the opening of the eye, and, divided into several branches, is spread to the muscles of the eye, and proceeds to the forehead itself for the purpose of movement.

units.la: Tertium par e duplici utrinq; radice, una crassiori, altera tenuiori & duriori initium sumit. Ortus gracilior per commune foramen cum fecundo pari transit in quatuor divisas propagines.
units.tr: The third pair takes its beginning from a double root on each side: one thicker, the other thinner and harder. The slender origin passes through the common foramen with the second pair and divides into four offshoots.

units.la: Prima in palpebras oculorum, cutem frontis, & adipem oculorum transit. Secunda superiori naso. Tertia carunculæ in interiori oculorum angulo inservit. Quarta vero, temporali musculo. Crassior origo descendit ad fauces, & efformat tunicam linguæ & palati, item inferioris maxillæ dentium radicibus & cuti infigitur.
units.tr: The first passes into the eyelids, the skin of the forehead, and the fat of the eyes. The second into the upper nose. The third serves the small caruncle in the inner corner of the eye. The fourth goes to the temporal muscle. The thicker origin descends to the throat and forms the covering of the tongue and palate; likewise it is fixed to the roots of the teeth of the lower jaw and to the skin.

units.la: Quartum par una cum tertio pari per commune foramen ad palati tunicam e-labitur, per eamque etiam dissemina-tur.
units.tr: The fourth pair, together with the third pair, glides through the common foramen to the covering of the palate, and is spread through it as well.

units.la: Quintum auditui inservit per foramen ossis petrosi ad auris cavitatem tendens.
units.tr: The fifth serves hearing, extending through the foramen of the petrous bone into the cavity of the ear.

units.la: Sextum ad omnia viscera in thorace & inferiori ventre, maxima ramorum soboles, sensus gratia distribuitur.
units.tr: The sixth is distributed to all the viscera in the thorax and lower belly, the largest offspring of branches, for the sake of sensation.

units.la: Septimum par à cerebri parte posteriore oritur, & praeest motibus musculorum laryngis, ossis Hyoeidis, & musculis à processu Styloeide ortum ducentibus, qui linguae movendae inserviunt.
units.tr: The seventh pair arises from the posterior part of the brain and presides over the movements of the muscles of the larynx, of the hyoid bone, and of the muscles that take their origin from the styloid process, which serve to move the tongue.

units.la: A Spinali medulla progredientes nervi sunt, qui motus praecipue gratia ad reliquas corporis partes à medulla spinae dorsi disseminantur.
units.tr: The nerves proceeding from the spinal marrow are those which are spread, chiefly for the sake of movement, from the marrow of the spine of the back to the remaining parts of the body.

units.la: Horum triginta numerantur paria, utrinque è medulla spinae singulis exurgentibus: quorum deductione totum corpus deorsum suas affectiones facilè percipit.
units.tr: Thirty pairs of these are counted, one arising on each side from the spinal marrow at each level; by their descent the whole body easily perceives its affections below.

units.la: CAPUT L.
units.tr: CHAPTER L.

units.la: DE ORGANIS SENSUS, tactus & gustus, ubi de LINGUA.
units.tr: ON THE ORGANS OF SENSE, TOUCH AND TASTE, WITH A DISCUSSION OF THE TONGUE.

units.la: Actenus communia fuerunt animalia membra: Sequuntur propria, quorum ministerio, vel sensitrix vel motrix facultas proprie & distinctè in suis edendis operationibus utitur.
units.tr: Hitherto we have considered the common members of animals. Now follow the proper members, by whose ministry the sensitive or the motor faculty carries out its own operations properly and distinctly.

units.la: Sunt igitur propria animalia membra organa vel sensitricis vel motricis facultatis.
units.tr: The proper members of animals, then, are the organs either of the sensitive or of the motor faculty.

units.la: Propria membra sensitricis facultatis sunt, quae sui usum exhibent sensibus exterioribus, seu quae sunt exteriorum sensuum sensoria.
units.tr: The proper members of the sensitive faculty are those which serve the external senses, or which are the sensoria of the external senses.

units.la: Suntq; vel primi generis, vel secundi.
units.tr: And these are either of the first kind or of the second.

units.la: Primi generis sensoria sunt eorum sensuum, quae sua sensilia admota, sive cominus sentiunt.
units.tr: The sensoria of the first kind are those of the senses which perceive their objects when they are applied to them, that is, at close range.

units.la: Et sunt sensoria organa vel tactus, vel gustus.
units.tr: And the sensoria are organs either of touch or of taste.

units.la: Sensorium tactus est, quicquid in corpore nerveum est. Estq; cum exteriorum membrorum, ut Cutis, & praecipuè ea, quae est in vola manus: quae ut singula tangibilia æquè reciperet sine excessu calidi, humidi, sicci, &c. esse oportebat veluti centrum ab omnibº tangibilibus æqualiter distans: Tum interiorum membrorum, ut propria membrana, quibus sunt donata & involuta.
units.tr: The sensorium of touch is whatever in the body is nervous. It consists both of external members, such as the skin, and especially that on the palm of the hand, which, in order to receive every tangible object equally, without excess of heat, moisture, dryness, and so on, ought to be like a centre equally distant from all tangible things; and of internal members, such as the membrane proper to each part, with which they are endowed and enveloped.

units.la: Sensorium gustatus est LINGVA, quae est caro ori indita, musculosa, porosa, per se sicca seu arida, plena nervis, venis & arteriis.
units.tr: The sensorium of taste is the TONGUE, which is flesh set in the mouth, muscular, porous, dry or arid in itself, and full of nerves, veins and arteries.

units.la: Lingua hæc per substantiam suam habet distributos nervos cum gustatꝰ, tum tactus, quorum beneficio sapores & qualitates primas secundasq; recipit.
units.tr: This tongue, through its substance, has nerves distributed for both taste and touch, by whose help it receives the primary and secondary flavours and qualities.

units.la: Deinde etiam est organum sermonis, siquidem sonum è pulmonibus per tra-cheam arteriam in os erumpentem, & ad dentes & palatum illisum format in distinctas & explanatas voces.
units.tr: Then, too, it is the organ of speech, since it shapes the sound that bursts from the lungs through the windpipe into the mouth, and is struck against the teeth and palate, into distinct and articulated voices.

units.la: Adjuvat deniq; masticationem, pervolvendo cibum in omnes oris partes.
units.tr: Finally, it also aids mastication, by rolling the food through all parts of the mouth.

units.la: Partes linguæ duæ sunt; radix seu basis, & mucro.
units.tr: The parts of the tongue are two: the root or base, and the tip.

units.la: Radix roboris causa crassior & major, fauces occupat. Mucro est tenuior & anterior pars, ut celerius moveretur.
units.tr: The root, thicker and larger for the sake of strength, occupies the throat. The tip is the thinner and forward part, so that it can move more quickly.

units.la: Porrò in linguam derivantur Nervi duo à cerebello profiliētes (ut placet Va-rolio) tangendi & gustandi facultate e-am imbuentes.
units.tr: Moreover, two nerves run into the tongue, springing from the cerebellum (as Varolius thinks), and imbue it with the faculties of touch and taste.

units.la: Cuticula etiam linguam & palatum oblinit, quæ cum saliva medium fit gustus, estq; tenuis, ut sapores eam facilè penetrent. Adjuvat gustatum Palatum, ad quod si lingua interventu musculorum cibos movet & atterit, vera fit gustatio.
units.tr: A cuticle also covers the tongue and palate, and together with saliva forms the medium of taste; it is thin, so that flavours can easily penetrate it. The palate aids tasting: if the tongue, by the action of its muscles, moves and grinds food against it, true tasting takes place.

units.la: CAPUT LI. DE VISUS ORGANO, OCULO.
units.tr: CHAPTER 51. ON THE ORGAN OF SIGHT, THE EYE.

units.la: Secundi generis sensoria sunt eorum sensuum, qui sensilia remota si-ne corporali contactu eminus percipiunt.
units.tr: The organs of the second kind are those of the senses which perceive their objects from a distance, without bodily contact.

units.la: Suntq; vel nobiliorum, vel ignobiliorum sensuum.
units.tr: And these are of either the nobler or the less noble senses.

units.la: Sensoria nobiliorum sensuum sunt vel vi-sus, vel auditus.
units.tr: The organs of the nobler senses are either sight or hearing.

units.la: Sensorium seu organum visus est Oculus.
units.tr: The organ of sight, or the sensory organ of sight, is the eye.

units.la: OCULUS est sensorium visus membranosum, sphæricum, tunicis humores suos continentibus constans, infra frontem ad narium latera utrinq; unum.
units.tr: THE EYE is the membranous, spherical sensory organ of sight, consisting of coats that contain its humours, one lying below the forehead on each side of the nose.

units.la: Partes itaq; oculi sunt cum tunicæ seu membranæ, tum humores.
units.tr: The parts of the eye, therefore, are both its coats or membranes and its humours.

units.la: Tunicæ oculi sunt quinq;.
units.tr: The coats of the eye are five.

units.la: Prima dicitur Conjunctiva, adnata seu alba, quæ est extima à pericranio pro-gnata, & corneæ anteriori parte adnata.
units.tr: The first is called the conjunctiva, or the white (adnata), which is the outermost, grown out of the pericranium and attached to the front part of the cornea.

units.la: Secunda dicitur Cornea, quæ durior est, è dura meninge orta, & omni ex parte toti oculo obnata.
units.tr: The second is called the cornea, which is harder, arises from the dura mater, and is grown over the whole eye on every side.

units.la: Tertia dicitur Uvea, quæ est à tenui meninge orta, instar iridis versicolor.
units.tr: The third is called the uvea, which arises from the thin membrane (pia mater) and is many-coloured like the iris.

units.la: Quarta est Retiformis tunica, exi-stens ex nervo optico ad posteriorem o-culi partem dilatato.
units.tr: The fourth is the retiform coat, existing as the optic nerve dilated at the back part of the eye.

units.la: Nervus opticus est primum nervorum par, à cerebri basi ortum, quod utrum-que oculum petens, in latam oculi tunicam expansum, oculo animales defert spiritus.
units.tr: The optic nerve is the first pair of nerves, arising from the base of the brain; it runs to each eye, spreads out into the broad coat of the eye, and conveys the animal spirits to the eye.

units.la: Quinta dicitur Aranea, quæ tenuis est, à tenui meninge orta, telam aranea-rum referens, in medio oculi humorem cristallinum in sua sede continens, & vitreum ab albugineo discernens.
units.tr: The fifth is called the aranea (the web), which is thin, arises from the thin membrane, resembles a spider's web, holds the crystalline humour in its place in the middle of the eye, and separates the vitreous from the albuginea.

units.la: Hæ fuerunt tunicæ : Humores oculi sunt tres.
units.tr: These are the coats. The humours of the eye are three.

units.la: Primus dicitur Aqueus, fluidus seu albugineus, qui est humor aquæ modo pel-lucidus, in anteriore parte oculi inter corneam & uveam comprehensus.
units.tr: The first is called the aqueous, the fluid or albuginous humour, which is clear like water and is contained in the front part of the eye between the cornea and the uvea.

units.la: Secundus dicitur Vitreus (quod vitri liquefacti & fusi sit similis) qui in posteriori oculi parte sedes est cristallini.
units.tr: The second is called the vitreous (because it is like melted and poured glass), which in the back part of the eye is the seat of the crystalline lens.

units.la: Tertius humor est Cristallinus, qui perspicuus est, & instar cristalli pellucidus, princeps videndi in oculo organum.
units.tr: The third humour is the crystalline, which is transparent and clear like crystal, the chief organ of seeing in the eye.

units.la: Oculi porro centrum instar puncti nigrum, dicitur Pupilla, in qua rerum conspiciuntur imagines.
units.tr: Moreover, the centre of the eye, black like a point, is called the pupil, in which images of things are seen.

units.la: Oculus denique ita constructus tegitur Palpebris, quæ sunt oculorum tegumenta, ex cute & carnosa membrana, & pericranio conflata.
units.tr: Finally, the eye so constructed is covered by the eyelids, which are the coverings of the eyes, made up of skin, a fleshy membrane and the pericranium.

units.la: CAPUT LII. DE ORGANO AU-DITUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 52. CONCERNING THE ORGAN OF HEARING.

units.la: AUditus organum, quo percipiuntur soni, quodque auditui proprie inservit, Exterius est vel Interius.
units.tr: The organ of hearing, by which sounds are perceived and which serves hearing properly, is either external or internal.

units.la: Exterius est Auris, quæ est organum auditus exterius, ex cute & cartilagine, anfractuosum, aerem & sonos exterius colligens, cosq; collectos ad interiora auditus organa transmittens.
units.tr: The external organ is the ear, which consists of skin and cartilage, is winding, and gathers the air and sounds from outside, transmitting them, once gathered, to the inner organs of hearing.

units.la: Auris pars alia superior, eaq; durior, quę prima dicitur; alia inferior, eaq; mollior, quæ fibræ & auricula appellatur.
units.tr: One part of the ear is upper and harder, and is called the first (or helix); the other is lower and softer, and is called the lobe or little ear.

units.la: In hoc exteriori organo videtur πόρος ἀκουστικός, seu meatus auditorius, qui est cavitas ab exterioribus versus interiora vergens, teres, editis sonis admittendis, & aurium sordibus excipiendis accommodata.
units.tr: In this external organ is found the auditory passage (πόρος ἀκουστικός), or meatus auditorius, a cavity running from the outside toward the inside, cylindrical, suited to admit the sounds that come in and to receive the dirt of the ears. [poros akoustikos]

units.la: Interius organum auditus est vel nerveum, vel osseum.
units.tr: The internal organ of hearing is either nervous or bony.

units.la: Nerveum est vel nervus auditorius, vel tympanum.
units.tr: The nervous part is either the auditory nerve or the eardrum.

units.la: Nervus auditorius est interius auditus organum, par scilicet nervorum, ortum (secundum vulgares) à cerebro, vel (secundum Varolium) à cerebello, in organa auditus implantatum, & in membranam meatus auditorii expansum & fusum, editum sonum excipiens, eumque, vel (secundum illos) in cerebrum, vel (secundum hunc) in cerebellum deferens.
units.tr: The auditory nerve is the inner organ of hearing: a pair of nerves, which arise (according to the common view) from the cerebrum, or (according to Varolius) from the cerebellum, are implanted into the organs of hearing and spread out and poured into the membrane of the auditory passage; it receives the sound that has been produced and conveys it either to the cerebrum (according to those) or to the cerebellum (according to this man).

units.la: Tympanum est membrana tenuis & robusta, meatum claudens, concava, sonum, seu soni speciem, extrinsecus advenientem, excipiens.
units.tr: The eardrum is a thin but tough membrane, closing off the passage, concave, which receives the sound, or the form of the sound, arriving from outside.

units.la: Osseum est vel Os petrosum, vel tria illa minutula ossicula auditui propria.
units.tr: The bony part is either the petrous bone or those three tiny little bones proper to hearing.

units.la: Os petrosum est, in temporibus, instar rupis, quod aliquot foraminibus pervium protuberat, in quo spiritus aërcus moratur.
units.tr: The petrous bone is, in the temples, like a rock, projecting, pierced by several foramina, in which the airy spirit dwells.

units.la: Ossicula illa tria sunt: Malleus, Incus, & Stapes, membrana invicem colligata.
units.tr: Those three little bones are the malleus, the incus, and the stapes, joined to one another by membrane.

units.la: CAPUT LIIII. DE ORGANO OLFACTUS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 54. ON THE ORGAN OF SMELL.

units.la: Sensorium sensus ignobilioris est organum olfactus, quo utitur odoratus ad percipiendos odores.
units.tr: The organ of the less noble sense is the organ of smell, by which the sense of smell perceives odours.

units.la: Estque Interius, vel Exterius: illud primarium & proprium; hoc secundarium dici posset.
units.tr: It is either internal or external: the former is the primary and proper one; the latter could be called secondary.

units.la: Interius & proprium odoratus sensorium sunt duo nervei seu Mammillares ductus, à media cerebri latitudine, non spinali medulla surgentes, & ad supremas nares descendentes. Per hos ductus animalis spiritus odores defert in cerebrum, quod, quia humidum est, aptè ab exhalatione odorabili, quæ ab objecto corpore continuò expirat, affici potuit: & quia expandi magis vapidus odor solet, quò longius à principio suo abit, omne cerebrum huic fertur tribuendum, ne arcto vase conclusus suffocaretur.
